product.title: Hangs on the loading screen and locks you out entirely
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after an update or a new phone, the app spins the Stardust logo forever and never lets users reach their data. Reinstalling, restarting, and clearing cache don't help — Android and Samsung users hit it hardest.

product.title: "Can't log into the future" — even though it's today
product.minus: A fresh, widespread bug: trying to mark a period that started today triggers "We do not allow logging into future." Users sarcastically point out that today isn't the future, and the tracker's core function breaks.

product.title: Symptoms save to the wrong day — or don't save at all
product.minus: Logging frequently misfires: entered symptoms land on the previous day, jumble across the calendar, or simply don't save. It guts the very feature people installed the app for.

product.title: You can't edit or delete wrongly logged days
product.minus: The app adds random period days, stretches cycles into weeks, and refuses to let users remove them. The inability to correct dates makes the tracker unreliable — and risky for anyone tracking fertility.

product.title: Beloved for its celestial aesthetic and gorgeous design
product.plus: The standout reason users love it: a deep blue-purple, witchy, celestial look instead of the tired bright pink. Moon-phase ties, hormone graphs, and a genuinely pretty interface make it an app people actually want to open.

product.title: Funny daily notifications that feel like a friend checking in
product.plus: A signature delight: daily push notes written with humor and slang about your cycle phase. Users laugh at them, look forward to them, and compare the app to a big sister or friend who reassures them on a rough day.

product.title: Inclusive language and women ownership — but it alienates some
product.plus: Many are won over by gender-neutral language, trans inclusivity, and the fact that it's built and run by women — it reads as genuine care. But some users bristle at "menstruating people" instead of "woman."

product.title: Can't handle irregular cycles and clings to 28 days
product.minus: A paradox: for regular cycles, predictions are praised as accurate, but with PCOS, endometriosis, or a long cycle the app clings to 28 days, claims a two-week "period," and won't let you adjust the length. For the people who need a tracker precisely because they're irregular, it's useless.

product.title: Partner mode inspires — but often just doesn't work
product.minus: Sharing a cycle with a partner or friends is exactly why many install it (couples and lesbians especially). But adding a partner has failed for years: requests don't go through, cycles don't sync, and you have to email support just to make the feature work.

product.title: Accused of selling "private" data, with a lawsuit brewing
product.minus: A serious trust blow: users cite a class-action lawsuit in the making over selling supposedly encrypted data to third parties, forced Google sign-in despite privacy claims, and the app "snitching" to a partner whenever you check.

product.title: Generous free version — but the key stuff is paywalled
product.minus: A mixed feeling: many praise that you can track your cycle ad-free without a subscription and the app doesn't nag for upgrades. But others resent that symptom definitions, stats, and the "encyclopedia" sit behind a paywall — women's health, they argue, should be free.

product.title: Glitchy, laggy, and even reboots your phone
product.minus: After a few months the app turns slow and unstable: blank screen on open, icons that take ages to load, and in the worst cases a full phone reboot (Samsung Galaxy especially). The Android build is noticeably worse than iOS.

product.title: Self-inflicted logout that wipes your whole history
product.minus: An especially painful failure: the app logs users out on its own, signs into a new empty account under a different email, or deletes data on reinstall — and years of cycle history vanish. It stings further that letting a subscription lapse wipes everything too.

product.title: "Free" means a 7-day trial requiring a card, and you only find out after a long onboarding questionnaire
product.minus: The price isn't disclosed before install: users complete the whole intro and cycle setup, hit a paywall, and the only "free" option is a trial that auto-charges ~$30/year. People feel tricked specifically because of the order — invest time first, get billed second.

product.title: It asks you to rate the app BEFORE you're allowed to use it
product.minus: After building a profile the app demands a rating before the user has tried anything, then immediately throws up the subscription screen. It reads as rating-gaming and erodes trust from the first minute.

product.title: Irregular or long cycles break the app: you can't log a period longer than ~15–20 days
product.minus: A hard cap on period length (15, 16, 20 days) plus the inability to edit dates makes the tracker useless for exactly the people who need it most — PCOS, postpartum, coming off birth control. The app silently truncates real data.

product.title: Predictions don't learn: it forecasts periods too early and invents an absurdly long luteal phase
product.minus: Even with a regular cycle the app is consistently 3–5 days off and won't revise its forecast from history — it "guesses then sticks to that guess." The luteal-phase logic is plainly broken (26 days after ovulation).

product.title: Partner sync constantly drops: every login means re-entering the code and re-registering
product.minus: The headline feature for couples won't persist login state: desyncs, a fresh code on every open, confusion between partner and user mode — even prompting a man to "track his period." Some leave for Flo specifically over this.

product.title: An endless "needs an update" screen: there's no update available, yet the app won't let you in
product.minus: After an update the app gets stuck on an "update Lively" screen even though no update exists in the store. Reinstalling, clearing cache, switching phones — nothing works, and the user is fully locked out of their data and partner.

product.title: Data vanishes: it logs you out, loses years of tracking, and won't save edits
product.minus: Sudden logouts and glitches wipe out 2 years of history; logged weight and symptoms disappear; the save button spins and reverts edits. For a health tracker, data loss is a fatal flaw.

product.title: The core value is phase-by-phase guidance: what to eat, how to move, what to expect each day
product.plus: People feel a real difference: food, activity and mood tips tailored to each cycle phase help them align workouts, diet and expectations. For many it's the reason to stay — the app explains WHY they feel the way they do.

product.title: A calm, aesthetic, ad-free interface without aggressive upsells — and dark mode
product.plus: The design earns its own praise: clean, not "bubblegum pink," ad-free, customizable to hide clutter. Dark mode is explicitly called a lifesaver during period overstimulation. The simplicity is the main selling point versus a cluttered Flo.

product.title: A lifeline for PMDD: seeing the phase explains sudden mood crashes and suicidal thoughts
product.plus: The strongest positive thread: for PMDD sufferers, opening the app to see "luteal phase" gives hope the state will pass. For some it literally held them through dangerous moments — a rare depth of value for a tracker.

product.title: The best features get moved behind the paywall retroactively — what was free is suddenly locked
product.minus: Long-time free users complain that the once-free "eat" and "do" tips got locked behind premium after an update, and the AI advisor is now paid too. The "bait then gate" move stings the most loyal users hardest.

product.title: The AI advisor is loved but constantly fails with "check your connection" on a strong network
product.minus: The new AI chat is one of the most praised features (helps with scheduling, symptoms, post-miscarriage), which is exactly why its breakage stings: it reliably returns "Something went wrong, check your internet connection" on a working network.

product.title: The day counter and visible progress are what keep people here
product.plus: Reviewers say again and again that the growing day count itself — and the fear of breaking the streak — keeps them sober better than anything before: watching the days, months and years pile up is the motivation.

product.title: Almost everything useful is locked behind a $40–120/year subscription
product.minus: The tools you need most in a crisis — logging urges, the "urge breakers," extra addiction slots — are all paywalled. Users say bluntly: if someone is struggling enough to download the app, give them at least one working tool for free instead of a $40–120-a-year journal.

product.title: The community is a lifeline: "you are not alone"
product.plus: People call the community the part that literally saves lives: it's easier to talk about addiction with others who get it than with anyone else, and the mutual support and check-ins keep them from relapsing. Many admit they wouldn't have made it this far without it.

product.title: Underage bans wipe out half the actual audience
product.minus: Users get permanently banned for being "underage" — often adults, often by what looks like AI moderation — and the ban wipes every post and story along with the account. The irony is that much of the audience is teenagers, so the ban cuts off exactly the people who need the community most and triggers relapses.

product.title: Your progress doesn't survive a new phone — backup is paywalled too
product.minus: Without a subscription progress doesn't sync: a new phone, a reinstall, or a stolen phone wipes every day, story and workbook entry, and there's often no way to log back into the old account. Several people directly blame this lost progress for relapsing.

product.title: Daily pledges and motivational reminders pull you back into focus
product.plus: The daily pledge, reminders and motivational messages land well: they keep people mindful, stop them letting their guard down, and remind them why they started. The ability to write down your own reasons to quit and reread them is a particular favorite.

product.title: The subscription is sprung only at the end of a long onboarding
product.minus: You only find out the price and that payment is mandatory after filling in a pile of questions about why you want to quit. It feels like a trap: you do all the emotional work and the reward is a paywall with "no way out," even when a free trial is promised.

product.title: Auto-moderation flags harmless posts and cuts you off from the community
product.minus: The auto-moderator repeatedly flags totally harmless posts (about dyeing your hair, wanting a pet) as guideline violations and blocks them. In a "support app" you end up isolated from the community precisely when you need it most.

product.title: Works for any addiction — not just alcohol
product.plus: Despite the name, the app covers a huge range: self-harm, smoking, vaping, porn, nail-biting, drugs, eating issues. People value how specifically they can tailor it to their own struggle, triggers and goals.

product.title: The free tier is strangled: only 2 addictions, no urge logging
product.minus: Even loyal users hit the free-tier ceiling: only two addictions at once, no urge logging, no helpful techniques. Anyone fighting several things at the same time is forced to pay or live with a crippled tool.

product.title: Doesn't shame you for relapsing — a gentleness people single out
product.plus: A key trait: the app doesn't make you feel bad after a slip and reminds you it's okay to make mistakes. For people in a fragile state that non-judgmental tone is itself a reason to stay — and for some it literally gave them "a reason to stay alive."

product.title: Pledge notifications are flaky and quietly die
product.minus: The daily-pledge and review reminders work for a day or two, then go silent, while community-reaction notifications keep coming. For forgetful users that's critical — reminders are the whole point — and they constantly have to reset them.

product.title: The redesign killed the app's whole point: simplicity
product.minus: A huge mass of loyal users (often 5-10 years in) unanimously hates the new version: confusing, not user-friendly, messy. They loved it precisely for the minimalism and clear calendar, and the update piled on extra sections and broke familiar navigation. The verdict is usually 'if it's not broke, leave it alone' and a switch to another app.

product.title: Updates wipe out years of accumulated history
product.minus: The most painful complaint: after an update or account login, 3-10 years of data vanish with no warning and no backup option. For women with PCOS, pregnancy planning, or prepping for a doctor's visit this isn't cosmetic, it's lost medical history. Data often disappears 'every couple of months', making the app fundamentally unreliable.

product.title: Aggressive premium pop-ups smother the actual logging
product.minus: Payment prompts pop up 'every 2 seconds', one after another, sometimes erasing the day's data you just entered. People come for one function, marking a cycle day, and physically can't reach it. The comparisons are brutal: 'It's a period app not a vpn'.

product.title: You can't backdate the start of a period
product.minus: A key regression in the new version: if you forget to mark the start day, the app only lets you set today's date, not the real past day. For women with irregular cycles or just busy lives, this throws off the whole calculation. The old version let you 'go back days', and that's exactly what everyone demands back.

product.title: The app freezes, won't load, or won't open at all
product.minus: After updates, many users get stuck on a blank screen, on the opening 'has your period started?' prompt, or on the login page. There are 404 and 502 errors and crashes tied to specific updates (July 4th, Samsung A21+). For a tracker you open once a day, 'great when it works, which isn't often' is a failure of the basic function.

product.title: Pregnancy mode was removed — the cycle counter keeps ticking
product.minus: The old version let you flag a pregnancy so the app would stop counting cycle days; the new one simply has no such option. Many people use trackers specifically to conceive, so the missing 'pregnant' state feels absurd. Postpartum tracking is broken too — the app keeps pushing the delivery date forward.

product.title: You can't export or take your own data without paying
product.minus: History export is locked behind the paywall, and for some the 'export' button simply doesn't work. So to move to another app people end up manually re-typing years of records. It's a hostage situation: you can neither leave with your data nor stay without subscribing.

product.title: Privacy fear: change of ownership and data being sold
product.minus: The app was sold (Bellabeat is named) and now demands login and consent to access sensitive cycle data. Users got emails saying their records were sold and shared, and fear the data being handed to police or the government. For a category where cycle data is intimate medical information, this is a critical blow to trust.

product.title: When it works, the prediction accuracy genuinely delights
product.plus: Those for whom the app is stable praise its accuracy: cycle and ovulation predictions often land within a day. Several women say they conceived by following the predicted ovulation dates. After a couple of months of data the algorithm adapts to your real cycle length, which is especially valued for irregular cycles.

product.title: The understated, non-girly tone is what's prized most
product.plus: Much of the appeal was that the app was discreet and free of saccharine styling: an inconspicuous 'P.D' icon on the screen, a clean interface, no loud 'girly vibes'. Users describe it as 'made for women by women', not 'for girls by men'. The new floral themes are exactly what breaks that sense of maturity and privacy.

product.title: A subset of users genuinely embraced the new design
product.plus: Not everyone is against the update: a smaller but visible group calls the new UI more intuitive, praising the 'coach', the algorithm, and the simplified start/end logging. They explicitly note the backlash comes from people used to the old way, and that it just takes a couple of minutes to learn.

product.title: You can't unsubscribe, yet the charges keep coming
product.minus: A distinct billing pain point: people can't find how to cancel, the auto-renew toggle doesn't work, and money is charged even after cancellation or without tapping pay at all. One user threatens legal action. This isn't ordinary 'too expensive', it's a genuinely abusive retention mechanism.

product.title: The paywall is hidden behind a long quiz and sign-up
product.minus: People spend 10-15 minutes answering health questions, create an account and hand over personal data — only to hit a subscription wall right at the end, just before the prediction, with no warning anywhere upfront. Many delete the account immediately and demand their data be erased.

product.title: Price doubled or tripled with no improvements — loyal users leave
product.minus: Long-timers since 2017-2018 say the sub jumped from £49 to £89 (or to $150/yr) with no warning and no meaningful new features. The hike is justified as "improvements" users never see, and many cancel, feeling the most loyal customers are the ones being squeezed.

product.title: You're forced to buy their thermometer, ring or band
product.minus: On top of the pricey subscription, the app demands a branded $40 thermometer, the NC band or an Oura ring — and blocks manual temperature entry from your own ordinary thermometer. Existing customers who already own the Gen 3 thermometer get hard-locked to the new device with no choice.

product.title: They auto-charge on renewal and refuse refunds
product.minus: The subscription silently auto-renews with no clear reminder email, charging people $120-168 even after they tried to cancel — then refunds are refused on a "once we have your money it's ours" basis. Tellingly, NC only refunds many of them AFTER a public one-star review.

product.title: The algorithm floods you with red days and confirms ovulation a week late
product.minus: Even with a regular cycle and Oura, the algorithm holds "waiting for ovulation" for weeks, then retroactively says it happened long ago. Red days are so frequent there are barely any green ones, and the day's colour flips green-to-red and back — which scares users and erodes trust in it as contraception.

product.title: Doesn't work with Samsung/Galaxy, Garmin or Fitbit — despite being advertised there
product.minus: People discover NC via Samsung Health ("powered by Natural Cycles") or a Galaxy/Garmin promo, subscribe — then learn the app only syncs with Apple and Oura, and their temperature-sensing watch isn't supported. In some countries it just says "no devices available."

product.title: The ads lie about being "the only" and "number one"
product.minus: Pushy ads claim NC is the only app that accurately tracks your cycle and is "number one"; in the UK the ads were forced to change for being misleading. Users bristle at the "we'll tell you when it's safe to have sex" framing — and come specifically to leave one star for the dishonesty.

product.title: Support is an AI bot instead of humans
product.minus: To reach support you first have to get past a useless chatbot posing as AI, then wait 1-2 (really 4+) days with no phone line. The contrast is stark: store reviews get instant replies while real billing tickets go unanswered. When a human does get through, though, they can be kind.

product.title: The recent redesign split temperature and symptom logging across screens
product.minus: After the update the most important step — entering temperature — was split off from symptoms and buried on the "today" screen, forcing a separate save per entry. Long-time users call it a step backward made by people who don't use the app themselves, and also dislike the new "blurry" look.

product.title: It teaches women about their own bodies — the core reason people love it
product.plus: Over years of use people say they've learned more about their cycle, hormones and phases than anywhere else, including school. The educational articles, reminders (PMS, breast self-exams) and seeing how the cycle ties to mood, sleep and energy give a real sense of bodily agency.

product.title: Works as non-hormonal birth control and helps people conceive
product.plus: For people off the pill, IUD or implant, NC reliably prevents pregnancy for years and, by switching modes, helps them conceive, then track and get through pregnancy. Users value that it's a non-hormonal, FDA-cleared method with no side effects — many staying 5-9 years.

product.title: Oura sync and the partner view make tracking effortless
product.plus: Syncing with the Oura ring (or NC band) removes the painful "take your temp the second you wake" ritual — a lifesaver for people whose sleep is broken by small kids or night shifts. The partner profile lets a husband see the red/green day and stay involved.

product.title: Insurance or an HSA often covers the subscription
product.plus: Many discover, often after paying, that the annual fee can be reimbursed through insurance or paid from an HSA via step-by-step instructions on the site — which makes the steep price tolerable or even free. Those whose insurance covers it 100% urge others not to let the price deter them.

product.title: The time, money and health counter is the core motivator
product.plus: People open the app daily to watch their smoke-free days, the money they've saved and how their body is recovering — these numbers are exactly what keeps them going.

product.title: Live advisors and community are the real lifeline
product.plus: Real people reply within minutes around the clock, and the forum and Facebook group make users feel they're not alone — for many it's this support, not the app, that made the difference.

product.title: Registration demands far too much personal data
product.minus: Just to start, the app demands full name, email, post code and phone number with no way to skip — people abandon onboarding before they even reach the first screen.

product.title: Email verification loops and blocks entry
product.minus: The link in the email doesn't activate the account and the page that opens just tells you to follow the email again — people reinstall dozens of times and still can't get in.

product.title: Half the features are locked behind a subscription
product.minus: The free version is basically just the counter: advisors, missions and advanced features require a subscription, and it's sprung on users as a surprise with constant upgrade prompts.

product.title: Badges, rewards and milestones give a sense of achievement
product.plus: Monthly certificates, ranks, a pet dragon and badges turn each smoke-free day into a small win users don't want to reset with a relapse.

product.title: Free NRT (patches, spray, lozenges) genuinely cut cravings
product.plus: Many note the app sends free nicotine-replacement aids, and it's these that got them through the worst cravings in the early days.

product.title: The app itself triggers stress and the urge to smoke
product.minus: Paradoxically, the painful onboarding and nagging notification dots drive people to want a cigarette — even after they'd already gone weeks without one.

product.title: Paid access gets lost and support goes silent
product.minus: Purchased Pro and Lifetime suddenly switch off, the premium link sends you back to the sales page, and support emails go unanswered — even for years-long paying users.

product.title: Updates and a move to a new app wipe out progress
product.minus: After some updates the app stops opening, and the move to a new version locks people out of the old one — they lose their quit date and the entire track they'd built up.

product.title: Promoting vaping as a substitute breeds distrust
product.minus: Some users are appalled that the app offers a free vape and advises switching from smoking to vaping — for those quitting nicotine itself it looks like swapping one addiction for another.

product.title: The free version is enough as a tracker for many
product.plus: Even without a subscription people use the app for years simply as a precise quit stopwatch: the counter, diary and health view all work in the free mode.

product.title: On Android the app barely runs: black screens, freezes, crashes
product.minus: A constant stream of Android complaints: the app hangs on the splash or logo, shows a black or white screen, lags and crashes. Many never even reach the home screen.

product.title: A mandatory account requirement scares people off at the door
product.minus: Plenty of users can't see why a time counter needs an email account with verification, and uninstall before they ever start. Some even read it as a risk of leaking sensitive addiction data.

product.title: Sign-up and login are broken: email won't type, verification never arrives
product.minus: Even those willing to register get stuck: the email field won't accept input, the verification email never lands with no resend button, and login loops on a wrong-password error.

product.title: The clocks are the core value that works even when nothing else does
product.plus: The sobriety counters are what keeps people coming back. You can run as many clocks as you need across different addictions and habits, and for many it's the one reliably working part.

product.title: Free with no paywall — its standout competitive edge
product.plus: Users love that it's entirely free, with no subscription and no ads, while rivals charge 8–10 dollars a month. For many that's the deciding factor.

product.title: Money and calories saved — the most motivating feature
product.plus: The tally of money, time and calories saved genuinely stuns people and keeps them going on hard days, making it vivid how far they've come.

product.title: The solo author's heart builds real trust
product.plus: People especially value that it was built by one caring person (Parker), himself in recovery, rather than a big company chasing money. It earns warm trust and a wish to support him.

product.title: No nagging notifications — the calm former addicts want
product.plus: For many it's precisely the absence of daily pushes and pressure that worked, where other apps' endless reminders made things worse. You check in only when you choose to.

product.title: Creating and resetting clocks often just fails
product.minus: The core function lets people down: they go through naming and time setup, reach finalising, and land on an empty 'My Clocks' list. Some can't even reset a clock.

product.title: Setting the time is agony: minute-by-minute scrolling and wrong timezone
product.minus: The non-standard time entry forces minute-by-minute scrolling, taking minutes to shift a few hours. There's no timezone option, so the day count is off for users outside the US.

product.title: The bottom ad covers the control buttons
product.minus: The bottom banner partly covers the toolbar and settings button, making it impossible to reset or edit a clock. When dismissed, Google blacks out the area itself, so the controls stay out of reach.

product.title: The community and support make sobriety less lonely
product.plus: The encouragement wall, accountability partners and a sense of 'one big family' help people ride out cravings: they read others' posts in a hard moment and draw inspiration.

product.title: A dated, neglected interface and navigation with no back button
product.minus: The design feels like 2005–2010, navigation is unintuitive, the back button closes the whole app, and by users' accounts the developer hasn't updated it in a long time.

product.title: No home-screen widget — a frequent request
product.minus: Users repeatedly ask for an Android widget so they can see the counter and milestones right on the home screen, especially when a craving hits, without opening the app.

product.title: Text fields and the journal don't work: the keyboard won't appear
product.minus: In the journal and input fields the keyboard won't pop up, you can't place the cursor or paste, and the encouragement button sometimes never appears, leaving whole sections unusable.

product.title: Touch misfires: scrolling registers as a button press
product.minus: While scrolling, the app mistakes a finger drag for a press and opens a random option, and the bottom of windows gets cut off, making it easy to misclick and hard to control.

product.title: Recognises any addiction or habit — flexible tracking
product.plus: You can track anything from substances to behavioural addictions, and even new healthy habits. That breadth and the customisation to personal goals is a strength in its own right.

product.title: A pushy rating prompt blocks you from using the app
product.minus: The 'rate this app' screen loops on startup: you can't get past it, yet you can't actually leave a rating either, rendering the app useless.

product.title: Everything in one place — the phone is always there, unlike a notebook
product.plus: The top praise: prayers, inventories, journal, gratitude and the day counter all live in one app that's always in your pocket. Paper notebooks get lost, pens go missing, but the phone is always with you — writing an inventory is easier right from bed.

product.title: Anchors the morning and evening ritual — the first and last thing of the day
product.plus: Many have woven the app into their routine: «On Awakening» in the morning, a nightly inventory at night. Notifications start the day on a positive note, and without it people literally feel off.

product.title: Inventories can be sent to a sponsor — built-in accountability
product.plus: A strong differentiator: spot-check and nightly inventories, step 10, can be forwarded to a sponsor straight from the app. It keeps people accountable, and sponsor and sponsee trade work through the same app.

product.title: The developer Nathan replies fast and personally — people remember it
product.plus: The creator's name (Nathan) comes up again and again: fast replies to emails, a caring attitude, the sense that a real person behind the app genuinely carries «the message of recovery».

product.title: A rich collection of prayers and daily reflections in your pocket
product.plus: Prayers («On Awakening», third step, serenity), the daily reflection and inspirational readings at your fingertips — that's what brings many to the app each morning.

product.title: The sobriety counter at the top — the motivation of seeing your «clean time» grow
product.plus: Many value seeing their sobriety day count at the top of the screen: it gives hope, motivates, and frees the user from having to count themselves.

product.title: Simple, clear interface — even «old timers» can use it
product.plus: The app is praised for being easy to learn: clear navigation, simple design, friendly even to the non-technical. «A simple app for complicated people».

product.title: Charging for recovery tools angers some users
product.minus: The sharpest objection: spiritual tools shouldn't cost money — «God is free». Even at $10 a year, some feel the very idea of charging is wrong for a recovery program.

product.title: The creator gives premium away during hardship — defusing half the pricing complaints
product.plus: The counterweight to the pricing debate: those who can't afford premium (in sober living, out of work, in financial hardship) say Nathan gave them paid features for free. It turns potential resentment into gratitude.

product.title: Missing core AA literature — users ask for the Big Book and «12 and 12»
product.minus: The most common feature request: add the full program literature — the Big Book and «12 and 12». Those who do have «12 and 12» access prize it, which highlights the gap for everyone else.

product.title: Registration crashes on launch — some users can't even get in
product.minus: A rare but critical failure: trying to register, the app closes itself and the person can't get started at all. For an app tied to a daily ritual, losing someone right at the door stings.

product.title: Fixed prayer texts can't be amended — small but nagging gaps
product.minus: Several users ask for text additions: the full Serenity Prayer, the full Resentment Prayer, a «when we retire at night» line to match «upon awakening», more character space in the first part, and the ability to edit the spot-check date. Small things, but one says the creator refused to add them.

product.title: The paywall hits at the very end, after they've already hooked you
product.minus: Users are walked through sign-up, plan selection and personalization, and the price only appears when they reach to hit play — it reads as a bait-and-switch, not an honest deal.

product.title: Advertised as free, but everything inside costs money
product.minus: The ads and listing promise free access, but in reality only the daily quotes are free — everything else is locked, and it feels like a flat-out lie.

product.title: The same content is free on YouTube
product.minus: Users recognize the clips and feel the app just repackages free YouTube and Spotify videos and sells them by subscription.

product.title: They charge after cancellation and before the trial ends
product.minus: People cancel the subscription or delete their account yet still lose $40-66; some get charge attempts several times a day.

product.title: Support is dead: emails bounce, tickets go unanswered
product.minus: The listed email is invalid and bounces, the widget keeps promising "back in 5 hours" forever — getting a refund or fixing a subscription issue is nearly impossible.

product.title: Demands a rating and payment before you can try anything
product.minus: The app asks for a review and payment before the user has seen a single full talk — there's nothing yet to rate or pay for.

product.title: Login and password reset just freeze
product.minus: The sign-in button freezes after typing the password, the reset link loops back into the app, and accounts fail with "unknown error" — you can't get in.

product.title: Your chosen idols are ignored, and the speaker roster is divisive
product.minus: Setup forces you to pick inspiring people with no "none" option, then serves someone else entirely; the roster is narrow and morally off-putting to some users.

product.title: Background music drowns the speaker, and playback keeps breaking
product.minus: The music plays too loud over the talk, the playlist restarts itself, audio cuts out with the screen off, and there's no background playback — using it on a commute or workout is painful.

product.title: Thin, repetitive content: the app feels abandoned
product.minus: No new clips for weeks, the same speeches scattered across different folders, some folders empty — it feels like the team took the money and ran.

product.title: For some, it has literally been life-saving
product.plus: The strongest reviews aren't about features but about daily talks pulling people out of depression, despair and even off the edge; for them the app became a voice that keeps them going.

product.title: A perfect daily ritual for mornings and workouts
product.plus: Loyal users' core ritual is one talk in the morning or at the gym/on a run; the short clips set the tone for the day, replace mindless scrolling and turn motivation into discipline.

product.title: The value is curated, distraction-free content from strong speakers
product.plus: Fans admit the material exists on YouTube, but value the curated, distraction-free collection in one place — it becomes an "inner voice" and spans faith, money and grit.

product.title: The «time since» counter is the core motivator: nobody wants to reset to zero
product.plus: People reopen the app every time they crave, look at the day counter and realise: one cigarette and it all goes back to zero. This simple loop genuinely stops relapses.

product.title: «Money saved» and «health improvements» — the stats that land hardest
product.plus: The money-saved figure, the count of cigarettes avoided and the health-recovery timeline give people a tangible, measurable reason to keep going.

product.title: Almost everything useful sits behind a subscription — the counter and a couple of badges stay free
product.minus: Users complain that 95% of the app is behind a paywall: achievements, chat, the breathing tool, the health timeline. What's left free is essentially a bare timer.

product.title: «It used to be free» — long-time users feel features they already had were taken away
product.minus: People who quit with the app years ago come back to find ads, forced sign-in and a subscription for features that used to be free or were bought outright. It feels like a betrayal of the community.

product.title: The community chat — for many it was the people, not the timer, that helped them quit
product.plus: Global chat rooms in many languages, support from fellow quitters and advice from people who succeeded — for a chunk of users this is the app's main value.

product.title: That same chat is also a site of bullying and unmoderated toxicity
product.minus: Newcomers run into rudeness, trolling and age-shaming; religious fanatics and creepy advances turn the «friendly community» into a stressor. Reports go unanswered by moderators.

product.title: On first launch a «Continue» pop-up drops you straight onto a payment screen
product.minus: Many never even get to learn the app costs money: the paywall pops before the questionnaire, before they try anything. People call it predatory and uninstall on the spot.

product.title: «Just a timer you could build in Excel» — the price doesn't match the simplicity
product.minus: For many, ~$20/year for a counter and some badges feels absurdly overpriced: they say a dozen students could build it in a week, and the savings math is just a formula.

product.title: The widget and timer often freeze at zero or stop updating
product.minus: The widget — billed as a key feature — shows 0 days, the timer doesn't advance on weekends or overnight, and achievements fail to unlock. People can't tell if it's a fake timer or just broken.

product.title: Surprise charges, vanished achievements and no way to get a refund
product.minus: The subscription charges without consent, the promised «health achievements» never appear after paying, and there's no way to reach support or get a refund — some users threaten legal action.

product.title: Intrusive ads and constant subscribe-nags annoy users — and even trigger cravings
product.minus: A huge banner on every open, endless subscribe prompts and floods of ads feel like pressure; one user says outright the ads stress them out and make them want to smoke.

product.title: Years of progress lost on Facebook login, plus sign-in failures
product.minus: Facebook login breaks and wipes out years of progress with no way to recover, while for some users sign-up simply fails with a «something bad happened» error.

product.title: Can't reset the date or restart the timer after a slip — the function is hidden
product.minus: After a slip people can't find the button to reset the date or restart the timer — it's buried — and logging a smoked cigarette isn't obvious either. They ask for a way to mark a relapse without starting from scratch.

product.title: Accurate, easy cycle tracking is the core reason users love it
product.plus: Reviewers repeatedly praise it for being simple and accurate: easy to log cycle, symptoms, mood and flow, with analysis that helps them understand their bodies.

product.title: The smart ring and thermometer pairing removes manual logging chores
product.plus: The Femometer ring and thermometer auto-upload data into the app, so users no longer have to log basal temperature by hand — for many it turns tracking into a powerful conception tool.

product.title: It actually helps users conceive — treated as proof it works
product.plus: Women trying to conceive credit the ovulation-test interpretation and tracking with helping them get pregnant, sometimes more than once — the strongest argument in the app's favor.

product.title: Forced migration to "Connect" wiped data and access
product.minus: The old Femometer app suddenly stopped working and vanished from the store, replaced by a totally different "Femometer Connect": users lost all their data and login info, and being unable to show years of cycle history at the doctor is no mere bug.

product.title: Removing the community/forum ("tribe") feels like losing what they paid for
product.minus: The new app dropped the "tribe" forum where women shared anonymously and asked questions; users say outright that the community was the main thing they paid for, and without it the app becomes just another period tracker.

product.title: Google sign-in breaks after the switch, especially on Android
product.minus: Many can't log in with Google — particularly after moving from iPhone to Android — and since the old app is already disabled, users are left with no access to their account at all.

product.title: Bluetooth sync with the ring is flaky and loses readings
product.minus: Connecting the ring and Vinca over Bluetooth takes multiple slow attempts; data from the ring is lost to a timeout, and sometimes readings simply fail to sync.

product.title: The ring mistakes a whole day awake for sleep
product.minus: Wearing the ring all day makes the app think the user has been asleep the whole time — the sleep-detection logic clearly can't tell waking from sleeping during daytime wear.

product.title: No way to escape the blindingly white theme
product.minus: The interface is white and blinding, and the new app's settings offer no option to change the theme — especially galling for those who upgraded from the previous version.

product.title: Small but irritating regressions in data entry
product.minus: Since the switch it's harder to flag a temperature as abnormal and to pick what shows on the chart; weight entry became a scroll instead of typed input, which is awkward, and some users can't figure out how to change their weight at all.

product.title: Being free and having solid support build trust
product.plus: Several reviewers single out that the app is free with no subscription and that customer service is top-tier — a real plus against paid competitors.

product.title: Partner account is promised but broken — instructions lie
product.minus: The instructions for setting up a partner account are inaccurate and don't work: the promised option isn't in the app, so a spouse can't join the tracking — for couples the feature is effectively useless.

product.title: Reminders and data sync silently fail
product.minus: Reminders never arrive even with all permissions granted and the app pinned in the background; data periodically unsyncs and not all health metrics come through.

product.title: The Glow merge is felt as the death of the old Eve
product.minus: People deliberately chose Eve over Glow for its simplicity — and the forced merge gave them literally the same Glow: an unfamiliar interface, alien logic, lost "vibe." Long-time users are leaving en masse.

product.title: The update freezes at 98% and goes to a black/white screen
product.minus: The forced in-app update loads to 98% and hangs for many people — then a black or white screen. Reinstalling and clearing cache don't help, support stays silent, and access to data is lost.

product.title: The update wiped out years of tracked cycle history
product.minus: After the update or a phone change, 5–10 years of data simply vanish: no past periods, no prediction. Especially painful for those who kept records for doctors due to health issues.

product.title: Logging a single day means dismissing a pile of premium pop-ups
product.minus: A wall of ads stands between the user and the calendar: 5–15 pop-ups and "buy premium" banners on every open. The basic act of logging a period start turns into a five-minute fight.

product.title: Your own cycle history is locked behind a paywall
product.minus: The most outrageous part: the data you entered yourself — period history, average cycle length — is now visible only if you pay. No warning, no chance to back it up first. Analytics behind a paywall is one thing, but not your own archive.

product.title: Fertility is forced on people who never asked — insensitive and hurtful
product.minus: The app is flooded with pregnancy and conception content with no way to opt out, even when you pick "period tracking only." It wounds those who can't or don't want kids, lesbians, and people who've had a loss — the constant "take a test" hits a raw nerve.

product.title: Simple period logging became an unintuitive maze
product.minus: The calendar "wheel" used to be the first screen; now you can't dig your way to it. The "+" button opens a fertility log instead of adding a period; people can't even find where to enter a start date.

product.title: The app crashes the instant you open it
product.minus: For some users the app crashes immediately on launch; clearing cache, restarting the phone and reinstalling don't help. For weeks on end it's impossible to even log a period.

product.title: After the update you can't log back into your account
product.minus: The update logs people out and won't let them back in: email and phone are "not recognized," and trying to sign in pushes you to register a brand-new account on top of a decade of data.

product.title: Logged periods don't save
product.minus: You enter a start date — it shows as saved, then next month it's gone. People log multiple times and records still vanish; the whole point of a tracker collapses.

product.title: Dark patterns: fingerprint auto-charges and fake profile activity
product.minus: The premium purchase screen opens on its own and sometimes self-triggers a fingerprint charge — even when exiting the app. On top of that the app posts "quiz" results as you, and PDF export invents periods that were never logged.

product.title: For loyal users the prediction was reliably accurate
product.plus: Those for whom it still works praise the accuracy for years — within a day or two, helpful for planning, and the free version is enough for many. That accuracy is exactly why people stuck with it for 5–10 years.

product.title: A warm women's community and forums kept people in the app
product.plus: The social side — forums, groups, talking with women worldwide — was a value in itself; for some people the community is the one reason they still keep the app even now.

product.title: The old Eve was simple, warm and clear from the first screen
product.plus: The old version is remembered as a benchmark: warm colors, a friendly tone (it called you "babe"), the wheel calendar right on open, approachable for young girls — a simple tool that did exactly what was needed.

product.title: Almost everything is behind a paywall — only bare tracking is left free
product.minus: Users who remember free articles and insights now hit a subscription wall on everything: reading an article, opening an answer card, asking the bot — it all requires premium. All that is left is logging days and symptoms.

product.title: Accurate cycle and ovulation predictions are the main reason for years of loyalty
product.plus: Those who stay praise Flo for accuracy: it correctly predicts the next period, ovulation and symptoms even with irregular cycles, and many have used it for 5–10 years.

product.title: Deceptive "free": a long questionnaire, then only a paid subscription at the end
product.minus: The app is advertised as free, makes you complete a 20-minute personal questionnaire, and only then reveals that nothing works without a subscription or 14-day trial. People feel their time was wasted.

product.title: Intrusive premium pop-ups and notifications on every tap
product.minus: Every app open and nearly every tap is met with subscription and discount ads. Notifications arrive even after being turned off, and logging the cycle takes far longer because you constantly have to decline premium.

product.title: Helps you understand your own body — educational value for newcomers
product.plus: Many users, especially those new to tracking, say they learned more about their body in a day than in years. The app explains phases, symptoms and emotions and removes the stress of waiting for a period.

product.title: The chatbot is locked into preset replies — you can't ask your own question
product.minus: The AI assistant pops up on every launch and won't let you type freely — only preset options. When a user already knows why her period is late, the bot still drags her through an irrelevant script, then asks for a subscription after a few replies.

product.title: Data loss and login failures after switching phones
product.minus: When users change or break their phone, the account often "isn't found" and years of logged data vanish. Sometimes the obstacle is the UI itself: the login button is unreachable past a hundred onboarding screens.

product.title: Charges after cancellation and a painful refund process
product.minus: Users cancel before the trial ends, yet the card is still charged — sometimes £34.99, sometimes several times over. Unsubscribing is hard, support goes silent for weeks, and refunds have to be forced through the bank.

product.title: Too much sexual content that settings won't remove
product.minus: Users who just want a period tracker complain about graphically sexual content across insights, chats and the calendar. Turning it off in settings doesn't work — sex buttons and prompts remain, putting off celibate, aro/ace users and parents of teens.

product.title: Not for everyone: age limit of 16, poor support for LGBT users and partners
product.minus: The app blocks girls under 16 (in the UK) even though periods start earlier; won't let same-sex couples share a cycle; pushes "girlhood" on trans users with no way to change pronouns. Partner mode barely works — beyond the calendar a partner sees nothing useful.

product.title: Anxiety around privacy and personal data
product.minus: The amount and nature of data requested feels alarming: health-data collection isn't optional, people fear data could be sold without consent, and some were unnerved by a "press and hold" onboarding step that revealed a thumbprint in the logo.

product.title: Handles pregnancy, perimenopause, PCOS and chronic conditions poorly
product.minus: The app struggles with non-standard states: it counts pregnancy as an "irregular cycle", offers no way to track PCOS or chronic conditions, pushes "could you be pregnant?" during infertility, and lacks options for perimenopause and postpartum.

product.title: An ad after every screen makes the app unusable
product.minus: Full-screen ads pop up after literally every tap and screen transition. Some users can't even finish the initial setup because the ads won't close — they have to kill the entire app just to advance to the next page.

product.title: Ads for gambling, drinking games and alcohol inside a sobriety app
product.minus: It's especially cynical that a sobriety tracker serves ads for the very things people are quitting: games with cocktails, "addictive" video games, and fake "your phone has a virus" banners. For people in recovery this isn't just annoying — it's a trigger.

product.title: A precise clean-time counter that motivates you to keep going
product.plus: The core value is seeing your exact accumulated clean time — down to the seconds, minutes, and even heartbeats. In moments of craving, users open the app, look at their progress, and find the strength not to relapse.

product.title: Journaling with daily prompts is an unexpectedly valuable tool for reflection
product.plus: Many come for the timer but stay for the journal: daily prompts and questions push you to reflect on your addiction and yourself. Even users who didn't expect to love this feature end up praising it.

product.title: A subscription instead of a one-time fee feels wrong for such a simple app
product.minus: Users find a monthly/yearly subscription disproportionate for a counter you could essentially keep in a notes app. Many would happily pay a couple dollars once to remove ads forever, but that option doesn't exist — and it reads as greed.

product.title: Flexible customization: backgrounds, fonts, colors and date format
product.plus: The app lets you change the background, font, color scheme, and date display format — down to the second. This personalization makes the counter feel like your own and delights users even amid the ad complaints.

product.title: Recycled quotes get stale, and some sound insulting
product.minus: The daily motivational quotes are a favorite feature for many, but they loop on a small set and get stale fast. Worse, some quotes read like a reproach to someone in recovery (calling them a "coward"), which demoralizes instead of supporting.

product.title: Tracks any addiction, not just alcohol
product.plus: Users track all kinds of things here: alcohol, drugs, smoking, porn, nail-biting, self-harm. The ability to keep multiple counters and track "any achievement" makes the app a universal recovery tool.

product.title: Your time survives even an uninstall and reinstall
product.plus: A pleasant surprise for many: after reinstalling, the app keeps counting accumulated time from where it left off. People return years later to find the counter didn't reset — which builds trust.

product.title: An in-app community makes you feel you're not alone
product.plus: Beyond the counter there's a chat and recovery community where people share the same struggle. For some users, this connection with others is exactly what makes the app truly valuable.

product.title: Confusing navigation: easy to enter a section, hard to get back out
product.minus: Beyond the ads, the app's structure itself frustrates: people can't always reach the chat, and once inside they can't get back out. Some call the app "over-engineered" for something as simple as a counter.

product.title: Premium doesn't remove ads and data loss wipes progress
product.minus: The most painful issue: people pay for premium and the ads remain while the widget breaks. And some find the app wipes their tracking entirely — a catastrophe for anyone who logged years of clean time here.

product.title: Long questionnaire, then a paywall: a bait-and-switch feeling
product.minus: By far the most common grievance: tens of minutes of questions about how much you'll save by quitting, a promise of a plan — and then a hard paywall at the very end, with no free version at all. People call it predatory, a scam, a con precisely because the cost isn't disclosed up front.

product.title: A trial that charges immediately or silently when it ends
product.minus: "7 days free" turns into a charge on the day you sign up, or a sudden yearly bill with no promised reminder. Amounts run from $40 to $89, and people often find out only from their bank statement.

product.title: No support: emails to the team vanish into the void
product.minus: Despite a "we're here to help" slogan in every email, refund and help requests go unanswered — people get ghosted after a first reply, or fobbed off with canned responses. Against an addiction backdrop, the silence feels especially cynical.

product.title: Login broken: email code never arrives, password "incorrect"
product.minus: The barrier starts at sign-up itself: the verification code never arrives, not even in spam, and on account creation the app keeps insisting "incorrect password" with no reset option. Some people can't get in at all — sometimes after already paying.

product.title: Buggy and crashing: freezes on the questionnaire, crashes on open
product.minus: The app freezes at the same point in the questionnaire, drops into an infinite loading loop, or crashes right after opening — and reinstalling doesn't help. Android owners (Pixel, Galaxy S24) complain especially that screens won't scroll.

product.title: Can't unsubscribe or get a refund: auto-renewal that won't let go
product.minus: Cancellation is buried so deep that people resort to disputing the charge through their bank; some get billed again after cancelling — a yearly sum months later. Refunds get denied citing "policy," sometimes keeping half the money.

product.title: Price feels high, especially when treating addiction with the money "saved on drinking"
product.minus: $80–160 a year is out of reach for many, and for this audience specifically: financial hardship is a common cause of drinking. Charging someone the exact amount they'd save by not drinking strikes many as ethically indefensible.

product.title: The science of alcohol is the most-loved part: you understand what's happening to your brain and body
product.plus: For happy users the heart of the app is the neuroscience and education: research-based daily material explains how alcohol affects brain and body, which lifts the "I'm broken" feeling and restores control through understanding.

product.title: Community, coaches and Zoom meetings: the support people stay for
product.plus: Live Zoom group calls, forums and coaches make people feel they're not alone — you can join without camera or voice. Many call the community the best part of the program and rate it above AA for its non-judgmental feel.

product.title: A gentle path with no cold-turkey or religion: an AA alternative
product.plus: The approach of small, steady change instead of cold turkey, and without the religious frame of the 12 steps, gives hope to those AA didn't fit. No pressure to quit entirely, no shaming — just learning to change your relationship with alcohol at your own pace.

product.title: Drink tracking and daily tasks that keep you on track
product.plus: Drink logging, cut-back goals and short daily tasks with check-ins create accountability and visible progress — plus they clearly show money saved and day-by-day health improvements.

product.title: More than just alcohol: mental health, habits and lifestyle
product.plus: Many note the app works on the whole person, not just drinking: sleep, anxiety, diet, neuroplasticity, relationships and finding meaning. Courses and meditations make it useful even for those simply on a wellness kick.

product.title: Android version is cut down and wipes entries: a platform penalty
product.minus: Even for loyal users the Android build trails iOS: rotating the screen erases everything typed into the journal, there's no Dry January challenge, group chats arrive empty — all at the same price as iOS.

product.title: A white pop-up box with a "0" covers the whole screen and won't close
product.minus: After a recent update, opening the app brings up a white rectangle with a "0" in the top-left corner that no amount of tapping will dismiss; reinstalling and clearing cache don't help, and the app becomes completely unusable.

product.title: The widget has been frozen on a single number for years and won't count down
product.minus: The widget — the very reason many keep the app — stops updating the day count and freezes on whatever day it was loaded; users have to keep deleting and re-adding it, and can only get an accurate countdown inside the app itself, which defeats the widget's entire purpose.

product.title: Switching phones wipes out years of history
product.minus: Moving to a new phone or recovering an account makes years of data vanish: the backup either fails to transfer or only pulls the last couple of months, leaving people to manually re-enter a full year of symptoms and temperatures.

product.title: A "lifetime" purchase suddenly turned into a subscription
product.minus: People who years ago paid a one-time fee for the ad-free "lifetime" premium now hit a paywall demanding a subscription for the same features they already had; they'd accept a one-off purchase, but the forced subscription feels like a betrayal and a reason to leave.

product.title: Predictions fall apart for irregular cycles and perimenopause
product.minus: The app forces irregular data into an average cycle: it silently rewrites the days you log into "prettier" numbers, flags everything past a certain point as spotting, and predicts a week off — so people with irregular cycles or perimenopause stop trusting it.

product.title: Notifications are set up but never arrive
product.minus: Despite notifications being on and double-checked, the app fails for years to send any reminder that a period is coming — the exact reason many switched to it — and complaints and support emails change nothing.

product.title: Login and sign-up fail with a server-communication error
product.minus: Creating an account, logging in, or resetting a password often fails with a "can't communicate with server" error, after which the startup pop-up can't be dismissed and access to a years-long diary is cut off entirely.

product.title: Partner mode shows stale status and can't be disconnected
product.minus: Shared tracking for a partner/husband has long been broken: cycle updates don't come through, the app reports the partner is hundreds of days "late," and there's no way to disconnect and reconnect — even uninstalling won't clear the link.

product.title: A decade-plus of loyalty for its minimalism and accuracy
product.plus: The app's core asset is users who've tracked here for 10–20 years and refuse to switch: they're won over by a clean, no-clutter interface and predictions that land within 1–3 days of the actual date.

product.title: Free and ad-light for basic tracking
product.plus: Basic cycle tracking stays free with barely any ads, and for many that's more than enough: against competitors that lock everything behind a paywall, people prize this as "the only decent free period tracker left."

product.title: Flexible notes and custom symptoms as a personal health diary
product.plus: Beyond dates, the app lets users log mood, mark intimacy, add custom symptoms and notes on any day — people keep it as a health journal that bails them out at the doctor's when memory fails.

product.title: Helps plan pregnancy and follow it week by week
product.plus: Many credit the app with helping them conceive — sometimes within a couple of months — thanks to its accurate fertile window, and expectant mothers value the pregnancy section with its week count and stage-by-stage info.

product.title: The anchor of a morning recovery ritual
product.plus: For most, it's the first thing they open in the morning: the reading, meditation and prayer set the tone for the day and keep the focus on sobriety. People describe it as a way to start the day right and stay grounded.

product.title: The book always in your pocket, no need to carry the volume
product.plus: The main reason people move from the paper book to the app is convenience: it's always on hand, on the go and while traveling, with no need to remember where the volume is. Long-time readers love having it at their fingertips.

product.title: The alarm clock icon won't leave the status bar
product.minus: The most concrete product bug: on opening, the app plants a stuck alarm icon in the Android status bar. The only way to remove it is to force-stop the app, and as a result people can't tell whether they've actually set an alarm — one user lost hours with Verizon over it.

product.title: Fidelity to the paper book is the core value
product.plus: Many have read the book for 20, 30, 40 years and trust the app precisely because it's word-for-word the original. To them it isn't "another app" but the same little black book that has kept them sober for decades.

product.title: Opens straight to today's reading — no hunting
product.plus: A strong design touch: the app opens to the right day and advances to the next on its own, so you don't need to know the date or hunt for the page. It removes the favorite excuse of "I couldn't find it / don't know what day it is."

product.title: No highlighting or note-taking
product.minus: The top feature request: people paid for the app as they would a book and want to highlight important lines and add notes to dates, but right now they can only dump the whole reading into favorites. Several also ask for an audio option.

product.title: Too religious for part of the non-believing audience
product.minus: The content leans heavily on God and the Bible, and some users — agnostics or those who don't see AA as the only answer — note it gets a little too churchy at times. It's not a bug but a worldview mismatch that lowers the rating for those who connect only with the meditative side.

product.title: The readings feel written for exactly your day
product.plus: The emotional core of loyalty: people are repeatedly struck that the daily reading seems to address exactly what they're wrestling with. That feeling of "how did they know what I needed" turns the app from a utility into a personal companion.

product.title: Went from free to paid without warning
product.minus: A sore point for some: what was free now costs money, and after switching phones people have to pay for the download again. Some are angry at making money off recovery, others reluctantly accept it while noting the paid version used to have no ads.

product.title: Configurable reminders and search help fit the reading into the day
product.plus: Beyond the text, people value the functionality: you can set a push-notification time, swipe to neighboring days or pick from a calendar, and search the content. It helps them not miss the reading and return to it through the day.

product.title: Easy to share the reading with friends in the program
product.plus: A quiet strength: people text the daily reading to dozens of others in the program and to the people they sponsor, using the app to stay connected and help others. The catch is the share function adds extra fluff, so many copy-paste the text instead.

product.title: Applies to any addiction, not just alcohol
product.plus: Though the book comes from AA, readers stress it works for NA, overeating, shopping and other addictions — even for those who never drank. That broadens the audience well beyond narrow alcohol recovery.

product.title: A paywall sprung at the very end, only after a long onboarding
product.minus: Users are walked through dozens of questions and promises, then hit with a subscription demand on the final screen. Many feel tricked: there was no upfront warning, and no free mode or trial exists at all.

product.title: Charging to escape an addiction feels morally wrong to users
product.minus: The core grievance: porn is free, yet the cure costs money. People argue such apps should be non-profit or at most have a tip jar, and accuse the developers of profiting off others' suffering.

product.title: Updates break login, locking people out of paid accounts
product.minus: After an update the app stops letting people in: it treats them as brand-new, streaks and progress vanish, and re-login through Google fails. It hits hardest those who already paid for a year.

product.title: Stuck on the «Continue» / «Let's Go» screen, can't get past the plan
product.minus: After onboarding and the «custom plan» screen, the «Continue» or «Let's Go» button simply does nothing: nothing happens and reinstalling doesn't help. People physically can't get into the app.

product.title: The site blocker — the headline feature — doesn't work
product.minus: The content blocker — the very reason many install the app — blocks nothing on Android: porn sites stay accessible. For a tool whose whole point is cutting off access, that's a failure of the core function.

product.title: Paid and got an «empty timer»: thin content, many features broken
product.minus: Those who do pay describe an empty shell: a bare day-counter, a couple of articles, no community or push notifications. The AI bot, the camera panic button, the research links — all advertised, none working.

product.title: Bait-and-switch pricing: the «80% off» becomes the full price at checkout
product.minus: A «one-time» 80–94% discount is dangled, but at the Google checkout the price is suddenly different and higher. The subscription is forced to a full year without clear consent, and refunds are impossible — read as outright deception.

product.title: The upsell pops up on every launch and blocks the app
product.minus: Even for those who used it free for a few days, the premium-purchase screen starts appearing on every open with no way to close it. People have to relaunch the app 2–3 times just to reach any features.

product.title: Frozen on the loading screen — the app won't start at all
product.minus: A separate cluster of complaints: the app simply won't load past the splash screen, hangs forever, and reinstalling does nothing. Sometimes it starts a day after paying for a subscription.

product.title: The paywall shuts out the teenagers who need it most
product.minus: Much of the audience are teens with no money or card, and the paywall lands squarely on them. An added «16+» gate (despite a store rating of «everyone») leaves younger users out — exactly where the addiction tends to start.

product.title: When it works, it genuinely helps people quit and hold a streak
product.plus: Those for whom it works are sincerely grateful: it helps them stay focused, count days without relapse, and «think twice» before falling back. For many it's the first support that actually worked against the addiction.

product.title: Motivates through identity — faith, masculinity, becoming a better self
product.plus: Its real strength isn't features but framing: it taps the desire to become more disciplined, closer to God, more self-assured. The «become yourself / alpha / righteous» angle resonates with its religious, young, male audience.

product.title: Payment goes through, access doesn't: money taken, no account created
product.minus: The worst case: money is charged (even for the lifetime plan) but the app won't open or log in — the profile never registered. There's no support, emails go unanswered, refunds are impossible. Users flatly call it a scam.

product.title: Asks you to rate it before you're even allowed to use it
product.minus: The rating prompt fires at the very start, before anyone has tried anything. It both inflates the score and annoys: people give five stars «to be at the top» or complain they're asked to rate blind.

product.title: A Clue Plus pop-up fires on every single tap
product.minus: By far the most common complaint: the subscription ad appears when you open the app, switch to any screen, and after every symptom you log. People describe it as a 'log a day, close an ad' game, 3-4 pop-ups per action, and leave for competitors despite years of stored data.

product.title: After an update the app won't open — just an endless spinner
product.minus: A whole wave of reviews: after a recent update the app hangs on a white screen with a spinning circle and won't load for days. Reinstalling helps only temporarily or not at all, and access to years of history — even to a paid subscription — disappears.

product.title: Once-free features got moved behind the paywall
product.minus: Long-time users (5-13 years) are furious: things that were free for years — trends, cycle history, sleep tracking, ovulation estimates, offline tracking — are now locked behind a subscription. It reads not as new paid features but as taking away what was already there.

product.title: Accurate predictions, especially for irregular cycles
product.plus: The app's core strength: it genuinely predicts periods and fertile windows accurately, using your own data rather than generic averages. Users with irregular cycles value it most — many credit it with helping them understand their body and even conceive.

product.title: You can't edit or delete dates entered by mistake
product.minus: An infuriating gap in core mechanics: if your period comes early/late or you tap the wrong day, you can't fix the date — and sometimes editing is itself paywalled. The app even logs phantom periods on its own with no way to delete them, wrecking the analysis.

product.title: Login failures and lost accounts lock you out of your data
product.minus: Sign-up and login frequently break: an error on account creation, password-reset emails that never arrive or lead to a 404, the system claiming an email both already exists and doesn't. Even paying users get locked out of their own history.

product.title: Chaotic billing and no way to get a refund
product.minus: Charges hit without warning — sometimes two subscriptions at once or after the app was deleted; cancelling is hard because it's hidden, and refund requests go unanswered even where EU law requires them. There is effectively no support.

product.title: Advertised as free, but the key functions cost money
product.minus: Many are drawn by 'free' ads, but the free tier is a bare calendar: fertility, pain intensity, analytics and articles sit behind a trial or subscription. People are especially angered at paying just to track a cycle or to try to conceive.

product.title: Educational articles and data privacy are what users love
product.plus: Beyond tracking, the app is praised for educational articles on cycles, pregnancy and menopause, and a clean, non-'childish-pink' design. Its privacy policy is valued in particular — especially post-Roe v Wade — along with the fact that many features really are free.

product.title: No integration with Samsung watches or Health Connect
product.minus: A frequent wish even among happy users: the app can't link to Samsung watches, Samsung Health or Health Connect, so sleep and activity data must be entered by hand. For many this is the sole reason they hold back the fifth star.

product.title: Clue Connect for partners is nearly useless and paywalled
product.minus: The partner-sharing feature disappoints: it's one-directional, doesn't show moods or other markers, is unhelpful for conceiving, and yet requires both partners to pay for a single cycle. The previously free sharing with a husband was removed too.

product.title: The 13+ age gate shuts out real young users
product.minus: Girls aged 9-12 who already menstruate can't register because of an 'underage' block — exactly those who need tracking most. Parents can't set up a profile for a younger daughter either, and the app has no multi-profile support.

product.title: People stay for years — the real trust signal
product.plus: Dozens of reviews mention keeping the app for 5, 6, 10, even 15 years across multiple phones. That kind of loyalty beats any marketing line: the tracker becomes a habit, not a one-off install.

product.title: Prediction accuracy is what keeps them
product.plus: The most common praise: next-cycle predictions are "almost accurate," often within a 1-2 day margin. For users that's not a stat, it's peace of mind — time to prepare and avoid getting caught out.

product.title: Partner mode turned the tracker into a couple's ritual
product.plus: Inviting a partner is a surprise hit: he sees symptoms and moods, knows whether to bring flowers or steer clear. Many say it genuinely improved their relationship rather than being just a "feature."

product.title: Pushy quizzes and notifications are the top irritant
product.minus: The stream of notifications begging you to take a quiz annoys even fans: there's no way to turn it off, it "begs" for attention, and users remind that the tracker should serve them, not the reverse. For some it was the reason they uninstalled.

product.title: The free version is genuinely enough — rare in this niche
product.plus: Users single this out: the app doesn't nag for a subscription at every turn, and the free tier lasts for years. Some buy the paid version out of gratitude rather than need.

product.title: Email backup rescues data when phones die
product.plus: Local storage with backup to your own email is a standout: data isn't locked on someone else's server, and it restores easily after a device dies. Veteran users tell newcomers to set up the backup right away.

product.title: Ads and bugs, up to a fully unusable screen
product.minus: For some users the app simply doesn't work: a grey film over the interface, drowning in ads, nothing clickable. Others spend months unable to figure out why the tracker won't function, and uninstall over unfiltered ads.

product.title: Cute pets and themes make periods a little less grim
product.plus: The mascot pets (capybara included) and themes aren't just decoration: users say the cute design literally makes cycle days less miserable. Crucially, a "not-cute" theme is available too.

product.title: Irregular cycles break the forecast — no manual override
product.minus: With irregular or long cycles the prediction misses: the app rigidly assumes an "average day" and won't let you set the ovulation day by hand or log why a cycle shifted (medication, illness). Users ask to show "predicted" next to "actual" dates.

product.title: Quizzes and partner mode beg for history and depth
product.minus: Even fans of the quizzes hit one wall: a partner's answers vanish the moment a new question appears — no history. They ask to save past quizzes, let the partner see mood and not just symptoms, and notify the partner in real time.

product.title: Feature bloat and a forced pregnancy theme alienate part of the base
product.minus: Long-time users notice new updates pile on the unnecessary and remove the useful, with no way to customize the home screen. Not everyone is trying to conceive, not everyone has a partner, and not everyone likes the wall-to-wall pink pastel "frou-frou" with animals.

product.title: Privacy worry over intimate data lingers in the background
product.minus: Some adult users, while recommending the app to teens, still doubt the safety of its data sharing. For others it's a plus that this company isn't on the lists handing data to "The State" — but the worry itself shows how sensitive this is.

product.title: The core pitch is NOT linking a bank: privacy sold as the product, not a feature
product.plus: Users deliberately choose manual entry precisely because nothing leaves for a server and the app never touches a bank account. This segment isn't looking for automation — it's fleeing from it, and pays and stays for years for the feeling that the money data lives only on their phone.

product.title: Speed of entry is the real engine of the daily habit
product.plus: "So fast to use, so little fuss" — the app wins not on features but on logging a spend taking seconds with an uncluttered UI. That's what turns tracking into a daily ritual instead of a chore dropped after a week: users report using it "every day" for 5-6 years.

product.title: No account means no safety net: all history lives on one manual backup
product.minus: Local-only storage with no mandatory login is the flip side of privacy: switch phones, reinstall, or hit a glitch and years of data vanish because the backup had to be made by hand. Users lose 4-6 years of records and realize the privacy "convenience" was the trap. It's a structural product risk: loyalty is built over years and collapses in a single day with no warning.

product.title: Cross-device sync is the retention backbone, not just a feature
product.minus: For a large share of payers, sync was the entire reason to buy — a shared budget with a partner, access from two phones.
