When sync was removed the app became instantly "useless" to them and they left for competitors; when it returned, the same people came straight back. It reveals what actually holds the top segment: not categories, but data following the person across devices.

product.title: Multi-currency silently recalculated all history at 1:1 and wiped years of stats
product.minus: For expats and anyone spending across currencies, conversion is the core of the value. After an update old transactions were retroactively recomputed as 1=1 (1 won = 1 euro) and all accumulated stats became meaningless. The nature of multi-currency tracking is that an FX error isn't local — it retroactively poisons every past report, fixable only by re-entering every transaction by hand.

product.title: The paywall hits the second account and second category — exactly where the habit matures
product.minus: The free tier doesn't cap an advanced feature — it caps a basic growth moment: the instant a user wants a second account or second category (i.e. actually starts budgeting), they're blocked. The limit sits right at the move from "tried it" to "built it into life," so it reads as confiscation of a working tool rather than an honest demo boundary.

product.title: Depth for power users: accounts, debts, lend/repay, subcategories retain the serious tracker
product.plus: Beyond simple entry the app handles credit accounts, debts with lend/repay mechanics, subcategories and fully editable transactions. It's this depth-with-simplicity combination that retains people who "tried 17 money managers" — they want flexibility without overload, and few apps strike that balance.

product.title: A loop hole: a spend deducts from the account but never shows in categories
product.minus: A bug broke the very point of tracking: a spend reduces the account balance but never lands in the category list/history, and sometimes entering an expense silently turns into a transfer between accounts. For a tracker this is fatal — the user stops trusting the numbers because balance and analytics diverge, and the app's whole value is that they reconcile.

product.title: The happiest users' top request — attach a receipt photo to a spend
product.minus: Happy 4-5★ users keep hitting the same ceiling: you can't attach a receipt or invoice photo to a transaction. This isn't a gripe but a signal of the next job-to-be-done — people want the tracker to replace the shoebox of receipts, not just the numbers. Closing this gap would turn the tracker into a proof archive and raise the switching cost.

product.title: Invisibility in Play Store search strangles the main growth channel — word of mouth
product.minus: Loyal users actively recommend the app to friends — but the friends can't find it: it doesn't surface in store search, as if shadow-banned. For a product that grows almost entirely on word of mouth rather than ads, this kills the very distribution engine: the referral exists but can't be acted on.

product.title: The redesign bloated fonts and added taps — the speed users came for regressed
product.minus: The UI overhaul hit exactly what was the strength: fonts grew larger, less fits on screen, the same actions take more taps, and scrolling appeared where everything used to be visible at once. When a product lives on "see your budget at a glance" and fast entry, cosmetics that break information density feel like degradation, not a refresh.

product.title: Recurring transactions exist, but without confirmation and timeline visibility they're half-blind
product.minus: Recurring transactions are implemented and valued, but users ask for the next layer: a confirm button for a scheduled payment, future recurrences shown on the timeline, and a calendar view. Without these the automation stays "blind" — you can't quickly verify charges matched the plan, yet predictability of recurring spend is the whole reason to set them up.

product.title: A rigid budget period hurts users whose payday shifts
product.minus: The budget is tied to a calendar month/week, but on a job change or non-standard payday, shifting the start date breaks already-closed past months. Users ask to "lock" prior periods and set an arbitrary interval. For a money app this is a meaningful segment — freelancers and job-switchers whose real financial cycle doesn't line up with the 1st of the month.

product.title: A loved product with no support net: emails to support vanish
product.minus: Even satisfied users go years without a single reply to support emails. For an app where data is local and there's no account, missing support is especially dangerous: when something breaks (restore, FX bug, missing transactions) the user has nowhere to turn and the only exit is a competitor. Support silence turns any minor problem into a churn trigger.

product.title: "Free and ad-free" is the number-one reason parents stay
product.plus: Over and over, parents thank the app precisely for being free and ad-free: no pop-ups for a child to accidentally tap, no subscription needed to start learning.

product.title: Kids genuinely learn letters and writing — and fast
product.plus: Parents and grandparents report a concrete outcome: the child learned the alphabet, learned to write letters and recognise words, sometimes as early as age 1–2; learning through play doesn't stress the toddler.

product.title: The tracing game accepts wrongly drawn letters
product.minus: The core mechanic — letter tracing — misfires: letters can be drawn wrongly across the screen and the game still accepts them, while the trace 'doesn't complete' when followed correctly. It undermines the teaching value.

product.title: Crashes and freezes, especially after updates
product.minus: Some users complain the app crashes, freezes or stops opening at all — sometimes right after an update or on specific devices like the Tecno Spark 10; the character freezes and only repeats one line.

product.title: A safe, risk-free environment lets parents relax
product.plus: Parents value how safe the app is for kids: no ads to tap, no data collection, a parent mode. It's one of the few apps they hand to a child without hovering.

product.title: Missing Tamil and other languages frustrates users
product.minus: A visible cluster of low ratings comes from a missing native language: Tamil (called the oldest), Dutch, Arabic. Users point out other languages are supported but theirs isn't, and it reads as a snub.

product.title: Kids genuinely engage and play for a long time
product.plus: Toddlers don't get bored, play for months, come back again; the app holds attention better than YouTube and replaces videos with learning. Parents note the bright visuals and the variety of activities.

product.title: Works offline — learning without internet or data cost
product.plus: Several users specifically note the app works offline and doesn't burn mobile data; that matters where connectivity is costly or absent, even in regions without kindergartens.

product.title: Jump to a $15/mo subscription angers long-time users
product.minus: Users who knew the app as free for years react badly to paid pricing: $15 a month is called a ridiculous price that drags an otherwise five-star app down.

product.title: Rewards, certificates and progressive levels keep motivation up
product.plus: The rewards-and-certificates system and stage-by-stage levels give the child a sense of achievement and fit different ages; parents like that there are apps for kids who outgrow this one.

product.title: The sticker collection goes blank and resets after one game
product.minus: A specific gamification bug: the sticker collection screen goes blank and white after a single section and doesn't persist even after updating — costing the app what would have been a five-star rating.

product.title: Requests to show stroke direction when writing a letter
product.minus: A constructive ask from loyal users: the tracing animation shows how to draw the line only once; they want the stroke-direction hint to repeat until the child completes the letter — it would help small kids a lot.

product.title: Cancellation is a maze, and they keep charging even after you cancel
product.minus: Parents spend months unable to cancel: the cancel button doesn't take, the account 'can't be found', and charges keep coming even after contacting the bank, changing the card, or closing the account. The single most common and most painful theme across reviews.

product.title: 'Free' in the ads turns into a mandatory paywall before the first screen
product.minus: The app is marketed as free, but you can't try it: payment is demanded up front, before the child sees anything. Parents feel duped by false advertising.

product.title: The 'free trial' charges you immediately, with no refund
product.minus: The '30-day free trial' actually charges the full amount within minutes, or after a trial you thought you'd cancelled, and refunds are refused under a no-refund policy — even when the child never used it.

product.title: Constant freezing and crashes break the lesson mid-game
product.minus: The app routinely freezes, crashes and forces restarts — across multiple devices. Kids can't finish a game, get frustrated and quit, while parents pay for a product that doesn't work.

product.title: You can't log in: the flow loops and asks you to 'download the app' from inside the app
product.minus: After paying, users hit login errors, broken password resets and an endless 'download the app' prompt while literally inside the app. They never get access to the content they paid for.

product.title: An onboarding survey and pop-ups trap you behind an un-skippable bug
product.minus: After entering payment, the app gets stuck on an 'optional' survey or a price-choice screen that can't be passed due to an error — leaving users trapped before they can even create a child's profile.

product.title: Reward tickets and virtual pets pull kids away from lessons toward grinding
product.minus: The in-app economy of tickets, pets and room decoration grabs attention more than the lessons themselves: kids pick the easy games to farm rewards, and the learning becomes a distracting backdrop.

product.title: Hidden add-on charges lurk behind the annual fee, with upsells at every step
product.minus: The advertised single annual price quietly grows with '$40 here, $30 there' add-ons and parallel charges for both the subscription and extras at once. The price is quoted as $45, then $80, then near $200 — a confusing structure that feels like a scam.

product.title: Support is a chatbot going in circles; you can't reach a human
product.minus: Instead of help there's an AI chat that repeats the no-refund policy and can't find the account, the phone line hangs up, and human agents are described as rude and useless.

product.title: Under the 'learning' label it's mostly games and videos, with little real progress
product.minus: Some parents see no learning effect: the content boils down to videos and a couple of repetitive games, rewards wrong answers, and doesn't help with, say, a first-grader's reading.

product.title: For its fans it's an educational foundation that works for years
product.plus: Many parents, grandparents and teachers praise it as best-in-class: kids ask to use it daily, pick up reading, math and letters, and end up ahead of grade level — families stay with it for 8-9 years across several children.

product.title: Age-based personalization and a 'go at your child's pace' design are what fans love
product.plus: A real strength is tailoring to each child's age and level plus broad subject coverage: reading, math, geography. Multiple profiles on one subscription let several kids in a family learn at their own pace.

product.title: The very idea of paying for kids' learning offends many on principle
product.minus: A distinct strand of anger isn't about bugs or charges but the model itself: parents find it unfair to pay for a child's education and expect free access like ordinary kids' games.

product.title: Basic functions are locked behind a paid subscription
product.minus: Recurring tasks, colours, kanban, even dark mode — things competitors give away — all require premium here. Users read it as greed and uninstall the moment they hit the first paywall.

product.title: Billing shocks: charges with no consent and hundreds of dollars
product.minus: A $4.99 plan turns into a nearly $500 charge; money is taken after unsubscribing and even a year of non-use. The trial is built so you can't cancel within 3 days, and refunds are nearly impossible.

product.title: Reminders and alarms fire unpredictably
product.minus: The one job of a reminder app — to remind — works only sometimes: missed alerts, no sound, repeats that switch themselves off. It's especially bad on Samsung and smartwatches.

product.title: Forced account just to use a simple checklist
product.minus: You must register just to open the app, and to delete it you first have to set a password. For people who only wanted a checklist this is a needless wall, and they bounce immediately.

product.title: Pushy premium pop-ups and ads break the flow
product.minus: Buy-premium prompts pop up at max volume and interrupt the work: users see "17 different ads" before even getting in and feel they're being pressured.

product.title: It auto-assigns dates and won't let you change them
product.minus: The app turns numbers in a task into a date and throws the task into the future, then won't let you change the day. It makes you less productive, not more.

product.title: Widget and calendar glitch: wrong month, lost dates
product.minus: The widget shows the wrong month, flickers, vanishes after reboots and updates; in the calendar you can't get back to today. For people who came specifically for the widget, that's a dealbreaker.

product.title: Updates break data and lock up the app
product.minus: After updates subtasks disappear with no way to recover them, old tasks get wiped during sync, and the app even managed to tangle itself into the phone's lock screen.

product.title: A lifesaver for people with ADHD and forgetfulness
product.plus: Many with ADHD call it the best: location-based reminders, an over-screen reminder and a simple daily brain-dump genuinely help them not forget and stay on plan.

product.title: Simple, clean interface without clutter
product.plus: Loyal users value the minimalism: nothing extra, easy to jot something down fast, intuitive. For those who want just a to-do list, this is the main draw.

product.title: Long-haul loyalty: years of use across devices
product.plus: Some have used it for 10+ years across phone, tablet and PC, praising solid sync, shared lists and cross-platform reach. It's a "trusted sidekick" that hasn't let them down.

product.title: Calendar and integrations weaker than rivals
product.minus: There's no native Google Calendar integration — only via paid Zapier; event colours aren't picked up, you can't select a time window, there's no time-blocking. People compare it to Todoist and leave.

product.title: The balance of simplicity and flexibility is the core reason people love it
product.plus: Over and over users hit the same note: it stays simple to use yet powerful and customizable. Not bloated, but it has everything you need — categories, colors, icons, groups, reports. That sweet spot is what keeps people for years.

product.title: People use it for years and don't leave — rare loyalty
product.plus: Dozens mention 7, 8, 10, even 14 years of use. For a time tracker that's unusual: the app becomes part of the routine and just works, day after day, across phone changes and life changes.

product.title: Shows you where your time really goes — and changes behavior
product.plus: Users describe not just logging but a shift in awareness: the pie chart and statistics force you to face the truth about your day and nudge you toward productivity. People with ADHD and 'time blindness' value it especially.

product.title: Easy to fix entries after the fact — forgiving of forgetfulness
product.plus: A big plus for real-world use: if you forget to start or stop a timer, you can edit the time manually. Multiple activities can run at once, and you can pause and resume the same entry.

product.title: The home-screen widget is loved — but it often glitches
product.minus: The widget is one of the favorite features for quick start/stop, which makes it more frustrating when it fails: it freezes, icons and names break until you restart the phone, the timer stalls until you open another app. People have to open the app itself to make the widget 'wake up'.

product.title: Updates destroy data — the most painful fear
product.minus: The most desperate reviews are about losing accumulated data. An update 'destroyed memory', logged activities vanish the next day, hours disappear over weeks. For an app trusted to track billable work, this undermines its entire purpose.

product.title: Sync and sign-in are a weak, unreliable spot
product.minus: Sync is a recurring pain: it stopped working after the paid version launched, throws 'Bad credentials' on sign-in, the backup option exists but doesn't fire. When you switch phones data won't migrate, and re-syncing asks you to pay again.

product.title: Paywalls on basic things irritate
product.minus: Some users hit the monetization: adding your own icon requires paying first, the bar chart is premium-only, a subscription appeared for basic functions. Against the many who praise the honest 'pay what you can' model, these paywalls feel like greed.

product.title: Reports and CSV export deliver real work value
product.plus: For freelancers, contractors and business owners the weekly and monthly reports and CSV export are a key reason to use it: they quickly show how time was distributed and help bill hours more accurately.

product.title: People want a Wear OS / watch version — and it's missing
product.minus: A recurring gap users feel: a smartwatch version (Wear OS, Galaxy Watch). People explicitly note that competitors offer both a phone and a watch app, and that makes them consider switching.

product.title: Weekly goals with the widget motivate — but goals get buggy
product.minus: The goals feature is liked and keeps people on track via the widget, but it has a persistent bug: after setting 2-3 weekly goals they get 'garbled', the last 10 weeks display incorrectly, and editing the hours afterward is hard.

product.title: A confusing, dated UI scares off newcomers
product.minus: The dark side of flexibility: for some people the interface is a jumble of features where it's unclear whether recording is on, and it's far too easy to delete a whole day instead of one event. Even loyal users admit the UI looks dated and the timer confuses at first.

product.title: Kids stay hooked and genuinely learn
product.plus: The core reason people keep it: toddlers play nonstop and pick up letters, numbers and shapes while building motor and speech skills. Parents notice real developmental progress.

product.title: Almost everything sits behind a paywall
product.minus: The most common gripe right after the praise: only a handful of games are free, the rest is locked. The toddler wants that one game and the parent has to pay just to stop the crying.

product.title: The price feels steep for a toddler app
product.minus: Even happy parents balk at $100+ a year: with a toddler's limited screen time, the full subscription feels too pricey and many hold off buying.

product.title: Sign-in throws out even paying users
product.minus: The sharpest technical pain: with an active subscription the app demands you subscribe again, keeps signing the child's profile out, and won't log in even after a password reset. What you paid for is locked away.

product.title: Charges nobody signed up for
product.minus: Parents find subscription charges they never made or already cancelled: billed after cancelling, three days into the app, sometimes for the whole year. Some flat-out call it fraud.

product.title: Lag and crashes break the play
product.minus: The app lags, freezes and crashes, which stings most against the high price: the child loves the games but constant glitches make it unusable.

product.title: The screen won't rotate and overflows
product.minus: A specific recurring bug: after an update the screen stops switching to landscape and the game overflows the display on both phone and tablet, making it impossible to play.

product.title: A wide variety for every mood
product.plus: A content strength: lots of varied activities and themes, with the child picking their own game, style and difficulty. The variety holds attention on long trips and for hours.

product.title: Simple, safe, ad-free interface
product.plus: Parents value that there are no ads, the space is child-safe, and the navigation is clear enough that a 2-3-year-old figures it out alone where other apps frustrated them.

product.title: A real help for special-needs kids
product.plus: A distinct, warm niche: parents of autistic and special-needs children report joy in learning and visible progress, filling a gap where schools fall short on support.

product.title: The subscription is impossible to read or cancel
product.minus: Billing is opaque: the subscription is invisible in Google Play yet active in app settings; cancelling is hard and support stays silent. Parents can't tell whether they're being charged.

product.title: Full-screen ads lock the phone mid-task while you create an event
product.minus: Ads pop up the moment you add or edit an event, go full-screen, and can't be dismissed until they finish playing — often unskippable video with a fake close button that dumps you into the Play Store. Users lose unsaved data and miss appointments.

product.title: The one-time Pro purchase was swapped for a subscription — paid features taken back
product.minus: Users who bought a perpetual Pro license years ago suddenly lose access after an update: basic features like drag-and-drop and widget font size move behind a paid subscription, with ads served instead. It reads as stealing from paying customers.

product.title: The best interface and customization of any Android calendar
product.plus: The core reason for years of loyalty: a thoughtful, information-dense interface, flexible week and month views, color-coding of calendars, and far more options than Google Calendar. People try rivals and come back.

product.title: Home-screen widgets are what people stay for
product.plus: Customizable month, week, and agenda widgets are a standout: you can shrink the font to pack the most onto a screen and keep several views at once. Smartwatch tiles and complications get praise too.

product.title: Google Calendar sync regularly stops working
product.minus: After years of reliability, Google sync breaks: events arrive days late, the weekly view shows different events than the monthly one, and manual refresh doesn't help. Missed new meetings push people back to Google Calendar.

product.title: Reminders and notifications fire unreliably
product.minus: Even paid Pro users get hit-or-miss notifications: after Android 14 reminders don't pop up for hours until you unlock the phone, and alarms sometimes make no sound at all. Some keep Google Calendar notifications on in parallel as a safety net.

product.title: Won't act as a separate calendar — demands personal access and deletes in Google
product.minus: An app called "Business Calendar" refuses to run without access to your entire personal calendar and can't stand apart from Google: delete a calendar in the app and it deletes the Google one too. For anyone wanting an isolated work calendar, that defeats the purpose.

product.title: All events and calendars suddenly vanish
product.minus: The scariest failure: one day all events or connected accounts simply disappear — even though they're still in Google Calendar — and re-syncing brings nothing back. For people who trusted the app with their whole life for years, it's the final straw.

product.title: Years of stability and one-time purchase — the loyalty bedrock
product.plus: Dozens report using it 7–10+ years without issues, install it on every device, and call it the backbone of their lives. Many specifically value that it was a one-time purchase, not a subscription, and gladly paid for Pro.

product.title: Weak non-Google support: Outlook, CalDAV, Microsoft accounts
product.minus: The Google focus leaves holes everywhere else: work Microsoft accounts demand admin rights and won't add, Outlook 365 sync breaks after the initial import, and CalDAV (Synology NAS, private CAs) stops connecting. It's the app's weakest area versus rivals.

product.title: Licenses don't carry across stores and regions — you pay again
product.minus: A license bought in the Galaxy Store or an old legacy purchase won't transfer to Google Play and won't survive a region change while travelling: the app breaks after an update or country switch and demands a new purchase. Pro isn't even buyable in some countries, including the US.

product.title: Calendar gets spammed with junk and the language switches on its own
product.minus: Beyond ads, odd bugs creep in: the calendar fills with junk "payment" events from unknown people and spam with no way to manage categories, while the interface or tasks suddenly flip to an Asian language the user can't switch back to English.

product.title: Double-entry bookkeeping is the moat that makes pros forgive everything else
product.plus: Bluecoins wins a narrow but high-value segment — people who think like accountants and need a balance sheet, P&L and reconciliation, not a cute spend tracker. It's the only app offering true double-entry on a phone, so users with an accounting background land here after sampling a dozen rivals and stay for years.

product.title: One-time purchase instead of a subscription is the filter that attracts lifers
product.plus: The pay-once-own-forever model acts as a selection mechanism: in a category exhausted by monthly charges, it attracts people willing to invest in a system for years rather than rent it. That's why users donate on top of the price and call premium "fair" — the absence of a subscription itself becomes a reason for loyalty.

product.title: Importing 30 years of Quicken/MS Money history is the moment of capture
product.plus: The real retention engine isn't features, it's migration: people bring decades of data from dead Quicken and MS Money, and the app swallows QIF/CSV across a dozen accounts. Once an entire financial life lives inside, the cost of leaving becomes prohibitive — that's the true moat, stronger than any feature.

product.title: Future-dated transactions folded into the balance is the feature people come for
product.plus: The core job-to-be-done isn't "log the past", it's "show me what I'll actually have left". Users pick Bluecoins precisely because an upcoming bill is subtracted from the balance on entry. That shifts behavior from accounting to planning — and when an update broke this, exactly these users dropped to one star: it killed the very reason they paid.

product.title: The v13/2.0 rewrite split the base into "refugees" and "adapters"
product.minus: The redesign broke the muscle memory of multi-year users: what took one swipe now needs many taps and scrolls. For an app where transactions get punched in several times a day, extra touches per entry are a tax on the core habit. Part of the base adapted, but the loudest voices are the loyal veterans whose daily ritual got broken.

product.title: Numbers users stop trusting is the death of a finance app
product.minus: After the update balances drift: totals don't add up, transfers between accounts show identical remainders, editing a note on an account changes the balance by a random number. For a spend tracker a bug is annoyance; for a double-entry app a wrong number is a betrayal of the core promise. Users start entering fake transactions to "force" the balance right — which means they no longer trust the system.

product.title: Performance doesn't scale for the very users who need the app most
product.minus: A paradox: the longer and more seriously you keep your books, the worse the app runs. At 30,000 transactions, adding one takes 15-20 seconds and lists won't load. The most valuable long-term users with deep histories hit the degradation precisely because they invested the most — and they're the ones loudest about leaving for a competitor.

product.title: The license is tied to the device Google account — premium silently vanishes
product.minus: This isn't a price gripe but a flaw in the access architecture: premium is bound to a Google account, and having a second account on the phone (or installing on a second device) drops paying users back to the ad-supported free tier. The mechanism meant to protect the purchase punishes the payers — the most loyal segment periodically loses what they bought for life.

product.title: Capturing transactions from SMS and notifications is the invisible habit engine
product.minus: Automatic parsing of bank SMS and push notifications removed the biggest friction — manual entry. When an update broke that capture, the habit fell apart: people used to transactions appearing on their own won't go back to typing them in and quietly drift away. The more "invisible" the feature, the more painful its loss — users never noticed it working until it was gone.

product.title: "Last-write-wins" cloud sync kills shared household accounting
product.minus: Sync is built as a whole-backup upload, not a merge of changes: when a husband and wife run a shared budget from two devices, each save overwrites the other's entries. The app markets itself for family finances, but the architecture supports strictly one user — an entire segment of couples discovers this only weeks in, after losing data.

product.title: Backup incompatibility across versions turns rollback into a trap
product.minus: A backup from a new version can't be restored in an old one — so users unhappy with an update physically cannot roll back: the app forces them to update again or the data won't open. This turns a voluntary migration into a one-way ticket and strips users of their only self-defense lever, the rollback. The v12/v13 incompatibility multiplies panic around an already painful redesign.

product.title: The app loses context on switch — and wipes a half-entered transaction
product.minus: The real entry flow is: switch to your banking app, check the amount, come back and finish logging. But after the update, returning resets the app to the home screen, losing the half-entered transaction. This breaks the natural workflow of exactly the meticulous users who verify every figure — and turns a simple entry into a source of frustration.

product.title: Local-first storage with no required account is a magnet for privacy-minded users
product.plus: Bluecoins wins the segment fleeing cloud finance services: data stored locally, backups to your own Google Drive or Dropbox, no account required to use it. For people unwilling to hand their financial life to someone else's server, this is the deciding factor — the privacy model itself becomes a selling feature, not a settings checkbox.

product.title: Inability to edit recurring transactions breaks trust in automation
product.minus: Recurring transactions are set once and then can't be edited: if you didn't set a reminder up front, you can't change or remove them later, and "ghost" recurring entries pop up every month with no way to delete them. Automation you can't correct is scarier than manual entry — the user loses control over their data exactly where they expected to save effort.

product.title: A no-frills tracker that does one thing and does it well
product.plus: The core thing people love: a clean interface with no ads, no gamification, no extra clutter. Start a timer on a project, stop it — that's it. This focus is what keeps users in the app for years.

product.title: No home-screen widget is the single most-requested feature
product.minus: To start tracking you must open the app every time, pick a project and a task — no quick start from the home or lock screen. People openly promise five stars the moment a widget appears.

product.title: On Pixel 9 the top buttons sit under the OS bar and won't tap
product.minus: The back button and the three-dot menu in the top corner overlap the Pixel notification bar, making it nearly impossible to delete or edit a record. The app hasn't been updated in ages, so for Pixel owners this has become a deal-breaker.

product.title: No cross-device sync — switching phones wipes everything
product.minus: Move to a new phone and your data and purchased premium don't follow: people log in with the same account and see an empty free version. Years of projects have to be set up again from scratch.

product.title: Makes studying visible and genuinely motivates students
product.plus: Students are the core audience: the app breaks time down by subject, shows progress charts and pushes you to keep a daily quota. For many it became a tool that literally nudges them to study more.

product.title: No way to attach a note to a record or task
product.minus: People want to jot down what they actually did in a given time block and tie a note to a record or task. It's missing — and for many that's the exact small thing standing between four stars and five.

product.title: You can't run two timers at the same time
product.minus: You can't track two activities in parallel — say a walk and a podcast. Manual entries support it but live timers don't, and users see the limit as artificial and easily fixable.

product.title: Premium purchase breaks: money taken, no access
product.minus: Some users got stuck on the payment page with money already deducted, others saw their bought "premium" vanish or suddenly be asked to pay again for "pro". Support emails go unanswered — a painful look for a paid product.

product.title: One-time purchase over subscription — trusted and appreciated
product.plus: Many specifically praise the honest model: one payment, no subscriptions, no add-on charges. Some grabbed lifetime access before the move to subscriptions and are glad they did — to them it's a sign of respect for the user.

product.title: Timers are locked behind premium with no way to try them
product.minus: The headline feature — the timer — is paid-only, and that isn't flagged upfront. There's no trial to decide whether it's worth buying, which puts people off right at the start.

product.title: Weak Pomodoro alerts: one quiet chime and you miss the end
product.minus: The Pomodoro timer chimes once with a quiet sound you can't make louder, repeating or different. People who get into the zone simply miss the end of the interval — making the feature near-useless for them.

product.title: Beautiful time visualizations genuinely motivate self-competition
product.plus: Charts, stats and the calendar make spent time tangible: you watch productivity climb project to project, and there's a thrill in beating your own past mark. For many it also exposes how much time goes to procrastination.

product.title: No tree structure: subtasks, categories and manual sorting missing
product.minus: Power users miss hierarchy: project → task → subtask, categories for projects, and the ability to arrange tasks in their own order rather than alphabetically. Right now one subject with several assignments becomes a mess.

product.title: Silent data loss undermines trust in long-term tracking
product.minus: Some users had months — even a year — of records vanish for no reason, and a deleted project can't be restored. For an app where people track for years, that kind of loss stings especially hard.

product.title: The free barcode scanner is the hook that pulls people off MyFitnessPal
product.plus: Rivals lock the scanner and custom foods behind a paywall; here they ship free, so the core scan-and-log loop works without paying and kills entry friction on day one. That's the actual switching trigger: users call the scanner fast, unlimited, and the deciding factor over paid competitors.

product.title: The crowdsourced database is both the catalog's breadth and the poison in its trust
product.minus: The same food sits in the database as several conflicting entries because users publish them with no moderation. For an app whose whole point is accurate macro counting, that breaks the core function: people stop trusting any number and end up hand-checking every entry, which eats the very time savings the tracker promised.

product.title: The recipe calculator does its own math wrong — and that hurts the core worse than bad user entries
product.minus: Even when the user enters verified ingredients themselves, the recipe and daily totals don't reconcile: 15g of carbs becomes 25–26, and the calorie budget contradicts the protein/fat/carb budget. This isn't crowdsourcing — it's the app's own arithmetic, and it's what finally breaks trust: a tracker that can't add up is pointless.

product.title: The "carb manager" promise collides with a calorie-first onboarding
product.minus: The name promises carb tracking, but the first screen forces a calorie goal and behaves like a calorie counter — which directly contradicts the low-carb audience's logic, who came to lower insulin, not cut calories. The most precise users (keto, diabetic) catch the conflict instantly and read it as a betrayal of the exact promise they downloaded for.

product.title: The custom-recipe builder turns the database into a personal one — loyalty is built here
product.plus: When the shared database lacks a food or lies, the user can build their own recipe and food with verified values — and that's what retains home cooks and complex-diet users who'd otherwise have nothing to lean on. The ability to "fix" the data for yourself turns the database's weakness into a retention tool: leaving means losing the personal library you've built.

product.title: The always-online architecture kills the app exactly where a tracker is needed most
product.minus: The app demands internet even for basic logging: on a weak connection a splash screen pops up and blocks access to your own data until the network returns. For a food tracker opened on the move — in a store, a cafe, on the road — that's a failure at the exact moment of use: people leave not over features but because they can't log lunch without wifi.

product.title: The captcha login locks out existing users — and cuts off the very people with vision issues
product.minus: To get into their own account, users must clear a visual hCaptcha puzzle that fails over and over — especially for people with vision problems who physically can't read the images. This isn't new-user onboarding, it's a returning user with all their data inside: the app locks the person out of their own history and pushes them to a competitor.

product.title: Long-term retention rides on visible weight and blood-sugar results
product.plus: The most loyal reviews aren't about features but measurable outcomes: 100–125 lbs lost in a year, glucose dropping, reaching maintenance. When the tracker attaches to a concrete health result it stops being an app and becomes part of a regimen — hence the multi-year users and the switching away from other trackers to this one.

product.title: Gamification (challenges, milestones, feed) turns logging into a habit for people who hate tracking
product.plus: Monthly challenges, milestones and a social feed turn dull food logging into accountability through competition with others — and that pulls in the audience that normally quits trackers within a week. Some users say outright they hate tracking but here it's "even enjoyable": the streak-of-progress and community mechanic keeps them in the loop.

product.title: Integrations with wearables shine — but the Samsung Health gap cuts half the Android base
product.minus: The app links easily to Fitbit, Garmin and Apple Health, but won't push data to Samsung Health or Health Connect — a huge slice of Android users on Samsung watches. People explicitly dock a star and keep a third-party workaround solely over this gap: an integration strength becomes a pinpoint loss exactly where the ecosystem is largest.

product.title: Ounces-and-cups defaults push out everyone outside the US
product.minus: The database and units are built for the US: weight only in ounces, portions in "cups", American brands, and the Australian/British net-carb logic has to be recomputed by hand. For an app where logging speed is half the value, this turns every entry into a conversion: international users leave not over quality but over the geographic blindness of the defaults.

product.title: The catalog is stuffed with packaged goods but fails on whole foods
product.minus: The database overflows with processed and brand-name items, but a plain carrot or some greens can't be found — exactly the audience that cooks from whole foods and needs honest keto tracking most. The barcode scanner, the headline hook, is useless on unpackaged food, so the most "clean-eating" users hit manual entry and leave.

product.title: Under the hood it's a wrapper over the website, not a native app — and the speed shows it
product.minus: The app essentially renders their website: javascript hangs, the loading screen drags, search lags, and building a single meal takes longer than cooking it. This architectural choice explains the whole scatter of "slow to open" complaints with one root cause — the product isn't native, and for a tracker valued for low-friction quick entry, that's a systemic ceiling on quality.

product.title: The missing Android widget is a quiet retention leak among loyal payers
product.minus: A tracker's core value is instant entry, yet Android has no home-screen widget while iOS does and reportedly once did. This isn't a whim: users have asked for years and say plainly it's why they'll stop paying for premium. A quiet pain among the most valuable cohort — long-term active payers for whom every extra daily tap costs the subscription.

product.title: The free tier is generous enough to be the product itself
product.plus: Unlike rivals where nothing works without paying, here basic calorie/carb/protein/water tracking, the scanner and custom recipes are all free — and many users stay on the free tier for years without feeling crippled. That generosity is the acquisition strategy: it defuses the "pay for everything again" fear and turns happy free users into word-of-mouth.

product.title: The visual macro presentation (pie chart) is what keeps visual learners
product.plus: The macro pie chart gives an instant at-a-glance picture of where you stand on protein/fat/carbs — and that hooks the audience that processes information visually and abandons table-of-numbers trackers. The presentation of data, not the data itself, becomes the differentiator: people name the pie chart specifically as why they finally understand their eating and stick with the app.

product.title: Lives in your pocket for years and survives every phone change
product.plus: The biggest praise isn't features but loyalty: people say they've used it 5, 10, even 13–15 years, and reinstall it first on every new phone.

product.title: Simplicity as the feature: nothing extra, doesn't eat time or attention
product.plus: People value the minimalism itself — lightweight, no lag, looks like a real lined notepad, doesn't overload the brain. Several outright beg the devs to change nothing.

product.title: Indispensable as a shopping list and memory for daily life
product.plus: Concrete use-cases recur: grocery lists, to-dos, reminders, recipes, grandkids' names, questions for the doctor. Several note it specifically helps with ADHD and forgetfulness.

product.title: Color-coding notes genuinely helps keep things organized
product.plus: The headline feature delivers: users color notes by topic and list, which makes navigation and visual sorting easier.

product.title: Works offline, no ads, no subscription — and that's why it's loved
product.plus: The combo of «free + offline + no ads + Google backup» reads as rare honesty. Many stay on the free version for years and are happy.

product.title: Updates break the familiar — and kill long-time fans' trust
product.minus: The most painful complaint: updates remove features (sub-folders), introduce editing bugs and push a paid «upgrade». Former 5-star users drop their rating.

product.title: Data loss and fragile restore without a matching account
product.minus: The scariest scenario for a notepad: people lose all their notes. The backup can't be restored without an account exactly matching the old phone, and the backup file can't be opened by another app.

product.title: Cross-device sync — people rely on it, but it's temperamental
product.minus: Google-account sync is praised as a key reason to stay, yet it also fails: after a transfer edits to notes don't stick, and migrating to a new phone is called «challenging».

product.title: Reminders only fire when you open the app
product.minus: A recurring reminder bug: notifications don't arrive on schedule by themselves, only when the user manually opens the app — so the reminder stops reminding.

product.title: Text only: no photos, no formatting, too few colors
product.minus: A common feature request: you can't insert a photo into a note, there's no bold/italic or highlighting, and the available colors are too few. For «just text», people want a bit more.

product.title: Walled ecosystem: no bulk export, no getting files out
product.minus: Notes are locked inside: no bulk export/email, you can't select multiple notes at once, and files can't be saved outside the app. This blocks anyone wanting to move their archive elsewhere.

product.title: No iOS or Windows version — cross-platform breaks down
product.minus: The Android lock-in becomes a trap: switching to iPhone makes devoted users lose the app, and it can't be installed on PC (Windows 11). They ask for at least a one-time purchase for iOS.

product.title: Lists randomly delete and reshuffle items
product.minus: After recent updates the shared lists have a mind of their own: items vanish mid-shop, things you add get wiped at random, and the row order rearranges itself. For the app's core feature — a shared grocery list — that's fatal.

product.title: Loved it for years — recent updates broke it
product.minus: The recurring refrain: families used Cozi for 10-15 years and adored it, but over the past year — or even the past month — it became unbearably buggy. People name the exact update that broke things and move to competitors.

product.title: Basic calendar features locked behind a paywall
product.minus: The app is marketed as free, but without a Gold subscription you can't view the calendar beyond 3-30 days — not even events you already entered. Month view, past appointments and planning ahead all cost money, and users call it a ransom.

product.title: Endless spinner, random logouts, refused logins
product.minus: The app spins the wheel of death for minutes or forever, logs people out at random, then refuses their correct password. Paying Gold users physically can't get into their own calendar and lists.

product.title: Lists and calendar don't sync between family members
product.minus: Cozi's whole point — everyone sees the same thing — breaks down: what one person adds never shows up for the others, especially across Android↔iPhone. Sometimes only one family member can add items at all; everyone else's get wiped.

product.title: Intrusive, interactive ads and constant upsells
product.minus: Ads pop up exactly as you're typing a list item, load on a delay so you tap them by accident and get thrown out of the app. Even paying Gold subscribers get a non-dismissible push to upgrade to the AI/Max tier.

product.title: The Android version is a crippled afterthought next to iOS
product.minus: On Android the month calendar shows no colors, dates sit below the cell instead of above, and the interface looks alien. Wives on iPhone love it; husbands on Android call the same app nearly unusable.

product.title: Swipe-to-delete with no confirmation wipes items by accident
product.minus: List items delete at the slightest touch, with no "are you sure?" and no undo. On a long grocery list it's easy to wipe half of it and not even remember what was there.

product.title: No offline access to lists — useless in a store with no signal
product.minus: The app needs a connection just to open the lists, and signal often drops exactly inside supermarkets. A shopping list that won't open at the store defeats the whole purpose.

product.title: One shared account keeps the whole family on the same page
product.plus: What users love most: spouses and kids share one account and see the calendar, shopping and to-do lists update in real time. Someone adds milk from home and whoever's at the store sees it instantly. It kills the endless "grab this too" texting.

product.title: A bridge between Android and iPhone, where native calendars won't talk
product.plus: For mixed-ecosystem couples, Cozi solves what the built-in calendars can't: a shared calendar and lists that work the same on the wife's iPhone and the husband's Samsung. That cross-platform bridge is exactly why many stay.

product.title: The whole household in one place: calendar, lists, recipes, birthdays
product.plus: Beyond calendar and groceries, people value recipes that turn into ingredient lists, meal planning, to-do lists and the perpetual birthday tracker with reminders. For families and people with ADHD this all-in-one is a lifeline against chaos.

product.title: The interface feels stuck in 2010 and is unfriendly to newcomers
product.minus: The design looks untouched since 2010: confusing navigation, too many tabs, no dark mode, text cut off at large font sizes. It's especially hard on the elderly relatives families install it for in the first place.

product.title: Support doesn't fix anything and blames the user
product.minus: Support tickets get months of off-topic auto-replies or advice the person already tried. In one case an agent claimed the events never existed, called it user error and offered no solution at all.

product.title: The real hook is micronutrients, not calories: it retains medically-motivated users
product.plus: Vitamins, minerals, omegas, fibre, sugar — this data layer turns food logging into a health-management tool, not a weight-loss one. It's what retains diabetics (A1C from 13 to 4.5), menopausal users and people whose doctor prescribed the tracker: they see what rivals don't show, so they don't leave.

product.title: The generous free tier is the funnel: users get hooked free, then pay voluntarily
product.plus: Barcode scanner, custom recipes and full nutrient summaries are free — enough to make a user settle in. Many say outright: "used the free version for a year, then upgraded not because I had to, but because I love the app." The free tier doesn't cripple the product, it sells it.

product.title: Ads kick in on day 4 — the product breaks the very habit it just built
product.minus: Ads don't appear at first — they switch on after a few days, exactly once the user is hooked on logging. And they arrive full-screen, mid-entry, stealing focus and the keyboard. This isn't "too many ads," it's a deliberate bait-and-switch: the product waits for the habit to form, then attacks that habit to force the subscription. The effect backfires: users describe wanting to uninstall, not to buy.

product.title: The food database is the retention ceiling: regional gaps push out non-Americans
product.minus: The app's strength is data accuracy, but it's also its weak spot: for Indian, Punjabi, South Indian, Algerian and UK dishes the database barely exists. A non-US user hits constant manual food creation — and the logging they came here to simplify becomes work. Regional food gaps are the quiet churn channel outside North America.

product.title: Barcode scan and photo-add are the engine that makes logging stick
product.plus: Free barcode scanning, and when an item isn't in the base, a photo of the front and the label that the app auto-fills from. This removes the friction that made users quit other trackers ("oops, this doesn't exist in our database"). It's frictionless input, not analytics, that gets people logging daily — and daily is the precondition for any result.

product.title: The app miscounts calories itself — and that kills trust in paying
product.minus: A known bug: when logging multi-component meals, total calories and macros are computed wrong and the user has to check the math by hand. For a product whose one basic job is "to count," that's fatal — people say outright it's why they didn't buy Pro. An error in the core voids the whole micronutrient superstructure on top of it.

product.title: You can't set a calorie goal manually — the app imposes its own plan on people who don't want it
product.minus: The app derives the calorie goal from profile data, and manual override is either hidden or broken. For a user who just wants to "track macros" against a specific doctor's or dietitian's advice, this turns the tool into an obstacle: they either fight imposed goals or start anxiously obsessing over them. Control over your own target is exactly what the medically-driven (not weight-loss) segment loses.

product.title: You can't edit a single ingredient in a saved recipe — for daily users this compounds into pain
product.minus: To change one ingredient's weight in a saved recipe (20g → 5g) you must delete the old entry and re-add a new one. For people who cook their own recipes daily and log meal prep — the most loyal, paying segment — small friction multiplied by frequency becomes "pulling teeth." The regression stings more because editing used to work.

product.title: The app for MyFitnessPal refugees: it catches the exact moment a rival gets greedy
product.plus: A huge share of users arrived after MFP stripped free features or Fitbit made logging "6x harder." Cronometer positions as "MFP before they got greedy" — and retains on exactly that contrast. It's a strategic moat: growth comes from rivals' mistakes, not marketing, and the refugees stay because the free tier here actually works.

product.title: Seamless tracker sync — what keeps the data-driven users in
product.plus: Integration with Garmin, Withings, Fitbit pulls in calories burned and biometrics and dynamically adjusts the day's calorie budget. For a user who's built a closed loop of eat-burn-weigh, that loop is the product: one user hit 10% body fat precisely on it. The hardware tie-in turns a food tracker into a body-management system.

product.title: Health Connect double-counts calories and meals — the product breaks on someone else's migration
product.minus: After Fitbit's move to Google Health Connect the integration turned hostile: meals and activity get duplicated, full BMR is added on top of the estimate — and the calorie budget becomes meaningless. The app's strength (hardware sync) turns against it when the ecosystem shifts underneath. Users can't tell Google's fault from the app's — and they leave the app.

product.title: The learning curve filters out novices, but it's what forges the advanced, loyal user
product.plus: The interface isn't intuitive at first, adding custom food needs an "operator's manual," and some features require googling. This sheds casual users — but those who cross the threshold call the "highly customizable" dashboard "pure genius" and stay for years. The entry barrier acts as a filter: it scares off the casual crowd and keeps the people who genuinely need the depth.

product.title: The rigid breakfast-lunch-dinner structure loses people who eat differently
product.minus: You can't add an extra meal (brunch, a second dinner for 5-meals-a-day eaters), there's no multi-add into one meal, and you can't copy yesterday's breakfast in one tap — even though people eat the same things in streaks. The default day model is tuned for an average user and creates small daily friction for anyone whose eating pattern doesn't fit three slots.

product.title: Default nutrient targets carry a dietary stance — advanced users argue with the app's philosophy
product.minus: By default the app steers toward a high-carb model (269g carbs/day as default), and for keto/low-carb users that's not a bug but an imposed stance they distrust. When a product is deeply about nutrients, its default recommendations read as a health claim — and part of the advanced, most valuable audience treats them as an ideological conflict.

product.title: It's a desktop tool in a mobile skin — the data depth lives on the big screen
product.minus: Veterans say it plainly: for all the data they prefer the web version, mobile is a compromise. The app doesn't rotate to landscape on tablets (where most people hold a tablet), there's no undo, charts are unreadable, and the 2022 redesign struck some users as a regression from a "super beauty app." The product is built around a rich desktop dashboard, and the phone screen is its bottleneck, not its home.

product.title: Five apps in one is the real hook — not the habit tracking itself
product.plus: Users arrive for habits but stay for the 'habits + spending + journal + mood + focus' bundle on a single screen: many say they deleted their other productivity apps because everything they needed was already here. The consolidation kills app-switching — and that, not the tracking, is what actually retains.

product.title: The 3-4 habit cap hits before the product can prove its value
product.minus: The free tier hits a wall exactly where a habit tracker starts to matter: 3-4 habits is fewer than one person's actual routine, so the user slams into the paywall on day one, before building a single streak or seeing any payoff. Activation lands after the payment ask — and many leave for HabitNow, which allows more habits for free.

product.title: Reminders don't fire — and that IS the habit-forming mechanism
product.minus: A habit runs on an external trigger, and here that trigger breaks: users with notifications fully enabled report reminders simply never arrive. Without a reliable nudge the tracker degrades into a passive list you have to remember to open — and people uninstall specifically over the broken reminder, not the design.

product.title: Widgets behind the paywall — can't judge the central feature before buying
product.minus: For a habit tracker the home-screen widget IS the always-on reminder people install the app for — but it sits behind the subscription. The user has to decide on buying without ever trying the one feature that determines whether they'll like the product, so the cautious simply won't gamble money blind.

product.title: The focus timer freezes mid-session and loses your progress
product.minus: Focus mode promises measurable discipline, but the timer hangs for 2-3 minutes near the final second or stalls around the 15-minute mark — and the session never counts. Worst of all the user breaks concentration to check what's wrong with the counter: the feature built to hold focus actively destroys it, killing the reason to come back.

product.title: No auto-sync — multi-device users do the work by hand
product.minus: The most engaged segment — people running their life across phone and tablet — is punished hardest: data doesn't sync automatically, so they manually back up on one device and restore on the other. For an app that wants to be the daily hub, manual sync breaks the very premise of 'always at hand everywhere'.

product.title: The journal corrupts non-Latin text — loses Arabic, garbles entries
product.minus: The journal is pitched as the reason not to install a separate diary app, yet it fails to preserve Arabic and non-standard characters: come back to an entry and it shows up as 'code'. For the most personal module this destroys trust — and quietly cuts off the entire non-English segment that valued having 'a diary inside the tracker' in the first place.

product.title: No streak or score on the main screen — the dopamine loop is missing
product.minus: Streaks and visible progress are the motivational fuel of habit trackers, yet the main screen shows neither a streak nor a score. For users driven by 'don't break the chain' and the daily check-off, the missing at-a-glance marker is a flat dealbreaker, even when they like everything else.

product.title: Stats locked in premium — removes the very reason to track anything
product.minus: The point of tracking is to see your trend, but basic statistics and analytics sit behind the subscription. The user diligently checks off habits, then hits a wall on 'so how am I doing?': they enter the data for free but can't read it back. It inverts the product's logic and leaves a feeling of logging into a void.

product.title: An active solo dev turns feedback into updates — and into loyalty
product.plus: A rare retention mechanism: the solo developer replies in public, takes suggestions and ships them fast, and users notice — 'the app keeps getting better'. A bug-driven downgrade doesn't mean churn here — the responsiveness turns critics into advocates and justifies buying 'because the project is alive'.

product.title: A clean, minimal UI wins those burned out on Notion and Trello
product.plus: Users explicitly compare it to Notion and Trello and pick this one for doing the same job without the complexity or feature bloat: 'minimal and without unnecessary bloat'. The self-described 'planner-app connoisseurs' have tried dozens and settle here precisely for the low learning curve — simplicity is a competitive weapon here, not a compromise.

product.title: The budget module pulls the user beyond habits
product.plus: The spending tracker turns out to be a hook of its own: people come for habits but realise they also need to keep money in check — and stay because it's already built in. Requests for multi-currency, carry-forward budgets and account sync reveal the budget is used seriously, not as a bolt-on — which widens the audience beyond 'habit tracker'.

product.title: A flood of new-tracker requests — the app is becoming a daily life dashboard
product.plus: A strong engagement signal: users don't ask to fix, they ask to add — sleep, water, health (BP/sugar), food, periods, gamification. That's how people treat a product that has already become their daily dashboard, not a mere habit tracker; each request is another module that would let them drop a separate app.

product.title: Students and teens love it, but it's a weak-to-monetize segment
product.plus: The app clearly resonates with young users: schoolkids, students, people with ADHD and autism say it's specifically what got them studying on schedule and keeping life in order. That's an organic, devoted word-of-mouth growth channel — but the same segment openly says it can't afford premium, so the love doesn't convert to revenue without a dedicated student mechanic.

product.title: Kids genuinely start reading in weeks, not months
product.plus: The headline praise is a concrete outcome: parents and grandparents describe a child recognizing letters, blending sounds and reading words within a week or two. Not «we liked it» but measurable progress.

product.title: Fully free with no ads — a rarity among kids' apps
product.plus: The «free + no ads» combo surfaces again and again as a standalone reason to love it: parents stress it's the only kids' app without ads they've come across.

product.title: English-only, no language switch — a wall for non-English kids
product.minus: The single most common complaint: the app teaches reading only in English and explains everything in English too. For a child who doesn't yet know the language, that turns learning into confusion — and there's no option to switch the interface language.

product.title: Crashes on launch and won't open on some devices
product.minus: For a chunk of users the app simply doesn't work: it crashes right after opening, kicks them out within a fraction of a second, or won't launch at all after install. Painful because even fans get locked out.

product.title: Child's progress gets lost, forcing lessons to be redone
product.minus: A painful bug: saved progress suddenly vanishes and the child has to redo the same lessons over and over. For a kids' app that hits motivation directly.

product.title: System nav bar covers the 'next' button
product.minus: A specific UI defect on several Android devices (Pixel, ZFold): the app goes full-screen but doesn't hide the system nav bar, so it covers the bottom buttons — making play impossible unless you switch to gesture navigation.

product.title: The game-like format hooks kids who used to find learning boring
product.plus: Kids don't just tolerate the app — they ask for it and get upset when it's turned off. Parents note that a child with no interest in learning games got hooked on this one specifically.

product.title: The short stories are a favorite and a tool for blending words
product.plus: The in-app stories earn their own praise: cute, inclusive, and useful for practicing blending sounds and rhymes. For many it's the part they come back for.

product.title: Spelling rewards guessing: letters magnetize into place
product.minus: Thoughtful parents spot a pedagogical flaw: in spelling exercises letters can be placed out of order and magnetize into the right spot — rewarding blind guessing over real learning. Related: teaching letter names instead of sounds makes blending harder.

product.title: No age personalization: same content for a 4- and 9-year-old, dull and repetitive
product.minus: Some parents and older kids fault the lack of leveling: children of different ages get identical content, material repeats to the point of boredom, and those who already know the alphabet find it too easy. A rigid «curriculum» with no freedom of choice deepens the feeling.

product.title: Whiteboard writing isn't recognized and the recording cuts off
product.minus: The interactive input mechanics break down: handwriting on the whiteboard isn't recognized, the bottom of writing activities fails to load, and when repeating after the narrator the mic only captures a second of sound. It breaks exactly the exercises the app exists for.

product.title: Emotionally manipulative reminder emails creep parents out
product.minus: A distinct, unexpected gripe: the daily reminder emails are cloying and guilt-trip the child («please put my heart at ease», «when you skip your lesson, I spiral»). Parents find it utterly inappropriate for a kids' product.

product.title: Paid content re-locks itself days after purchase
product.minus: The single biggest and most painful complaint: people buy the full version, play for a few days, and then the letters lock again as if no purchase happened. It effectively turns a one-time payment into something that simply stops working.

product.title: No purchase restore — you pay again on every device
product.minus: There's no restore-purchase button: switch phones, reinstall, or add a second child, and the app demands you buy everything over again. Parents end up paying for the same content multiple times.

product.title: Only A–C are free, the rest sits behind a paywall
product.minus: Only the first three letters are unlocked for free; everything else is one paid unlock at ~8.99. Parents resent that the child gets hooked on the opening letters and then hits a wall and melts down.

product.title: Purchase doesn't share across Google Family or tablet profiles
product.minus: The paid version is tied to one account: it doesn't transfer to kids via Google Family Library, and you can't add it to a second profile on a shared tablet. Each child and parent has to buy their own copy.

product.title: Teaches not just letters but words, sounds and their meaning
product.plus: The app's core strength: two- and three-year-olds pick up letters, phonics and the meanings of new words — parents repeatedly report a sharp jump in letter recognition and reading within a week or two.

product.title: Charming monsters, sounds and animations hold a toddler's attention
product.plus: Silly letter sounds, adorable monsters and funny cartoons after each word turn learning into play — parents laugh along with their kids, and the reward animation eases frustration with longer words.

product.title: Powerful nostalgia: those who grew up on it return with their own kids
product.plus: A rare emotional bond: teens and adults who played as kids rediscover the app 10+ years later — now for their own children, nieces and grandkids. It's an unusually long-lived loyalty.

product.title: A favorite tool for teachers and parents of special-needs kids
product.plus: Early-childhood teachers and educators recommend it to their families, and parents of autistic children note it makes learning letters and speech accessible and non-frustrating.

product.title: Words aren't sorted by age — a jumble for three-year-olds
product.minus: There's no difficulty filter: a three-year-old gets words like ARTISTIC and CONTRAPTION mixed in with simple ones. Parents ask for age-based sorting and a mode that forces letters in order for phonics.

product.title: The reward animation after a word disappears after updates
product.minus: The closing cartoon after a completed word — the child's main motivation — simply stops playing for some users, especially after updates. The content seems bought, but the reward never arrives.

product.title: Purchases get auto-refunded, and support stays silent
product.minus: Some payments reverse themselves without any refund request, content won't download, and emails to support go unanswered. People can neither get what they paid for nor get their money back.

product.title: Users ask for more words, languages and content expansions
product.minus: The content is finite and grows stale: kids memorize the same ~7 words per letter. The most engaged parents ask for a rotating word pool, digraphs (ch, sh, ck) and other-language versions.

product.title: An intrusive review prompt blocks the child mid-play
product.minus: A pop-up asking for a rating flashes right while the child is playing and distracts them. It especially annoys people who already paid for the full version and don't expect that nagging.

product.title: A paywall blocks the app before the very first page
product.minus: The subscription is demanded right at the entrance: you can't see what's inside or try a single book — pay or leave. People uninstall without ever opening a single book.

product.title: The ads promise "free" — and that's a lie
product.minus: It's advertised as free, and people install it for exactly that reason — only to be asked for money inside. They see it as outright deception and false advertising.

product.title: No "X" button — you can't escape the free-trial screen
product.minus: The "7-day free trial" screen pops up on every entry and won't close: no cross, no skip, no decline. Your only options are to agree or delete the app.

product.title: Sign-up breaks on entering the birth year
product.minus: Creating an account often fails: after you enter the birth year it throws an "we can't sign you in" error, over dozens of attempts and reinstalls — even on a stable connection.

product.title: Surprise charges hit accounts for large sums
product.minus: People report unexpected charges of tens or hundreds of dollars — sometimes for an app that isn't even installed, or after refusing the service. Getting a refund is nearly impossible.

product.title: Cancelling and refunds are their own ordeal
product.minus: The cancel button on the site doesn't work, refund emails go unanswered, and two subscriptions can somehow run on one email at once. Trust in the company collapses.

product.title: Free for schools, but families have to pay
product.minus: Teachers and students get free access at school, but reading the same books at home costs money. Homeschooling parents and families in poorer countries feel cut off from learning.

product.title: Kids start reading on their own — the core value
product.plus: Parents say again and again that after Epic their child starts reading voluntarily, won't put the tablet down and asks for more. It genuinely pulls in kids who used to dislike books.

product.title: A huge library: books, audio and videos in one place
product.plus: Thousands of books, beloved series like Cat Ninja and Diary of a Wimpy Kid, learning videos and audiobooks — for every age and level. There's so much content it serves both a classroom and a family.

product.title: "Read to me": narration with word highlighting teaches reading
product.plus: The mode where the app reads aloud and highlights the words helps kids who struggle with reading and supports English as a foreign language. You can read yourself or listen.

product.title: Gamification: badges and reading "buddies" keep kids hooked
product.plus: Badges for books read, cute reading-buddy pets and quizzes turn reading into a game — kids take pride in their collection and keep coming back. A safe, "productive" alternative to games.

product.title: Pricing stings, and access is capped by time of day
product.minus: The subscription costs more than premium Netflix for arguably less content, and the free school access only works until 4 p.m. — so kids can't get in after school or on weekends.

product.title: Book previews are just 3-4 pages, and progress gets lost
product.minus: Even once inside, without a subscription you only get a 3-4 page "preview" of each book. And paying users lose profiles, favorites and reading progress — sometimes along with the series they paid for.

product.title: The price multiplied — long-time loyalty was betrayed
product.minus: People describe the subscription multiplying 2-4x in a couple of years: 49 to 199 EUR, 79 to 150 pounds, 40 to 232 dollars. Users of 10-17 years are cancelling en masse, calling it extortion and greed.

product.title: Your notes are held hostage — the free plan was strangled by limits
product.minus: The core tactic: let you accumulate notes for years, then lock them away. A 50-note cap on a single device, access to your own records only after paying. Many say they have fewer than 50 notes yet still can't create a new one.

product.title: Upsell pop-ups bury the notes themselves
product.minus: Just to open a note you have to dismiss a pile of subscription pop-ups. Prompts intrude on every page and block navigation. People uninstall specifically because of this aggression.

product.title: An unskippable promo video on every launch
product.minus: Opening the already-installed app greets you with a 30-second unskippable ad for Evernote itself, the continue button greyed out. Absurd: advertising the product to someone who just downloaded it.

product.title: Laggy and freezing — opening a note has become painful
product.minus: The app takes a minute or more to open, lags 5-10 seconds while typing, freezes and closes on its own. People complain nothing has been fixed for years despite the sluggishness reports.

product.title: Forced AI overlays your notes and can't be turned off
product.minus: AI features rename notes for you, a "suggest title" button covers the text, and AI search buries the right notes among irrelevant ones. Even with the settings off it still gets in the way.

product.title: Can't stay logged in — endless logouts and lockouts
product.minus: The app constantly demands re-login, throws you out, and sometimes won't let you in at all, neither sign in nor sign out. For some, only reinstalling lets them reach their notes.

product.title: A one-device limit breaks cross-platform use
product.minus: Free sync is limited to one device, and detaching old phones (even long-sold ones) is impossible — the link doesn't work. People get stuck and can't reach their own records.

product.title: Support goes silent and cancellation is deliberately hard
product.minus: Tickets get no reply or an AI-generated one; a scheduled call is cancelled at the last minute. Cancelling is hard too: the cancel button isn't where they say, and some are charged even after deleting their account.

product.title: Backup and export are obstructed — leaving with your data is hard
product.minus: Notes can't be exported in bulk, print-to-PDF is broken, .pdf export is missing — you end up moving thousands of notebooks one by one. Many migrate anyway to Obsidian, OneNote, Joplin, UpNote, Google Keep.

product.title: Updates lose and corrupt the notes themselves
product.minus: Updates wipe out some notes and photos, a "view only" mode blocks editing, and clicking a notebook lands you in a random note. On large notes performance collapses and text simply vanishes.

product.title: For devoted fans it's still the number-one "external brain"
product.plus: Despite the backlash, a long-loyal core calls Evernote their most essential app and "external brain": first thing installed on every new device, praised for reliably storing and organizing notes for years.

product.title: Some users do see real improvement under Bending Spoons
product.plus: A minority notes the new owner fixed bugs, added genuinely useful features and finally enabled offline access; the app is now noticeably faster and more stable, and some of the intrusive ads and the 30-second video were removed.

product.title: They keep charging after you cancel
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people cancel (often still inside the trial) and still get charged weeks and months later. The subscription shows up neither in the app nor in Google Play, so the only way to stop the charges is to block the card.

product.title: Unauthorized and duplicate charges at sign-up
product.minus: Signing up for a single plan triggers multiple back-to-back charge attempts, often for large amounts and from different countries. Frequently the only thing that saves users is their bank flagging the transactions as fraud and declining them.

product.title: Bundled into a stack of separate subscriptions for other apps
product.minus: During onboarding users get quietly signed up to 5+ "bundle" apps, each of which must be cancelled separately. Cancelling the main subscription doesn't cancel the add-ons, and they get billed for them anyway.

product.title: Dark patterns: "Continue" silently agrees to pay
product.minus: The paywall flow is built so the "Continue" button at the bottom confirms add-on purchases (sometimes with non-refundable "setup fees"), while the opt-out is hidden in a faint "Skip this offer" at the top. One tap — or a child poking the screen — charges money with zero confirmation.

product.title: Preys on people with ADHD and those who are vulnerable
product.minus: The app is deliberately marketed at people with ADHD, depression and self-control struggles — exactly those most likely to forget to cancel. Users read it as cynical exploitation of the very audience it promised to help.

product.title: Cancellation is made deliberately hard
product.minus: You can't cancel inside the app — you're sent to a website that often doesn't work, made to take a quiz, or pushed through several "discount" offer screens. Cancellation only takes effect next billing cycle, and support replies with bots or not at all.

product.title: Cluttered interface drowning in upsell pop-ups
product.minus: Even paying users get a screen buried in "rate me", "invite a friend", "buy another app" pop-ups, coaching and banners. Getting to the actual habit tracker is a slog, and many avoid opening the app at all because of the visual noise.

product.title: Forced animations and cut-scenes on every check-off
