product.title: Missing text formatting and headings
product.minus: Formatting is thin and in places stripped back: title styling was removed, you can't bold or underline, and formatting is lost on copy-paste. Users ask for bold, italic, headings and font size — without them the app only suits short notes.

product.title: People want more colors and backgrounds for notes
product.minus: The palette is stuck at 12 colors and a handful of background patterns, in 2026 no less. People want more shades, custom colors and the option to set their own gallery image as a note background — often the only gripe from otherwise happy five-star users.

product.title: "Free and ad-free" is the number-one reason for the love
product.plus: Parents repeatedly single out that the app is completely free, ad-free, and has no mandatory subscription — for a kids' learning app this is felt as a rarity and a reason to trust it.

product.title: Kids reach for it on their own — learning feels like play
product.plus: Many parents say the child is "hooked", wakes up wanting to open it, and doesn't notice they're learning — the lessons are disguised as play so well that it holds even toddlers' attention.

product.title: Crashes, freezes, and won't launch on a range of devices
product.minus: Stability complaints pile up: the app crashes on launch, freezes "on almost every other song", and lags or hangs even on brand-new flagships like the Pixel 10.

product.title: English-only — a barrier for non-English families
product.minus: The most common structural complaint: the language can't be changed, everything is English-only. Parents from India, Bangladesh, Arabic-speaking and other regions ask for localization and note that without it the app feels "for the rich" and their kids can't follow the content.

product.title: Content is too easy and stops at preschool age
product.minus: For first-graders and kids aged 6+, the material quickly turns dull: lessons are "too easy", there's no way to manually set the difficulty edge, and parents ask to raise the ceiling (around 2nd grade) up toward K-12.

product.title: Tablet incompatibility — and tablets are exactly what's needed
product.minus: A paradox: the best experience is on a tablet, yet it's tablets where the app often refuses to install or launch (Lenovo Tab M11, Galaxy Tab S11, etc.) — even when the parent bought the tablet specifically for it.

product.title: Especially valued by parents of neurodivergent kids
product.plus: A distinct strong note: parents of autistic, non-verbal and neurodivergent children report real progress — a child starting to learn opposites, to read, to speak — and thank the app for it.

product.title: An indispensable free homeschooling tool
product.plus: Homeschooling families use the app as a full supplement across subjects and stress that it covers reading, math, logic and writing — and many voluntarily donate to the developers.

product.title: Login loop: email/Google sign-in dead-ends
product.minus: Sign-in is its own pain zone: the app endlessly demands you re-check your email, falsely reports "no internet" over working Wi-Fi, or gets stuck forever on the loading animation after login.

product.title: Too-continuous flow with no clear activity boundaries
product.minus: The continuous format makes parental control hard: it's unclear where one activity ends and the next begins, you can't pick a single specific exercise for the child, and the only way "back" is to exit the app.

product.title: Managing child profiles is clumsy and inflexible
product.minus: Child profiles can't be deleted or corrected, you can't create a new one with the same names, and the level is locked to age — parents would rather have a placement test so the child lands at their real level.

product.title: AI sits in FRONT of the log, not beside it — it became a gate, not an accelerator
product.minus: The «+» used to open a list and logging took seconds; now the same button routes into an AI chat where you describe food in words. The muscle-memory reflex «open — pick yesterday's — log» is replaced by a dialogue that types one letter at a time and gets things wrong. For logging meant to repeat 5x a day forever, the extra steps kill the habit itself — people quit not over AI quality but because the fast path vanished.

product.title: Number accuracy was the only asset — AI traded it for a «guess»
product.minus: A calorie tracker sells exactly one thing: you can trust the number. The same food gets different values run to run (carrot — protein from 4 to 12g, coffee — 7000 cal), and the user loses the reason to keep a diary at all: if numbers are invented, the diet is built on noise. This hits the product's core — not «inconvenient» but «pointless».

product.title: A hidden «multimodal tracking» toggle restores the old app — but they kept silent about it
product.plus: Buried in settings is a toggle that disables AI and restores the old search-with-database flow; those who find it instantly get the fast input and accuracy back. It's an escape hatch that retains a slice of would-be churn.

product.title: Silently removing the intermittent-fasting timer pulled out the single reason some people paid
product.minus: For a whole paying segment the IF timer was the core of usage — not calories, the fasting window. It vanished with no warning and no way to bring it back, and these people aren't «disappointed in a feature» — their reason to subscribe disappeared mid paid-term. Deleting an anchor feature from a paying segment turns manageable churn into resentment.

product.title: Killing meal-sharing evicted the couples who dieted together and doubled retention
product.minus: Logging meals jointly with a partner wasn't a nicety but a social lock-in: two accounts hold each other and neither leaves. Removing sharing turned the couples scenario into manual double-entry of the same food — and now both look for a new app at once. The stickiest cohort became the angriest.

product.title: A rich multilingual database and fast barcode scan — that's what actually held people for years
product.plus: The real retention engine isn't AI but the catalog: almost any brand is in the database, the barcode pulls a product instantly, and it works across many languages with no wall on the basic flow. This is exactly what brought people over from MyFitnessPal and kept them for 5-10 years.

product.title: Merging photo and barcode into one button broke autofocus — and killed the most frequent gesture
product.minus: Fusing photo recognition and the barcode scanner into one button sounds like simplification, but in practice the camera stopped focusing on barcodes: people describe a workaround of «add new food → scan → confirm item exists». The single most frequent daily gesture — barcode scan — became a quest because it got subordinated to the AI flow.

product.title: No «same as yesterday» forces every repeated meal through a fresh entry — against the nature of tracking
product.minus: People eat the same things day to day — the base pattern that makes logging effortless. The AI version won't let you favorite a meal, doesn't remember ingredients individually, and suggests not «lunch for lunch» but «yesterday's dinner». Every repeat is forced through a fresh AI query — the product fights the very repetition that makes tracking sustainable.

product.title: The clean, beautiful diary is the reason people forgive the rest
product.plus: Even scathing reviews almost always note the interface is pleasant, the main-screen navigation tidy, the colors and visuals enjoyable. That aesthetic is an emotional anchor: it pulled people to premium and makes them give the app «one more chance» instead of deleting instantly.

product.title: An auto-assigned 870-1198 kcal goal undermines trust with the very people it's meant to help
product.minus: The app auto-sets dangerously low daily goals, and a newcomer can't change them. For someone who doesn't know nutrition, this isn't just a limit — it's a risk: a health product nudges toward an unhealthy deficit. The disordered-eating segment is hit by this mechanism directly — trust in a «healthy» app turns into a hazard.

product.title: The keto/diabetic scenario hinges on net carbs — and that's exactly where AI misses most dangerously
product.minus: The keto/diabetic segment came for one thing: accurate net-carb accounting and sugar tracking. Here the AI errs critically (chia as 10 net carbs instead of zero), and you can neither exclude fructose recipes nor reliably fix macros. For a user whose blood sugar spikes, a wrong number isn't an inconvenience but a medical risk — and the product loses its most motivated segment.

product.title: Logging depends on the server — every entry waits on the network, and the offline habit falls apart
product.minus: AI recognition routes every entry to the server, so the simplest food log hits 10-30 second delays and timeouts, and on mobile data it doesn't work at all. A food tracker by definition is needed at the moment of eating — in a cafe, on the road, off Wi-Fi; by tying the basic log to an online call, the product broke the scenario exactly where it matters.

product.title: «AI» in the name became a distrust signal for an audience that came for honest accounting
product.minus: A food tracker's audience is people who want verifiable numbers and control over their data, not a «guessing game». For them «AI» in the name and the forced upload of their diet to the cloud read as a negative, not a feature: they explicitly refuse to give AI access to their data and leave to find an AI-free alternative. A brand built on trust in the number slapped on a label that repels its own core.

product.title: Multi-year discipline (day 105, 700 days) is the real product; the streak IS the retention
product.plus: The strongest value signal is people who log hundreds of days straight and drop 21-150 pounds, crediting the result to daily logging in Lifesum specifically. These streaks aren't a metric, they're the product: as long as the app made repeat logging frictionless, it was effectively selling discipline. Any change that lengthens the daily gesture hits this asset directly.

product.title: Minimalism isn't styling here — it IS the product promise
product.plus: People come back precisely because the app doesn't try to keep them inside: tick the habit and leave. This 'anti-engagement' becomes the core differentiator — the user focuses on the goal, not the UI. For an audience burned out on bloated trackers, it's the deciding factor.

product.title: No ads and no paywalls turn trust into loyalty
product.plus: In a category where widgets and basic features hide behind subscriptions, making everything free reads as an ethical stance, not marketing. Users explicitly contrast it with 'money suckers' and stay for years. That builds a moat a freemium rival can't leap by simply cloning features.

product.title: No cloud sync pushes away the most engaged users
product.minus: The most loyal users — those with several devices and years of history — hit manual backup export/import as the only way to move data. The longer someone uses the app, the more this wall hurts: they're invested but can't work across a second phone or tablet. It systematically loses exactly the audience that would otherwise stay forever.

product.title: A long habit list breaks the product — no groups, no search
product.minus: The app shines for 5–10 habits, but a 'successful' user who adds dozens falls into endless scrolling through a flat, category-less, search-less list. The paradox: the more actively someone builds habits, the less usable the tool becomes. Collapsible categories are the single most-requested feature, and the gap hits the engaged core hardest.

product.title: Measurable habits are an afterthought — manual entry kills the routine
product.minus: Users who came to count water, runs, or pills expect a quick increment but get a popup keyboard for manual number entry. That turns a 10-second gesture into annoying labor and erodes the very habit of logging. +/− buttons with a custom step are the obvious fix that's missing, and it makes measurable use-cases lose to rivals.

product.title: Flexible 'X times per Y days' frequency is a killer feature rivals lack
product.plus: Letting users set a habit as '3 times a week' rather than 'every day' matches how people actually live, and it's exactly why users abandon other trackers. It turns the app from a checklist into a tool for realistic, irregular goals. For people frustrated by binary 'done/failed', this frequency model is the reason to stay.

product.title: Widgets are the core return mechanism — they work without opening the app
product.plus: Home-screen tile widgets let users tick a habit with a single tap without launching the app — perfectly aligned with the minimal-friction philosophy. The widget, not the app screen, becomes the daily touchpoint that sustains the routine. Users explicitly credit it for making logging 'fuss-free'.

product.title: The streak is buried inside the card — the main motivator is hidden
product.minus: The streak is the whole reason people track habits, yet seeing it requires opening the habit and scrolling down. It's absent from the home screen and widgets, so the daily 'dopamine' signal is lost. Surface the streak count on the home screen and daily motivation would rise with no new feature at all; as is, the product hides its own hook.

product.title: Deliberate absence of gamification keeps adults but loses reward-seekers
product.minus: The app deliberately offers no animations, rewards, or sounds — for some that's a plus (they even ask to make confetti toggleable), for others it's why the habit doesn't 'stick'. A segment explicitly asks for stars, applause, a Duolingo-style streak widget. It's a strategic fork: the product picked the mature audience and knowingly forgoes those held only by external reward.

product.title: Unreliable reminders undermine the very point of a habit tracker
product.minus: For a habit tracker, the reminder isn't an add-on but the retention core, and when it silently stops firing (even with battery optimization off) the user loses the exact signal they came for. A separate pain is inflexible logic: with an 'every N days' goal, reminders don't follow the floating day. A broken reminder doesn't annoy — it quietly severs the habit, and the user leaves.

product.title: Android-only lock-in cuts off entire user scenarios by itself
product.minus: The lack of iOS and web versions doesn't just cap reach — it makes a habit ecosystem impossible: a mixed-device household, a work computer, switching to an iPhone, and the accumulated history is cut off. For some users it reads as 'outdated', even when the app is functionally stronger than rivals. Platform lock-in works against the very idea of long-term tracking.

product.title: Charts and analytics promise insight but don't earn trust in the data
product.minus: Users who want to track weight or metrics and see a trend hit charts that, by their account, don't reflect their actual data and won't let them plot real captured values. When the visualization stops being trustworthy, analytics flips from a strength into a reason to switch. For the data-oriented segment, a broken chart nullifies the point of tracking numeric habits here at all.

product.title: A narrow 5-day view window breaks the sense of weekly rhythm
product.minus: The home screen shows only the last 5 days, and users who think in weeks can't see the full picture without exporting or scrolling. Habits live on a weekly cycle, but the interface clips that cycle — a tiny default decision that breaks the natural mental model. For some, this alone is the reason to 'try something else', even though the tracking itself satisfies them.

product.title: A single closed-off developer turns 'maturity' into stagnation
product.minus: Some long-time users read the unresponsiveness to requests and rare updates as a signal the product has frozen: three- and four-year-old requests go unimplemented, and people start eyeing rivals after years of loyalty. For an open-source tracker that lives on trust and longevity, the feeling that 'development has stalled' is more dangerous than any single missing feature — it undercuts the 'I'll stay forever' bet.

product.title: Supporting medical and work routines makes the app indispensable, not just 'nice'
product.plus: When people use it to track pill schedules, day-specific work tasks, and health metrics, the app stops being a self-improvement toy and becomes a critical tool they don't abandon for years. This 'high-stakes' use-case is the strongest retention driver: here reliability and simplicity matter more than any decoration. These are the users who stay 6–7 years and bring others in.

product.title: Logging speed is the real reason people return, not features
product.plus: The core hook isn't charts or a plan — it's how fast food gets into the log: barcode scan, photo, and voice strip friction out of a daily ritual, and it's that speed that pulls people off MyFitnessPal and brings them back for years. The habit lives on the seconds saved per meal.

product.title: The streak and the act of logging change behaviour on their own — even without precision
product.plus: The strongest mechanism isn't the math — it's the daily act of honest logging: people lose tens of pounds simply because they finally see how much they actually eat. Multi-year streaks (300+, 600+ days) turn tracking into identity, and the ritual works even when the numbers are only approximate.

product.title: A no-pressure tone breaks perfectionist paralysis — a rare design choice
product.plus: Tips like "don't worry if your tracking isn't exact, just do it as well as you can" disarm exactly the users whom a demand for perfect measurement usually kills. For someone with food anxiety this isn't cosmetic — it's what lets them start at all and not quit, a behavioural move most trackers never make.

product.title: Broken fitness-tracker sync nullifies the whole point of premium
product.minus: People pay for premium for exactly one thing — to merge calories-in and calories-out in one place. When Fitbit, Google Health, or Samsung Health pull steps but not burned calories (or report double), the entire reason to subscribe evaporates: the user is back to juggling two apps and computing their deficit by hand. It's the failure of the core job they bought it for.

product.title: A duplicate-ridden crowdsourced database quietly destroys the accuracy the whole app is for
product.minus: The database is huge but clogged with duplicates carrying different calorie values and no way to flag the correct one — users log a wrong number for years and think they're in control. There's no thumbs-up and no way to report bad entries, so the junk never gets cleaned. For a tracker whose one job is accuracy, this rots trust from the inside.

product.title: No gram-level logging pushes out the most disciplined users
product.minus: Users with a kitchen scale — the most motivated, most retainable cohort — hit a wall where many foods only offer "cups" and "servings," never grams. For someone weighing food for precision this makes the app nearly unusable: the design is tuned for the casual logger and loses exactly the accuracy-obsessed core willing to pay for it.

product.title: The default starting calorie target is so high it breaks trust on the first screen
product.minus: The app hands out a starting goal like 2400 kcal "per FDA recommendation" before it knows the person's actual day — and the user feels nudged to overeat. Trust in a weight-loss tracker hinges on the plausibility of that first number; an inflated default reads as incompetence at the exact moment the stay-or-go decision is made.

product.title: A buried "done logging" button breaks the ritual for the most loyal users
product.minus: The daily "close the day" tap is where the streak and the sense of control are forged. Moving that button and killing Quick Add as "underused" hit the heaviest users — they close the day multiple times daily. When a product breaks the micro-ritual the habit rests on, even multi-year users start shopping for a replacement.

product.title: An endless onboarding quiz kills intent before the first log
product.minus: People arrive with one intent — log food — and are met with 30-40 screens of questions about their family and world cuisines, with no skip button. Intent is finite: users uninstall at question #18, #30, never reaching the interface. The long quiz exists to personalize, but it torches activation for exactly the people who wanted simplicity.

product.title: Constant UI reshuffling punishes veterans' muscle memory
product.minus: A familiar tracker's power is that your hands already know where to tap. Monthly button moves, colour swaps, and toggling macros through settings erase that muscle memory and turn a habitual action into mental effort. For a product that retains people for 5-10 years, frequent cosmetic rebuilds sabotage its own greatest asset.

product.title: Forcing users to confirm pre-planned meals punishes the planners
product.minus: People who plan a week ahead are among the most engaged users, yet the app greys out future items and forces a manual tap to confirm each one after eating. For a planner that's hundreds of extra taps a year across a fussy hit-zone. A design that should reward discipline instead penalizes it — directly alienating the power-user core.

product.title: Switching phones wipes progress — and trust in the longest habit
product.minus: The entire point of multi-year tracking is the accumulated history, and for this cohort the data is emotional capital. When a phone reset or reinstall loses days and years of logs (and the web version doesn't save you), the one irreplaceable thing breaks. Data fragility hurts the most loyal harder than any barrier — they leave for good.

product.title: Cross-metric tracking (weight, measurements, body fat) turns the tracker into a long-haul retention system
product.plus: Keeping calories, weight, measurements, body-fat %, and macros in one place is what moves a user from "losing weight" to "watching my health for life." After the goal, what remains isn't calorie counting but a body-metrics dashboard — and that's what retains people for years and feeds lifetime purchases. A rival can't just clone the food log; they'd need the whole metric history.

product.title: The social layer adds accountability but rots without moderation
product.plus: Support groups and recipes shared with a partner add accountability a solo tracker lacks — for some users that's the very reason they pick it. But without moderation or blocking the layer rots: some treat it as a dating app, and removing "challenges" killed the one thing that made it the best. The social mechanic is both a hook and an unmanaged liability.

product.title: Free, no ads, no subscription — the parents' headline reason
product.plus: The same point comes up again and again: the app is fully free, with no ads, no upsells and no paid subscription. For budget-conscious parents and volunteer teachers, that is precisely why they install it and trust it.

product.title: Kids genuinely start doing arithmetic — adding, subtracting, multiplying
product.plus: Parents describe concrete progress: a five-year-old learned to add and subtract within a couple of weeks, a child can now «add up to 20», a sibling learned to divide. These aren't vague compliments but an observed jump in skill.

product.title: Hints can't be turned off: a hand just points to the answer
product.minus: The core systemic bug: a parent unchecks «hints» in settings, yet after 5 seconds a hand appears anyway, pointing straight at the correct answer. The child never gets to think and just taps where it points — defeating the whole purpose of a learning app.

product.title: The Lucas character carries engagement — kids learn without noticing
product.plus: The bond with the character Lucas and friends turns the lesson into play: kids «don't even notice they're learning» and won't put the tablet down. Teachers and volunteers note it's the characters that hold a class's attention.

product.title: There's a mindless mini-game where the child hides from the math
product.minus: The app exposes a pointless point-and-click game, and the child slips into it without solving any problems at all. Parental controls don't block it — for a learning product that's a hole in the core mechanic.

product.title: A safe alternative to «violent» games — parents feel calmer
product.plus: Parents explicitly contrast the app with shooters and violent mobile games: the child is busy with age-appropriate educational content that builds thinking and focus. It's a strong emotional reason to stay.

product.title: It's hard to quit — even parents are baffled by the close button
product.minus: Quitting the game is hard even for an adult: a non-obvious close button turns «time to hand back the phone» into a fight, especially when the child won't let go of the tablet.

product.title: Crashes on the splash screen and freezes on the stickers — you just close it
product.minus: Some users can't get past the door: the app sticks on the title screen and never opens, or freezes at the stickers stage with closing it the only way out. There are also glitches that scare the child.

product.title: A lifesaver for homeschooling and the classroom when the parent is busy
product.plus: It fills a real need: it helps parents who don't have time to teach the child themselves, and first-time homeschooling teachers. Whole families use it (4 kids) and it's used in classrooms.

product.title: Safety alarm: the child reportedly reaches «adult» content
product.minus: Several parents are seriously alarmed: by their account, the child gets from the app to «adult» YouTube or an «adult only» tab via a basic number test. Even if it's an edge path, for an app «for the littlest ones» that perception is a reputational risk.

product.title: Too easy and «babyish» — older kids get bored
product.minus: The content is pitched at first-grade level, and for older kids (12+) the tasks feel primitive and dull: «a baby game because the maths is so easy». What's a plus for a preschooler is a reason for an older child to quit.

product.title: It used to work offline, but after an update it needs Wi-Fi
product.minus: Part of the app's value was working without a connection — key for kids on the go and families with poor internet. After an update users complain it now needs Wi-Fi, and ask whether it can be played offline at all.

product.title: One-tap entry is the engine of the daily habit
product.plus: Monefy's core value is the speed of logging a spend: open, tap a category, type the amount on the built-in calculator. That instantaneity is what turns expense tracking into a daily ritual people keep for years instead of abandoning in a week. This IS the product; everything else is secondary.

product.title: The pie chart isn't a report — it's the emotional hook
product.plus: Users describe a feeling, not numbers: "see at a glance where money goes," "makes money fun." The home screen's category pie gives instant feedback with zero report-building — and that's what actually changes behavior and makes people cut wasteful categories.

product.title: It's a spend tracker masquerading as a budgeter — and it loses the planners
product.minus: Budget mode is built so that changing the budget figure rewrites it across all past months, and the surplus or deficit never carries forward to the next month. For anyone who wants to plan rather than just record the past, budget mode becomes unusable. The app brilliantly answers "how much did I spend" but not "how much can I spend."

product.title: A rigid category model: one global set across every account
product.minus: Categories are shared across all accounts: delete an "unneeded" one in a single account and it vanishes everywhere, notes included. No sub-categories, no separate sets for "cash" vs "savings." Users who build multiple accounts for different goals hit a flat structure and lose data trying to organize it.

product.title: Transfers between your own accounts log as expenses — breaking the balance picture
product.minus: When someone moves money from their own account to another of their own, Monefy records it as an expense. For a user with several accounts (cash, bank, savings) this distorts both total spend and each account's balance — the app doesn't grasp that the money never left the owner. The base "every movement is income or expense" model never accounted for internal transfers.

product.title: Horizontal month-swipe fights the vertical list scroll
product.minus: The core month-switching gesture — a side swipe — fires when a user merely tries to scroll the expense list vertically. The screen keeps jumping to the previous month, with no way to turn it off. A gesture designed for speed becomes a constant irritant on long lists.

product.title: No reports or exports — a glass ceiling for the power user
product.minus: There's no report generation, no printing, no per-category breakdown over a period. A user who matures into tracking and wants to analyze "how much went to transport over six months" or share a summary finds nothing there. Monefy onboards perfectly but doesn't grow with the user — the ceiling arrives exactly once the habit is locked in.

product.title: Manual entry is the convenience ceiling — no SMS or voice capture
product.minus: However fast manual entry is, it's still manual — every spend must be keyed in by hand. The most engaged users ask for auto-capture of amounts from bank SMS or voice commands, and it's precisely this missing automation that caps how deeply someone keeps tracking. The "remember and log" friction quietly attrits part of the audience.

product.title: Per-transaction notes choke the app as history grows
product.minus: Users who diligently add a note to every transaction eventually hit freezes: when entering a note the app pulls similar past entries and stalls, offering to close or wait. The most disciplined audience — those who fill in everything — is punished with slowdowns precisely for heavy use.

product.title: Daily granularity, not timestamped — loses the minute-by-minute logger
product.minus: Monefy is built around daily and monthly totals: a spend is tied to a day, not a moment. For a user who wants to see spends in time order or sort the feed by entry time, that data model simply doesn't exist. It's a deliberate focus on "how much per day" that cuts off the segment keeping a chronological ledger.

product.title: No guard against accidental wipe — one touch erases months of tracking
product.minus: Several users describe the same scenario: an accidental touch erased all their entered data with no confirmation and no auto-save. For an app whose value compounds over months of daily entry, the absence of an "are you sure?" dialog and a local backup destroys the very asset the person keeps the app for.

product.title: A thin icon set bumps into the urge to make the app one's own
product.minus: The cute category illustrations are part of Monefy's charm, but there are too few, and users keep asking for more icons, custom images, or at least renaming. The urge to "make it mine" is strong precisely because the app is opened daily; the limited icon palette undercuts the sense of ownership the habit feeds on.

product.title: The spartan design reads as clean to some, dated to others
product.minus: Monefy's minimalism cuts both ways. Part of the audience praises the clean, pleasant interface, but another part calls it "90s window software" and notices the app hasn't changed in years. The same stability that makes the habit dependable looks like stagnation to newcomers — a perception risk against fresher competitors.

product.title: Multi-year retention — the product embeds into life for years
product.plus: A striking number of reviews measure usage in years, even a decade: "since 2016," "almost a decade," "5 years and never looked back." That's an unusually strong PMF signal for an expense tracker — people don't just download it, they fold it into their financial routine for the long haul. The habit built on entry-simplicity turns out to be remarkably sticky.

product.title: An ad-free experience — a rare value in a free finance app
product.plus: Users specifically call out the lack of intrusive ads even in the free version — against rivals where ads won't even let you see how to use the thing. In a category where the app is opened several times a day, an ad-free flow isn't a detail — it's a reason people stay and recommend.

product.title: License tied to device and account makes switching phones a failure point
product.minus: The mechanism meant to protect the product — binding access and backup to a device or Google/Drive account — turns against the long-tenured user at phone-switch time: years of accumulated data suddenly become inaccessible on the new device. It's a structural transfer flaw: the highest-value moment in the lifecycle (migrating to a new phone) is exactly when the product most often fails its most loyal users.

product.title: Frictionless manual entry IS the product — it's what earns forgiveness for everything else
product.plus: The habit core is logging a spend the instant it happens: people who never tracked money before get hooked precisely because entering an expense is easier than skipping it. That converts one-time skeptics into daily users who stay 5-10 years.

product.title: Multi-wallet plus inter-wallet transfers is what retains people who run several accounts
product.plus: Being able to keep separate wallets (cash, card, credit) and move money between them makes the app the single hub for people with complex finances — and this is the exact feature users name as the reason they stay instead of switching to simpler rivals.

product.title: Broken sync hits the exact center of trust — and drives even paying users to competitors
product.minus: Cross-device sync was sold as the main reason to pay, so when a new device hangs forever on "syncing your data", what breaks isn't a feature but the contract itself. A user who has already moved their entire financial history in finds themselves locked out of their own data and leaves — often mid-review.

product.title: When the balance stops adding up, the product loses the one thing it exists for
product.minus: A finance tracker sells exactly one thing — a number you can trust. So a balance that silently changes or doubles isn't merely a bug but the collapse of the whole reason to use it: people who trusted the totals for years start re-checking them on a calculator and, once they find a mismatch, never trust them again. That's deadlier than any crash.

product.title: Duplicate entries on save sabotage the very mechanic of manual logging
product.minus: The habit rests on trusting the Save button: one tap, one record. When the button "doesn't work" and a restart spawns a dozen identical transactions, the user loses control of their own data and has to clean up the mess by hand. It destroys the very ease-of-entry the whole product is built on.

product.title: Global categories across all wallets — a simplification that actually took away control
product.minus: Making a new category global to every wallet by default inverted the expectation: people created a category for one specific account and it spread everywhere, breaking their nesting. Control over the structure of one's own ledger — the thing that makes a tracker feel like yours — was taken away, and power users read it as a loss of control, not a convenience.

product.title: Smart amount-based category suggestions made entry near-automatic — losing them feels like a regression
product.minus: The app used to predict the category from the amount entered and recent spends, turning logging into a single tap — that was the secret of the "ease". The new update either removed the hint or made it inaccurate (referring to the oldest, not the latest transaction), and every entry now requires a search again. The main lever of habit retention is gone.

product.title: Shared wallets for couples are a strong acquisition hook — but sync inside them breaks and corrupts the main account
product.minus: Running a household budget with a partner is a frequent reason to pick this app specifically. But when the shared wallet won't sync, drops transactions and — worse — dumps them into the owner's main wallet, the one reason people came becomes a source of corrupted data. A couple loses trust two users at a time, not one.

product.title: The web version going read-only kills the desktop-entry use case people paid for
product.minus: A segment bought premium specifically for convenient entry and editing from a computer via the web. Pushing the web to read-only left them with view-only — the lever that turned a phone tracker into full household accounting is gone. For heavy loggers, mobile-only entry without desktop reduces the product to a viewer, not a tool.

product.title: Budgets are locked to one wallet and one category — and don't match how people actually plan
product.minus: People think of a budget as a "cap on a group of spends" (food + cafe + delivery), but the app only lets you budget either one category or all of them with no exclusions. Being unable to assemble an arbitrary set of categories makes users abandon the very feature they came to plan with — and it's a request repeated for years.

product.title: Future and recurring transactions don't feed the projected balance — breaking planning around payday
product.minus: The key use case "how much will I have left after all my bills" only works if future and recurring payments correctly subtract from the forecast. The app doesn't do this right for non-standard pay periods, so a user who isn't paid "on the 1st" can't trust the projection and loses the main reason to plan ahead.

product.title: The missing savings tracker pushes users into a parallel app
product.minus: Expense tracking is only half of financial life; the other half is savings and goals. Without a proper savings tab, loyal users keep a second app alongside just for savings, which lowers their dependence on Money Lover and makes leaving at any point less painful. An unclosed use case is an open door to a rival.

product.title: Responsive support is an underrated asset that single-handedly rescues retention
product.plus: When bugs wipe data or reset premium, it's the live support fixing the issue in a couple of days that flips an angry review into gratitude. Many users say outright they stayed only because the team resolved their case — support acts as a safety net for a mature but fragile product.

product.title: The redesign traded minimalism for "mess" — alienating the very users who valued simplicity
product.minus: These users came for a minimalist, easy-on-the-eyes interface — that was their reason to pick the product. The new design reads as "confusing" and "messy", and basic actions (viewing transactions by date) now take extra taps. When an update changes the thing people stayed for, the loyal core considers leaving for the first time.

product.title: Forcing an account at the door turns away the privacy segment before the first transaction
product.minus: A budgeting app handles the most sensitive data, so demanding an account and personal info right at the entrance — before the product has proven anything — is an instant no for the privacy-minded segment. These users uninstall before the first entry: the barrier stands up before any value appears.

product.title: Locking past history behind the paywall turns "your own notebook" into a hostage — activation breaks before value lands
product.minus: A strategically fatal choice: what got hidden behind premium isn't an advanced feature but access to one's own past spending history — the thing a user sees as "my notebook on my phone". The paywall lands on data the person entered themselves, so it hits the sense of ownership before the product can prove the value of advanced features. It converts loyalty into a feeling of betrayal and triggers churn among exactly the most engaged users, the ones with the most history.

product.title: Manual entry isn't a flaw — it's the habit-building mechanism
product.plus: The most loyal users value precisely the fact that they must type expenses by hand: the act of logging forces awareness of every purchase, and within 20 days people see for the first time that they spend recklessly. Forcing entry turns the app from a spreadsheet into a behavioral-discipline tool.

product.title: No SMS reading is the single biggest reason users defect
product.minus: An entire segment is ready to switch to any app that parses bank SMS itself: the manual entry that retains loyalists repels those who value speed over ritual. Competitors with SMS auto-capture are named outright as the reason to switch — this is the product's sharpest hole.

product.title: Manual-only Google Drive backup makes users lose years of data on phone change
product.minus: Backup must be enabled by hand, and nobody learns this until they switch phones and find years of transactions gone. An app whose value is accumulated history jeopardizes that history through a 'backup off by default' design decision. The loyal user is punished precisely for loyalty.

product.title: No cross-device sync breaks the family and multi-platform use case
product.minus: Data is locked to one device: a couple with an iPhone and an Android can't share a budget, and a phone-plus-tablet owner can't see the same expenses. For a household-finance app, the inability to co-track cuts out an entire segment of families and two-OS users.

product.title: Double-entry makes spending transparent for those who know debit-credit
product.plus: Accounting-style accounts and transfers between them give 'proper' bookkeeping to the financially literate: for them it's not a toy but a real ledger. The same mechanism filters out novices but firmly binds those who understand debit and credit — a narrow but devoted core.

product.title: Inability to change main currency traps expats and travelers
product.minus: You can't change the main currency without breaking all old balances — moving to another country turns accumulated history into a mess of wrong exchange rates. For an app praised for multi-currency support, it's a paradox: it tracks several currencies but won't let you switch the primary one, losing the very mobile, international segment.

product.title: Stats won't filter by category, account or subcategory — analytics stalls halfway
product.minus: Data goes in cleanly but you can't pull the slice you need: there's no stats filter by category, account or subcategory, and no subcategory totals. The advanced user — the one who logs the most data — hits a ceiling: the app collects but won't let you truly analyze.

product.title: Moving money to savings and investments counts as spent — the app hides net-worth growth
product.minus: Money moved into savings or investments is flagged as 'gone,' so the app hides real net-worth growth. Strong at controlling daily spending, it's blind to long-term wealth: there's no unified view of cash, savings and investments. For those who outgrow expense tracking, it's the ceiling.

product.title: Ads between every entry destroy the core use case — fast logging on the go
product.minus: The app sells speed of entry but inserts an ad at the exact moment you add an expense — breaking the very fast-logging ritual the habit depends on. The ads hit not patience but the core value: 'quick and efficient' becomes impossible, and in real life the tool stops working.

product.title: Editing an amount wipes the whole number instead of one digit — micro-friction at every step
product.minus: When editing an amount you can't delete a single digit — the whole number is wiped and you retype it. In an app whose entire point is fast manual entry, this small thing repeats dozens of times a day and erodes the core promise. The frustration accrues to the most active users, who type the most.

product.title: Deep category and subcategory customization is the retention engine for power users
product.plus: The freedom to create your own categories, subcategories and accounts gives a sense that 'the app bends to my life,' not the reverse. That flexibility is what turns casual users into people who've tuned the system to themselves and won't leave — customization is the moat.

product.title: No future cash-flow forecast — users fall back to spreadsheets
product.minus: Recurring income and expenses don't roll up into a forecast of future months — the single most powerful budgeting tool is missing. People keep a separate spreadsheet just for this and can't abandon it. The app records the past brilliantly but is blind to the future, losing the planners.

product.title: Being free without forcing a subscription builds trust and brand advocates
product.plus: That the full feature set is available free and without subscription pressure is something users flag as rare and a reason to recommend the app. The absence of coercion turns the budget-conscious segment into advocates: they buy premium voluntarily, out of gratitude and long-term attachment, not because of a paywall.

product.title: A low entry barrier rewires beginners' financial behavior — from chaos to awareness
product.plus: Entry friction is so low that people stick with tracking as a habit for the first time in their lives and say outright the app 'changed' their life and financial decisions. Even users with ADHD note the interface doesn't distract — the product wins where complex rivals scare people off, turning tracking into a durable habit.

product.title: Clean, minimalist interface is the reason for decade-long loyalty
product.plus: The core asset is the absence of noise: the app does exactly what it promises without bloat, which is why people stay for 7-10 years. In a category where rivals compete on features, the 'nothing extra' discipline wins — and it is itself the switching barrier.

product.title: The home-screen widget flickers and reloads endlessly
product.minus: The widget — the main reason people install the app — has been continuously flickering, stuck on "loading" or "all done," and ignoring taps for months for huge numbers of users. The only fix is deleting and re-adding the widget or restarting the phone, and even then only for a few hours. Reinstalling, clearing cache, switching launchers — nothing fixes it for long.

product.title: In long notes the keyboard covers the text and you can't scroll to it
product.minus: Once a task note grows past a certain length you can neither see nor edit the bottom: the on-screen keyboard covers the text and scrolling down stops working. Reviewers say the bug is literally years old (one counts from 2016), returned after an update, and turns note-editing into a guessing game.

product.title: Every launch it nags you to turn on notifications and won't take no for an answer
product.minus: Anyone who deliberately turned reminders off gets a "Reminder settings turned off" pop-up or an enable-notifications prompt on every single launch. There's no "never" option, so you dismiss the same dialog over and over — reviewers furiously write "No means No, Microsoft."

product.title: Simple, clean, ad-free — and that's exactly why people love it
product.plus: The core value is zero clutter and zero ads: nested lists, steps within tasks, "My Day," and sharing lists with family. People keep everything here for years — from grocery lists to career goals — and call it the best to-do app they've tried.

product.title: Free sync across phone, PC and Mac is the main hook
product.plus: Tasks appear instantly on every device, fit neatly into the Microsoft 365 and Windows ecosystem — and it's all free. For many that's the deciding factor: jot it on the laptop at work, see it on your phone.

product.title: Forces you to re-login every few days, even corporate users
product.minus: The app demands a login almost daily, while other Microsoft apps (Outlook) keep the session for 5 days under the same policy. For To Do this has gone unfixed for years, annoying people enough to leave for Google.

product.title: A painful Microsoft-account sign-in — too many hoops for a simple list
product.minus: Just to start a to-do list you're forced through multi-step verification — password, last digits of phone, a puzzle captcha, a code, a backup email, then verifying that. People give up at step 6 or 7. And tying it to a work/school account means losing your data when you leave the company.

product.title: The Wunderlist shadow: Microsoft is seen as having ruined what worked perfectly
product.minus: Long-time users remember Wunderlist and say in unison that after the Microsoft acquisition the app became less intuitive, buggier, and lost its charm. "If it ain't broke don't fix it" is a recurring refrain; for them it's a symbol of a good product being enshittified.

product.title: No way to bulk-delete completed tasks
product.minus: Completed tasks pile up forever and you have to clear them one by one — there's no "delete all completed" or "uncheck all." For recurring lists (groceries, packing, checklists) it's tedious; people openly envy Google Tasks' "Delete completed" button.

product.title: Recurring tasks and reminders get garbled — DST, time zones, snooze
product.minus: The reminder logic is unreliable: at DST changes the recurrence shifts by a day or hour, while travelling reminders stay in the old time zone, and dismissing one notification of a recurring task kills the next. Snooze glitches too. For an app whose whole point is reminders, that's critical.

product.title: Bottom-edge buttons land under the system nav and become useless
product.minus: The "More"/save/delete-list buttons sit right at the bottom edge and get covered by the gesture bar or the phone's Google button — you can't reach them. Worse, the delete-list button in the corner is easily brushed by your palm.

product.title: Won't merge tasks from multiple Microsoft accounts or show them in the calendar
product.minus: Anyone with work and personal life in separate MS accounts is forced to keep switching — the app won't show everything together. On top of that, tasks don't surface in the calendar and there's no Outlook integration on Android, pushing people toward the Google or Apple ecosystem.

product.title: Far too easy to accidentally complete a task — and it vanishes with no history
product.minus: A swipe or a stray tap on the widget instantly marks a task done and it disappears — you can't disable the swipe, there's no history and no trash for accidental deletions. It hits hardest for people whose hands shake or who tap with a thumb.

product.title: The food database carries the whole product — even furious users stay for it
product.plus: The one real moat is the huge, user-built food database. People who hate everything else say outright they stay only for it: type grams off a kitchen scale and get accurate macros in a second. That turns a one-off tracker into a daily ritual nobody wants to abandon.

product.title: The 2026 redesign killed the at-a-glance day — and that drove out decade-long veterans
product.minus: The whole food diary used to read on one screen; now each meal is hidden behind its own tap and you can't see the day as a whole. For a calorie diary that's fatal — the product exists for the quick 'how much is left' glance, and the redesign buried it under taps and scrolls. Users with 10-15 year histories leave over exactly this, not over price.

product.title: Swiping between days was muscle memory — removing it breaks the daily flow
product.minus: Swiping left-right between days was wired into the habit: open, swipe to yesterday, check. The redesign replaced it with a date picker at the top, so people get stuck on the wrong day, log food into it, then delete. A tiny gesture, but it was the heart of the daily ritual — without it every session became friction.

product.title: Removing batch actions turned fixing a mistake into a punishment
product.minus: You used to delete a whole meal or copy an entire day in one action. Now it's one item at a time. This compounds a second flaw: the UI makes it easy to accidentally copy yesterday's food onto today, and you can only clean it up line by line. The product creates the mistake and then removes the fast way to undo it.

product.title: Accumulated history is the strongest lock-in: quitting means throwing away years of data
product.plus: Saved recipes, custom foods and a years-long log become a personal asset you can't carry to a rival. That keeps people through redesign rage — leaving means losing 'years of recipes.' But the lock is brittle: when an update wipes workouts or history, the exact thing holding people vanishes, and the exit is instant and bitter.

product.title: Switching from 'calories remaining' to a count-up broke the point of the diary
product.minus: The core value of a calorie diary is the instant answer to 'how many calories can I still eat.' The update swapped the counting-down remainder for a counting-up total, so users lose the main cue for 'eat or not.' This isn't cosmetic, it's a mental-model swap: the product stopped answering the single question people open it for before every meal.

product.title: Habit and accountability are the real product, not the number-crunching
product.plus: The strongest emotional hook isn't accuracy, it's the feeling of being accountable to yourself. People recount multi-year stories of losing 20, 80, 150+ lbs and say it 'holds me accountable' and won't let them gaslight themselves. Logging becomes a near-automatic ritual. That explains the abnormal loyalty: the product sells discipline, and the numbers are just its instrument.

product.title: Streak notifications flipped from support to 'cringe' — and push people toward the door
product.minus: Streak gamification is meant to pull people back into the habit, but the new 'quirky' notification tone ('not logging? you'll make us sad') reads as manipulative and infantilizing. For an audience that already logs automatically the streak is useless, and you can't turn it off. A retention mechanism became an irritant people explicitly cite as making them want to uninstall.

product.title: Step and workout integrations are a promise that barely works
product.minus: Pairing with Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung and Health Connect is sold as the edge — burned calories sync automatically. In practice steps are off by multiples, workouts either never arrive or duplicate five times and wreck the calorie remainder, and you can't enter steps manually. Half the 'eaten minus burned' equation is unreliable, so the product falls short of the one-stop health hub it pitches.

product.title: The open database is double-edged: depth versus the noise of duplicates
product.minus: The very thing that makes the database huge — open user entry — also clogs it. A single food surfaces a dozen entries with different calories and you have to guess which is right; even 'verified' ones can be wrong. Logging quality hinges on whether the user picked the correct row, which quietly erodes trust in the number the whole thing exists to provide.

product.title: Rigid dashboard presets won't let you see the nutrients you actually track
product.minus: The diary only shows fixed nutrient sets, and you can't see, say, protein and fiber at once — you must pick one. For users with a specific goal (diabetes, keto, fiber) this defeats the point: they pay yet can't assemble on one screen the exact metrics they came for. Customization — the thing that would turn a tracker into a personal tool — is locked away.

product.title: AI photo logging can't tell portions apart — so it saves no manual entry at all
product.minus: Photo food recognition is the flagship new feature, but it can't tell a 60-calorie small yogurt from a 250-calorie full cup. And since you end up typing the quantity by hand anyway, it removes none of the logging friction it was pitched to kill. It becomes a demo feature: impressive at install, useless in the real daily loop, and people fall back to manual entry.

product.title: US-only units and week-start quietly alienate everyone outside America
product.minus: Recipes in 'cups,' a week that starts on Sunday, salt only as 'sodium' — small things that, for a non-American, turn every entry into a conversion. You can't align the week to your weigh-in day, can't track salt by the European standard. Individually trivial, together a constant friction tax that leaves international users feeling second-class.

product.title: Forcing a US data transfer as a condition of entry scares off privacy-minded users at the threshold
product.minus: To use the app at all you must consent to transferring your data to the US — and a segment of users balks right here, especially given how sensitive health data is. This isn't a buried policy line, it's a blocking screen at the very start: the product loses cautious users before it ever proves value, and declining means you can't get in at all.

product.title: A long onboarding before the wall — the failure lands after the time is already invested
product.minus: This is the single money card — and it's about a mechanism, not a price gripe. The app walks you through 20 minutes of goal and meal-plan setup, then reveals the subscription only at the very end. The user invests time, feels the sunk-cost pull — and hits the wall right there. Activation arrives after trust is already spent, so the refusal reads as bait-and-switch and people score it zero before a single real use.

product.title: The free tier does almost everything — and it's what builds the habit
product.plus: The core retention mechanism: the essentials — logging, the database, barcode scanning, recipes — all work unpaid, so people weave the app into a daily ritual before money ever comes up. The habit forms on free, and payment later feels like a thank-you, not an entry toll.

product.title: It's the landing pad for MyFitnessPal refugees
product.plus: Growth comes not from beginners but from a rival's disillusioned base: people leave MyFitnessPal once it walled off familiar features, and land here because they find those features free. This segment already knows how to log food and judges not 'is it easy to start' but 'are they greedy' — and the comparison lands in this app's favor.

product.title: Visible weight-loss results turn users into evangelists
product.plus: The strongest growth engine isn't marketing but the numbers themselves: people credit the app with specific pounds and kilos lost and then retell it to family and friends unprompted. When the product is woven into a successful weight-loss story, the review becomes a personal referral — the cheapest and most persuasive acquisition channel there is.

product.title: A long onboarding questionnaire scares off people who just want a quick count
product.minus: The costliest funnel leak: the product makes people grind through a multi-step survey about their diet, body and goals before they ever reach the tracker. The 'I just want to know the calories in this dish' segment reads it as friction and uninstalls before logging a single meal — before the product ever proves its worth.

product.title: AI photo meal-recognition delights exactly as much as it disappoints
product.plus: For a chunk of users the photo-recognition of a meal is the 'wow' moment that removes logging's biggest pain: snap a picture, the app guesses the food and the calories, and the habit sustains itself. For people eating out or estimating, 'close enough' is enough — and that one feature is what binds them to the product.

product.title: When the photo-scan misses, it misses loudly and erodes trust in the numbers
product.minus: The flip side of the same mechanism: for some, the meal recognition guesses 'wildly wrong,' and that's worse than a simple glitch — a calorie tracker is only worth its accuracy, so a crude AI miss undermines trust in the whole product. Those who came specifically for photo-logging as the headline feature feel cheated and leave.

product.title: The barcode scanner and database depth are the speed that keeps logging alive
product.plus: Food logging only survives if it's fast, and here the combo of 'barcode + a huge catalog + restaurant menus' removes the core friction: no manual thinking or counting. That speed mechanism is what keeps people for years and makes them call the app a 'habit' rather than a chore.

product.title: The database is Western-skewed and loses anyone eating non-Western food
product.minus: A hidden market boundary: the catalog and scanner cover Western foods well, but users in Turkey, Japan, India and Pakistan hit a dead barcode and missing dishes without macros. For them fast logging collapses — they must hand-enter everything — and they defect to local rivals. The product quietly loses its entire non-Western segment.

product.title: Overestimated maintenance calories quietly sabotages results
product.minus: The most insidious failure because it's invisible: the calculation engine overstates maintenance calories and the deficit, so a person faithfully 'follows the app' yet doesn't lose weight. Since the product's entire value is an accurate budget, an error in the very core nullifies results — and the user only realizes it after months of lost progress, then leaves blaming the app for being 'inaccurate.'

product.title: Wearable sync locks users in — until it silently breaks
product.minus: A two-edged lock-in mechanism: tying into Fitbit, Garmin and Samsung Health makes the app the hub of a fitness stack, and people move here precisely after Google broke the native Fitbit app. But when sync silently stops, or the app ignores Health Connect's burned calories and substitutes a 'wild assed guess,' it breaks the exact reason the person chose the product — and trust drops harder than it would for an app with no integrations at all.

product.title: Rigid measurement units repel people who think in grams
product.minus: A narrow but decisive friction: the product pushes servings, cups and ounces, and for some won't let them type a food's weight in grams directly. For people used to a kitchen scale and precise weighing — the most disciplined, loyal segment — being unable to work in their own units is reason enough to delete on the spot, before judging anything else.

product.title: 'It used to be simple' — feature bloat is smothering the original value
product.minus: A mature product's strategic debt: veterans remember a clean, simple app and now face an overloaded interface with ten buttons for one function and six menus for a single action. The more that's crammed in, the harder it is to keep the habit — yet simplicity was once the very advantage. The product risks losing the same 'I just want to count calories' segment it keeps attracting.

product.title: Recurring weigh-ins and visible progress are the built-in motivation hook
product.plus: A quiet retention engine: the app turns weight loss into a measurable ritual — weekly weigh-ins, charts, auto-adjusting calories to the past week. This 'measure → see the shift → keep going' loop is what turns dull bookkeeping into something people come back to daily, and keeps the disciplined users for years.

product.title: Constant premium nagging reads as manipulation — even to paying users
product.minus: Not a complaint about 'too expensive' but a strategic self-sabotage: a product whose strength is a generous free core aggressively pushes premium banners and pop-ups on every open — and does so even to users who have ALREADY paid for a year. It thereby destroys with its own hands the 'they're not greedy' feeling that draws people over from MyFitnessPal. The upsell's intrusiveness strikes at the exact positioning advantage that makes the app win.

product.title: It sells thought-retraining, not tracking
product.plus: Noom's core product isn't the calorie counter but the daily psychology-of-eating micro-lessons and habit work; people who failed every diet because they hate restriction stay precisely because the program explains WHY they eat rather than banning foods. It retains the segment that needs meaning, not a spreadsheet.

product.title: Duolingo-grade gamification turns weight loss into a game
product.plus: Seeds, levels, streaks and micro-challenges pull people back daily — users openly admit they're "ridiculously motivated by earning meaningless seeds." It's a rare case where the behavioral hook drives the daily logging habit rather than one-time novelty.

product.title: The same gamification crossed the line into annoying noise
product.minus: When seeds, unskippable streak animations and "art break" pushes pile on top of logging, the same hook starts to repel: people force-quit the app over animations and cancel specifically over the "distractions." By over-tuning engagement, Noom drives out the very users it used to retain.

product.title: Photo meal logging is the wow-hook that breaks on a real plate
product.minus: Noom sells AI photo food recognition as a flagship feature, but it consistently misreads: a cup of spinach with an apple is graded "red," a labeled 280-cal cookie logs as 190. The onboarding wow-moment turns into distrust of every number — and trust in the tracker is the whole product.

product.title: The food database is US-only and empty for everyone else
product.minus: The barcode scanner and search find US, Canadian, UK and Australian products — and nothing else; users outside those markets simply can't log their food. For an app whose core is logging, this isn't a localization bug but a total loss of the international segment, which leaves for MyFitnessPal.

product.title: Logged food vanishes — the tracker's memory leaks
product.minus: Again and again users add a food to the database, then can't find it on the next visit; identical meals return different calories. A tracker that doesn't remember what you ate breaks the entire reason to keep a diary — and people leave for MyFitnessPal specifically for reliable re-logging.

product.title: Android is a second-class citizen with no recipes or custom meals
product.minus: The recipe builder and saving your own meals exist on iOS but are cut on Android — users discover it after the fact and abandon the app. For people who cook their own food, the absence of reusable recipes makes daily logging unbearable, and it's a stated reason not to renew.

product.title: The calorie budget is tied to steps, and steps don't count
product.minus: Noom computes the daily calorie budget from activity, but step sync with Samsung/Fitbit/watches broadly fails and manual entry was removed. The result breaks not one feature but the program's whole math: without correct steps you can't trust the calorie goal either, leaving the user with no compass.

product.title: The green-yellow-orange color system punishes healthy food
product.minus: The traffic-light classification is Noom's signature teaching tool, yet it drops vegetables, vegan protein and whole foods into the "orange" zone, contradicting actual nutrient density. For a nutritionally literate user it undermines trust in the app's core pedagogical mechanism.

product.title: The human coach was swapped for AI — and the reason people came back left
product.minus: Personal human coaching and psychological support used to be what set Noom apart from plain counters; laying off coaches for AI hollowed the coach out — it just points to materials the user already has. Loyal past customers return, see the AI shift, and leave in disgust.

product.title: The GLP-1 pivot turns a habit program into a drug-sales funnel
product.minus: Users come for a behavioral program, then after months of lessons the app starts pushing its own GLP-1 drugs — a "slap in the face" to a paying customer. Strategically Noom monetizes meds on top of the subscription, but at the cost of the very "healthy without drugs" positioning that brought its audience in.

product.title: Navigation bloated: simple calorie counting is now buried in menus
product.minus: What used to be quick food and exercise logging now takes several screens: activity logging is hidden in a "get your steps in" section, viewing past days is unobvious. Interface bloat raises friction on the core daily action and actively demotivates — people quit over the navigation itself.

product.title: Spinning-dial serving entry — small friction that breaks the habit
product.minus: To set a serving size the user must "spin a dial for five minutes to enter 160" instead of typing the number directly. In an app where logging should be instant, this per-meal micro-frustration compounds and erodes the daily discipline the whole product depends on.

product.title: The weight loss genuinely works — but only for those who follow the plan
product.plus: Despite the chaos, the program's core delivers durable results for the disciplined segment: people lose 40-55 lbs and keep it off for years, attributing it to compounding habits and lessons rather than a quick fix. This is the success cohort whose stories sell the subscription to newcomers.

product.title: The mobile app lags and freezes compared to desktop
product.minus: The number-one pain is the mobile app: multi-second delays on every tap, freezes, constant restarts — while desktop and web run great. Users say outright the mobile version feels neglected and unusable for quick notes on the go.

product.title: AI is forced everywhere and can't be turned off
product.minus: The AI assistant is shoved into every corner of the UI, hijacks note creation, replaced normal search — and there's no way to disable it in settings. Some users uninstall specifically because of this.

product.title: Endlessly flexible platform — a "second brain" for anything
product.plus: Those who get the hang of it run their whole life and work here: client notes, budgets, databases, projects, journals, recipes. The core strength is flexibility plus a generous free tier — limited only by your imagination.

product.title: Sudden loss of notes and unsaved edits
product.minus: The scariest scenario: the app stops saving edits, notes vanish, pages open blank. People kept important data for years — and lost it all, with no way to recover.

product.title: Pages won't open offline — and often not even online
product.minus: The app demands a constant connection just to open tables and notes you already made, and offline mode is buggy — it shows "you're offline" with a live connection. When you urgently need your notes away from home, they're gone.

product.title: You can't copy your own text out of the app
product.minus: A text editor you can't copy text out of: content never reaches the clipboard, highlighting keeps breaking. People are forced to retype everything or import files instead of pasting.

product.title: Scrolling breaks during selection and in menus on mobile
product.minus: A specific mechanical bug: when you try to select text or pick a background color, the page refuses to scroll up/down, and the background and action menus freeze and won't swipe. Maddening on certain Samsungs.

product.title: The back button throws you out of the app and the note
product.minus: The system back button doesn't behave as expected: instead of stepping back through a menu it dumps you on the home page or out of the app entirely, and returning from another app opens the home page instead of the note you were on.

product.title: Steep learning curve, but worth it
product.plus: Almost everyone admits Notion is overwhelming and confusing at first, but those who push through the learning curve end up loving it and can't imagine life without it. The number-one request: add a proper tutorial.

product.title: Constant updates break what used to work
product.minus: Loyal users complain about regression: a new update lands every week, something stops working, old bugs never get fixed, and familiar handy features get removed. It feels like the app is degrading.

product.title: Enterprise focus at the expense of the single user
product.minus: Former note-taking fans feel abandoned: the app gets stuffed with workplace and team features while the single-user case is ignored, and support locked people out of their own data. The result — migration to Obsidian.

product.title: Confusing pricing: pricey subscription, plus extra for AI and add-ons
product.minus: The subscription is called overpriced, and on top of it you're asked to pay for AI credits and add-ons. A separate trap: buy the subscription via Google Play and you can't purchase add-ons — with no warning up front.

product.title: Text selection and copy-paste on Android simply doesn't work
product.minus: The single most common complaint: «Select All» doesn't select all, the highlight randomly deselects, and «copy» claims it saved to clipboard but nothing is there. Copying a paragraph or a long note becomes torture, and many leave just for this.

product.title: Long-pressing a file or folder freezes the whole app
product.minus: To get the context menu in the file tree you long-press a file — and the app freezes with the item stuck highlighted purple, fixable only by force-closing. Often triggers on the second attempt, breaking the core flow of creating a note and moving it to a folder.

product.title: The new UI moved buttons under system bars and enraged users
product.minus: A redesign toward Google's guidelines stripped accent colors, moved the nav and vault bar to the bottom, and pushed buttons into the corners under the status bar — on foldables and big screens they're literally unclickable. A flood of «bring back the old UI» pleas.

product.title: Paid sync is framed as mandatory and pops up before you even open the app
product.minus: Many believe the app went paid: setup leads through account creation straight to a Sync subscription bill, and without it you feel locked out. Nowhere is it stated upfront that sync costs money (~$48-$100), even though local use is free — but that's not obvious.

product.title: Notes vanish: deletions, corruption, and data loss with no backup
product.minus: The scariest class of reviews: people lose years of notes. Notes disappear after a sync error with no version history, a document corrupts when the phone dies, and «new note» on a folder wipes its contents. For a notes app, this is fatal.

product.title: Sign-up and login are broken: 2FA codes never arrive, «challenge verification failed»
product.minus: Enabling sync requires an account — but sign-up dies with «Challenge verification failed», and password reset demands a 6-digit 2FA code that never arrives. With no error message or explanation, people can't even begin to use it.

product.title: Demands access to all files on the device and scares users
product.minus: To keep notes outside the app you must grant read/modify/delete access to ALL files on the device — a legacy permission newer Androids no longer need. Users call it «data mining» and suspect surveillance.

product.title: Heavy and slow on phone: long startup, lag, overheating
product.minus: Built on a Capacitor/Electron stack, the app feels non-native: 8-10 seconds to start at a blank screen, lag that grows with vault size, long documents with tables and attachments crawling, and on older phones it overheats and drains battery.

product.title: Steep learning curve: powerful, but a newcomer has no foothold
product.minus: Everyone recommends it, but out of the box the interface is unintuitive: a baffling «vault» concept, ten ways to do one thing, a demand to «invest time». For anyone who just wants to jot a thought fast, it feels over-engineered.

product.title: Local markdown files — you own your data, no vendor lock-in
product.plus: The core reason for the love: notes are plain .md files on your device, openable in any editor, movable by hand, free of cloud lock-in. For privacy and a «second brain» this is decisive, and many donate for the philosophy itself.

product.title: Plugins, themes and the link graph make it endlessly customizable
product.plus: The community and plugin ecosystem turn it into anything: graph view, note links, themes, canvas, automation for D&D campaigns and writing. Users build a «second brain» and praise that it's all free and endlessly extensible.

product.title: The best tool for writing and a knowledge base — for books, stories, and a «second brain»
product.plus: For writers and knowledge-base builders it's the gold standard: linking and back-links genuinely change how you think, helping organize book chapters, character lore, and research. Many call it the best they've found in a decade of searching.

product.title: Free and ad-free — a rarity users thank and donate for
product.plus: In a world of subscription notebooks, people specifically value that local use is fully free with zero ads. Many voluntarily become donors or buy Sync just to support the team.

product.title: No real widgets and no official Google Drive sync
product.minus: Two recurring requests: widgets that actually show note text (not an empty icon) like Samsung Notes; and official Google Drive sync/backup for Android — current manual and third-party methods feel unreliable for keeping notes safe.

product.title: The editor forces code-style formatting and stumbles on markdown
product.minus: The editor is built for code: it auto-formats prose for writers with no way to disable it, aggressively «helps» with punctuation, breaks nested lists and quotes, and renders LaTeX and non-English scripts (Bangla) poorly. Basics like in-document font size and a table of contents are missing.

product.title: Sync breaks and flips every note into read-only
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after an update the entire library suddenly turns read-only. The app gets stuck in a "syncing" state, and while it "syncs" you can't edit anything — you can only stare at outdated notes. None of the recommended fixes (cache clear, reinstall, desktop repair) help.

product.title: Loses years of notes when sync fails
product.minus: An app with one job — to save your notes — fails at it. People describe notes vanishing on sync, reverting to old versions, or disappearing entirely, with nothing in the recycle bin or misplaced-notes section. Microsoft's own recommended fix (log out/in or reinstall) itself wipes any unsynced files.

product.title: Constant page conflicts fixable only on desktop
product.minus: On shared or frequently-used notes a "page conflict" pops up about once a week, and to resolve it you must open the note in a desktop browser — even if you only ever use the phone. There's no list of all conflicts, so you stumble into them one at a time.

product.title: Forces a fresh login on every open
product.minus: The app keeps signing you out of your Microsoft account, so you have to log in almost every time. The login itself often works only about a third of the time, and sometimes dumps you onto an endless black or blank screen.

product.title: Hangs on launch: white screen and endless spinner
product.minus: For many the app simply won't open: a white screen with an endlessly spinning wheel, an instant crash on launch, or a frozen loading screen. Reinstalling, restarting and clearing cache change nothing — the app is completely unusable.

product.title: Noticeable typing input lag on Android
product.minus: Even in a simple text editor on Android the input lag runs past a second, and that's on strong devices. For people whose same notebook flies on PC, it makes the phone version unusable.
