product.title: A stripped-down desktop: key features missing on mobile
product.minus: The Android version feels like a watered-down desktop OneNote: no subpages, can't paste images, no keyboard shortcuts, no label search, no math editor. People who love it on Windows hit a wall on the phone.

product.title: Stylus either won't write or confuses finger for pen
product.minus: On pen devices (Galaxy S25 Ultra, S Pen) the pen is detected but you can't write with it; switch to finger and the page just scrolls. After an update inking lags, has no real-time tracking, no palm rejection, and you can't erase handwriting.

product.title: Cross-device access to everything in one place — the core love
product.plus: When it works, this is what wins people over: jot on the phone and it's on the laptop, everything within reach anywhere. Notebooks, sections, pages, photos, links — all stored neatly in one place, replacing piles of paper scraps.

product.title: Flexible organization: notebooks, sections, mixed content
product.plus: Over the years it has replaced dozens of paper notebooks: text, images, audio, files, drawings, task lists — all in one notebook-and-section structure. And the interface stays beginner-friendly and minimalist while doing it.

product.title: Free and ad-free with a rich feature set
product.plus: A big repeated draw: all of this is free and ad-free. For many it's the deciding reason to stick with OneNote despite the bugs.

product.title: Review-nag popups that can't be dismissed
product.minus: A small but pointedly noted irritation: the app keeps begging for a rating with popups you can't dismiss, getting in the way of actually taking notes.

product.title: The timer ends, but the bell never rings
product.minus: The most frequent and damaging complaint: the interval runs out and there is no notification, sound or vibration at all. Users have to keep checking the screen, which defeats the whole point of the method.

product.title: Interval over — the counter slips into negative time
product.minus: Instead of moving to the next interval, the timer starts counting negative seconds. You can't pause or reset it — only kill the process and restart manually.

product.title: With the screen off, the timer goes silent
product.minus: Lock the phone or turn the screen off and the alert simply doesn't fire. Yet that's exactly how people want to use it — hide the distracting screen — and then the notification disappears.

product.title: Ad-free minimalism is exactly what people love
product.plus: A clean, non-distracting interface with no ads and no paywalls is the headline reason for the praise. It does exactly what it promises and nothing more.

product.title: The alert is too quiet and too short
product.minus: Even when the bell does sound, it's easy to miss: a single short beep instead of a sustained melody, with no volume control. Users ask for a continuous, alarm-style ring.

product.title: The timer freezes and lies about the time
product.minus: The countdown gets stuck in the final seconds, the notification freezes, and a five-minute break stretches to nearly ten. Sometimes a short break runs as a long one instead.

product.title: No statistics — you can't see your weekly progress
product.minus: There's only a timer, no stats section. Students want to see how many hours they've put in over a week or month, and for many this gap is a dealbreaker.

product.title: Perfect for studying and focus
product.plus: When it works, it measurably boosts productivity: students break cramming into blocks, stop getting distracted every ten minutes, and start enjoying studying again.

product.title: Customisable intervals and themes
product.plus: You can set your own Pomodoro, short- and long-break lengths, a daily goal and a background colour — enough to build a custom '50/10 student' routine.

product.title: The cycle doesn't reset between days
product.minus: There's no way to start the day fresh: unfinished Pomodoros carry over, so the next morning the very first interval hands you an ill-timed 'long' break.

product.title: An intrusive persistent notification and watch spam
product.minus: A persistent notification stays up the whole time the timer runs, and the watch gets a new ticking update every second. You can't toggle the 'persistent' and 'reminder' types separately.

product.title: Users ask for a quick-start widget
product.minus: Starting the timer means opening the app every single time. A home-screen widget would let users launch it instantly without the distraction of unlocking and hunting for the icon.

product.title: A 4-habit free cap hits before the product can prove its worth
product.minus: Building habits inherently means tracking several at once — and the 4-habit cap hits the paywall during setup, before the user has lived a single streak. The pay-or-leave decision lands before activation, so churn happens before the product ever works once.

product.title: Reminders ARE the product — when they go silent, only a useless list remains
product.minus: A habit tracker sells one promise: "I'll remind you, you'll act." The widespread Android notification failure removes exactly that lever, and users say plainly that without reminders the product is pointless. It bites hardest for the ADHD segment that came for an external memory — for them a silent tracker equals no tracker.

product.title: The don't-break-the-chain effect is the core retention engine
product.plus: Progress visuals and streaks turn tracking the habit into a habit itself: people return so they won't reset the chain. This game loop is why fans keep the app for years and call it their favorite on Android.

product.title: Streaks can't be backfilled — one missed mark destroys the motivation
product.minus: You can only mark a habit complete on the same day: forget at night and the streak resets with no way back. Since the whole product rests on the streak, this rigidity backfires — instead of motivation the user gets punished for ordinary forgetfulness and quits.

product.title: Completion only works by swiping — a hidden gesture breaks the core action
product.minus: The product's most frequent action — "I did the habit" — is buried in a swipe that no tap reveals. Users tap the item and can't figure out how to mark anything done; some are tripped up further because the left swipe means skip, not complete. A core gesture you can't pass without the tutorial loses people in the first minute.

product.title: Onboarding demands a fixed wake-up time — it filters out anyone with a shifting schedule
product.minus: The first setup screen asks for a wake-up time and won't move on without one. But the very people with chaotic sleep — a common habit-tracker audience — have no fixed time, and they delete the app right at that question. A rigid onboarding step rejects the segment that needed the product most.

product.title: Signing in doesn't sync — a reinstall or new phone wipes everything
product.minus: Users create an account expecting a backup, but habits and streaks don't carry across devices and don't survive a reinstall. For a product built on a months-long streak, losing the history is losing all the accumulated meaning; the user who invested in the streak leaves for good.

product.title: Without a timer, habits collapse to a checkbox — no effort tracked, no accountability
product.minus: Habits like meditation, working out or reading are measured by time, not by a binary "done." A plain checkmark creates no sense of accountability, and users say themselves they're more likely to cut corners without a timer. A product promising behavior change under-serves exactly the habits where effort matters more than the tick.

product.title: Ready-made habit sets and presets cure beginners' blank-page paralysis
product.plus: Suggested habits and preset sets hand a user who doesn't know where to start a concrete list instead of an empty screen. For self-improvement beginners — the core segment — this lowers the entry barrier: no need to invent anything, just pick and go.

product.title: A completion sound and micro-celebration give a dopamine hit for each check-off
product.plus: A small animation and sound on completing a task turn a routine check-off into a pleasant moment — fans name the sound itself as the reason they stick with the app. This sensory reward reinforces the desired behavior and works as a habit-forming mechanism, not just decoration.

product.title: No Android widget keeps the app out of sight — and out of mind
product.minus: A home-screen widget is a passive trigger that keeps the habit in view without opening the app. On Android there isn't one (iOS only), and users admit outright: without the widget they simply forget the app exists. For a product whose job is to remind, missing the most visible reminder is a structural retention failure.

product.title: Rigid daily/weekly/monthly intervals don't fit real habit rhythms
product.minus: Many habits run on non-standard schedules — "every Tuesday," "twice a week every two weeks" — but the app only knows daily, weekly and monthly. Advanced users either clutter the calendar or can't set up the habit at all. Inflexible frequency caps out exactly the most engaged segment.

product.title: Pushy premium and "challenge" pop-ups poison the speed of the daily check-in
product.minus: A habit tracker lives on the instant "check and go" open. But every launch greets users with a subscription screen or a prompt to start a challenge, breaking the very speed they came for. Friction in the most frequent action quietly trains people to open the app less — and so to log habits less.

product.title: A clean, minimalist interface is what keeps the "non-planner" crowd
product.plus: A tidy, uncluttered UI wins the segment that gets distracted easily and drowns in complex planners — including people with ADHD. They name simplicity and the lack of clutter as the reason they stay: the product isn't intimidating, so starting a habit doesn't feel daunting.

product.title: Progress shown as a bare percentage — users miss richer feedback on results
product.minus: Feedback is reduced to a completion percentage, with no notes on why you did or didn't, no levels or gradations. For a product meant to motivate, a dry number feels meaningless: people want context and growth, and get an abstract metric instead. A thin feedback layer weakens the emotional attachment to progress.

product.title: The program actually teaches reading — parents see progress within weeks
product.plus: The core reason people forgive everything else: kids go from non-readers to reading sentences within weeks, and parents notice it on school tests.

product.title: Constantly logs you out — you have to sign back in several times a day
product.minus: The most frequent pain: the app doesn't hold a session, kicks the child out multiple times a day, and each time a parent has to stop and re-enter the login.

product.title: Glitches, freezes and loses progress — the child repeats the same lesson
product.minus: The app freezes mid-lesson, then fails to save progress, forcing the child to redo the same map — motivation drops, young kids cry and give up.

product.title: Wild volume swings: cartoons blast, but the instructions are barely audible
product.minus: No audio normalization: videos and the «Well done!» jingles blast at max volume while the teaching speech the child actually needs to hear is barely audible — parents are forever adjusting the volume.

product.title: The subscription is nearly impossible to cancel, and money is taken even after you cancel
product.minus: Cancellation sends you in circles or claims «already unsubscribed» — yet keeps charging for months, sometimes yearly amounts, from people who left long ago.

product.title: After the update the screen gets stuck forever on "please rotate your device"
product.minus: A specific recent-update bug: a «rotate your device» message appears that won't clear no matter how you turn the device, blocking both the placement test and the program itself across all devices.

product.title: The «free» claim is a lie: no play without paying, and the trial often vanishes
product.minus: Ads promise free access, but you can't even try it without entering payment details, and the promised 30-day trial suddenly turns out «ineligible» or charges you immediately.

product.title: You pay — and the content is still locked, including Mathseeds
product.minus: The worst case: you pay for a yearly or monthly plan, and the app either won't load past the main screen or says Mathseeds «requires a subscription» — money gone, no access, refund denied.

product.title: Crashes on launch and after updates — the app simply won't open
product.minus: Recent updates turn a working app into a broken one: crash on launch, endless loading, «oops something went wrong» — reinstalling doesn't help.

product.title: Opens as an in-browser site rather than a proper native app
product.minus: It's essentially a web wrapper: the «app» opens a browser version, forces a login every time, lags, and has no offline mode — many give up and switch to a computer.

product.title: Too much distraction around the lesson — library, store, rude «furballs»
product.minus: Beyond bugs there's a design gripe: the lesson is buried under clutter (store, market, library), young kids get lost, and characters that taunt a wrong answer hurt the child instead of encouraging.

product.title: Genuinely good for neurodiverse kids and for homeschooling
product.plus: A distinct strength: it's praised by parents of autistic kids and children with learning difficulties, and by homeschooling families — kids work independently and love it, freeing up the parent.

product.title: When support does respond, it's fast and helpful
product.plus: Against the «no one to contact» complaints there's a flip side: some parents praise support for replying fast, even over holidays, and fixing the issue same-day.

product.title: A visible per-step timer removes the «decide what's next» moment — that's the whole product
product.plus: The core mechanism: a routine is split into timed steps and the app walks you from one to the next, removing the «what now» decision. For ADHD and decision-paralysis users this turns morning chaos into autopilot — they leave on time and finally hold a pace.

product.title: An alarm with no on-screen button that overrides silent mode turns the app into a sound bomb
product.minus: The routine-start alarm is loud, has no snooze and no visible off-button — users panic and kill the app process to stop it. It overrides system volume and silent mode, switches itself back on after updates, and must be disabled per-routine. A tool meant for a calm morning is the thing that wrecks the morning.

product.title: Reminders only fire at «time's up», not during the task — a failure for the exact users it's built for
product.minus: The app sells itself as a cure for time blindness, yet it only reminds you once a task has already ended — announcing failure after the fact. Distracted mid-way through a 10-minute task, you get no nudge; the notice arrives when it's already time for the next step. The most paying segment leaves precisely over the missing mid-task reminders.

product.title: «Pause / reorder / delay» flexibility is what separates a coach from a dumb schedule
product.plus: Being able to pause, extend and reorder steps on the fly makes the routine survive real life — parents with unpredictable kids keep the structure without it shattering at the first disruption. It turns a rigid timetable into an adaptive helper and keeps people for years.

product.title: Broken drag-to-reorder kills the exact flexibility the product is built on
product.minus: Dragging steps glitches: a task slams to the bottom, hides behind another, snaps back to the original order. You have to restart the app to move a single item. This strikes at the heart of the promise — «adapt your routine to the day» — and angers even five-year loyalists who otherwise worship the app.

product.title: The free 2-routine cap blocks the very core use case — separate routines
product.minus: The product's value is running distinct routines — morning, gym, evening, weekends. But free gives only two, so the core use case hits a wall before the user ever sees the payoff. People defect to unlimited gym-workout timers: the verdict is «two slots is the product, not a teaser».

product.title: The voice coach and «robot» offload mental load — no constant checking of what's next
product.plus: Speaking steps aloud means you don't hold the phone and check — the voice tells you what to do while your hands are busy. For an overloaded brain this frees working memory: users describe «decreased mental load» and calm as the main effect, not the task list itself.

product.title: Hard time-binding turns help into stress for perfectionists
product.minus: The same timer that rescues ADHD users repels another segment: when every step is on the clock, perfectionists and anxious users feel rushed and start rejecting the task itself. The product's mechanism splits its audience — it cures time blindness at the cost of pressure, and for some that pressure outweighs the benefit.

product.title: A huge «Done» button with no undo marks the whole day complete on one mistap
product.minus: A giant complete button and no back/undo mean one accidental tap marks a step — or the whole day — done, with no way to reverse it. For the ADHD users who are exactly the ones to mistap and to test a routine, this breaks the key motivator — streaks and honest progress — and forces re-running the routine to get back a step.

product.title: Losing months-built routines after updates burns the most loyal users
product.minus: Updates wipe routines users built over months of analyzing their own behavior and roll data back to old versions. That accumulated setup is the switching cost and the attachment; destroying it, the app demolishes the very thing that held the user. The longest-tenured leave precisely after losing what they invested in.

product.title: The watch as a standalone device is the unkept promise: a wrist timer would solve the core pain
product.minus: People install the app specifically for the watch — a wrist timer would solve their biggest problem: glance at the phone for something and forget the routine. But the watch app crashes, returns a null countdown, and sync forces you to end a routine twice, on both phone and watch. The most valuable scenario — «timer always in view» — doesn't work.

product.title: A lock-screen widget/player is the most-asked feature to keep the routine from getting lost behind other apps
product.minus: Users repeatedly ask for a lock-screen widget or media-style player showing the timer with next/skip buttons. The reason is behavioral: apps get closed and forgotten, and the routine gets lost. The current widget is called poor. Without an always-visible timer, the core mechanism — holding attention on the current step — breaks.

product.title: Social features and AI contradict why users came — to escape feeds
product.minus: The app adds a social feed, video anime ads and AI features, but the audience came precisely to escape Instagram/TikTok and focus. These don't just annoy — they work against the stated value (focus, calm) and make the app heavier and less stable. Paying users explicitly ask for an opt-out.

product.title: Randomized free-tier icons punish the exact segment that shouldn't waste time
product.minus: In the free version task icons are handed out at random via a «shuffle», so to get the one you want you press again and again. For an ADHD audience already struggling with time management this isn't an upsell but a time trap — it reads as mockery. The monetization design hits the target segment's exact pain point.

product.title: No per-weekday task scheduling — a flexible weekly plan is impossible without subscribing
product.minus: You can't assign specific tasks to specific weekdays (gym on weekdays, cleaning on weekends) — the basic way people run a paper planner. Without it the app doesn't replace the thing it's adopted for. The segment that needs a flexible weekly rhythm hits a wall and goes back to paper.

product.title: Almost all content is locked behind a subscription — nothing left to play
product.minus: The overwhelming majority of reviews are about one thing: after install only 1–6 mini-games are playable, everything else is locked. Kids drive parents crazy asking to buy more, and the child just hits a lock screen.

product.title: It used to be free — betrayal felt by those who grew up on it
product.minus: A huge share of reviewers are former kids returning to their childhood game. They remember the separate free apps and the 7-day trial, and now see a paywall. The feeling of a ruined childhood comes up again and again.

product.title: A monthly subscription feels too expensive for a kids' game
product.minus: Parents object not to paying as such but to the model: $7–13 or €60–88 a year for a simple toddler toy. Many — single or low-income — say outright they can't afford it and ask for a one-time purchase instead of a subscription.

product.title: Ads promise free, but the app demands payment right away
product.minus: Users feel deceived: ads don't mention the subscription, the "try for free" button immediately tries to charge, and features promised in ads (like character customization) aren't available.

product.title: Charges after cancellation and after a promised free trial
product.minus: An alarming billing cluster: charged despite cancelling, charged for a "free trial", refused refunds, and cancellation hard to find. Money keeps leaving the account even after deleting the app.

product.title: Sign-in, accounts and connecting the subscription don't work
product.minus: Even paying users get stuck: the subscription won't link to the child's account, sign-in kicks them out, the password is "wrong" when it's right, and switching Google account or device loses purchases. Support is effectively absent.

product.title: Requires Wi-Fi to download the mini-games
product.minus: The app is marketed as offline, but mini-games must be downloaded online: on mobile data or without good Wi-Fi even the one free game won't run, which especially hurts kids on the go.

product.title: Glitches, black screen, crashes and slow loading
product.minus: Technical failures spoil even the available content: a black screen on launch, crashes, the child being kicked out, endless loading and slow downloads. On older devices the game stops working after updates.

product.title: Removed favorite worlds upset the kids
product.minus: Parents of special-needs kids and plain fans raise the alarm: favorite modes (Monsters, Dress-up, the gnome camping, daycare, Friends) were removed or locked. Autistic children especially struggle to accept that a beloved game suddenly vanished.

product.title: The content itself is loved: cute, calming, educational
product.plus: When content is unlocked, it's genuinely adored: dozens of games in one app, adorable characters, no ads and nothing toxic. It teaches, builds imagination and suits kids of every age — and even grown-up fans.

product.title: Calm and sensory regulation — especially for neurodivergent users
product.plus: An unexpected strength: the game helps with anxiety and sensory overload. Parents of autistic and nonverbal children, and adult players, describe it as a safe, calming anchor worth paying for.

product.title: For paying families the subscription genuinely pays off
product.plus: The minority who do pay find it justified: one subscription covers multiple devices and kids, works cross-platform, has no ads, and keeps a child busy with educational games for a long time.

product.title: A paper replacement for everyday lists and reminders
product.plus: The core use case is everyday memory: grocery lists, to-dos, birthdays, reminders. People say they use it daily and literally can't go without it.

product.title: Notes travel with you across phones
product.plus: A big draw is account sync: switch to a new device and all your notes are still there, available across devices, even moving over from iPhone. For many that's the clincher.

product.title: Updates break what used to work
product.minus: The most painful theme: each new update breaks something. Notes get hard to find, copy-paste stops working, useful features vanish, the familiar layout shifts. People say outright that an update makes them want to uninstall.

product.title: Free, no ads, no subscriptions
product.plus: People value that it's fully free, with no ads and no subscriptions — and they explicitly ask not to add purchases. For a built-in notepad that's a real edge over third-party apps.

product.title: Simple, fast and intuitive from the first open
product.plus: A core strength is the low friction: it opens fast, has no clutter, and is handy for jotting on the go. Many specifically praise the simple, user-friendly design.

product.title: Frequent crashes, lag and lost unsaved work
product.minus: For some users the app is unstable: it crashes right after opening, lags while typing, makes the tablet stutter. Worst of all, it closes on its own and loses what was written.

product.title: Wants more font and styling customization
product.minus: A common ask is more fonts, colors, stickers and templates. The default font feels dull, there's no way to set title size and color, and people want custom note covers. They wish styling were as rich as Google Docs.

product.title: Easy PDF export and file sharing
product.plus: People like that notes turn into PDFs easily, letting them share documents and personal info. It covers light paperwork without office apps — though some ask to speed up PDF creation and drop the size limit.

product.title: Strong clipboard for long pastes
product.plus: A standout is handling big chunks of text — the clipboard holds far more than rivals like Google Notes. Handy for collecting information when researching a topic.

product.title: An emotional outlet, not just a utility
product.plus: A surprisingly strong thread — the app doubles as an emotional journal: people vent feelings, write poetry, journal, relieve stress. For some it's almost a personal confidant.

product.title: Handwriting, dictation and tables fall short
product.minus: For advanced use the app falls short: complaints about drawing and handwritten notes, weak dictation, a missing mic for voice input, broken tables, and no way to set an image as a watermark.

product.title: No proper view or edit on a computer
product.minus: A clear limitation — notes are effectively stuck on the phone: people want to open and edit them on a computer, but there's no convenient way. Deleted notes also vanish for good after 11 days.

product.title: The circular clock face, not a linear list, is the whole point
product.plus: The core thing users love: the day rendered as sectors on a clock face, so you instantly grasp how much time is left until the next thing and how full the day is. For many it clicks far better than the usual vertical calendars.

product.title: A lifeline for ADHD and time blindness
product.plus: A huge share of the rave reviews come from neurodivergent users: the visual clock literally helps them "see" time and stay on schedule where ordinary planners failed them.

product.title: The home-screen widget is what people install it for
product.plus: Users keep the sectograph widget on their home screen as their main planner: one glance shows what's coming. For many the widget, not the app itself, is the product.

product.title: Watch sync keeps breaking — and the watch is why people bought Pro
product.minus: The most painful complaint: events vanish from the watch face and sync drops out — and Pro was bought precisely to see the schedule on the wrist. When it fails, the purchase feels wasted.

product.title: WearOS updates break compatibility with Samsung/Pixel/Galaxy watches
product.minus: Time and again newer watch models drop out of support: "device isn't compatible", the face won't install. For users who chose it specifically for the watch, that turns the app useless.

product.title: The Pro purchase doesn't carry across devices or accounts
product.minus: A recurring pain: paid Pro reverts, isn't recognized on a second device, there's no restore button and no way to migrate the purchase to a new phone or account — users are forced to pay again.

product.title: Hard dependency on Google Calendar — no Proton, flaky Outlook
product.minus: The app stores almost nothing itself — it just draws someone else's calendar. Anyone who left Google (for Proton) or lives on Outlook/Exchange hits a wall: events don't pull in and the app becomes useless.

product.title: The free tier is generous — Pro feels optional
product.plus: A real draw: the essentials aren't paywalled — the free version works fully, the widget is available, and people buy Pro more to support the devs than out of need.

product.title: Constant ask: show tasks (Google Tasks, TickTick, CalDAV), not just events
product.minus: The top feature request from fans: the app only draws calendar events, with no task integration. People would pay for Pro to get Google Tasks/CalDAV, but for now they keep a separate to-do list.

product.title: Widget glitches: clock freezes, resizes itself
product.minus: The very widget people install it for has its own ailments: the clock freezes and won't advance until you open the app, and the widget resizes itself due to a bug.

product.title: Steep learning curve; the dial can overwhelm at first
product.minus: Some users stumble at the start: the dial feels chaotic and hard to parse, a single sector crams in too many numbers, and labels collide. Many get the hang of it, but the barrier to entry is real.

product.title: Paywalled color hurts colorblind users; no desktop/web version
product.minus: Two structural limits: changing colors sits behind Pro, which locks colorblind users out entirely, and there's no desktop/web version — your schedule is trapped on phone and watch.

product.title: Sign-up wall before the first note
product.minus: People are furious that a «simple note» app demands an account and email before you can type a single word. Many uninstall on the spot without ever reaching the notes: there's no «skip» option and no Google sign-in.

product.title: Cursor jumps to the end of the note while typing
product.minus: The most hated bug: pause for a couple of seconds while editing (especially on the Samsung keyboard or in checklists) and the screen jumps to the very bottom of the note. The complaints stretch back years with no fix, making the app «practically unusable» for writing.

product.title: Sync breaks and loses data
product.minus: The headline feature — sync — is also the headline pain: notes fail to match across devices, revert to old versions, or vanish entirely. People describe losing hours of work, text duplicated thousands of times, and fresh edits overwritten by stale ones.

product.title: The sign-up email never arrives
product.minus: Even those willing to make an account get stuck: the verification email simply never arrives, no matter how many tries or different addresses. Password reset is just as silent and support doesn't reply — onboarding becomes a dead end.

product.title: Crashes after Android updates
product.minus: After OS updates (especially Android 14/16 and One UI 6 on Samsung) the app crashes right at launch or freezes solid. Access to notes disappears for weeks with no fix in sight — people migrate to Joplin and Google Keep.

product.title: Free, ad-free, no subscriptions forever
product.plus: Users' core love: unlimited notes on unlimited devices, zero ads and zero paywalls. Many can't believe years in that this quality is given away, and thank the Automattic team for keeping the app free.

product.title: Instant cross-platform sync, when it works
product.plus: When sync behaves, it's almost magical: edits land on phone, tablet and PC in seconds, and you can watch text change in real time. This is exactly why people pick Simplenote as a bridge between devices.

product.title: Clean, distraction-free simplicity — the reason people stay
product.plus: The minimalist, no-frills interface is the main draw for those who just want to open, type and close. People call it the best replacement for Apple Notes and Evernote precisely because nothing extra gets in the way.

product.title: No Undo/Redo button
product.minus: The missing undo is a recurring plea: accidentally delete a big chunk of text and there's no way back except digging through version history, which rolls back more than intended. For a basic editor this feels like a missing fundamental.

product.title: Search can't find inside a note
product.minus: Search scans across all notes but can't find and highlight a word inside a single long note — you have to scroll manually. For those holding large texts, this is repeatedly the reason they walk away.

product.title: Feels abandoned and dated
product.minus: Loyal long-time users worry the app has frozen: no updates for years, support silent on tickets, known bugs lingering for months. Against Notion and Obsidian it feels «stuck in 2016».

product.title: No images or attachments
product.minus: The plain-text nature is the main ceiling for many: you can't insert a photo, PDF or scan, though it's constantly requested. Some users say outright they'll leave or stick with rivals purely over the lack of media.

product.title: Manual entry isn't a flaw — it's the accountability mechanism users stay for
product.plus: Users who deliberately skip bank sync describe manually logging every expense as a self-discipline ritual: the moment of entry forces the question 'do I need to spend this?'. That turns a plain tracker into a behavior-change tool and creates loyalty without any automation.

product.title: Shared wallets with live sync are the real hook for couples and families
product.plus: Running one wallet together and seeing your partner's spending in real time across devices is exactly why people pick Spendee over solo trackers. It's a household network effect: the more members in a wallet, the higher the switching cost.

product.title: The cross-platform, web-based layer is what local-only competitors lack
product.plus: Data lives in the cloud and is equally reachable from iOS, Android and the browser under one login — users explicitly contrast this with rivals where data is trapped on a single device. It removes the fear of losing history when switching phones and makes the product a long-term 'home' for records.

product.title: Visualization and color categories make tracking pleasant, not a chore
product.plus: A clean minimalist design, color-coded categories, tags and charts make the act of budgeting enjoyable — users call it 'fun' and 'beautiful'. Aesthetics function as retention here: people come back because they like looking at their data.

product.title: Geo-tagging and photo receipts are surprise features that sell the product
product.plus: Pinning a transaction to a place on the map and attaching unlimited receipt photos are details users flag as unexpectedly valuable. It signals that depth of data per transaction — not just the amount — is an underrated differentiator in this niche.

product.title: Responsive support rescues trust where the product itself stumbles
product.plus: When something breaks, prompt support with fast fixes and refunds repeatedly turns an angry user into an advocate — people raise their rating specifically because of how the team handled them. It shows the human layer is an underrated retention lever in finance apps.

product.title: The free 'one wallet' ceiling kills the exact job people install the app to do
product.minus: The free tier allows only one wallet and one budget — yet comparing 'cash vs card' or 'personal vs shared' is the very reason people install it. Someone trying to see where they overspend hits the wall before the first insight: the product blocks its own core job.

product.title: You can't hand-fix a synced bank — auto-sync strips control over transactions
product.minus: When transactions are pulled automatically from the bank, users lose the ability to correct them: you can't mark a transaction cleared, can't split a purchase across categories, can't turn a refund into a correct entry. The automation that should save effort actually strips control over the picture — and people leave for Wallet/Snoop to regain manual edits.

product.title: Linked credit cards break net worth: debt counts as income
product.minus: The app treats a credit-card balance as cash and a debt payment as income, so 'net worth' grows the deeper you go into the red. For the core job — knowing how much money you actually have free — this is a fatal inversion: the product lies in exactly the number people install it for.

product.title: No transaction split or subcategories — tracking stays coarse where life isn't
product.minus: A single purchase can't be split across categories, and categories can't nest. For families and precise budgeters this is a detail ceiling: a real basket of groceries plus a gift collapses into one line — and that's exactly why people migrate to Wallet.

product.title: Categorization misfires: the app forgets your choice and overrides it
product.minus: Auto-categorization picks 'public transport' over the user's own 'taxi' and doesn't remember how similar purchases were filed. In a tracker where the category is the core unit of meaning, this breaks trust in the stats and forces manual re-sorting of nearly everything.

product.title: Clunky transaction entry wears down the single most frequent action
product.minus: Adding an expense is the action repeated many times a day, yet it's awkward: you can't duplicate an entry as a template, can't switch currency on the fly, and have to hunt for the right category every time. Accumulated friction in the core flow is the top reason people abandon daily tracking.

product.title: No widget robs the app of instant quick-entry
product.minus: A quick-add widget that once existed was removed — and users have been asking for it back for years, because without it every expense means opening the app and walking the full path. For a tracker that lives on entry frequency, losing the fastest entry point directly erodes how regularly people log.

product.title: Scheduled transactions can't be edited — the planning feature is half-broken
product.minus: You can set a recurring or scheduled payment, but then can't change its amount, move the date, or delete it from the list. For people budgeting ahead, this turns a useful feature into a source of stuck, wrong entries and undermines trust in the forecast.

product.title: AI Magic Scan was bolted on top of the UI — a trendy feature crowded out core utility
product.minus: The AI scanner tab was added so that it covers the labels list and degrades navigation, while still not splitting a receipt into categories. It's a textbook case of chasing the AI trend at the expense of the daily flow — long-time users explicitly ask for optimization instead of 'trendy' features.

product.title: Export is capped at one year — the app holds history hostage on the way out
product.minus: Leaving with your own data is nearly impossible: the Excel export returns only the last year, there's no CSV import/export, and years of history can't be moved. It creates a hard data lock-in — people stay not out of love but because years of records are effectively trapped inside.

product.title: Manual entry isn't a flaw — it self-selects the audience
product.plus: The app deliberately makes you type each expense by hand and never touches your bank — and that is exactly what retains people who want to feel every dollar leave. They describe it as a daily ritual of open-log-see-the-balance, and that micro-habit makes the product irreplaceable for years.

product.title: Simplicity is the product, not a phase it'll grow out of
product.plus: Users openly compare it to fancier rivals and choose it precisely for what it lacks: a clean screen, no setup, instant entry. For them any extra button is a loss, not a gain, and that stance wins a loyal niche that complex apps scare away.

product.title: All history lives on the device — a new phone wipes out years
product.minus: Because data lives locally, switching or breaking a phone wipes out multiple years of records — and people learn this at the worst moment. The product is kept for years precisely for its history, yet it fails to protect the one scenario it exists for, turning the most loyal users into the most burned.

product.title: Dropbox-only backup excludes anyone in another ecosystem
product.minus: The only way to save data is Dropbox, leaving Google Drive, OneDrive and local-storage users unprotected. People plainly say they don't use Dropbox and will therefore lose everything when upgrading; tying backup to one cloud makes the promised sync unreachable for a whole slice of the base.

product.title: One global budget instead of per-category limits breaks real budgeting
product.minus: It tallies where money went well, but only lets you set one global budget figure rather than a limit per category. People who came to plan, not just record, hit a wall: there's tracking but no forward control of spending, pushing them toward more 'real' budgeting apps.

product.title: Fixed periods (day/week/month) hurt anyone paid biweekly
product.minus: The app slices time only into day, week, month and year — but a huge group is paid fortnightly or every four weeks and can't align tracking to their real pay cycle. The mismatch between period and paycheck makes the balance meaningless for exactly the paycheck-to-paycheck users it should serve.

product.title: No custom date range blocks trip- and project-level analysis
product.minus: The single most common ask from multi-year users is a custom date range — expenses for a trip, a project, or a personal month running the 10th to the 9th. Without it the product only shows calendar periods, and people who need to cost a specific event hit a ceiling they'll forgive but that keeps them off five stars.

product.title: Manual carry-over of the balance triggers false panic
product.minus: The unspent balance doesn't roll into the new period automatically — you must re-enter it as income. As a result, when a new week or month starts people think they've lost all their money and panic until they figure it out. A default that scares the user at the start of every cycle is a behavioral bug, not a setting.

product.title: Widget and quick-add turn tracking into an impulse micro-action
product.plus: A home-screen shortcut and built-in widget let people log a purchase at the register in seconds — and that speed is exactly what keeps expenses from being forgotten. Users note that small cash, otherwise written off as lost, now gets captured on the spot; the product wins by cutting friction to near zero.

product.title: Custom categories with color and icon make the ledger feel personal
product.plus: Being able to create unlimited custom categories and change the name, symbol and color makes the app feel built around the user's life rather than the other way round. This personalization is a quiet retention engine: people have invested setup time tuning it to themselves and don't want to start over with a rival.

product.title: Deleting a category erases all its history — a trap for long-timers
product.minus: You can't delete an outdated category without losing every past-year entry tied to it, so long-term users' lists fill up with dead items. The people who've tracked the longest are punished for loyalty with a cluttered interface, and the workaround (rename with a prefix) is something they have to invent themselves.

product.title: No shared access — the product loses users at the moment of marriage
product.minus: The app is built strictly for one person: no shared account, no sync between partners. Users describe the exact turning point — they were single and loved the simplicity, now they're married and forced to leave because two people can't share a budget. The product misses the natural life-stage upgrade.

product.title: Multiple accounts can be created but not switched — a feature that teases
product.minus: People set up several accounts (personal, family, investments) but then can't switch between them or reopen them — and they cut their rating specifically over this. A half-working feature is worse than none: it promises multi-account tracking, draws the user in, then locks their data inside an unreachable account.

product.title: Spreadsheet export makes the data yours, not the app's hostage
product.plus: Being able to export entries to a spreadsheet and pull a yearly report matters to people who need to do taxes, report, or simply own their numbers outside the app. This data openness lowers lock-in fear and paradoxically retains: users stay calm knowing they can take everything with them, so they stay.

product.title: Years of 'invisible' daily use is the clearest sign of product-market fit
product.plus: Dozens of users say they've tracked here for 5, 7, 10, even 15 years and carried it phone to phone — and the highest praise is 'it's one of those apps you never think about because you use it every day and it just works'. That invisible daily habit is the strongest moat a niche tool can have.

product.title: Pro doesn't survive updates or device changes — trust breaks after payment
product.minus: The core protective value — ad-free for a one-time payment — collapses on updates and migration: Pro buyers see ads again, lose their status, and can't find 'restore purchase'. When the very paid trait fails to survive basic lifecycle events, the product punishes its most committed users, and churn arrives not at onboarding but after payment — where trust should be highest.

product.title: The best "second brain" for people who forget everything
product.plus: Long-term users run their whole life on it for years — tasks, habits and reminders in one place; for many it's literally a memory replacement.

product.title: Downloads as "free" but basic features sit behind a paywall
product.minus: Event duration, the full month view, more than 10 lists, sharing and even a simple reminder all hit the subscription wall — users feel cheated and uninstall.

product.title: The free tier is enough for everyday work
product.plus: Despite the paywall complaints, many run the free version for years and get reminders, lists, tags and widgets with no ads.

product.title: A lifesaver for the ADHD brain
product.plus: People with ADHD specifically call out that it helps their executive function and keeps the chaos of tasks in one clear view.

product.title: Cross-device sync misbehaves
product.minus: Tasks and habits fail to sync between phone, PC and watch for hours, sections reset to "not sectioned" — even on a paid account.

product.title: The home-screen widget gets things done in seconds
product.plus: You can check items off straight from the widget without opening the app — for many that's the decisive convenience.

product.title: Forced to pay before you even see the product
product.minus: An onboarding of a dozen screens demanding your email and pushing the purchase before letting you try anything reads as predatory, and many uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Lists, calendar and Pomodoro fused into one app
product.plus: Its core strength is that tasks, calendar events, habits and a Pomodoro timer all live together instead of across five separate apps.

product.title: Unusable without an account and constant connection
product.minus: Just to make a to-do list you're forced to create a Google account, and the model expects the app stay open — otherwise reminders don't arrive.

product.title: Reminders and alarms fire blind
product.minus: The alarm rings with no notification and no idea which task it's for, and for some the phone vibrates even after notifications are fully disabled — the app ignores Android permissions.

product.title: False ads for an AI feature that isn't there
product.minus: People buy Pro for an advertised AI tool that doesn't exist and feel scammed; others are angry that AI was added where they didn't want it at all.

product.title: Watch and Wear OS are a stripped second-class experience
product.minus: On Galaxy Watch some functions don't work and bounce you back to the phone, with no tiles or complications — users envy the Apple Watch experience.

product.title: Voice task entry simply doesn't work
product.minus: Creating reminders by voice consistently fails even with the Google app installed.

product.title: Ads took over the app even for people who already paid
product.minus: Users who paid years ago for 'pro' or a one-off upgrade suddenly saw large banners covering up to half the screen, plus a new offer to pay again to remove them — read by many as a bait-and-switch.

product.title: Logged hours vanish — and it wrecks invoicing
product.minus: Sudden data loss — after an update, a reinstall, or just out of nowhere — is the most painful failure: people can't invoice clients because worked shifts disappear from the calendar, sometimes even with a backup in place.

product.title: Restore from Google Drive often fails when switching phones
product.minus: Moving to a new device is a weak spot: the Google Drive backup won't import back, auto-sync between phone and tablet fails, and 'restored successfully' sometimes brings back nothing.

product.title: Paid once — yet asked to pay again
product.minus: The 'not a subscription, just a one-off payment' promise doesn't hold: people hit the invoice fee again, discover a £15.99 surcharge to share Excel files, and can't tell 'No General Ads' from 'No All Ads' — the monetization is confusing and stacked in tiers.

product.title: A hidden paid trial: 'free' turns into a costly trap
product.minus: The app looks free, and only after sinking days into setup does the user find buried in a menu that it's a trial — with a 'pro' price (around $37) that feels several times too high for a phone app.

product.title: Updates break what worked fine for years
product.minus: Recent updates bring regressions: date sorting removed, the date picker now covers the whole screen, punch-out loops entries into a 9-to-5, and old version 13.2 is the only one where the timer notification still works.

product.title: Years of reliability as a simple offline timesheet with no account
product.plus: The core value is simplicity and stability: people track hours for 5+ years, love that it works fully offline with no cloud or login, and rely on the punch-in/out button and widget for a quick start.

product.title: Invoices and automatic earnings calc save a ton of time
product.plus: For freelancers and contractors the killer benefit is that the app calculates earnings, overtime and holiday pay itself, and turns punches into a professional invoice you send and mark paid in one tap.

product.title: Flexibility across many clients, rates and pay types
product.plus: A standout for complex billing: different rates and flat/hourly per client, billable and non-billable lines, multi-project tracking — users say flat-out that other apps can't do this.

product.title: A responsive developer who actually ships requests
product.plus: A rare asset for a niche app — the developer corresponds with users directly, fixes bugs within a couple of days, and incorporates ALL the suggestions people raise, which deepens loyalty.

product.title: Overtime and night-shift math doesn't work as expected
product.minus: There are gaps under the hood: overtime won't calculate or works incorrectly, a 18:00–06:00 night shift is read as one giant day, and OT isn't pooled across multiple projects for the same client.

product.title: Power comes at a setup cost — and there's no iOS version
product.minus: The depth of features comes with a learning curve: initial setup is involved and unintuitive, it's overkill for simple needs, and what users call the best app of its kind can't be installed on iPhone.

product.title: The 2024 update turned an instant tool into a slow, laggy one
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after the major update, every action — start, stop, switching project, changing screens — comes with seconds of waiting and a spinning circle, where everything used to be instant.

product.title: The update wiped years of records, and backup restore didn't work
product.minus: For a tool people bill clients from, this is fatal: users lost projects, tasks and months or years of logs with no warning, and backup files would say "restore complete" yet show nothing.

product.title: Relentless email spam even after uninstalling and unsubscribing
product.minus: Installing the app signs you up for emails you can't escape: people uninstall, hit unsubscribe, mark as spam — and the messages keep arriving weekly, sometimes for years.

product.title: A $100+/year subscription hidden behind a "free" trial
product.minus: Nowhere in the store does it say this is a subscription: people install it as free, then get locked out after a trial and asked for roughly $100–120 a year, forced to a separate website to even find the price.

product.title: Text fields jump the cursor to the end, and dates land a day early
product.minus: Two specific post-update bugs enrage daily users: editing notes or names forces the cursor to the end of the line, and the calendar picks the previous day — making entries nearly impossible to edit.

product.title: Every update resets your settings, including backup frequency
product.minus: A small annoyance that hits the most sensitive spot: after each update settings and preferences reset and the backup schedule flips itself back to "daily" — which users only notice once they've already lost something.

product.title: Cross-device sync — the main paid feature — disagrees on the numbers
product.minus: People pay the subscription specifically for sync, yet get different totals on two phones and find hours, locations and billing material don't transfer — the paid feature failing at the one job it's bought for.

product.title: On Galaxy Watch the app crashes and won't sync
product.minus: Wear OS is an advertised draw that pulls buyers in, but in practice on the Galaxy Watch 4 the app crashes instantly, clock in/out won't sync, and you can't scroll the project list with the bezel.

product.title: One-tap start-pause-stop plus a widget make tracking thoughtless
product.plus: What users love most: open it, hit start, and you're tracking — no login, no fuss. The home-screen widget lets you clock in even with dirty hands, and tracking becomes a habit you don't think about.

product.title: Excel export turns hours into ready-to-send client invoices
product.plus: For freelancers and contractors this is the decisive feature: a clear, customizable Excel export handles invoicing and reporting, and some users replaced both QuickBooks and a punch clock with it.

product.title: A generous free tier that doesn't cripple the app and earns "buy a coffee" donations
product.plus: A rare honest freemium: the free tier is fully functional, ad-free and pop-up-free, so people use it for free for years and then donate a "coffee" out of sheer gratitude.

product.title: Project, tag and rate flexibility handles many clients and roles
product.plus: The app's strength is in slicing time: projects, tags, colors and rates let you split hours across clients, roles and tasks, while the interface still isn't cluttered for those who only want start-stop.

product.title: Auto-playing audio ads blare out in waiting rooms and offices
product.minus: The single most common complaint: open a date and a video ad unmutes itself at full volume, sometimes even in silent mode. People are scared to open the app at the doctor's, at work, in a restaurant; you can mute it, but moving to another date brings the sound straight back.

product.title: Burying memos deep in menus broke a feature families relied on
product.minus: Memos (shopping lists, to-dos, notes) used to open right from the home screen, but after the update they're buried several taps deep inside a specific calendar. For many users memos were the whole reason they used the app, and now they're leaving for competitors.

product.title: The calendar-navigation revamp overcomplicated everything
product.minus: After the redesign you must first pick a calendar, then hunt for the right tab; buttons move from page to page, events land in the wrong calendar by accident, and labels get scrambled. Many long-time users beg for the old interface back, or at least an option to keep it.

product.title: A forever-subscription for "just a calendar" reads as greed
product.minus: Paying monthly forever for a calendar feels absurd to people, especially when the subscription can't be bought once and shared with the family — each person needs their own paid account. Many ask for a one-time purchase or a family plan and leave, calling the ad-removal-by-subscription model extortion.

product.title: Updates cut off support for older devices
product.minus: Users suddenly lose access: the app demands an update, but the Play Store says it's "no longer compatible with your device." People who'd been on TimeTree since 2020 are left with a locked calendar and no way back in.

product.title: No export or sync — your data is trapped
product.minus: You can't export TimeTree events to Google Calendar or Outlook, and deleting them means going one at a time through a multi-step process. After piling up years of entries, users find themselves locked in: either start a fresh calendar from scratch, or stay forever.

product.title: Sync failures and vanishing events erode trust
product.minus: After updates people lose saved appointments, events won't save, a partner's additions don't sync, and shopping-list items disappear on their own. For an app where users keep hospital appointments and work schedules, these losses cut especially deep.

product.title: AI training on user data and a new privacy policy spook users
product.minus: The fresh policy lets the app collect names, notes, locations, photos and behaviour and feed it all into AI services. Some users see this as selling their personal data and leave on principle; bolting AI onto a calendar also strikes them as pointless.

product.title: Multiple colour-coded calendars in one app — a lifeline for families and couples
product.plus: What users love most: you can keep separate calendars (work, family, personal, business) yet see them all at once, everything colour-coded. Mixed iPhone-and-Android families, couples, divorced parents, small businesses — all praise it as the thing that finally brought order to their lives.

product.title: The free version genuinely does the job — a rare honesty
product.plus: Many use it free for years and stress that everything they need is available without a subscription, storage is plenty, and some even pay "to support the devs" rather than out of necessity. For a subset of users the ads really are unobtrusive and stay out of the way.

product.title: Per-event chat and notes turn the calendar into a comms tool
product.plus: Users value that every event has its own message thread and that you can attach photos, notes, locations and reminders. For collaborating, coordinating shifts and planning hangouts with friends it works as an extension of the group chat.

product.title: Simple, visual, ADHD-friendly — it lifts the schedule anxiety
product.plus: Many call it a lifeline for organising their lives: intuitive design, clarity, colour-coding. Several note it's the only planner they've managed to stick with consistently, including people with ADHD.

product.title: Missing flexible recurrence and editing options
product.minus: Users miss recurrence options like "every 4 weeks" or "the last Saturday of the month," bulk-deleting events, and quick time edits without extra taps. For bills, shifts and cyclical tasks the current repeat options simply aren't enough.

product.title: Notifications and reminders keep silently breaking
product.minus: The single most common complaint: notifications, reminders and the persistent alert work for a day or two, then go silent. Without them the whole point of the planner is lost — the user gets no cue when a block starts.

product.title: Basic features are locked behind premium
product.minus: Many bristle that marking a block 'done', the time tracker and focus mode aren't free. The 'done' checkbox feels like a basic feature, not a premium one — even the phone's default Notes app has it.

product.title: Visual time-blocking rescues people with time blindness
product.plus: The biggest love: the visual block layout of the day helps people with ADHD and time blindness actually see and manage their time. For visual thinkers it just clicks.

product.title: Simple yet powerful — usable even without premium
product.plus: For many the free tier is plenty: clean, no bloat, barely any ads. Simple enough not to overwhelm, deep enough to genuinely plan a day.

product.title: Day templates are loved, but repeat and template paste misfire
product.minus: Templates and day-repeat are the headline feature, but for some they break: 'repeat day' duplicates blocks in the wrong order with wrong timings, and a saved template never pastes back.

product.title: No cross-device sync or cloud backup
product.minus: The schedule lives on one device only: no cloud, no sync across devices. Switching phones means re-entering everything.

product.title: Weak Google Calendar integration
product.minus: Google Calendar sync technically exists, but its events show without notifications and the schedule has to be rebuilt by hand — which puts off would-be paying users.

product.title: Affordable pricing and a rare lifetime option
product.plus: Premium is praised for fair pricing and, above all, a one-time lifetime option instead of a subscription. People buy lifetime even just to support a good app.

product.title: Can't schedule more than a month ahead
product.minus: A hard horizon limit: even in the paid version you can't schedule beyond a month ahead — which hurts students who need to plan a whole semester.

product.title: Widget fails to refresh or show the current block
product.minus: The widget often won't refresh or show the current time-block in real time, even though other calendar widgets on the same phone work without any tweaking.

product.title: Updates break the familiar look and removed the white background
product.minus: Some long-time users resent the redesigns: the clean white background is gone, replaced by a distracting colored one, and the day view changed — people miss the old version.

product.title: Users want subtasks, notes and a dedicated to-do list
product.minus: A recurring ask to expand: subtasks inside blocks, daily notes, file attachments and a separate untimed to-do list. As it stands, users keep a second app alongside it.

product.title: A steep start that pays off once it clicks
product.minus: The learning curve is higher than expected: at first the app confuses and takes time to get used to. Many admit it didn't click immediately — even those who later praise it.

product.title: Natural-language task entry is the standout reason people stay
product.plus: You write or speak a task in plain words and the app parses the date, time and recurrence itself. Users call it a joy and the single thing that makes Todoist great.

product.title: The $60/year price and the doubled tariff are a reason to leave
product.minus: The sharp price hike (up to 3100 INR in India vs TickTick's 1390) angers even loyal users. People say the app helped with their disability but is now unaffordable, and they switch to free alternatives.

product.title: Core features (calendar, deadlines, reminders) are locked behind the paywall
product.minus: Calendar view, deadlines, more than one reminder, more than 5 projects and filters are all behind Pro. Users find charging for deadlines in a to-do app absurd and call the free tier a limp trial.

product.title: Reminders simply don't fire — it breaks the core use case
product.minus: Notifications for individual tasks stop arriving (often after an update), while the morning and evening summaries still come. People miss things because of Todoist and leave after turning off every battery saver.

product.title: The send button turns into a mic after you switch away
product.minus: After the voice-input update the red send button shares space with the record button: switch away and back and it no longer turns into save, forcing a force-close after every single task.

product.title: Forced sign-up before you can even try it drives people off
product.minus: You can't even try the app without an account and email. Many delete it on principle, and for others the sign-up just freezes on the welcome screen or fails outright.

product.title: Login and sign-up are broken: Google fails, every password is 'too weak'
product.minus: Google auth throws exceptions, and on sign-up the password is rejected as too weak even at 25–128 characters with special symbols. People can't get in and uninstall before they start.

product.title: Engagement spam emails you can't unsubscribe from in one click
product.minus: The app sends daily 'create/check a list' emails and signs you up for newsletters without asking, while unsubscribe works one category at a time or not at all — people block the sender as spam.

product.title: Completing a recurring task late corrupts the next day's schedule
product.minus: Mark yesterday's daily task done today and the app also completes today's, and shifts the time the user set by hand. Plain daily repeats sometimes just don't show up the next day at all.

product.title: Tasks vanish and don't save, and sync diverges from the web
product.minus: Entries disappear, duplicate or revert to an old version; collapse a list and 20 tasks are gone. Meanwhile the web shows a completely different state and manual sync does nothing — fatal for a to-do app.

product.title: Gamification and 'helpful' nudges feel hostile to neurodivergent users
product.minus: Confetti, achievements, 'overdue' labels and '0/5' counters create artificial shame and anxiety. ADHD users call it the opposite of accessible, even as other ADHD users call the same app a lifesaver.

product.title: Demand for a one-time / lifetime purchase instead of a subscription
product.minus: The very idea that a to-do list is a subscription service strikes people as insane. Many, especially from lower-income countries, explicitly ask for a one-time or lifetime option and refuse to pay recurring.

product.title: Cross-platform sync and widgets keep people for years
product.plus: For most this is an indispensable daily tool: clean sync across phone, desktop and web, great widgets, watch support and an API. People call it the best to-do app after trying many others.

product.title: The widget breaks after almost every update
product.minus: The home-screen widget is a favorite feature, yet it stops loading or loses its add-task button on practically every update, forcing users to delete and re-add it.

product.title: Silent, unresponsive support even for paying subscribers
product.minus: Support requests (calendar-sync failures, a cancelled subscription with no refund, Pro reverting to basic with money still charged) go unanswered for days, directly hurting users' productivity.

product.title: A lifesaver for people with ADHD and for students
product.plus: Many ADHD users and students call it life-changing: it helps them see what needs doing, remember the small stuff and lower cognitive load, all with a short learning curve.

product.title: Removed the "start from previous entry's end" button — breaking the core workflow
product.minus: The single most common complaint: an update killed the one-click button that snapped a new entry's start to the previous one's end. Now you have to drag a circular slider — slow and imprecise, especially when reconstructing the day after the fact.

product.title: Low-friction timer: one tap and tracking is on
product.plus: The headline love: an interface where starting, stopping and resuming a task takes seconds. You can start the timer before even naming the entry, and a home-screen widget begins counting in one tap without opening the app.

product.title: Mandatory sign-up: you can't even peek inside without an account
product.minus: People are put off that you can't see the app without handing over your data — no local storage, no demo. For a time tracker, a forced login plus a marketing opt-in reads as data harvesting and instantly kills trust.

product.title: "Free" with a catch: a month of premium, then a paywall
product.minus: A frequent grievance: the app presents itself as free, silently enables a premium trial, then after a month hides basic things (report export, viewing old data, others' hours) behind a ~€10/mo subscription. People feel baited.

product.title: Cluttered, unintuitive UI for simple needs
product.minus: For people who just want to "start a timer and see hours", the mobile UI feels like a chaotic pile of text and buttons. Many admit the web version is excellent — it's the app, trying to do too much at once, that frustrates them.

product.title: Login buttons dead, constant logouts
product.minus: A painful class of bugs: the Sign in / Sign up, SSO and Apple buttons simply don't respond (only Google works), and after an update the app keeps kicking users out. Logging back in mid-workday is agony.

product.title: Sync breaks: "you're offline" and lost hours
product.minus: Trust in a tracker is undermined when it loses sync with the web and stubbornly shows "offline" with a live connection, or even drops already-recorded hours. For a tool where the data is a client's money, that's critical.

product.title: "You were removed from a workspace" bug locks out new users
product.minus: A brutal first-run bug: a brand-new user gets stuck on a message that someone removed them from a workspace that doesn't exist. "Try again" and "create workspace" buttons do nothing — there's no way in at all.

product.title: Pomodoro with no end-of-session sound — a years-old bug
product.minus: Many love the built-in Pomodoro, but it has an annoying hole: the sound plays only at the start of a session and break, not at the timer's end, so you can't tell when it's done. Users note the bug has lingered for three years.

product.title: Cross-platform: phone and desktop, seamless
product.plus: What keeps people for years: the same tracking lives seamlessly across phone, PC and browser, with effortless switching between devices. For people who work wherever they are, that's the decisive advantage.

product.title: Generous free tier covers real needs
product.plus: Despite the paywall gripes, many are won over by how much the free plan gives: reports, weekly goals, no ads. For personal tracking by students and freelancers, the free tier is enough without any subscription.

product.title: Projects, tags and reports reveal where time goes
product.plus: A strength for those who stay: flexible categorization by project, client and tag, plus clear reports and weekly goals. People say they finally saw their patterns for real and became more productive.

product.title: Premium sells bank sync, which is the least reliable part of the product
product.minus: People pay (often lifetime, up front) for one feature — automatic bank sync — and it drops every few days, demands constant re-authorization, and stays broken for months. Activation and value diverge: the user has already paid, but the exact feature he paid for doesn't work, which produces the angriest reviews.

product.title: Bank coverage ends where half the user base lives
product.minus: Sync is built for the US and Europe, while the reviews come from India, Mexico, Indonesia, Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Qatar, Botswana. A user buys premium specifically for his bank — then learns after paying that his country or bank isn't on the list. This isn't a bug but a structural segmentation failure: the product sells a feature globally that it supports only regionally.

product.title: You can't create top-level categories, only ones under a subcategory
product.minus: Everyone's spending structure is different, but the app only lets you add sub-sub-categories inside its bloated default list — never a root category. For an app whose whole job is to mirror YOUR money, being unable to make your own category breaks the basic premise; it surfaces from both fans and people who therefore can't use the app at all.

product.title: Manual entry isn't the fallback — it's the happiest path
product.plus: Paradox: the people who never connect a bank and type expenses by hand are the most satisfied segment. They get the visuals (pie charts, category breakdowns), spending awareness, and zero dependence on fragile sync. The product effectively rests on manual trackers while monetizing automation. The signal for a competitor: the core value lives in fast simple entry and visualization, not in integrations.

product.title: Spending visuals turn logging into awareness
product.plus: The core behavioral effect isn't 'I logged it' but 'I saw it'. Pie charts and category breakdowns give people their first-ever overview of where money goes and catch accidental overspending. The exact words — 'aware', 'whole picture', 'reality check' — recur among the most loyal. The product sells not bookkeeping but the feeling of being in control of money.

product.title: The lifetime license is the main trust anchor in a category of forever-subscriptions
product.plus: The 'pay once instead of an endless subscription' option is its own reason to love the product: people explicitly say they chose it because they weren't forced into a forever subscription, and switched from competitors like YNAB for it. That's a strong trust signal in a category where everyone milks you monthly.

product.title: Forced login wipes local data and destroys trust
product.minus: An update that forces account login wiped some people's prior records, and spontaneous sign-outs 'lose' all data. For a finance tracker the data IS the product; making it vanish because of a login requirement turns multi-year users into ex-users in a single update. The 'tie everything to the cloud' decision works against retention here.

product.title: A chunk of the audience refuses to hand over banking passwords — and wants offline
product.minus: A whole segment deliberately refuses automation because sync demands their net-banking username, password, and OTP. These people just want offline tracking with no email and no account access — and run into a product that pulls ever harder toward cloud and integrations. Strategically it's a fork: the privacy segment and the sync segment want opposite things, and the product optimizes for the latter.

product.title: The web + app combo with cross-device sync holds the most devoted users
product.plus: When the cloud works, it works for retention: people value that the same data lives in the browser and on the phone and syncs fast across devices. For multi-year users that's the reason not to leave — the app becomes part of a daily routine, not a one-off utility.

product.title: Frozen exchange rates break the books for multi-currency users
product.minus: The app does multi-currency, but rates are fixed and don't update, and changing a rate rewrites the entire history instead of keeping the rate as of each transaction's date. For people with foreign accounts and several currencies this turns the 'financial overview' into wrong numbers — breaking exactly the use case they picked a flexible app for.

product.title: A rigid monthly cycle doesn't match people's pay rhythms
product.minus: Budgets and periods are tied to the calendar month or 'last 30 days', but people live on their own cycles: paid every 4 weeks, twice-monthly, a personal period from the 7th to the 7th. Not being able to shift the period start forces manual budget re-entry every time and breaks planning — for a budgeting app that hits the core.

product.title: Logging a single expense is a 'circus' of extra swipes and taps
product.minus: The most frequent action — quickly jotting an amount and a name — is made clumsy: adding a description requires swiping into a side panel, and labels appear by default so you remove them every single time. For an app that lives on daily manual entry, friction in this micro-flow directly erodes the very habit it's installed for.

product.title: Sync that duplicates and loses records poisons shared use
product.minus: When two people (a couple, a family) or several devices share the app, sync spawns duplicates, drops records, and jumps between accounts. The demand for a 'shared budget with your partner' is right there in the reviews, but the current sync engine makes exactly that scenario unbearable — the product misses a natural growth path through households.

product.title: Income analysis is the blind spot of an app that nails expenses
product.minus: The app's whole strength is breaking down spending by category with charts, but it shows income flat: no equivalent breakdown of how much comes from where. Users explicitly ask for mirror-image income analytics. For a product that builds its identity on the 'full financial picture', it's an asymmetry that leaves half the picture in the dark.

product.title: Years-long loyalty: "the only one I always come back to"
product.plus: The core of the 5-star reviews are people who've used it for 2-10 years: the first thing they install on a new phone, an indispensable daily tool for lists, tasks and notes.

product.title: Ads pop up instantly and get in the way while you're typing
product.minus: Ads greet you right at launch, flood the screen and intrude while typing and reading; for a note app that feels absurd.

product.title: Pricey subscription instead of a one-off purchase puts people off
product.minus: The price to remove ads and unlock basic features is a monthly or yearly subscription ($40/yr, £6, Rs 2600), not a one-off; many would pay once but won't subscribe.

product.title: Notes vanish on sync and when switching phones
product.minus: After a sync or a move to a new phone, people lose years of accumulated notes — they end up in the trash, in an empty app, or gone entirely.

product.title: Cursor jumps to the end of the document after every keystroke
product.minus: When editing a long note the app keeps snapping the position to the end or top of the document, forcing you to scroll back — a real obstacle for heavy writers.

product.title: Rating prompt pops up before you've even used it
product.minus: The app asks for a rating right after install, before you've tried anything; some users read this as a red flag and a trick to farm stars.

product.title: Consent screen hands your data to hundreds of ad vendors
product.minus: A pop-up offers to share your data with hundreds of third-party vendors, with toggles on by default — this drives privacy-conscious users away and gets the app uninstalled.

product.title: Calendar and widgets keep your whole life in one place
product.plus: The combo of calendar, notes and home-screen mini-widgets is a top loved feature: appointments, medications, shopping lists and tasks all at hand — something even Google Calendar doesn't give.

product.title: Color-coding and category tabs make notes easy to find
product.plus: Splitting notes into category tabs, colors and emoji on the nav bar is exactly what people praise: everything stays neat, organized and quick to find.
