product.minus: By far the most common complaint: things that were free for years — group games, adding players, HCP rounds, basic stats — now require a Gold subscription. People say outright they're switching to competitors.

product.title: GPS rangefinder is paid yet frequently wrong
product.minus: GPS is locked behind payment while rivals give it free, and when it does run it confuses holes, sends you to the wrong tee box, or pins you on a different course. No front/middle/back option.

product.title: Sign-up is broken: «bad request» and you can't decline notifications
product.minus: Many simply can't create an account — declining notifications throws a «bad request» or «something went wrong» error and setup won't continue. The forced mandatory login annoys people on its own.

product.title: The subscription jumps in price and is hard to cancel
product.minus: Prices leap (from £4 to £15/mo, from $25 to $80), people get charged more than promised, and cancellation is buried so deep they delete the account to stop paying. Double-charges and refused refunds too.

product.title: Lag, freezes and crashes on Android
product.minus: It freezes mid-round, crashes on launch and lags through menus — especially on Samsung and Pixel. Often only a reinstall helps, which is maddening on the course.

product.title: A long influencer splash screen slows every action
product.minus: Before every interaction — entering scores, checking distance — a 5+ second loading screen with YouTube golfers appears. Longtime users feel the «influencer» turn has bloated and slowed the app.

product.title: Forced fullscreen mode hides the navigation buttons
product.minus: The app runs in a forced fullscreen mode, so on Samsung its on-screen buttons sit on top of Android's system buttons — some options simply can't be reached.

product.title: Ads even after paying
product.minus: The free version is buried in ads and slow menus, but the real sting is that ads remain even for paying Gold users — and support ignores the complaints.

product.title: No smartwatch support — a recurring request
product.minus: The top feature request: a client for Wear OS, Samsung Galaxy Watch, Garmin and Pixel Watch. Several say they'd subscribe outright if a watch were supported.

product.title: The live group leaderboard is what people love it for
product.plus: The core strength: on tournaments, golf trips and big groups everyone sees each other's scores live and can follow other flights. For group play it's best in class.

product.title: Easy score entry and clear stats to analyze your game
product.plus: Happy users praise the easy score entry instead of a paper card and the clear stats — fairways, GIR, putts, chips — that help spot weak areas and improve.

product.title: Lots of game formats — but people want even more
product.plus: A rich set of formats — Ryder Cup, skins, Stableford, better ball — makes rounds more varied and fun, and the new Ryder Cup mode draws special praise. Still, many ask for yet more formats and individual games.

product.title: A timer that needs the internet breaks the entire point of fasting
product.minus: The single simplest action — ending a fast so you can eat — was made dependent on a server round-trip. A user stands at the fridge unable to close their fast while the app syncs; for a tool whose only job is to mark a moment in time, that's absurd, and people leave for offline alternatives like Fast Times.

product.title: Years of loyalty became the loudest source of anger
product.minus: The angriest reviews come not from new users but from 5-7-year veterans with hundreds of logged fasts and long streaks. They're trapped by their data history, watch the app rot, and leave feeling betrayed — which destroys the brand's core asset: word-of-mouth from long-time advocates.

product.title: 30+ second load times in real time kill the motivation to fast
product.minus: To start or end a fast at the right minute, users have to relaunch the app several times and wait. For a habit tracker this is fatal: instead of motivation it injects frustration at the exact moment accuracy matters, so people start back-dating their times or quit entirely.

product.title: A white screen instead of the timer — the core product simply vanishes
product.minus: The most common failure hits the one thing the app exists for: the main timer screen renders as a blank white box while secondary tabs (calendar, premium) load fine. Users can neither see their current fast nor stop it — the product keeps everything except its reason to exist.

product.title: A mandatory onboarding questionnaire scares people off before the first timer
product.minus: Just to start a timer, the app forces account creation and a long questionnaire of personal data, then overrides the user's own target with a 'recommended' weight. For the impulsive 'I'll start fasting right now' intent this is too high a barrier — people quit during onboarding before ever reaching the product.

product.title: The inability to edit or delete a fast breaks trust in the data
product.minus: An accidental one-minute fast can't be deleted, and editing times throws an 'overlaps an existing fast' error. For a tracker whose value is a clean history and streaks, one uncorrectable mistake poisons all the stats, and the user leaves to find a tool they can trust.

product.title: Forcing the timer to never go past 'now' blocks recording a real fast
product.minus: The time selector snaps the choice back if it goes past 'now' and won't save a fast longer than the preset. As a result you can't manually enter an already-running 48-hour fast or log when a fast ran over plan — the app imposes its own model of time instead of the user's reality.

product.title: Bloating into a health platform crowded out the simple timer people loved
product.minus: Goal rings, water, steps, food, sleep and 'four pillars' piled on top of the timer and effectively buried the quick answer to the only question: how long have I been fasting. Users who want fasting alone can't switch the extras off — and leave for minimalist competitors or a paper journal.

product.title: Broken streaks and badges snuff out the exact motivator that held the habit
product.minus: 1800+ day streaks suddenly reset, and 50-day badges fail to unlock or repeat themselves. Gamification is the core retention hook of a habit tracker; when it starts lying about progress, the disciplined user loses the reason to keep logging here at all.

product.title: No watch app keeps users chained to their phone
product.minus: Many users beg for a Wear OS / Samsung / Garmin version to start and end fasts from the wrist. Fasting is a background process measured in hours, and having to pull out the phone for a single tap rubs against the habit itself; this is the one missing thing keeping the most loyal users from five stars.

product.title: The widget is the lifeline when the app itself won't load
product.minus: The home-screen widget became the only way to start and end a fast for users whose app hangs — but it too works only half the time, shows blanks or weird numbers, and won't let you change a fast's length. The last fallback into the product turned out as unreliable as the main one.

product.title: When it works, it's the category's best — a simple, visual fasting tracker
product.plus: Despite the failures, the core is still praised as the benchmark: a clear progress wheel, a toggle between time-elapsed and time-left, fasting stages, and encouraging notifications near the finish. This legible visualization of progress is exactly why people stay for years and recommend it to IF beginners.

product.title: Built-in content and fast stages turn the timer into a coach for the hard moment
product.plus: For beginners the strongest asset is the educational articles, videos and the explanation of what the body does hour by hour. When willpower fades mid-fast, users open the app to re-motivate themselves — the product retains them not with the timer but by answering 'why am I doing this'.

product.title: Broken health integrations force manual entry and kill the convenience
product.minus: Links to Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung Health, Health Connect and Oura either don't sync or broke entirely after the Google Fit API shutdown. A user who wants 'everything in one place' is forced to re-enter weight, sleep and activity by hand — and leaves for a tool where the data flows in automatically.

product.title: The paywall lands before the product ever proves its value
product.minus: A full-screen trial pop-up covers the app with no close button and reopens after every swipe, so a new user sees not the timer but a demand for card details. The activation gate slams shut before the first fast — churn happens before the person ever learns what the product is for.

product.title: The AI food scanner is the hook that removes the biggest barrier to tracking
product.plus: Photographing a plate to get calories and macros removes the manual-entry grind that makes people quit trackers. This is the feature that converts skeptics into payers: users say they didn't believe it would work, tried it, and subscribed. The scanner does the very job the app exists for, and becomes the reason people come back.

product.title: Visualizing fasting stages turns abstract waiting into observable progress
product.plus: By showing what happens in the body hour by hour — ketosis, autophagy, HGH — the app makes users feel the fasting window is working for them right now. It turns a dull timer into an educational narrative that sustains motivation through the hard hours and sets Fastic apart from a plain stopwatch.

product.title: A long quiz before showing the product is a filter that drives away the curious
product.minus: Before a user sees a single screen of the app, they're marched through dozens of personal questions for 10–30 minutes. People who searched for a 'simple fasting timer' bail halfway and uninstall before ever reaching the value. The onboarding was designed as a funnel to payment but works as a wall — it filters out exactly the people who wanted to try first.

product.title: A thin, inaccurate food database undercuts the AI scanner's own promise
product.minus: The scanner sells itself on 'no manual entry,' but the database is so small and inaccurate that half of foods aren't found and calories land multiples off. Users end up typing and correcting everything by hand — the exact chore they were fleeing. The app sells automation but delivers manual labor, and that's what breaks trust in the numbers.

product.title: Gamification and 'frosties' destroy accuracy for serious fasters
product.minus: Built to demand daily engagement, the app starts inferring behavior for you: skip a few days and it auto-marks 'frosties' — freebie non-fasting days — and treats long fasts as unfinished. For the disciplined faster who came precisely for accurate tracking, this turns the history into fiction that's painful to correct by hand.

product.title: Rigid measurement units alienate anyone who doesn't think in grams
product.minus: Food logging only accepts portions in grams or fluid ounces — no cups, spoons, or package servings. American users, who measure food differently in the kitchen, are forced into a calculator at every meal. A small product decision makes the core daily task — logging what you ate — so laborious that people give up.

product.title: No fasting widget removes the app from sight at the exact moment of fasting
product.minus: The app has widgets for steps, water, and weight, but none for fasting itself — the core function. Without it, the timer isn't visible on the home screen, and users lose the constant nudge that they're in a fasting window. Long-time paying users have asked for years and been ignored, which pushes them to competitors over one missing piece.

product.title: Refusing to sync with fitness ecosystems makes the app an island
product.minus: The app won't pull from Samsung Health, Google Fit, Fitbit, or Garmin, forcing users to manually duplicate steps, weight, and sleep. For anyone with an existing health ecosystem, that means double entry and inaccurate numbers — and a direct reason to leave for Cronometer or Noom. The missing integrations turn 'all-in-one' into just another siloed data source.

product.title: Community and shared fasting turn discipline into a social commitment
product.plus: Small beginner groups starting the same day, fasting alongside a friend inside the app, and moderated chats create the mutual accountability a solo timer can't. For the core audience — beginners who struggle to hold a routine alone — this turns an abstract goal into a commitment to real people and keeps them in on the hard days.

product.title: Explaining the 'why' makes Fastic a teaching tool for fasting beginners
product.plus: Beyond the timer, the app offers lessons, articles, and recipes that explain how to do intermittent fasting and eat well. For a beginner who doesn't know where to start, this lowers the entry barrier and builds the habit through understanding rather than blind rule-following. Users name this educational layer as the reason they stay for years.

product.title: Bundling fasting, food, water, and steps into one screen is the core of loyalty
product.plus: Users stick with the app because it closes the entire weight-control ritual in one place: the fasting window, calories and macros, water, steps, weight. It removes the hopping between several apps and lowers the friction of daily tracking. For a weight-loser who values simplicity, this all-in-one flow is what makes Fastic a product they return to.

product.title: Real weight-loss results are the strongest proof the method works
product.plus: The warmest reviews are about results: people lose 20, 50, 56 pounds, one user 100 over two years, and keep it off. The app supplies structure, motivation, and habit, and for many it's the only thing that has ever worked — and that proven payoff is what creates years-long loyalty and word-of-mouth.

product.title: The product's main hook sits behind a monetization wall that hits before value is proven
product.minus: Strategically, Fastic puts its best feature — the AI food scanner — and basic tracking behind a wall and a barrage of promos that fire on every action: start fast, end fast, log a meal. Users hit the wall before the product proves its value; long-time fans who praised the free version for years leave at the exact point where monetization friction outweighs benefit. Churn lands before activation, not after.

product.title: Explaining fasting phases during the fast turns endurance into curiosity
product.plus: The real retention engine isn't the timer — it's the feed that tells you in real time which stage your body is in (fat-burning, autophagy, etc.). It reframes hunger from 'enduring emptiness' into 'watching a process': users deliberately open the app in the hard final hours to read what's happening inside, and that gives them a reason to wait it out.

product.title: The faster wants a stopwatch and gets a quiz and a 'contract'
product.minus: A huge segment arrives with one job — 'just time my fast' — and slams into a multi-screen onboarding that demands an account and 'signing a contract' for what they see as a stopwatch. This entry friction repels pragmatists before the product proves anything: they delete it right at the sign-up step.

product.title: Rigid plan presets break anyone whose fast doesn't fit the template
product.minus: The app pushes its own fasting windows and resists manual editing: people on 23:1, 18:6, OMAD or shift schedules find their window simply isn't offered or can't be set by hand. For experienced fasters with their own protocol it's a disqualifier — the product argues with their body instead of serving it.

product.title: The weekly plan reset punishes you for one missed Monday
product.minus: The design forces you to rebuild your plan every week and can't recur or shift the start day. Forget to restart once and you're manually editing each day's times to get back on track. It turns a habit routine into weekly admin work and burns out exactly the people who'd already committed.

product.title: A genuinely generous free tier converts skeptics into defenders
product.plus: In a niche where almost everything sits behind a paywall, BodyFast wins by making the free tier actually sufficient: tracker, water reminders, daily tips, custom plans. This creates a rare class of loyal free users who return for years and themselves rebut the 'scam' accusations in reviews — the free tier functions as proof of value.

product.title: Water reminders, not the fasting itself, turn out to be the most-loved feature
product.plus: A paradox: users repeatedly name the water reminder, not the fasting timer, as their favorite feature. It's an easy-to-complete micro-habit that delivers a daily sense of accomplishment — it hooks the user on a small win while the big goal (weight loss) is still far off. A cheap feature carries an outsized share of retention.

product.title: A forced weight-loss-and-BMI frame alienates already-lean users
product.minus: The app is hardwired to weight loss: it computes BMI, labels the user 'overweight,' and pushes them to drop weight — even those fasting for autophagy, mental clarity, or maintaining shape at low body fat. This segment (fit users, men, non-dieters) feels the product isn't for them and leaves — the name 'fasting tracker' promises something the inside doesn't deliver.

product.title: The AI food scanner dazzles but falls apart on edits and accuracy
product.minus: Photo-scanning your plate is a hook that pulls people in ('it nailed what was in my food!'), but it can't retain them: recognition is wrong, the result can't be edited, and for some it just stops working after a couple of days. A flashy demo feature without reliability becomes a letdown right when the user starts to trust it.

product.title: The paid 'coach' turns out to be googlable tips and kills trust
product.minus: Those who do pay for the coach expecting a personal mentor get generic fasting tips available in any article and a feedback-free PDF. The gap between 'coach in your pocket' marketing and the 'drip-feed of facts' reality erodes trust in the very users most willing to pay — they feel cheated not by the price but by the hollowness of the promise.

product.title: The locked weekly evaluation holds the free user's progress hostage
product.minus: The 'evaluate your week' screen is tied to paid coaching, and for free users it freezes, trapping them with no way back to fasting tracking. The paywall sits across the core loop, not on an add-on feature — the user is locked in an upsell screen that blocks the very thing they came for. It's the worst kind of paywall: it breaks the free product rather than extending the paid one.

product.title: Low blame for slipping is the real stress-reliever for those who break
product.plus: A core retention strength is the absence of judgment. People who fear diets precisely because of the guilt of breaking them note the app doesn't pressure: you can shift the window, break the fast, and get no scolding. This retains the 'slipper' segment that quits stricter trackers — the product forgives, so users return after a lapse instead of deleting it.

product.title: A 'phase right now' widget is the missing link for an out-of-app habit
product.minus: The most common power-user request is a home-screen widget showing whether you're fasting or eating and how long is left. The ask reveals a behavioral truth: for the habit to hold, status must be visible without opening the app. The missing widget forces a full open every time, and that friction is where rivals with widgets win.

product.title: No count-up timer — the app won't let you savor what you've already endured
product.minus: The timer shows only the countdown to the goal, not how many hours you've already held. It misses a powerful motivator: pride in distance covered. Fasters want to see accumulated progress as an in-the-moment reward, while a countdown only highlights the pain remaining. A simple mirror metric would turn the ordeal into an achievement — its absence flattens the motivation loop.

product.title: The update meant to streamline time changes broke the one edge it had
product.minus: Changing fasting windows used to be instant — 'boom boom boom and done' — and that's precisely what set BodyFast apart from rivals. After an update the same step became a multi-tap slog through each day. The app dismantled the very feature people chose it for and turned loyal fans into churners — a lesson in the cost of regressing the core of the experience.

product.title: Drip-fed daily tips keep the IF beginner on a short hook
product.plus: For total fasting newcomers the winning mechanism is the drip: a new tip, habit, or phase explanation each day. It gives a reason to open the app daily and lowers the fear of a method that looks complicated. The beginner segment stays because the app leads them by the hand in small steps rather than dumping everything at once — for them the 'coach in your pocket' feels real.

product.title: The mascot overseer IS the product: it hooks some and shames others out
product.minus: When you miss a log the cartoon (Blinky/Pinky/Avo) turns passive-aggressive — "hoping I'm happy without him," a sad face, crossed arms. For users who came to get healthy this backfires: shame reads as punishment, not motivation, and they quit over the tone itself, not the features.

product.title: For another segment the same mascot is the core retention hook
product.plus: Users wired for the playful attachment log their food specifically to get the character's reaction: "I like logging my meals because of the positive feedback." The mascot turns the chore of tracking into a tiny relationship, and people return daily for the approval, not the data — that's the daily-open engine.

product.title: The ad promises tai chi and walking; inside it's diet and fasting — the funnel breaks trust on screen one
product.minus: People are acquired by ads for a "free tai chi / walking / sore-knee exercise plan," then land in a fasting-and-food-logging app. Expectation and product don't match, so users bail before any first taste of value — the acquired traffic is mismatched to the core.

product.title: The AI coach botches basic nutrition and undermines the whole point of tracking
product.minus: The headline feature — "smart" food analysis — fails systematically: plain chicken breast gets 13 carbs, raw spinach is flagged "too high in sodium," brands and ingredients aren't recognized. Users came for tracking accuracy and instead get numbers they must fact-check — the product fails its core job.

product.title: The AI overrides the medical limits users explicitly enter
product.minus: People spell it out — wheelchair, back pain, need regular meals — and the coach still prescribes standing workouts, a bike ride against doctor's orders, or fasting until noon. The most vulnerable segment (seniors, people with limitations) is both the frequent audience and exactly who the product actively loses.

product.title: The fasting timer — nominally the core — breaks for exactly the serious fasters
product.minus: The schedule won't hold the window: start times autofill wrong, long fasts (24–40+ hours) lose their data, days bleed into each other. The paradox: the app is named for fasting, yet the advanced faster is precisely whom the timer fails — only beginners on standard windows get the value.

product.title: The "macros over calories" design is both a draw and a quiet risk
product.minus: Some users pick the app precisely because it ditches calories — it lowers food anxiety. But the same logic cuts the other way: the "energy" goal closes before the real intake target, signaling "stop eating" too early — for eating-disorder-prone users that nudges behavior in a dangerous direction.

product.title: Inability to edit a logged meal destroys trust in the data
product.minus: After an AI mistake (and it makes many) the user can't fix the entry — no editing of the dish or the scanned portion weight. The error becomes permanent, careful tracking loses its point, and the most motivated "disciplined loggers" hit this wall hardest.

product.title: Duplicate reminders for already-done actions turn motivation into annoyance
product.minus: The app pushes "log your weight/food" when it's already checked off hours earlier, and prompts snacks in the middle of a fasting window. The reminder system doesn't reconcile with its own state — the nagging undermines the very habit it was meant to cement.

product.title: Accountability via the daily check-in is the strongest real driver of results
product.plus: Users who click describe the same mechanism: the daily logging of food, water, weight and movement keeps them honest, and on that they drop 10–34 lbs. The value isn't fasting per se but the ritual of honest daily tracking — the app wins people who need external accountability.

product.title: The AI coach removes confession-shame — users are more honest with a bot than they'd be with a human
product.plus: An unexpected mechanism: some users admit it's easier to disclose "shameful" eating slips to a non-human, which raises logging honesty. For people embarrassed by a live dietitian, the AI format lowers the barrier — and that, not accuracy, is what retains them.

product.title: Plans adapted to age, illness and low mobility win a forgotten segment
product.plus: When personalization lands, it captures people fitness apps usually ignore: 70–80-year-olds, PCOS sufferers, post-surgery recoverers. Low-impact at-home workouts tuned to energy level deliver results where generic apps scare them off with difficulty.

product.title: Teaching "what to eat" rather than just counting is what makes users stay
product.plus: The loudest praise isn't for the timer but for the app teaching diet composition — protein, fiber, portions, single-serving recipes. People frame it as "learning to eat for the rest of my life": the product sells a skill, not a diet, which yields retention beyond the first weight drop.

product.title: The "calibration" progress gimmick punishes the most disciplined
product.minus: The "calibration percentage" meant to reward consistency gets stuck: the user checks in every single day, yet the counter hangs on "day 29" and threatens to reset. Gamification that punishes the ideal user destroys faith in the progress system — losing the very best, paying-through-term customers.

product.title: Broken step sync and data drift undercut the "all-in-one" promise
product.minus: The "all-in-one place" promise rides on data integration, but steps don't sync, 3,000 garden steps have nowhere to go, and entered weight and times silently change. When the aggregator can't aggregate reliably, users fall back to MyFitnessPal — the product loses on its own positioning.

product.title: The quiz promises a personalized plan, but inside you just pick the same options yourself
product.minus: A long quiz about age, weight and goals sets up the expectation of an individualized program — yet after payment the user picks their own fasting window, decides what to eat and logs their own workouts. The gap between the pitch and the product turns "personalization" into the single biggest source of regret and refund demands: people pay for an algorithm and get a set of presets.

product.title: Activity sync is locked to Fitbit and Google only, blinding the app to everyone else
product.minus: Steps and activity are pulled exclusively from Fitbit or Google, with no manual entry at all. A huge slice of users on Samsung, Garmin, Apple or Polar watches is shut out: their workouts, swimming and aerobics simply never reach the daily picture, and the app sees only part of their real effort. For a wellness product this is a blind spot that hollows out the log for an entire segment.

product.title: Explaining the fasting stages changes behavior — that's the real retention hook
product.plus: Tips about what happens in the body at each stage (entering fat-burning) act as a behavioral anchor: knowing fat-burning is about to kick in, users skip the snack and push the fast to the finish. That turns the timer from a passive counter into a motivator, and it's exactly this effect beginners reward with high ratings — the app gives the wait a meaning instead of just ticking off hours.

product.title: Custom meals don't persist, turning food logging into a daily grind
product.minus: The food database is thin, so most items must be entered by hand — but those custom entries don't carry across categories and get wiped fast: what you log for lunch can't be picked for dinner, and "recent" holds data a day or two. So someone who eats the same things spends ten minutes re-entering them every time. This breakage kills the daily logging habit and pushes people to MyFitnessPal.

product.title: The barcode scanner and calorie counts are wrong — the core tracking tool erodes trust
product.minus: The barcode scanner fails even on mass-market products, and the database calories diverge from the labels: a 70-kcal serving suddenly jumps to 540 when selected. When the very tool people install a weight-loss app for hands back wrong numbers, users stop trusting it and count calories by hand via Google — meaning the product no longer does its core job.

product.title: For the IF audience the timer is a commodity easily replaced by the phone clock
product.minus: The core of the product — counting down the fasting window — is something users see any free alarm or calendar already does. Over and over comes "it's just a timer, I can do this on my phone." This positioning vulnerability means all the value rests not on the timer but on the layer above it (recipes, stages, reminders) — and if that layer doesn't convince, the product instantly collapses to a free alternative.

product.title: Start/end-fast notifications don't "stick" — and the app punishes users for its own glitch
product.minus: When users start or end a fast via a push notification, the action often fails to record, and the app then accuses them of "missing a fast." Inside the app everything is fine — so the failure is in the engagement channel itself. Users work around it by turning notifications off and doing everything manually. But that breaks the main retention mechanism — the reminders that should pull people back instead manufacture false reproaches.

product.title: A scolding message for missing the eating window alienates the users it should support
product.minus: If a user steps even a couple of seconds past the allotted eating window, the app fires off a reproachful message. For an audience already wrestling with eating habits, a judgmental tone is a sure way to push them out: discipline turns into guilt. This is a product decision about voice, and it works against retention precisely for the people who need gentle support, not punishment.

product.title: The branded scale is a proprietary brick without the app — a risky hardware-to-software lock-in
product.minus: The DoFasting smart scale measures not just weight but muscle mass, water, bone density and BMI — yet all of it is unlocked only through the app. When the app breaks or the subscription lapses, the expensive device drops to being a plain scale. Tying valuable hardware to unstable software creates a double point of failure: a user who bought the scale feels held hostage, and a single pairing error zeroes out the whole purchase.

product.title: Simple onboarding and water tracking win the beginners who need structure
product.plus: For first-time intermittent fasters, the low barrier to entry is the real strength: the app sets the schedule, reminds you when to start and stop, and keeps water, calories and weight in one place. That tidiness and the "third-eye" feeling give a beginner the structure they can't impose alone, and this is exactly where the early-weeks weight-loss success stories cluster.

product.title: Recipes hold the Western user but miss real diets and keto/Asian cuisine
product.minus: The recipe library is a clear plus for many, but the "personalized" selections ignore the stated diet: a keto plan surfaces pasta, bread and potatoes, and there's almost no Asian or Indonesian cuisine. A user who doesn't know better won't lose weight on that plan, and an experienced one won't trust the curation. Recipes create the appearance of personalization, but without a diet filter they undermine trust in the program as a coherent nutrition system.

product.title: US-only measurement units with no toggle alienate the international audience
product.minus: Water in ounces, no millilitres, litres or pints, prices and calories in dollar logic — and no toggle to familiar units. British, South African and other non-US users immediately hit the need to convert every figure just to enter data. This localization gap creates instant friction in the most frequent action (logging water and food) and tanks engagement across an entire geographic segment.

product.title: Marketing under "Fast Like a Girl" promises cyclical fasting the app doesn't have
product.minus: The app surfaces in searches for the popular book Fast Like a Girl about cycle-synced fasting for women — yet there is no cycle tracking and no adjusting of fasts to its phases inside. Women who came specifically for that feel misled, all the more since the product team has a female Head of Nutrition. The mismatch between positioning and functionality loses exactly the segment the targeted marketing attracted.

product.title: No back-dating of food entries breaks logging for busy and forgetful users
product.minus: If a user forgets to enter food on time, they can't add it for yesterday — logging only works on the day of consumption, before day's end. For a busy, forgetful audience this hard limit means gaps in the diary that can never be filled, and therefore a wrong calorie picture. The product demands the very discipline it should be compensating for, and loses the people whose day doesn't always go to plan.

product.title: The subscription charges before the product ever proves its value
product.minus: The quiz dead-ends straight into a "subscribe" screen, with full access gated until payment — so the user must pay before seeing any value at all. In a niche where the skeptic's core objection is "a free timer does the same," demanding money up front is a strategically losing moment: churn happens before activation, before the fasting stages and recipes ever get a chance to hook. This isn't a price gripe — it's a sequencing error in how value gets proven.

product.title: You can't fix a window after the fact — and that kills tracking for the most disciplined users
product.minus: The app's core promised job — an honest record of fasts — breaks on the simplest scenario: you forget to tap start at night or stop in the morning. You can't move to yesterday's date to correct the time, and you can't delete a mistaken fast. So the app punishes exactly the people who take fasting seriously and want an accurate picture: one missed tap and the whole day is lost, the streak broken. This isn't a bug, it's the absence of basic edit mechanics.

product.title: The timer opens and closes windows on its own — users lose trust in their own data
product.minus: Many users describe the exact same behavior: the app ends a fast in the middle of the night, or opens an eating window at 2–3 am, on its own and even while closed. Because you can't fix it by hand, the user sees provably false numbers in their stats — '43 hours fasted instead of 19.' For a tracker whose only value is timing accuracy, a timer that resets itself voids trust in the entire product.

product.title: Real-time 'what's happening in your body right now' turns a timer into a motivator
product.plus: The strongest retention mechanic is the notes tied to each hour of the fast, explaining fat-burning stages and what the body is doing. People read them at exactly the moment they need willpower to push through, which turns a boring counter into a source of motivation. It's the rare content that pulls users back into the app rather than just glancing at a number.

product.title: Manual mode with a backdated start is the one feature that forgives real life
product.plus: Unlike the rigid preset plans, manual mode lets you start the count and, when needed, push the fast's start back to 'yesterday, 10 pm' for someone who only opens the app in the morning. For people who fast intuitively — longer on weekdays, shorter on weekends — it's exactly the flexibility the rest of the product lacks, and it's what earns five stars.

product.title: Quiet notifications and auto-windows remove the burden of deciding from the user
product.plus: When notifications work, they deliver exactly the right amount of nudging — 'time to eat,' 'fast starting,' 'drink water' — without the intrusiveness people complain about in competitors. The window schedule fires automatically per your setup, so you don't have to manually start each day. This 'just-right amount of reminders' is what separates it from a plain phone alarm and keeps IF beginners on track.

product.title: Challenges and a daily journal turn tracking into a habit through gamification
product.plus: Beyond the timer, the app adds daily challenges and a one-minute journal you complete. This turns passive tracking into an active engagement ritual: the user has something to 'do' every day, not just watch a clock. This combination is what keeps people longer than a bare tracker, and it's repeatedly named as the reason they stay.

product.title: The eating window shows in the timeline but not in the stats — half the audience never gets their number
product.minus: A meaningful share of users track not the fast but the length of the eating window — for them that's the control metric. The app draws the eating window in the timeline but never surfaces it in the monthly stats or overview, and on Android the toggle to switch the view is missing entirely. So a whole segment sees their key number only in passing and can't lean on it — the product silently denies them the very job they came for.

product.title: No cross-device sync, and history vanishes when you switch phones
product.minus: The app never builds a real account with cloud history: data doesn't carry to a tablet, doesn't sync between phone and web, and on a device switch or reinstall the entire progress is gone for good. For a product whose value is the long arc of progress and a months-long streak, the lack of sync makes accumulated motivation disposable — and breaks retention precisely once the user has already invested.

product.title: Knowing the fasting stages gives beginners a sense of grounding and lowers anxiety
product.plus: For people trying IF for the first time, the app works less like a counter and more like a coach: step-by-step explanations, tips and context remove the fear of 'am I doing this right.' Users describe feeling 'supported and connected,' confident to continue. This positions the product as an onboarding ramp into intermittent fasting for beginners rather than a tool for veterans — and in that segment it wins.

product.title: The actual product (fasts longer than 12 hours) sits behind a wall — free users hit it before any value
product.minus: Strategically the app gives away for free exactly what IF practitioners don't need: a single 12-hour preset and a 'manual' timer. But the classic 16:8, Warrior, and ADF — the very reason someone installs a fasting tracker — are locked. So the user hits the wall before the product ever proves its value: 'start plan' leads straight to payment. It's an inverted funnel — the wall stands before activation, not after — so churn lands earlier than engagement ever does.

product.title: Notes with photos exist but get cut off when read — the journaling feature is half-useless
product.minus: The ability to attach a note and photo to a fast attracts people who keep a reflective journal, but the implementation breaks the use case: a long note shows in preview, yet on opening the text starts in the middle and some lines are unreachable; on some phones the keyboard covers the input field. A feature that could be a retention anchor for the thoughtful segment instead repels exactly them — the people who write a lot.

product.title: Rigidly linking the eating window to the fast won't let you end early without shifting the whole day
product.minus: The fast and eating windows are rigidly coupled: end a fast 30 minutes early and the app immediately shifts the eating window's start 30 minutes earlier, firing notifications at the wrong time. There's no setting to 'end the fast early without touching the next day.' For a flexible practitioner whose days vary, this turns a helper into an irritant and breaks the feeling of control over one's own schedule.

product.title: Water and weight are built in but cut off and uneditable — the companion trackers are half-baked
product.minus: The app pulls adjacent habits — water and weight — into one dashboard, which many see as a plus. But the execution limps: weight can be logged only a few times before a wall; yesterday's missed water can't be entered due to the same no-edit-past-days flaw; there's no Fitbit link, so you double-enter everything. The companion trackers fail their job and push users toward parallel apps instead of keeping them inside.

product.title: A clean, uncluttered interface lowers the barrier to the discipline of fasting
product.plus: Visual simplicity is a real competitive strength: users explicitly call the interface modern, pleasant and not overloaded, contrasting it with heavier rivals like Fastic and Zero. When the task demands daily discipline, low interface friction directly raises the odds the user keeps going. It's not cosmetic but a retention factor: 'just what I need to get started.'

product.title: Ads are pinned to the moment of logging — the very action that builds the habit
product.minus: The free tier's monetization is strategically self-defeating: ads fire not on a session timer but after every food entry — 1-2 full-screen clips (dismissable only by opening a Play Store page) plus premium screens. Yazio thus drowns in ads the exact action that should become a habit — logging. A 10-second entry stretches into minutes, the new user never feels the product's value, and leaves: impression revenue kills activation.

product.title: Duolingo-style gamification annoys even paying users
product.minus: Streaks, a yeti mascot, chests, diamonds, and an "I'm committed" screen on every launch turned a simple tracker into a clingy game. There's no way to switch it off even with premium, and long-time subscribers leave repeating one thing: "Don't be Duolingo."

product.title: An endless onboarding survey scares people off before they ever reach the app
product.minus: Before the first use you must answer dozens of personal questions (down to "how many kids you have" and "which clothes you'd wear after losing weight"), you can't skip them, and at the end there's a paywall and a discount wheel. Many uninstall mid-signup.

product.title: Animations and meal tips can't be turned off, even with premium
product.minus: After every logged meal there's a screen of slow animations and "meal tips" you have to wait through or click away. Users have begged for a toggle in settings for years — Yazio's answer is that it's "by design."

product.title: AI photo recognition systematically underestimates calories
product.minus: The headline feature — calories from a photo — consistently misses, underestimating by 30-40% versus manual entry and barely knowing non-European cuisines. You can't correct the scan, so people end up entering everything by hand — after paying for the AI.

product.title: The May 2026 update took the app down: "no internet" on a working Wi-Fi
product.minus: After the April-May 2026 update, paying users couldn't log food for whole days: the app demands a constant connection, throws "no internet" on working Wi-Fi plus 502/412 errors, and there's no offline mode or status page.

product.title: Replacing manual entry with an AI chat and the redesign broke the familiar workflow
product.minus: Recent updates removed the "add manually" button in favor of AI text, buried Recently/Frequent/Favorites inside a dropdown, and swapped icons for menus — so a simple action now takes several extra clicks. Long-time users are furious.

product.title: The onboarding survey repeats every time you pause for a few days
product.minus: Skip the app for a few days and on return it drags you back through the same long survey about weight and goals, with no skip option. It happens even to paying users and feels like punishment for using it irregularly.

product.title: The AI "tips" pressure your eating and trigger disorders
product.minus: The mascot and AI critique your food choices after every meal and push you to "swap for something healthier" with no context, which for people with eating disorders feels insulting and drags them back to dark days. Requests for an off toggle are ignored.

product.title: A huge food database and convenient search — the main reason to stay
product.plus: Even the angriest reviewers admit it: Yazio's food database is huge, you can find almost anything, plus you can create custom meals and scan barcodes. It's the reason people endure the ads and stay, calling the database the best thing about the app.

product.title: A pretty, simple, intuitive interface that genuinely helps people lose weight
product.plus: Under the layer of ads sits a beautifully made, simple, pleasant tracker that people actually lose weight with — 9 to 21 kg in a couple of months, streaks of 150+ days. For many it was a years-long favorite, and they cling to it regardless.

product.title: When you get past the bots, support replies fast and actually solves things
product.plus: Despite a wall of AI chatbot, Yazio's human support exists and works: people flip an angry review to 5 stars after a fast reply, a refund, or a bug fix — often within ten minutes.

product.title: Yazio does listen: a snooze for tips appeared — and ratings climbed back
product.plus: Some criticism doesn't fall on deaf ears: the developers added a "snooze tips for 2 weeks" option and a way to skip the post-scan hints almost entirely — and several users publicly raised their rating, noting logging is enjoyable again.

product.title: Double-counting steps and calories — dangerous for anyone tracking a deficit
product.minus: When syncing with trackers, Yazio counts activity twice (both phone steps and watch data), inflating burned calories by up to ~1000 kcal. For an app people rely on to stay in a deficit, that's a direct risk of overeating.

product.title: The fasting timer decides when to end and won't let you edit the past
product.minus: The very reason people install it — the intermittent-fasting tracker — is half-baked: it's locked to the chosen fasting type and ends your fast for you, with no way to set the real start/end or edit past entries, even on the paid plan.

product.title: Basic analytics and data export are locked away or simply missing
product.minus: Even paying users can't export their data (no API or file export for a doctor), weight history is trimmed, and weekly/monthly nutrient summaries simply don't exist — for a tracker, that reads as a missing core feature.

product.title: The real hook isn't the timer — it's the running narration of what your body is doing right now
product.plus: People come back not for the stopwatch but for the per-hour explanation of which fasting phase the body is in. It turns an invisible process into watchable progress and keeps beginners engaged who would otherwise have nothing to look at while fasting.

product.title: A timer pinned in the notification shade makes the fast impossible to forget
product.plus: A persistent counter in the corner and an icon you tap to see fast length embed the app into the background of daily life: users don't open it on purpose but always see their status. This passive nudge is what turns a one-off attempt into a habit.

product.title: Editable start/stop times are the feature that forgives real life
product.plus: Users constantly forget to log the fast start — at work, in a rush. Those who can backfill the time stay. Those who lost the option after an update feel the system is imposing its rules on them and get angry — a direct churn driver.

product.title: Manual start is the silent leak: people 'fast' while the clock never runs
product.minus: The app needs a manual start and stop tap, but the real fast isn't synced to when the user happens to have a phone in hand (work, forgetfulness). Logged hours then diverge from lived hours — which destroys trust in the one number the whole app exists to produce.

product.title: The food diary and barcode scanner spit out garbage data and undermine trust in the core
product.minus: The most ambitious part — photo and barcode food recognition — returns wildly inaccurate numbers you can't correct on the spot. A user who came for honest calorie tracking gets data worse than pen and paper, and carries that distrust onto the whole product.

product.title: The meal scanner is a hook for one segment and dead weight for another
product.plus: One slice of the audience stays precisely because they can photograph a plate and instantly see calories — it removes the friction of googling every dish. But another slice came for a simple fasting timer and sees the whole food module as needless 'just another food diary' bloat.

product.title: Visible weight loss in week one ignites the motivation loop
product.plus: Users repeatedly report losing 2-5 kg in the first days or weeks — it's the fast doing the work, not the app, but it gets credited to the product. An early tangible result locks in the habit faster than any gamification and fuels word-of-mouth.

product.title: Schedule flexibility around real life is what brings lapsed users back
product.plus: Being able to tune the fasting window to your rhythm and resume easily after a break makes the app a 'home' people return to after months or years. It's not a one-shot tool but a tracker that survives the user's own lapses — hence the 'uninstalled, came back, chose it again' reviews.

product.title: A long ad ON LAUNCH turns app open into a waiting room
product.minus: The ad sits not in pauses but at the very entrance — two minutes pass between wanting to log a fast and reaching the screen. For an app whose value is to quickly check status, an entry delay strikes the core use case: people set the phone down and walk away, and some never come back.

product.title: A long onboarding questionnaire scares people off before they ever taste the value
product.minus: Before the first fast, the app runs users through dozens of personal questions and pushes payment right away. Some read this as 'data harvesting, not help' and leave before reaching the main hook — the body-state narration. The activation barrier sits before the value moment.

product.title: Water reminders quietly upgrade the app from fasting timer to daily coach
product.plus: The water tracker with reminders is a surprisingly frequent reason for love: busy people forget to drink, and the app covers that pain alongside fasting. It widens the reason to open it beyond the fast and makes the product feel 'all-in-one' for health rather than a single-purpose stopwatch.

product.title: Fasting reminder notifications sometimes manufacture the hunger they remind about
product.minus: Overly frequent 'you're fasting now' reminders backfire psychologically: the constant focus on hunger makes the user feel a hunger that wasn't there. The retention mechanism works against the very goal — getting through the window without breaking.

product.title: No Google Fit/Health sync cuts off the most valuable segment
product.minus: The most engaged users — those who run their health inside an ecosystem (Google Fit, Health Connect, glucose readers, fitness bands) — hit the app's isolation. Manual weight entry and no data export force duplicate work, and these are the very people who say 'add it and I'll give 5 stars.'

product.title: Broken BMI math is a reputational landmine for a health app
product.minus: When a health tracker calls a thin person 'overweight' and nudges them to lose more, it isn't just a wrong number — it hands potentially dangerous advice to people at risk of eating disorders. For a product claiming the health-coach role, this error costs the trust of the whole category, not one feature.

product.title: Streaks and daily tips are the lightweight gamification that holds the beginner
product.plus: The streak challenge and daily tips give a beginner a reason to open the app every day and the thrill of not breaking the chain. In a category where the main enemy is quitting after a week, this cheap hook works directly on retention during the most fragile stretch of the habit.

product.title: No diet constraints or non-standard regimens make the app feel 'not for me'
product.minus: The app recommends chicken to a vegetarian and can't handle OMAD or custom plans — it imposes an averaged scenario. Users with their own regimen or diet feel the product doesn't see them, and either ignore the recommendations or leave for a more flexible competitor.

product.title: Narrating fasting stages turns a timer into a lesson and keeps beginners hooked
product.plus: The real retention hook for a beginner isn't the countdown — it's the app narrating which fasting stage you're in right now and why. That gives the boring wait a meaning: people come back to read what's happening to their body rather than stare at a number. This is exactly what first-time fasters give five stars for.

product.title: Water reminders are the real product people actually change behavior for
product.plus: The strongest behavioral lever here isn't fasting, it's water: the nag pushes retrain people who barely drank for years. Someone on 200ml a day reaches a litre within a week and credits the app directly. For a non-techy, often older audience this is a micro-habit they genuinely acquire — and it's what makes their pocket friend feel like more than a stopwatch.

product.title: Manual start/stop breaks for anyone who gets distracted — and that's the whole app
product.minus: You must start and stop the fast by hand, and the app can't detect that you've begun. Forget to tap and the day simply isn't logged, or the clock runs forever past your window. A product whose only job is tracking loses the data at the exact moment life distracts the user; people explicitly ask for auto-detection and a start/stop alert that doesn't exist.

product.title: No watch or fitness-tracker sync — steps only count if you carry your phone in your pocket
product.minus: The single most common gripe even among happy paying users: it connects to no Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung Health or smartwatch, and won't let you enter steps manually. Steps only count from a phone in your pocket — yet the target audience (often older, at home) doesn't carry it. The activity core silently zeroes out, and support's advice to just keep your phone on you reads as mockery.

product.title: Under the educational wrapper sits a plain stopwatch, and experienced users see it instantly
product.minus: Once novelty wears off, the product is exposed: for someone already doing 12:12 or 16:8, it does nothing a clock and a notebook can't. Zero personalization, no food database, no barcode scanner — everything is manual. That turns the paid sub into a tax on a timer and pushes anyone who already knows how to fast toward free alternatives.

product.title: The cookie-cutter meal plan ignores allergies, diets and age — breaking trust exactly where it promised personalization
product.minus: The long intake quiz sets the expectation of a tailored plan, then delivers generic: a vegetarian is offered meat, an allergic user gets their allergen, lactose-intolerant gets cheese, a 77-year-old gets a plan with no metabolic adjustment. The promise that your answers mattered is contradicted by the very first recipe, and that feels like a bigger betrayal than any price.

product.title: A hard 23-hour fasting cap shuts out advanced long-fast practitioners
product.minus: The app won't let you set a window longer than 23 hours with a one-hour eating window — exactly what advanced fasters want: 24–36h fasts, alternate-day, author-specific protocols. The hard cap silently tells the advanced user this isn't for you and pins the product at beginner level, losing its most motivated, retainable segment.

product.title: A ~23-screen intake quiz before the paywall defers any proof of value to the very end
product.minus: The one genuinely defining strategic mechanism of the funnel: a long personal-question quiz sits BEFORE any proof of value. The user invests ten minutes and personal data, then discovers nothing works without paying — not even the timer. That moves the is-it-worth-it decision to a point where the product has shown nothing, so churn lands before activation rather than after.

product.title: The onboarding body-image step (flabby/extra) repels the very audience it invites to lose weight
product.minus: The first screen shows photoshopped ideal bodies and forces you to pick a figure type from normal / flabby / extra. For an overweight person — i.e. the target user — that's an instant insult before the product has shown any value. The result is immediate uninstall: an onboarding meant to motivate instead shames and loses the user at first touch.

product.title: A 331-lb starting-weight cap pushes out the heaviest users — the ones who need it most
product.minus: The starting-weight field rejects anything above 331 lb (~150 kg), with no override. Someone at 360 lb who came to lose weight can't even create a profile — the product turns away precisely the segment for whom weight loss matters most. A pounds-to-kilograms auto-conversion bug also corrupts the number at step one. This isn't cosmetic; it's denial of entry at the gate.

product.title: The daily log-meals-water-weight ritual builds a sense of accountability — the core motivator for returners
product.plus: The manual entry that annoys advanced users works as a feature for the target beginner: the very act of logging what you ate and drank makes you more mindful of what goes in your mouth. The app becomes a friend that keeps you honest; accountable, mindful, on track are the words that recur among those actually losing weight. The value is the daily conscious ritual, not automation.

product.title: No way to edit recipes or logs on the fly kills trust in the daily ritual
product.minus: The logging ritual — the beginner's core value — trips over rigidity: you can't fix a same-day logging mistake, can't drop a nut you're allergic to from a recipe, can't add your own dish or swimming/cycling as activity. The menus aren't flexible and repeat month after month. A product that lives on daily engagement punishes every attempt to bend it to your life.

product.title: No built-in calorie counter or food database — users get pushed into MyFitnessPal mid-product
product.minus: Calories must be looked up and typed in by hand, with no food database and no auto-count. Users say outright they keep MyFitnessPal or Fitbit open alongside for the thing this app should do itself. It's a critical hole: a product sold as a nutrition tracker hands its key function to a competitor and undercuts its own why-pay argument.

product.title: Round-the-clock water pushes wake users at night and contradict the app's own sleep advice
product.minus: The very water mechanism that retrains habits becomes a saboteur without scheduling: drink-up pushes fire every two hours including at night, waking and annoying users — even as the app itself teaches that good sleep is critical to weight loss. There's no quiet window, and turning notifications off entirely breaks the core. The main retention lever becomes a cause of churn.

product.title: The lessons and recipes give beginners the structure they lack trying to fast alone
product.plus: For someone who doesn't know where to start, the value is ready-made structure: daily lessons on the science of fasting, recipes matched to the chosen plan, small achievable goals. It removes the what-do-I-even-do paralysis and replaces willpower dieting with a guided process. Users who failed to fast on their own credit exactly this structure and prompting for keeping them on track and delivering first results.

product.title: Onboarding feels like signing a contract, not starting a timer
product.minus: The first-run flow is framed as a "contract" with pledges and commitments — which cements adherence for those who want a program, but repels the large segment who came for a simple fasting window: they quit before their first fast even starts.

product.title: You can't set your own window manually — the app imposes its plans
product.minus: Custom windows like 18/6, 20/4 or 23/1 are either unavailable or locked behind the paid "coach" plan: the product refuses to serve people who already have a routine, losing the segment most committed to fasting — experienced practitioners.

product.title: No manual start/stop — the app won't trust your actual fast
product.minus: No free start/stop and no way to log a fast that began yesterday means the tracker records the plan, not reality: a user who fasted on their own terms can't log it — and leaves for an app that just listens to a button.

product.title: The window must be rebuilt by hand every week — plans don't repeat
product.minus: Each week the schedule resets and must be re-entered day by day; there's no recurring week or saved plan — turning a routine into manual labor and hitting people with irregular schedules (night shifts) hardest, who churn on friction rather than on fasting itself.

product.title: The headline feature — the "coach" — turns out to be a PDF of generic tips, not a mentor
product.minus: The paid "coach" that the whole subscription sells turns out to be generic internet-grade tips with no personal feedback or workouts — the promise of a personal mentor goes unmet, and payers feel they overpaid for what Google gives free.

product.title: Explaining fasting stages hour by hour is what keeps people in
product.plus: A feed that shows in real time which phase the body is in turns dull waiting into learning and gives meaning to each hour — it's this education, not the timer, that keeps beginners on the program and helps them time workouts.

product.title: Water reminders are the unexpected hook that retains even non-payers
product.plus: Simple prompts to drink water and log fluids become a daily habit people keep the app for — a small, unobtrusive mechanic makes fasting bearable and brings users back every day, even on the free tier.

product.title: The weight-and-BMI framing alienates the already-lean and the maintainers
product.minus: The app is hard-wired around weight loss, BMI and dropping pounds — pushing "lose more" even at people with low body fat and ignoring those who fast for health or maintenance, expelling a valuable segment that could have stayed for the long term.

product.title: Photo food scanning impresses — then breaks on day three
product.minus: Scanning a plate by photo wows users at first and pulls them toward the paid tier, but it can't be corrected when wrong and simply stops working after a couple of days — the lure feature breaks exactly when the user starts relying on it, undermining trust in the paid product.

product.title: The generous free tier — not the subscription — is the real retention engine
product.plus: A free tier rich enough to deliver real value without paying (plans, tracking, tips, water) is what keeps people for years and creates advocates — those who can't or won't pay still stay and recommend the app.

product.title: Ready-made weekly plans remove choice paralysis for beginners
product.plus: Pre-built weekly plans and the "power week" give a beginner rails: they don't have to decide how long to fast — the app tells them when to eat and when not, and that structure turns a tentative attempt into a sticky habit with visible results.

product.title: Editing the hours in the schedule is the core daily pain
product.minus: Even happy users stumble on time-editing: it's unintuitive, snaps back to 00:00, demands clicks per day — and a recent "improvement" made it slower, turning a former killer feature of instant edits into a source of frustration.

product.title: No home-screen widget and no count-up timer — a gap versus rivals
product.minus: Users miss a home-screen widget and a count-up timer (how long you've already fasted, not just what's left) — small things, but exactly what keeps someone connected to progress between sessions, and their absence drives people to rivals that have them.

product.title: A bare timer wrapped as a "program" — repelling those who just want a countdown
product.minus: An account, a quiz, goals and BMI are bolted onto what the user wants as a simple countdown — the excess scaffolding raises the bar and pushes minimalism-seekers out: "why an account for a timer?" is a structural positioning conflict, not a bug.

product.title: A no-pressure, judgment-free tone retains the anxious and the lapse-prone
product.plus: No shaming for slipping and a gentle framing of goals create a safe space for those who fear "failing" — people who quit other diets stay because the app doesn't make them feel guilty, turning a one-off attempt into a lifestyle.

product.title: The paywall lands before the product proves its value
product.minus: Core actions — choosing your own window, evaluating your week, unlocking OMAD — hit a subscription before any first result, so the user meets the demand to pay before getting any payoff: churn arrives before activation, not after.

product.title: Subscription ads hit the people who already paid for maps
product.minus: You buy the World Pack or offline maps as a one-time payment and still get full-screen "go Premium" popups on every launch and screen switch. There's no way to turn it off, and it's the number-one reason long-time fans are leaving.

product.title: Lifetime licences and the World Pack suddenly turn into a pumpkin
product.minus: People paid for a "lifetime" licence or world pack and now hit a paywall as if they'd just installed the app. A region promised "free for life" demands payment, and restoring the purchase or getting a refund is impossible.

product.title: Route discovery is what keeps people around
product.plus: The standout strength: it surfaces quiet, safe trails and bike routes even in unfamiliar areas, steers you away from highways and traffic, and leans on its community. For hiking, gravel and MTB it's often called the best mapping out there.

product.title: Post-update the map lags and drops a pin on every tap
product.minus: Recent updates turned a smooth map into a mess: scrolling stutters, every tap drops a stray pin, and planning a route becomes impossible. Many say outright the app became "unusable" right after an update.

product.title: Drains the battery faster than any other map
product.minus: Power draw is its own pain: the phone or watch dies within 1.5–3 hours of a ride, the screen won't sleep despite the settings, and there are reports of wakelocks held even when the app isn't in use. For multi-day or long hikes that's a dealbreaker.

product.title: Navigation sends you the wrong way — onto highways, into rivers, into dead ends
product.minus: Turn-by-turn navigation lets you down: it routes onto dangerous main roads instead of local cycleways, through rivers and private property, instructions arrive late, and dead-end U-turns are routine. Several say the app literally "insisted I walk off a cliff".

product.title: One-time map purchase instead of a subscription — that's the love
product.plus: A historically loved feature: you can buy a region or world pack once and use it with no monthly subscription, unlike Strava and AllTrails. This is the model people paid for and recommended the app over.

product.title: Cancelling a subscription and deleting an account are built like a trap
product.minus: You can't unsubscribe in-app — you're pushed to a browser; the delete-account button doesn't work and loops you through endless auth screens ending in an error. The trial charges immediately, and cancellation is "hidden so well it's close to a scam".

product.title: The Bending Spoons takeover feels like the start of enshittification
product.minus: Long-time users tie the decline directly to the sale to Bending Spoons: the dev team was laid off, ads and AI support replies appeared, and useful features get cut or paywalled. The word "enshittification" comes up again and again.

product.title: The elevation profile now goes full-screen and breaks navigation
product.minus: A specific regression that infuriates many: the elevation profile used to open in a small window you could scroll and measure distances on. After the update a tap expands it full-screen, hiding the map, with no interaction — a loss of a key feature for mountain hikes.

product.title: You can't just follow a route — it forces you to record and save the trip
product.minus: The basic "plot A→B, ride it, leave" flow is broken: navigation only works coupled with activity recording, and at the end the app forces you through 8 save screens. Want to just ride without tracking and social features — you have to fight the UI.

product.title: Garmin, Wahoo and watch sync — when it works, it's brilliant
product.plus: A prized combo for serious riders: routes push to Garmin Edge, Wahoo and smartwatches, with turn-by-turn on the wrist saving phone battery. Many stay with the app specifically for this integration.

product.title: You can't shut up the voice prompts
product.minus: An annoying detail with no off switch: the voice keeps shouting about lost GPS signal or "Let's go!", cutting into your music, with no way to disable it. For some that alone makes the app unusable.

product.title: Mandatory Google/Facebook login often breaks
product.minus: You can't do anything without an account, and the login itself fails: Google and Facebook sign-in errors out, sometimes loops endlessly, and trying to register without internet is pointless. A barrier before you even reach your first route.

product.title: Once-free features moved behind the paywall — a bait-and-switch feeling
product.minus: Long-time users are furious: features they relied on for free for years now require a subscription. Maps, search, activity breakdowns, sharing — they all migrated into Premium one by one, and without paying the app «won't let you do anything».

product.title: Subscription popups on every tap make the app nearly unusable
product.minus: The loudest complaint: you can't press a single button without a «buy Premium» popup. Two popups just for finishing an activity, ads blocking the record button — users call the UX «desperate» and «pathetic».

product.title: Recording cuts out mid-activity and loses the whole route
product.minus: The core technical failure: the app silently stops recording, then greets you at the end with «Strava recovered from a problem» — with nothing actually saved. People lose half-marathons and long rides, and it has gone on for years.

product.title: GPS «bounces» and miscounts distance — stats come out wrong
product.minus: Distance is systematically off: a 30-mile ride logged as 16, a 21-mile ride as 0.11. GPS throws you into the next street from inside a stadium, and in the mountains or among skyscrapers the track falls apart entirely.

product.title: Charges without consent after a «free trial» — money meant for school and food
product.minus: A whole stream of identical stories, especially from the Philippines: 1500–2999 pesos pulled from GCash/bank accounts without confirmation, often money set aside for school. The «free trial» quietly becomes a yearly plan, and refunds get delayed or denied.

product.title: One-time-code login breaks and locks you out of your account
product.minus: Removing Facebook login and switching to 6-digit email codes left people locked out — including paying subscribers. Codes «aren't accepted», an endless «try again with a new code» loop, and support tickets sit unanswered for weeks.

product.title: Support goes silent, and accounts get banned with no explanation
product.minus: Tickets sit for weeks with zero reply, and some users get banned «for logging workouts» with no reason given. Support is described as «non-existent» — not afraid to take your money, but unwilling to help.

product.title: Screenshot interception forces «share» and gets in the way of saving ride data
product.minus: Take a screenshot of your own data and a window pops up saying «just share it through us», with no way to turn it off. It breaks scrolling screenshots and annoys people whose actual share function doesn't show what they want.

product.title: Poor syncing with watches and third-party services
product.minus: Galaxy Watch and Samsung Health, Whoop, Oura, Huawei Health, Shimano E-Tube — integrations either won't connect or import garbage (a 21-minute swim becomes 1h 34min). People end up running two apps at once.

product.title: Forced AI and bloated updates crowd out what used to work
product.minus: Long-time subscribers beg them to «not go down this AI nonsense»: AI insights and AI workouts are useless, the «muscle map» is constantly wrong and can't be disabled, new animations lag. The app gets «worse every update».

product.title: The gold standard for accurate tracking and analytics — when it works
product.plus: For its happy users this is the best tracker out there: accurate GPS, clean breakdowns of distance, pace and segments, clear progress over time. Many call it the «gold standard» for runners and cyclists and praise the low battery drain.

product.title: A social network for athletes that motivates and hasn't drowned in ads or toxicity
product.plus: Its strongest side is the community: kudos, segment leaderboards, challenges and following friends genuinely motivate people to train on days they'd rather not. It's one of the rare social networks people call «good for you».

product.title: Minimize the app and the workout pauses
product.minus: After recent updates, recording stops the moment the screen locks or you switch apps: a nagging "resume" button appeared, and workouts come back fragmented or reset entirely.

product.title: Recorded workouts vanish without a trace
product.minus: The app says "saving" but the history stays empty; it crashes mid-ride and loses the whole result, sometimes hours of it. For people who use it precisely to log workouts, that defeats the entire point.

product.title: You pay for the trainer, then pay again to control it
product.minus: After buying expensive hardware, basic functions — erg mode, resistance control, routes — got locked behind an $18–25/month subscription. Users see it as blatant double-dipping.

product.title: An update yanked heart rate and cadence off the workout screen
product.minus: The "simplified" interface stripped heart rate, cadence, power and calories from the live screen — sometimes leaving just a clock. Those readings were the whole reason people used Wahoo.

product.title: Health Connect sync was suddenly cut
product.minus: The autumn 2024 update removed Google Health Connect / Google Fit sync that many had built their routine around; some manually rolled back to an old version. At times the sync even corrupted other step data.

product.title: Simply pairing a sensor or trainer became a lottery
product.minus: The app fails to find or connect its own Wahoo gear — Bolt, Roam, Kickr — even when it shows up in system Bluetooth. Connections drop mid-ride, and some models are flatly declared "not supported".

product.title: Demands location permission just for a Bluetooth sensor
product.minus: To connect a trainer or heart-rate monitor over Bluetooth, the app insists on precise location access; users read this as data harvesting and refuse, losing the ability to use it.

product.title: The home screen is clogged with junk widgets and social features
product.minus: Once-simple, the app bloated: a home screen littered with suggestions, extra taps before starting, AI "mental fitness" check-ins, constant browser pop-outs. Setting resistance now means navigating a maze of menus.

product.title: Endless prompts to rate the app, even mid-ride
product.minus: The app aggressively begs for a rating and won't let you skip surveys, interrupting the workout. After hundreds of dollars on hardware, that pestering stings.

product.title: Deleting your account is nearly impossible
product.minus: Just to request account deletion you must hand over extra personal info, and the account still isn't deleted. Users suspect the app's main purpose is harvesting data for marketing.

product.title: Pairs any third-party sensor straight to your phone, for free
product.plus: For those it works for, this is the draw: it freely connects heart-rate, cadence and power sensors of any brand — Garmin, Polar, Coros, Scosche — directly to the phone, no separate bike computer needed.

product.title: A serious free alternative to paid subscriptions
product.plus: For many it's a full fitness hub with no subscription or ads: customizable screens and HR zones, support for many activity types, .FIT export — it even replaces Zwift and dodges Strava's data "tax".

product.title: Custom HR zones and profiles for every sport
product.plus: A real strength for zone-based training: custom zones, voice cues, separate profiles for cycling, running, strength, even a wheelchair, plus big readable numbers and zones that light up in real time.

product.title: Seamless auto-upload of workouts to Strava
product.plus: Many keep the app for reliable auto-export to Strava (plus Garmin Connect and Fitbit) — especially those on a stationary bike that Strava can't track on its own.

product.title: A long-hauler that just works for years
product.plus: A substantial group of loyal users have kept it 5–10 years without major issues; some even note responsive support that genuinely resolves things over email.

product.title: Long-free core features got moved behind a paywall
product.minus: What enrages users most isn't the subscription itself but that it walls off things that were free for years: route comparison, maps, progress, audio cues. Many would pay a one-off fee but not a monthly one for what used to be included.

product.title: Tracking dies mid-workout and loses the route
product.minus: The most common failure: recording just stops mid-run or walk, leaving half the distance or nothing at all. It's often blamed on power saving, but people disable everything they can and nothing helps.

product.title: Constant 'always' location demands feel like surveillance
product.minus: The app demands location access even when not in use and spams pop-ups at every screen unlock. People check and see it really pings GPS in the background for no reason — hurting battery and trust.

product.title: Forces a login every single time you open it
product.minus: A recent update stopped remembering the login: the app demands sign-in on every open, which means it's unusable without internet. For tracking in the mountains or woods off-grid this is a flat-out dealbreaker.

product.title: Locking audio feedback behind premium stings the most
