product.minus: The defining wound of the update: the «adaptive» AI changes weights and reps in saved workouts on its own — sometimes to absurd numbers — breaking the entire point of a workout log. For many the settings toggle simply does nothing.

product.title: Intrusive AI insights and pop-ups fire on every single set
product.minus: The app interrogates you after every set about why you didn't follow its suggested weight and throws «insights» at the start, middle and end of a workout, knocking you out of your flow. You can't turn it off, and it annoys even paying subscribers.

product.title: Even basic logging is now locked behind a «start free» paywall
product.minus: Marketed as the best free app, but after a long questionnaire everything — from your own plans to plain weight tracking — hits an unclosable pay screen. Many call it a bait-and-switch.

product.title: After updates the app hangs on screens like «accumulation» and won't open
product.minus: Recent updates freeze the app on intermediate screens — «accumulation», «intensification», «on ramp», «adapting» — that you can't swipe past. Clearing cache, reinstalling and restarting don't help.

product.title: Updates wipe years of data: notes, plans, workout history
product.minus: Users with 10+ years of history report updates zeroing out saved sessions, per-exercise notes and past records — every lift suddenly a «new PB». For long-timers it's the loss of a journal built over years.

product.title: A huge exercise library with videos is the core that keeps people
product.plus: The most extensive exercise database around: form videos, filters by muscle group and equipment, plus the ability to add your own movements and machines. It's the thing even unhappy users still praise.

product.title: The free tier is genuinely enough — a rarity in the category
product.plus: Long-time users say the free version covers nearly everything you need, with no nagging ads (at least historically). Some pay for Elite not for features but out of sheer affection for the app.

product.title: The go-to long-term progress tracker — across years and decades
product.plus: The anchor strength: people keep 10-15 years of history, value the volume/set/rep tracking, calendar, muscle-group breakdown and the playful volume comparisons (elephants, bridges). It's the «I always come back to it».

product.title: Switching dumbbells to «per dumbbell» broke totals and 1RM
product.minus: The new «per dumbbell» logic mangles total volume and one-rep-max math: with 30kg in each hand it counts only one side, or reports a 1RM of 30kg. Old records logged as total weight get scrambled too.

product.title: Relentless subscription upselling wears down even paying users
product.minus: The «Elite» promo invades the logging screen, pop-ups and notifications — even for people who already subscribed or earned upgrade points they can't spend. The constant «buy» actually makes people want to use it less.

product.title: The interface has bloated: ending a workout drags on for minutes
product.minus: Once simple, the app turned clunky: opening and saving a workout can take up to two minutes, navigation is confusing, and it checks the connection constantly. Cache-clearing and reinstalling don't fix it.

product.title: Integrations (Strava, watch, Fitbit) are promised but half-broken
product.minus: Strava sync works only half the time and doesn't push data back, the watch app got paywalled and shows mismatched weight totals, and Fitbit integration has been requested for ten years with no reply.

product.title: A password leak and spam with no notice erode trust
product.minus: Users report a leaked password surfacing in identity-protection services with no notification, and a flood of spam to the address they gave only to Jefit. Trust in the developer is sliding.

product.title: "Lifetime" access turned out not to be lifetime
product.minus: Hundreds of people paid years ago for a "lifetime" Power Pack — only to find one day that the access was revoked and a subscription demanded instead. Users read it as outright deception and a betrayal of trust.

product.title: Paid-for features were taken away and locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Warmup sets, the plate calculator, history — the very things people paid a one-time fee for — suddenly stopped working with no notice. Users aren't asking for Pro, they just want back exactly what they already paid for.

product.title: Your own workout history held for ransom
product.minus: The most painful part: people lost access to years of their own data — sometimes 10-15 years and thousands of workouts. Just to see your own numbers you now have to take out a subscription.

product.title: Subscription pitched as high-value, though the app is a timer and a spreadsheet
product.minus: For an app that logs numbers and counts plates, a ~$60/year subscription feels absurd. Many say the same thing is easily replicated with a spreadsheet, ChatGPT, or pen and paper.

product.title: You can't even try it without a paid trial sign-up
product.minus: New users are made to go through setup and enter their details, only to hit a mandatory 7-day trial that auto-rolls into a yearly subscription. There's no free version anymore, and it feels like a bait-and-switch.

product.title: The "free" trial charges immediately, and refunds are impossible
product.minus: Several users report that accepting the "one-week free trial" charged them the full yearly amount ($80) on the spot, and Google and the developer point fingers at each other while no refund happens.

product.title: Constant pop-ups and subscription ads get in the way of working out
product.minus: Even before the full lockout, the app nagged with Pro ads on every action — even for those who already owned the Power Pack. Pop-ups blocked working features like warmup sets.

product.title: The simple 5×5 program genuinely gets beginners results
product.plus: For those not driven off by the subscription, the program wins with sheer simplicity: no math, no overthinking — just do it. People describe weight lost, muscle gained, and seeing real strength progress for the first time.

product.title: Automatic weight progression takes all the mental load off the lifter
product.plus: The app manages weight progression, alternates workouts and times rest — users love not having to guess what or how much to lift. For many that's the whole point of value.

product.title: Flexible plan editing and a large exercise library with videos
product.plus: Power users praise the plan editor, rest timers, set variety (regular/drop/pyramid), custom exercises, and form videos. For them it's the best workout tracker around.

product.title: Mehdi's emails and the community are a value of their own beyond the app
product.plus: Loyal users trusted founder Mehdi's advice for years: daily emails, spreadsheets and a mentoring tone gave them knowledge and motivation. It's exactly that trust that makes the subscription turn sting so much.

product.title: Bugs: crashes on launch, resetting workouts, data loss when switching phones
product.minus: Beyond monetization, there are technical complaints: the app crashes on launch even for paid users, workouts reset on their own, and weeks of progress are lost when moving to a new phone.

product.title: The migration to the new app wiped out years of workout history
product.minus: Dozens of users with 10-15 years of history lost everything when moving from BodySpace — workouts, progress photos, stats — nothing carried over and there was no export option.

product.title: The app constantly crashes and freezes mid-workout
product.minus: Crashes on launch, freezes when opening the calendar, and network errors — people spend more time relaunching the app than actually working out.

product.title: Finished workouts don't save and get stuck on the "You crushed it" screen
product.minus: After hitting "end workout" the "You crushed it" animation appears and the app freezes on it — the workout never closes and program progress stays stuck at 0%.

product.title: One accidental tap of "back" wipes out all your logged progress
product.minus: No resume button and no autosave: one wrong swipe or tap sends you back a screen and erases all the weights and reps you entered — you have to start the whole workout over.

product.title: The once-free BodySpace became a $10-15/month paid subscription
product.minus: Free user-made programs were locked behind a paywall and the price was hiked to $15 a month — for a version almost everyone considers worse than the free original.

product.title: A paid subscription isn't recognized — the app demands you pay again
product.minus: People who bought an annual subscription get told to pay again or start a free trial when they try to open a workout, and support replies only with AI templates or stays silent.

product.title: Workout logs don't save and history gets randomized with junk data
product.minus: Weights and reps don't log, history either disappears or fills with random values — tracking real progress through a program becomes impossible.

product.title: A workout tracker was turned into an intrusive social network
product.minus: Instead of easy program browsing there's an Instagram-style feed, people's faces popping up in the menu, and influencer videos at the start that can't be turned off.

product.title: Stripped-down customization: no custom programs and no multiple programs at once
product.minus: Old BodySpace let you build custom workouts and run several programs — now it's one at a time, with no custom exercises, supersets, drop sets, or equipment filters.

product.title: A bloated, unintuitive interface with side-scrolling and too many extra clicks
product.minus: Reaching simple things takes too many clicks, the screen is crowded, side-scrolling is awkward, history is buried in the calendar, and the layout doesn't adapt to foldable screens.

product.title: The programs and coaches themselves are still good — it's all that keeps the app afloat
product.plus: Even amid scathing reviews people admit the content is strong — great programs, coaches like Hannah Eden and Kris Gethin, a useful exercise library. The problem is the engineering, not the material.

product.title: A year of negative reviews and not a single fix: the developers seem to ignore everyone
product.minus: People come back a year later hoping for fixes and find the same bugs; the common refrain is lost progress, crashes, broken history — with no response from the company, only a prompt to buy.

product.title: The sheer variety of programs and coaches is why people stay for years
product.plus: A huge library of workouts for every level, goal and equipment — from bodyweight to gym — with new programs added regularly, so users don't get bored even after 5 years.

product.title: Not just workouts — a holistic bundle of food, meditation and recovery
product.plus: Users value that everything lives in one app: programs, recipes, meditations, sleep and mobility — it feels like complete wellness, not just a set of exercises.

product.title: The coaches motivate you — it feels like training with a friend, not a script
product.plus: Clear exercise delivery, banter and coach encouragement keep people coming back: videos show proper form and the coaches feel like real people guiding you.

product.title: Real results — and a replacement for an expensive personal trainer
product.plus: Users cite concrete numbers — kilos lost, shape gained — and compare a year's subscription to a £200/month personal trainer, deciding the app wins.

product.title: Constant logouts that wipe saved progress
product.minus: The app logs you out on every launch, forces a password reset and erases all recorded progress and saved recipes — for months, with no fix from support.

product.title: A recent update kills music from other apps during a workout
product.minus: After an update you can't play Spotify and keep the workout beeps at once: starting the session kills your music and starting music pauses the session — a choice between no music or no music.

product.title: "Sorry we dropped a dumbbell" — the error that breaks login and workouts
product.minus: The branded error message greets users at sign-up, login and program start; reinstalling doesn't help, and even the cancel-subscription button serves up the same dumbbell excuse.

product.title: Subscription charges even after cancellation — and you can't unsubscribe
product.minus: Annual charges of $80–$153 hit months after cancellation and even after deleting the app; there's no unsubscribe button in-app, and the website loops you back to the app.

product.title: The paywall is hidden until the end of onboarding — "free" in name only
product.minus: Users aren't told the app is paid until they've finished onboarding and handed over personal data; the promised "3 free months" with equipment turn into a 7-day trial demanding a credit card.

product.title: Workouts can't be customized — you take what's forced on you
product.minus: No exercise swaps, no building your own workout or adapting for knees/beginners, no logging weights in guided sessions — the app rigidly dictates what to do with no alternatives.

product.title: Videos and timers freeze right in the middle of a workout
product.minus: The demo freezes, the video won't "play", rest timers stop counting and the beeps vanish — forcing you to skip an exercise or restart the workout; unfixed for months.

product.title: The app "went downhill" after the company was sold — nostalgia for old Centr
product.minus: Long-time subscribers mourn that after the ownership change the Australian feel and community faded, programs grew repetitive with a HYROX bias, and each update makes the app worse.

product.title: Bought Centr-branded equipment — but the app has no workouts for it
product.minus: People buy Centr cable machines, multi-gyms and resistance bands, yet the app offers no programs for that equipment and isn't even compatible with the Inspire gear they bought — money on hardware effectively wasted.

product.title: The library of programs from real coaches is the main reason to stay
product.plus: Again and again, even in angry reviews users concede the program selection is fantastic. Ready-made plans like 5/3/1, Reddit PPL, GZCLP from real coaches and content creators, with auto-progression, technique videos and animations. It is the thing people put up with the app for.

product.title: Sluggish, laggy, and burns seconds on every tap
product.minus: The most frequent complaint: a fundamentally simple app behaves as if it's grinding something heavy in the background. 5+ second startup, a delay on every button press, lag when entering weight and reps. People literally compare it to an Excel spreadsheet — and Excel wins.

product.title: Crashes on launch, stuck on the 'checking for updates' screen
product.minus: For a whole tier of users the app never even reaches the home screen: it shows 'checking for updates' and immediately shuts down with a bug message. Clearing cache, Wi-Fi, reinstalling — nothing helps. For them the product is simply unusable.

product.title: A long onboarding questionnaire that dead-ends at a paywall
product.minus: Advertised as free, the app walks you through a long 'we're tailoring your workout' questionnaire, harvests your data — and only at the end tells you a subscription is required to use it. Many call the questionnaire itself a disguised ad rather than real personalization.

product.title: Swapping an exercise and the rest timer moved behind the paywall — and that stings most
product.minus: The most painful pattern: features that were free for years (swapping an exercise, the rest timer, dark mode, the plate calculator) got steadily locked into Pro. Longtime users read it as a betrayal and drop their rating specifically for it.

product.title: Two full-screen subscription prompts on every single open
product.minus: The redesign brought an aggressive upsell: every launch greets you with one or two full-screen Pro prompts you must dismiss by hand, even mid-workout. People pointedly note these two screens work flawlessly — unlike everything else.

product.title: Loses data on save: you hit 'done' and the day wipes itself
product.minus: The core of the product — the workout log — breaks: after hitting 'save' the day clears, weights don't save on the first try, history gets erased. For a tracker this is fatal, and paying users are especially furious to lose the very thing they paid for.

product.title: Restarts itself the moment you leave the app during rest
product.minus: Switch away to change a song and the app reloads from scratch, eating 15–20 seconds, resetting the rest timer and sometimes kicking you out of the current workout. Against the real gym scenario it turns every set into a fight with the app.

product.title: The new UI broke what was already perfect
product.minus: The redesign is near-unanimously seen as a step back: text overlapping text, everything too big and 'still in beta', programs now hard to find. Many just ask for the old UI back or an option to revert.

product.title: A genuinely generous free tier — that's what wins people over
product.plus: Those who get lucky on performance are delighted: genuinely free programs, progress tracking, technique videos and a PR indicator — all of it ad-free. For many it's the rare case where the free version is so complete it makes them want to pay out of gratitude.

product.title: The subscription feels overpriced — people want a one-time buy, not a rental
product.minus: Even loyal users balk at the price: ~€17 or $20 a month for what amounts to 'automated spreadsheets' feels absurd next to Spotify and Netflix. The recurring ask is a one-time purchase instead of a subscription — many would pay that, but not subscribe.

product.title: 'Home, no equipment' programs still hand you a barbell and parallel bars
product.minus: Equipment-based personalization doesn't work: pick 'home' or 'only bands and a pull-up bar' and you still get barbell bench, dumbbells and parallel-bar raises. People literally suggest scrapping the feature since it fails at its one job.

product.title: The program builder won't reliably save your work
product.minus: The standout feature — building your own program — is in practice unreliable: a created plan drops back to a draft after a day or two, only week one saves, custom workouts get deleted. The rigid UI on top of that won't even let you enter a rep range like '4-6'.

product.title: The rest timer gets fixed, then broken again
product.minus: The rest timer — for many the key reason to buy Pro — has been unreliable for months: doesn't ring, doesn't count, stops when you switch apps. One update fixes it, the next breaks it. For paying users that especially stings.

product.title: Support is barely there — a single co-founder handles tickets
product.minus: Paying users wait weeks for a reply: the in-app 'report issues' link is broken, emails go unanswered, and tickets — by users' accounts — are handled by the co-founder himself. Against the backdrop of subscription charges, the silence pushes people to bank chargebacks.

product.title: The team actually ships fixes and features people ask for
product.plus: The bright side of that same active development: users note requested features (notes, a timer) were actually added, the background timer got fixed, the data-draining issue and the intrusive popups were resolved — and they bump their rating back up to five stars for it.

product.title: A hard «3 workouts then pay» wall hits with no warning
product.minus: By far the most common complaint: the app is presented as free, but after 3 workouts (or ~3 days) it locks you out and demands a subscription. People are furious less about the price than about not being told up front — you only find out when you hit the wall.

product.title: Clear instructions and animations teach proper form
product.plus: The strongest praise: detailed descriptions, videos and animations for each exercise help beginners learn proper form. Many say this is exactly what turned them from «never worked out» into regulars.

product.title: Best pick for a beginner: easy entry and ready-made plans
product.plus: Users repeatedly call it the best of the apps they've tried specifically for starting out: a clear interface, ready-made plans by level, nothing to figure out yourself — just follow along and train.

product.title: You can't swap, reorder or skip exercises in the plan
product.minus: The rigid structure frustrates: the app forces «its» workout of the day, won't let you swap an exercise for your equipment, reorder, or do something other than what's assigned today. Some complain even after paying.

product.title: You can't add your own exercises — the catalog falls short
product.minus: Experienced users are blocked by the inability to add an exercise that isn't in the database: the catalog feels limited, especially for home no-equipment options. Several explicitly promise a 5-star return if the feature is added.

product.title: Huge exercise variety and custom programs
product.plus: For those who value freedom, this is a plus: advanced users note the biggest exercise selection among the apps they've tried, including functional and mobility moves, plus the ability to build your own programs and progressive-overload settings.

product.title: Progress tracking and workout history keep you motivated
product.plus: Long-term users (18 months, 2 years) stick around precisely for tracking weights, sets and history — it keeps motivation up and shows results. Many see body changes within a couple of weeks.

product.title: Set logging is clunky — no editing and no «to failure»
product.minus: The real-time data entry itself annoys: you must input info after every rep, can't fix an already-completed workout, there's no «to failure» option instead of an exact number, and you can't log yesterday's session.

product.title: Kills your music — the timer cuts playback off
product.minus: A specific technical irritant: the app shuts off third-party music (YouTube Music etc.) every time the rest timer fires or you simply switch screens. For training to music that's a deal-breaker.

product.title: Billing breaks: charged, but the subscription never activates
product.minus: A painful cluster: people pay but workouts stay locked; they're charged twice; a refund is shown but never arrives; charges continue after cancellation. Unsubscribing is also called confusing.

product.title: Condescending coaching messages demotivate
product.minus: A surprisingly strong irritant: when you don't complete sets, the app fires snarky «What a pity right?» remarks. Paying users find this disrespectful and demotivating, especially when the workout was actually done.

product.title: Won't sync with trackers and watches
product.minus: A frequent deal-breaker for wearable owners: no working sync with Google Fit / Health Connect, Samsung Health, Huawei Watch, and no watch app for Android. Heart-rate and step data stay siloed.

product.title: Calories and units are handled sloppily
product.minus: Small but grating flaws: the calorie count is clearly off if weights aren't exactly as recommended; no kg-instead-of-lbs option or you must dig into settings; height is entered in feet without inches. For some it's reason enough to call the app unusable.

product.title: Paid for premium, premium never unlocks
product.minus: The single most common complaint: money taken, receipt issued, the Google Play transaction shows complete — yet the app still shows basic. Trying to activate throws an «already purchased» error and the loop closes. Support is silent and refunds are near impossible.

product.title: Used to be the best — now won't even launch
product.minus: A crowd of years-long users come back to find the app simply won't open: an endless spinner on a blue background, a white screen, or a crash within 5 seconds. Reinstalling doesn't help and the issue lingers for months.

product.title: The redesign stripped out features users already paid for
product.minus: People bought the «plus»/full version years ago for the huge library and custom workouts. The update hid all of it behind a new subscription: exercises vanished, custom plans locked, leaving a generic shell with «social media» bolted on.

product.title: Workout logging breaks mid-set
product.minus: The core job — log weight, reps, progress — fails: the app crashes mid-workout and loses the whole day's data, fills in a random weight, won't show last session's numbers, and the timer resets on every touch.

product.title: The Android build is a stripped clone of the iOS one
product.minus: Users who switched from iPhone are stunned: Android is missing half the exercises, has no progress graphs, won't show last weight, has no auto rest-timer, won't sync with Samsung/Google Health, and crashes constantly. The same app is «great» on iOS.

product.title: Subscription shoved in your face before you can even enter
product.minus: Just to set up a free account or peek inside, you have to fight off the buy-premium prompt several times. It's annoying enough that people delete the app before ever reaching a workout.

product.title: Demands suspicious permissions for a fitness app
product.minus: Location, access to all files, phone status, even the flashlight — with no explanation and no opt-out: deny location and the app won't launch at all. Many smell phishing and delete it without ever running it.

product.title: The bought full version was abandoned, replaced by a subscription clone
product.minus: The old paid app stopped getting updates (last one 2015) while a near-identically named subscription version was launched alongside it. Paying customers weren't migrated — their data is stuck in the cloud and they're forced to pay all over again.

product.title: Subscription doesn't carry over when you change phone or platform
product.minus: Buy premium, switch device (especially iOS→Android) and access is gone, history wiped, you must pay again. Support blames «different platforms» and Google, and no refund comes.

product.title: A huge exercise library with animations — the reason people love it
product.plus: When it works, this is the standout strength: hundreds of exercises sorted by muscle group, animated gifs showing correct form you can check right at the gym so you don't look lost at the machine. Many have used it for years.

product.title: Custom workouts and progress tracking — when not broken, they keep you coming back
product.plus: Fans value building their own workout, logging weight/reps, seeing last session and progress charts, keeping it all handy at the gym and offline. This is exactly what many pay to upgrade for.

product.title: A great starting point for beginners and gym ideas
product.plus: For beginners the app builds confidence: it suggests how to plan a program, what to do for which muscles, helps you avoid «hitting anywhere» at the gym, and brings fresh ideas to veterans — which is why it gets recommended to friends.

product.title: Expands your emotional vocabulary and finally helps you name feelings
product.plus: The single most-praised value: people who got by for years on "mad/sad/happy" suddenly get a hundred precise words with definitions and learn to tell shades apart. Neurodivergent users and those struggling with alexithymia respond especially strongly.

product.title: Completely free, ad-free and subscription-free — from a non-profit team
product.plus: Against a market of paywalled mental-health apps, this model draws almost embarrassing delight: every feature is free, no ads or microtransactions, the project lives on donations. Many are ready to donate just to keep it that way.

product.title: Android is the second-class app: no custom emotions, body map or guided entries
product.minus: The loudest pain point: key iPhone features stay unavailable on Android for months. You can't add a custom emotion, there's no body-sensation map (somatic scan), no guided journaling. Users who switched from iOS feel cheated and can't understand why their version was shortchanged.

product.title: The two-emotion cap and fixed list can't capture a mixed state
product.minus: The paradox of an app about emotional precision: you can pick at most two emotions per check-in, and (on Android) can't add your own. People often feel more than two things at once, or can't find the right word in the list — and have to flatten the very state they came to capture.

product.title: The pleasant/unpleasant grid leaves no room for neutral or numb states
product.minus: The four-quadrant model (high/low energy × pleasant/unpleasant) forces a choice between extremes. When someone feels neutral, numb, or "somewhere in between," there's literally nothing to pick — and some people skip logging entirely.

product.title: Therapists and psychiatrists recommend it as a real between-sessions tool
product.plus: A strong trust signal: many users came on a therapist's or psychiatrist's recommendation, and clinicians themselves rate it highly. It helps people arrive at sessions with a detailed emotional picture and builds a skill rather than replacing therapy.

product.title: Privacy dread: a vague policy, chatty Firebase, fear of a data sale
product.minus: The most psychologically sensitive data — moods and notes — breeds deep distrust. People are alarmed by the privacy-policy wording, notice constant Firebase calls without consent (in the EU), and fear that if the company is sold, their "psychological profile" goes with it.

product.title: A pushed-in AI "therapist" and Reflect alienate part of the audience
product.minus: Rolling out generative AI split users. Some quit over the very idea of an AI "therapist," calling it harmful; others complain Reflect's answers feel stiff and unnatural. Meanwhile those who noticed the AI is optional and off by default are grateful for the choice.

product.title: Losing all entries on a reinstall or phone switch
product.minus: Several users lost months and years of entries: data didn't sync even when signed in with Google, photos don't carry over on import, and turning off social features wiped everything. For an emotion diary kept "religiously," it's a devastating loss of trust.

product.title: Nagging updates, seasonal surveys and in-app feature ads disrupt reflection
product.minus: Long-time users note a decline: after a check-in the app buries you in videos and lessons, slips feature promos between entries, and the seasonal "mood snapshot" can't be dismissed — it hounds you until you fill it in. Constant update nags knock you out of the calm state you opened the app for.

product.title: A beautiful, calm, intuitive interface you want to come back to
product.plus: The design is its own reason for love: clean, gentle, not like "an app working against you." A check-in takes seconds via a widget that changes color with your mood. Many say it never feels like a chore and actually motivates them to log several times a day.

product.title: The Analyze section won't show data and collects logging bugs
product.minus: The core value — seeing patterns over time — simply breaks for some users: Analyze says "not enough check-ins" with dozens of entries, new logs stop saving after a hundred, the weekly AI analysis fails. Plus smaller bugs: emotions flicker on the grid, notifications fire after being turned off, the entry screen jams.

product.title: No way to set day boundaries — night shifts break tracking
product.minus: A day is hard-coded midnight to midnight, with no way to set your own start and end. For night-shift workers and night owls, half their moods slide to the next day and exercise doesn't count — wrecking the very tracking accuracy the app exists for.

product.title: Brings couples, friends and loved ones closer through shared mood check-ins
product.plus: The social feature works not as a feed but as a closeness bridge: seeing a partner's or friend's mood, adding a photo, replying and leaving a message genuinely improves communication. Couples — including long-distance — and people learning to be more responsive to others especially value it.

product.title: Cancelling sends you in loops, and the charge hits anyway
product.minus: The single biggest pain: people cancel before the trial ends, delete the app, and still get charged, sometimes twice or a year later. The cancel button doesn't work, the subscription shows up neither in Google Play nor in the profile, and confirming cancellation takes 5 to 12 taps.

product.title: Support is a dead end: chat loops to FAQ, emails bounce, no one replies
product.minus: When a billing problem hits, there's literally nowhere to turn: the "Chat with Support" button leads to a FAQ, the email field won't click, messages bounce as undeliverable, and refund requests go unanswered for weeks. For people in crisis it's the final straw.

product.title: Long quiz, then a paywall — 'free' turns out to be bait
product.minus: The app walks you through 10-20 screens of questions and promises of a personal plan, then demands a card at the end: you can't try features without subscribing. Many are angry that the store lists it as "free" when it's really a paid service, with data collected before you pay a cent.

product.title: The 'free trial' bills you instantly or at the full yearly price
product.minus: They promise to charge after 7 days with a reminder first, but money comes off on signup day, without warning, often a full year instead of monthly. Overdrafts, a yearly sum off the card, zero trial-end notifications.

product.title: Blue or purple screen: the app just won't open
product.minus: A huge Android pain: after install or on day two, instead of content there's a blank blue (sometimes purple) screen, endless loading, or "server down." Often it works once, then dies, and reinstalling helps for only a day.

product.title: Buggy, crashes, and loses progress — especially when saving plans
product.minus: Even for those who get in, it crashes right before saving an action plan, won't scroll, loses what you typed, and resets checked-off tasks. People resent paying for something that feels like beta-testing a finished product.

product.title: The AI cat genuinely comforts and eases anxiety
product.plus: Users' biggest love: chatting with the Shmoody cat feels like talking to a real person, replies in seconds, lets you vent without fear of judgment, and genuinely lowers anxiety. For many it's support when there's no one else to turn to.

product.title: Gamification, cats, and music make self-care feel approachable
product.plus: Cute cat design, confetti for completed tasks, soft soothing music, and a game-like flow turn routine into something pleasant. It pulls people in and lifts moods where more "serious" apps pushed them away.

product.title: Breaks goals into tiny steps — helps with ADHD and anxiety
product.plus: Those it clicks with praise how it breaks tasks into doable steps, guides gently without pressure, and helps build habits without shame. Several call it the best of a dozen ADHD apps they've tried.

product.title: AI-generated art is off-putting, and AI can't be turned off
product.minus: A chunk of the audience is openly annoyed by the "AI slop": backgrounds are AI-generated and the mandatory AI features can't be switched off. For people who care about privacy and ethics, it's a reason to delete on the spot.

product.title: Heavy onboarding and pushy pop-ups overwhelm the very ADHD audience it targets
product.minus: The paradox: an ADHD app loads a long mandatory questionnaire with no "none of these" option, forces you to "schedule your joy," and shoves an Upgrade button on every screen. The cat talks agonizingly slowly with no skip button — people run out of patience before reaching any benefit.

product.title: When a refund does come through, it's quick and clean
product.plus: A counterpoint to the complaints: some users, especially among the 3-5 star reviews, got refunds within 24 hours and praise support by name (Glasiele, Glasielle). For them the honest refund outweighed a rough start.

product.title: The free version hits the paywall almost immediately
product.minus: Without premium you get just 3 journals, while unlimited pages and most else cost money — barely anything stays free.

product.title: The app nags too hard to get you to subscribe
product.minus: Constant pressure to subscribe pushes some users to the point of deleting the app.

product.title: Genuinely helps with studying — useful for school and college
product.plus: Users say the planner really helps in high school and supports their studies.

product.title: A wide, fun variety of beautiful templates
product.plus: A big, creative range of templates to pick from delights users.

product.title: The best journal-planner, now on Android and not just iOS
product.plus: iOS fans are glad their favourite app is finally available on Android too.

product.title: Missing customization: custom images and a draw tool
product.minus: Users ask to put custom images on journals and want a drawing tool added.

product.title: Store screenshots don't match the actual app
product.minus: One user complains that even the paid version looks nothing like the pictures shown.

product.title: Newcomers can find it confusing at first
product.minus: Despite the love, some users admit the interface is confusing to start with.

product.title: An ad to save every entry — even to fix a typo
product.minus: By far the loudest pain: to save a day's entry — or even to edit something you already typed — the app forces a full-screen video ad. Users call it absurd: watching 30 seconds of ads just to log a bad day, repeatedly per session because of small fixes.

product.title: Updates wipe years of entries — with no way to recover
product.minus: People lose 2-4 years of entries and photos after an update, phone change, or creating an account. Images turn into "failed to load", whole months vanish, and there's no official recovery — only a manual Google Drive backup nobody was warned about.

product.title: It used to be free — now even your own old entries sit behind a paywall
product.minus: Long-time users return to find what was free is now premium: even viewing and re-reading your own 2021 entries requires a subscription. People feel betrayed — for a "mental health" app, charging to access your own diary feels especially cruel.

product.title: After the update, entries simply don't save
product.minus: A recent bug breaks the core function: you write about your day, hit done, and it doesn't save or vanishes when you reopen. Worse — editing a day wipes everything you'd entered, as if starting fresh. For the poor-memory users who keep the diary precisely for this, it's devastating.

product.title: The cute, simple tap-to-log design is the heart of the love
product.plus: The strongest praise: a clean, minimalist interface where you log a day with a couple of taps on cute "beans" and emojis. It takes the pressure out of journaling — people who quit other apps in a day stick here for years because there's no "essay" to write.

product.title: A genuine support for mental health and mood tracking
product.plus: For many it's not just a diary but a therapeutic tool: people with depression, bipolar disorder, autism track mood, sleep and triggers, and see patterns in their condition over a year. They call it a "godsend", "therapy", a place that feels less lonely.

product.title: The "lucky clover": ads for currency that almost always pays 1 instead of the promised 100
product.minus: Themes are bought with "clovers" earned by watching ads with a chance of "up to 100". In practice it nearly always pays 1 or 5 — users call it false advertising and a gambling mechanic shoved into a diary app. Saving for a single theme takes weeks or months.

product.title: Adorable customizable themes and "beans" are the engagement hook
product.plus: Cute seasonal themes, customizable icons and self-defined categories are what bring people back daily. Users chase specific themes (matcha, Winnie the Pooh, cherry), love the yearly "recaps" and custom activity blocks. The aesthetic directly sustains the habit.

product.title: Lag, crashes and a bloated size after a recent update
product.minus: Since a recent update the UI turned noticeably sluggish, the app crashes (especially on photo upload), and its size ballooned to where people delete other apps to make room. A simple "few buttons" tool suddenly demands disproportionate resources.

product.title: Premium is pricey — and even after paying, themes still cost extra
product.minus: The annual subscription ($30-85 across currencies) feels overpriced for a "simple diary", and the core gripe is it doesn't unlock everything: themes still cost extra in clovers or cash. People just want a one-time payment to remove ads, not a subscription bundled with features they don't want.

product.title: Photo and word limits frustrate people who want to write and keep memories
product.minus: The free version allows just 1 photo per day, caps image size (1.5MB), and imposes a word limit that cuts off longer thoughts. For people who treat it as a real memory journal, these limits strike at the product's whole point.

product.title: The devs genuinely respond and fix things — and it wins people back
product.plus: Despite all the gripes, there's a steady signal: the team replies to tickets, restores lost data and accounts, fixes bugs, and even adds requested features (like a save button). Several users explicitly raised their rating back to five stars after a fix.

product.title: The app works as a confidant, not a notebook
product.plus: The core value isn't typing text, it's feeling heard: people write "as to a friend", get the anxiety out of their heads and feel lighter afterward.

product.title: The lock and password are why people choose this one
product.plus: The password protection feels real rather than decorative: teens hide it from parents, adults from prying eyes, and it's often the deciding factor.

product.title: The best stuff is locked behind a subscription: themes, stickers, fonts
product.minus: The most wanted decorations — cute themes, stickers, wallpapers — require premium, and even fans get annoyed that the pretty shell is paid, with some deleting over it.

product.title: An ad after every page-to-page move
product.minus: Ads pop up on practically every click and after every entry — it shatters the intimate moment of self-reflection and drives people to other apps within a week.

product.title: Photos, audio and keepsakes are the main functional joy
product.plus: Being able to attach photos, voice notes and documents turns the diary into a living archive of memories — trips, a child, a pet — not just text.

product.title: Data loss with no undo and no recovery
product.minus: The most painful failure: entries vanish on a phone switch or accidental delete, there's no undo, and auto-backup overwrites the already-erased version — no way to get it back.

product.title: Helps with anxiety, stress and for neurodivergent users
product.plus: People explicitly describe a therapeutic effect: less anxiety, a cleared head, help with ADHD — one was even sent by their therapist to journal here.

product.title: An easy on-ramp for people who never journaled before
product.plus: The barrier is low: the app asks how your day went, and even people who never wrote on paper start easily and get pulled into a daily habit.

product.title: Aggressive pressure to buy premium
product.minus: Beyond locked features, the app itself nags you toward the subscription — promo screens won't let you leave until you tap the X several times, and users feel milked.

product.title: Photo caps and a shortage of free customization
product.minus: Even happy users hit limits: you can't add as many photos as you want, there are too few free wallpapers and emoji, and they ask for a reward system to unlock looks without paying.

product.title: Login, sync and update glitches
product.minus: Some users hit refused logins with the correct password, lost network and mood emoji, an app that won't update, and no desktop version.

product.title: "Pay what you want" for results turns into a hidden $15-30 charge
product.minus: Users agree to a token $1-2 for their test results, then right after the "Continue" button get hit with another $14.99 (or $19.99, $29.99) with no separate confirmation. This is by far the most common complaint, repeated in nearly every review.

product.title: "Continue" is placed where "Skip" should be — the UX is engineered for an accidental yes
product.minus: The add-on screen makes a prominent "Continue" button charge the subscription while "Skip" is hidden below the fold. People tap "Continue" thinking they're just proceeding to their results.

product.title: The subscription doesn't show in Google Play — there's nothing to cancel, yet money keeps going out
product.minus: The charges don't appear as an active subscription in Google Play; it's buried inside the app's own settings. People can't find where to cancel, and deleting the app doesn't stop the billing.

product.title: They keep charging after cancellation — sometimes for months
product.minus: Even after cancelling and deleting the app on day one, people keep getting hit with $29.99-42 charges for weeks and months; only blocking the card through the bank stops it.

product.title: The "free 7-day trial" charges you within minutes
product.minus: The screen promises billing only after the trial ends, but the second charge lands instantly — same date and time as the first. The "free" trial is never free.

product.title: Support is an auto-reply, and refunds are denied "by policy"
product.minus: Refund requests get a templated bot reply; negative reviews get the same "sorry you feel that way" with a link that loops back. Refunds are denied on the grounds that "web purchases are non-refundable."

product.title: The tests are shallow BuzzFeed-style quizzes whose results miss the real picture
product.minus: Some users call the tests a rehash of free pop quizzes and "pseudo-Jung," with results that miss badly: one person with severe childhood trauma and suicidal thoughts was told they were "fine and normal."

product.title: It targets the most vulnerable — people in mental-health crisis
product.minus: Social-media ads funnel in people with trauma, ADHD, autism and depression; the very users it "assessed" as traumatized are the ones it immediately pushes into a hidden charge.

product.title: It pushes you into BetterHelp on top of its own paywall
product.minus: After all the charges, the app funnels hard into a BetterHelp partnership — much of the content feels like a pipeline into yet another paid subscription rather than a standalone product.

product.title: For those who actually go through the program, the trauma work genuinely helps
product.plus: Some users — including a practising clinician — say the app helped them understand themselves and work through childhood trauma: the structure, daily tasks and self-assessments give a real sense of progress and relief.

product.title: When support does respond like a human, refunds happen and impress
product.plus: A minority had the opposite experience: they asked for a refund and got one quickly and graciously, with support that left them feeling genuinely cared for.

product.title: Nagging rating prompts before you've even started using it
product.minus: The app keeps begging for a rating every couple of actions — before the user has really started — which annoys even otherwise positive reviewers.

product.title: A clean, non-overwhelming interface is the main reason people love it
product.plus: Users repeatedly praise the simple, intuitive interface: writing and browsing entries is effortless, it doesn't overwhelm like Notion or Obsidian, and it feels cozy and pleasant to use.

product.title: The paywall blocks basic functions — especially the one-photo-per-entry limit
product.minus: The most basic things — multiple photos per entry, video and audio, using two devices — are locked behind a subscription, and many feel you can't add more than one image per entry on the free plan.

product.title: Force-fed AI with no off-switch angers users over both privacy and clutter
product.minus: A recent update added AI features that stay visible even when supposedly off and can't be removed: people fear their private entries feed model training and resent AI being forced into a place meant for their own thoughts.

product.title: Entries and formatting vanish — the most painful bug
product.minus: People regularly lose their writing: entries fail to save, paragraphs disappear when adding a photo, template and table formatting is dropped, and some are forced to manually save every thirty seconds after an update.

product.title: A repeated-text bug when fixing typos has gone unfixed for years
product.minus: When you fix a typo and hit backspace, the app duplicates the whole word instead of correcting it ("exampexample"); users say the bug has been open for over three years and they're told to change their keyboard settings.

product.title: Endless syncing blocks input — even when sync is turned off
product.minus: Switching between apps freezes Day One on "Synchronizing" for tens of seconds and blocks writing; maddeningly, it happens even to people who disabled sync or have no account at all, and it drains the battery.

product.title: You can permanently lose your journal: encryption key, phone reset, expired subscription
product.minus: Several users lost everything: losing an "encryption key" locks you out forever, data fails to load after a phone reset or switch, and an expired subscription becomes a "login → payment screen" loop that holds years of writing hostage.

product.title: Crashes on large journals and when editing entries
product.minus: For some users the app has become unstable and crashes reliably: with a large volume of entries, when trying to create or edit an entry, and reinstalling, clearing cache, and force-closing don't help.

product.title: Streaks and "On This Day" genuinely pull people back to writing
product.plus: Streaks and the streak-reminder widget motivate people to write daily, while the "On This Day" feature and revisiting past entries are exactly what keeps people journaling for years and attached to the app.

product.title: Multiple journals, templates and prompts are why people pick it
product.plus: The ability to keep many separate journals, a rich set of templates, and thoughtful prompt questions help people start writing and organize their thoughts — cited as key reasons they chose and stuck with it.

product.title: A design update with the round calendar split users
product.minus: The recent redesign triggered a wave of complaints: the all-blue calendar makes photos hard to see, round date icons replaced the familiar squares, and tags vanished from the home screen — many beg for the old look back (though a few actually liked the new round icons).

product.title: A barrier to entry: login, Google sign-in and a mandatory password scare people off at the start
product.minus: Many never even reach the app itself: Google sign-in throws errors, the login screen greets you first, and being forced to create a complex password with symbols and capitals feels absurd for a simple diary.

product.title: Minimalist UI is the number-one reason people love it
product.plus: The clean, calm, aesthetic design is named as a value in itself — it doesn't distract, it's pleasant to look at, and everything is easy to find.

product.title: Paywall at the door: it used to be free, now basics are locked
product.minus: Long-time users remember a free, feature-rich version; now even basics — an account, a PIN, many tools — sit behind the subscription. For many this kills the app before they even try it.

product.title: Android is the poor relation of iOS
product.minus: People who switched from iPhone say it in unison: the Android build is missing the special details, lags behind on updates, doesn't sync, and feels like just another generic wellbeing app.

product.title: Morning/evening prompts ask questions at the wrong time of day
product.minus: A recurring gripe: in the evening it asks "are you prepared for the day", in the morning "what bad thing did you curb today". Prompts ignore the time of day and break the logic of reflection.

product.title: The journal won't save — lost entries
product.minus: The save button "does nothing", autosave works only sometimes, sessions don't record. Losing what you wrote is what hits trust — and the will to keep going — hardest.

product.title: Prompts and routines genuinely help you start writing
product.plus: The core functional value: guided questions kill the blank-page fear, reconnect people with their feelings, and sustain the journaling habit even for those who'd quit five times before.

product.title: Trial trap and non-refundable charges
product.minus: The free trial silently rolls into a yearly charge with no warning; no end-of-trial reminder, no receipt, and refunds get denied. People lose money on an app they opened once.

product.title: No real sync and no cross-platform account
product.minus: There's no shared login across Android, iOS, Mac and web: a purchase on one platform doesn't transfer, the web only logs in with an Apple ID, and there's no Google backup — your data is stuck on one device.

product.title: The free tier is enough to sustain the habit
product.plus: Despite the paywall complaints, a chunk of users praise the free tier specifically: morning/evening exercises, no ads, and a solid core — enough to start and keep going.

product.title: Questions repeat and grow stale
product.minus: The same prompts day after day, with no variety: reflection turns mechanical and "predictable", people get bored answering and drift off to look elsewhere.

product.title: Awkward wording and typos undermine trust in the product
product.minus: Grammar mistakes, weird out-of-nowhere questions ("are you married?", "how old were you then?"), reading like machine translation — for an app about clarity of mind it's jarring and erodes trust in the paid tier.

product.title: Crashes on meditation, breathing and the "journey" tab
product.minus: Starting a meditation, the breathing exercises and opening the journey tab routinely crash back to the home screen — breaking exactly the features people stay for.

product.title: Forced religious quotes on a "secular Stoic" app
product.minus: Notifications and prompts suddenly started pushing Christian/religious quotes, even though Stoicism is a secular philosophy; for part of the audience it feels like forced religion and a reason to drop a star.

product.title: One-tap logging turns journaling into a habit that sticks for years
product.plus: Users' deepest love is the minimal effort per entry: just tap mood and activity icons. That lightness is exactly what lets people build multi-year unbroken streaks and makes Daylio the rare habit they never abandon.

product.title: Charts and stats reveal what actually drives your mood
product.plus: People value the insight, not just the logging: weekly and monthly reports, graphs and activity search surface patterns — which activities, meds and symptoms correlate with mood. Many bring these screenshots to their therapist.

product.title: Deep customization: your own moods, activities, colors and templates
product.plus: Daylio is praised for bending to any use case — from tracking tics and long-covid symptoms to cycles and medication. Users add dozens or hundreds of their own activities, recolor icons, and build templates.

product.title: Ads for sibling AI apps (calorie/weight) alarm vulnerable users
product.minus: Inside a mental-health app, users get pop-ups for the company's own AI calorie, weight and BMI trackers. For people recovering from eating disorders and those who distrust generative AI, it feels like a breach of trust — enough to uninstall.

product.title: Subscription and pricing have soured long-time loyalists
product.minus: People who recommended Daylio for years — often after buying a cheap lifetime license long ago — now call the yearly sub and ~$60–79 lifetime out of proportion for a simple app that barely changes. The price stops them from recommending it.

product.title: The free version delivers almost the whole product — and that wins people over
product.plus: What holds many users is the generous free tier: moods, activities, notes, reports, photos and backup work without paying. Premium reads as cosmetic and a way to support the devs, not a mandatory unlock.

product.title: The forced free trial charges users without warning
product.minus: A raw complaint: the app demands a card before you can even try it, auto-starts the trial, then charges automatically. Several users describe it as a scam or theft, sometimes with no refund.

product.title: Backup-restore data loss is catastrophic for a years-long archive
product.minus: Because people treat Daylio as a lifelong archive, a failed restore hurts the most: users lose entries, thousands of photos and years of memories. It's worse because automatic backup sits behind the paywall.

product.title: Streaks and reminders motivate — but streak pressure breeds anxiety
product.minus: Gamification cuts both ways. The streak system motivates many to keep logging, but for some users the reminders and fear of breaking the streak turn entries into a dreaded chore and amplify anxiety.

product.title: Intrusive 'achievement' and offer pop-ups annoy during setup
product.minus: The app's attempt to encourage backfires: every small setup action triggers an "achievement" pop-up, and constant offers and questions make the interface feel invasive exactly when you just want to get set up.

product.title: No real free-writing journal and no cross-device sync
product.minus: The name promises a journal, but there's no real free-writing mechanism — it's a tracker with a note field. Users also miss accounts that sync across phone, tablet and computer, plus easier access to past entries.

product.title: Technical glitches: battery drain, cache bloat, crashes and slow load
product.minus: Against a generally stable reputation, specific bugs surface: the screen stays on overnight and drains the battery, the cache balloons to gigabytes in days, the app crashes on startup and loads slowly on older phones.

product.title: Design and customization are what people love most
product.plus: The most common praise is the pleasant, cute interface and flexible setup: you can tune the mood scale to yourself, and the set of events and icons is huge. Many say that after trying other trackers, this is the one they stuck with.

product.title: Basic features locked behind a paywall
product.minus: The most frequent complaint: too much is locked behind a subscription — not nice extras, but things that feel basic. It frustrates people that you can't trial the full feature set before buying; you only get stripped-down options at download.

product.title: A forced tutorial scares people off at the start
product.minus: The mandatory step-by-step guide can't be skipped, and for some that's a dealbreaker: a few get stuck inside the tutorial and lose access to features, others just abandon the app before reaching the point. Even fans ask for a way to skip the walkthrough.

product.title: No ads and doesn't push the subscription
product.plus: A huge plus for users is the absence of ads and the respectful treatment: the app doesn't shove premium in your face every few minutes. Many are willing to pay voluntarily for that reason alone, just to support the developer.

product.title: Reminders arrive late or not at all
product.minus: The reminders — a mechanic central to a tracker — are unreliable: they arrive half an hour to two hours late, and for some people they don't fire at all, even after sorting out permissions and following the FAQ.

product.title: Logging an entry takes too many steps
product.minus: For people who just want to quickly log a mood, the multi-screen flow gets in the way: a single entry is stretched across several pages, and the unwanted events section can't be removed — it still blocks the path and eats half the stats page.

product.title: Helps people see and understand their emotions
product.plus: Many note real mental-health value: the app helps spot triggers, see mood patterns, and feel more in touch with yourself. For some it revealed a burnout, others use it alongside therapy.

product.title: Pricing feels steep, especially outside Western regions
product.minus: The subscription price strikes many as too high for this kind of app, and the lack of region-adjusted pricing hits users from India and elsewhere. People ask for a more affordable one-time payment and discounts.

product.title: People value being usable for free
product.plus: Despite paywall gripes, many find the free version enough: basic mood tracking, a couple of color themes, one reminder and simple stats are available without paying. Some people, precisely because the free tier is generous, then become willing to support the developer.

product.title: Bugs, crashes and lost entries
product.minus: Stability lets people down: for some the app lags, crashes on launch or doesn't work at all, and the X and ✓ buttons in pop-ups don't respond. The worst case is losing recent entries, after which the user uninstalled.

product.title: Light text on pastel backgrounds — a readability problem
product.minus: White lettering on pastel backgrounds is hard to read even at the largest font, while a dark theme and text-color change are hidden behind the paywall. People with dyslexia and weak eyesight suffer most — it reads as accessibility gated behind money.

product.title: Missing widgets and sync
product.minus: Users who love the app keep asking for the same things: a home-screen widget showing the weekly mood (already on iOS, not Android) and cross-platform sync. It's the most common feature request among satisfied people.

product.title: Updates reliably break what used to work
product.minus: The number-one pain: after each update the app starts crashing, logging people out, losing progress or refusing to open at all. Users openly regret updating.

product.title: Logging a single book is a marathon of taps
product.minus: Recording one session takes a pile of screens: find the book, tap log again, pick the reader, save. With several kids or a fast reader it becomes torture, and many just give up.

product.title: The screen jitters and flashes when you save
product.minus: A very common complaint: the moment you enter pages or minutes and hit Done, the screen flashes and jitters, the button jumps, and the log doesn't save. For some the flickering even hurts their eyes.

product.title: "Something went wrong" and the vanishing library
product.minus: The app suddenly logs you out and then insists your library or school "doesn't exist" or "doesn't use Beanstack" — even though you logged in through it yesterday. Reinstalling and clearing cache don't help.

product.title: Streaks vanish even though reading is logged
product.minus: The streak — the big motivator for kids — keeps resetting: every day is there in the log, but the streak shows zero. Children whose months-long streaks get wiped lose the will to read.

product.title: One account, one child: switching means logging out
product.minus: You can't keep several kid profiles or two libraries connected at once: to switch you must log out and back in, and adding a second library deletes the first.

product.title: Book search finds nothing, ISBN scanner fails
product.minus: The catalog is full of holes: even common books are missing, searching by title/author/ISBN returns nothing, and the barcode scanner often fails. So you end up typing almost everything in by hand.

product.title: After an update the camera scanner just won't open
product.minus: A recent regression (especially on Android/Pixel): the barcode-scan button no longer opens the camera even though permission is granted. A favorite feature suddenly stopped working for many.

product.title: Logged reading and whole books just disappear
product.minus: The most painful kind of failure: after updating, hours of reading, past years of challenges and whole kid book-lists vanish. People lose months of accumulated progress with no way to get it back.

product.title: Minute caps: the child "read too much"
product.minus: An odd limitation: the app refuses to record honest minutes, claiming they're "too many," forcing the parent to understate them and "promise" the child really read that much.

product.title: A perfect bridge to library reading programs
product.plus: When it works, the app is a great way to join summer reading challenges, collect badges and earn real prizes from your local library. This connection is exactly why people put up with the bugs.

product.title: Genuinely gets people reading more — kids and adults
product.plus: The gamification works: streaks, badges and challenges motivate people to read more than ever before. Parents watch their kids' reading levels climb and a real love of books take hold.

product.title: Asking for the basics: audiobooks, dark mode, notes
product.minus: Even happy users hit the gaps: no proper audiobook tracking (only pages/minutes), no dark mode, no private per-book notes, and no Goodreads/Kindle integration.

product.title: The app is a stripped-down shadow of the desktop site
product.minus: Half the basic actions are impossible in the app and force you to a browser: changing the edition, viewing your highlights, finding past reads, editing data. The website is richer in every way, and it has dragged on for years.

product.title: Dark mode turns on but makes text unreadable
product.minus: When you switch to dark mode the background stays light while the font turns white or pale, making it impossible to read. The setting exists but has been broken for a very long time, and reinstalling does nothing.

product.title: A sudden flood of ads, including porn
product.minus: After a recent update ads flooded in — you can't scroll a couple of titles without one, sometimes outright porn with no way to report it. Many ask for a paid option to remove them.

product.title: You can't pick the edition you're actually reading
product.minus: The app won't let you switch a book's edition — especially galling for Android users who had it on iPhone. Many editions (e.g. Arabic ones) aren't in the database at all, and you can't add them yourself.

product.title: The read-count and challenges miscount
product.minus: The app adds and then quietly drops books from the count, shows the wrong number of reads, fails to log books toward challenges and won't award trophies. For people who track for the stats, it kills the whole point.

product.title: An outdated, slow and glitchy interface
product.minus: The design feels like it's from 2008: list-only views, endless scroll, constant 'load more'. The app loads slowly, freezes and often throws a 'come back later' error, essentially crashing.

product.title: Can't log in or create an account
product.minus: Sign-up and login routinely break: password resets don't take, Amazon login hangs on authentication, and 7-10 character passwords are rejected as 'too short'. Some users simply can't get into their own data.

product.title: Amazon ownership feels like a conflict of interest
product.minus: Users resent that Goodreads is owned by Amazon: it dumps every Amazon-touched book onto your shelves, negative reviews seem to get flagged and removed with a warning, and the app gets no investment because the monopoly keeps users anyway.

product.title: Syncing with Kindle and the website fails
product.minus: Despite the Amazon link, Kindle purchases don't sync, reviews posted on desktop never show in the app feed, and read updates now arrive hours late instead of near-instantly.

product.title: No half-stars and no way to sort reviews
product.minus: Things that should be basic for a book app are missing: you can't give 3.5 stars, and you can't sort or filter the reviews under a book. These requests recur for years with no response.

product.title: An indispensable tracker that motivates reading
product.plus: Despite everything, it's the beloved way to log what you've read, set an annual goal and watch your progress. Many say updating progress in Goodreads is their biggest motivation to read more, and for some it's a memory aid.

product.title: The community and reviews help pick your next book
product.plus: The core value is the living community of readers and honest reviews. People trust the ratings to decide whether a book is worth their time and money, see what friends are reading, and discover new titles through recommendations and giveaways.

product.title: An unmatched catalog and convenient shelves
product.plus: The catalog is huge — 'it has every book I've ever searched for' — and the Read / Currently Reading / To-Read shelves are intuitive for managing a personal library. The long-awaited DNF ('did not finish') shelf finally arrived.

product.title: The barcode scanner returns the wrong books and covers
product.minus: Scanning a barcode often returns 'unknown author', the wrong cover, or a description in the wrong language (Greek, Polish) for an English edition. In a bookshop it's nearly useless for checking whether you own a book in a series.

product.title: Reading stats and graphs are the reason people stay
product.plus: Detailed graphs, moods, pace, monthly and yearly wrap-ups — the data visualization is exactly why people switch and stay. For a stats-loving brain it's a feast.

product.title: Better than Goodreads and free of Amazon — an ethical choice
product.plus: People leave Goodreads and don't look back: an indie team, no Amazon, no ads. "I'm not the product, I'm the customer." Importing a Goodreads library is usually painless.

product.title: Blank/grey screen with only the bottom bar — the app just won't load
product.minus: A mass failure of recent months: the app opens to a blank white or grey screen showing only the bottom tab bar, and nothing loads — neither on wifi nor mobile data. Reinstalling doesn't help.

product.title: Lag, freezes and crashes that have gotten worse lately
product.minus: The app is slow to open, pages don't load, buttons don't respond, it freezes and crashes. Many note it's gotten worse recently, forcing constant closing and restarting.

product.title: Broken navigation: the back button drops you on a random page
product.minus: The back button and system swipe misbehave: they send you to the wrong place, into loops, sometimes don't even exit the app. Reaching recent reads takes three taps and you still tap wrong.

product.title: AI features in a book app enrage readers
product.minus: Adding generative AI (AI summaries, running requests through an LLM) feels like a betrayal for a literature app. Some uninstall on the spot, the rest demand the AI be removed on principle.

product.title: Goodreads import is either painless or completely broken
product.minus: For some the Goodreads move takes minutes; for others it simply fails: import only works from a computer, mangles dates, marks books finished on every progress update. And without import the app won't let you do anything.

product.title: The ISBN scanner doesn't work on Android — the one reason to use the app
product.minus: The barcode scanner — the app's main edge over the website — barely works on Android: camera access is wired up wrong, it errors out, fails to read even in perfect light. A quick scan becomes a chore.

product.title: The developer genuinely listens and ships updates constantly
product.plus: The tiny team (the founder is often mentioned) asks for input on social media, lets users vote on features and responds quickly. People value that their requests actually show up in the next updates.

product.title: Flexible logging: editions, formats, quarter-stars, DNF and rereading
product.plus: You can log the exact edition, switch audio/ebook/physical, rate in 0.25 increments, mark DNF, pause, rereading and owned books. This granularity is what people missed in Goodreads.

product.title: Search returns junk: an exact title drowns in look-alikes
product.minus: Even with a full title and author, search shows piles of irrelevant results and the right book has to be hunted out of hundreds of look-alikes. There are no decent filters or author sorting beyond alphabetical.

product.title: Vanished books and lost data with no way to recover
product.minus: After switching phones or logging back in, completed books disappear, the counter resets, data is lost — and support says nothing can be recovered. For a tracker whose whole point is keeping a reading history, that's critical.

product.title: Challenges, buddy reads and community keep motivation up
product.plus: Buddy reads, book clubs, reading challenges, streaks and giveaways turn reading into a game and pull people back into the habit. The social features exist but don't crowd out the tracking.

product.title: The app just won't load: blank white screen and an endless spinner
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after an update the app hangs on loading, opens blank, or spins for minutes. Feed, profile, lists and clubs won't load, and reinstalling doesn't fix it.

product.title: Android is a second-class citizen: features and updates land on iOS first
product.minus: Android users are furious: dark mode, widgets, Fable Plus and weekly updates were iPhone-only for a long time, and the Android build is far glitchier. People who switch from iPhone find the app simply 'doesn't like' them.

product.title: The book community and clubs are the real reason to stay
product.plus: What people genuinely love: a warm, friendly community of readers, with clubs, discussions and buddy reads. Many call it 'Instagram for books' and come specifically to connect with fellow book lovers.

product.title: Constant crashes only fixed by reinstalling, over and over
product.minus: Just to mark a book finished or open a club, people have to uninstall and reinstall — sometimes several times a day. System 'app not responding' dialogs and crashes when switching screens have become routine.

product.title: Search is terrible and the books you want simply aren't in the database
product.minus: Type the exact title and author and you get random books or nothing. You often need the ISBN to find a book. Many editions are missing entirely, and adding a new book gets stuck in review for months.

product.title: Duplicate editions break your counts and 'most-read authors' list
product.minus: A single book exists as several separate edition cards that the app won't merge. A series won't gather under one author, marking one edition 'read' doesn't carry to the other, and the Goodreads import duplicates your whole list.

product.title: Paywalled Fable Plus and a vanished Scout — best features moved behind a paywall
product.minus: People who left Goodreads for the free charts and the Scout recommender feel betrayed: half the features got locked behind a $5.99/mo subscription, Scout was 'ruined', and some book clubs now charge fees just to vote.

product.title: Tracking glitches: finished books don't count, or count two or three times
product.minus: The core feature — tracking — is unreliable. Finished books don't count toward your goal and monthly wrap, or get counted multiple times and break your reading challenge. Books drift into DNF on their own, and fixes require contacting support.

product.title: Beautiful interface and stats genuinely motivate you to read more
product.plus: The aesthetics, clean design, annual wrap, charts and streaks genuinely nudge people to read. Many admit Fable looks nicer than Goodreads and has increased how much they read.

product.title: The feed drowns in pet pics and romantasy instead of books
product.minus: The feed algorithm ignores your interests: instead of books you get endless cat-and-dog photos and a flood of romantasy. Muting books or curating your library doesn't help, and there's no filter by content language.

product.title: Removing direct messages cut off people's book friendships
product.minus: Direct and group messaging were removed without warning — and for many that was the whole reason they joined, to chat with book friends without handing over their personal socials. Conversations vanished, and it's cited as a top reason to leave.

product.title: No web version — long reviews and desktop access are impossible
product.minus: The website exists only to push you to download the app and has no real functionality. Writing thoughtful long reviews on a phone is painful, and you can't hop on a laptop to add a book — a desktop version is a frequent request.

product.title: An AI assistant inside a reading tracker feels unwanted
product.minus: The beta AI assistant and 'AI reader profile' put people off: they call it unnecessary, unethical over its environmental impact, and pointless — they already know what kind of reader they are.

product.title: Catching duplicates right in the store — the number-one reason people love it
product.plus: The most repeated praise is the same scenario: you're at a store or a yard sale, you open your library on your phone, and you don't re-buy a book you already own. For collectors it's literally money saved.

product.title: The 100-book free cap plus a steep lifetime price feel like a bait-and-switch
product.minus: Many arrived after reading that storage was free and unlimited, only to hit a 100-book ceiling — useless for collectors with hundreds of volumes. The price to lift the cap strikes them as wildly out of proportion.

product.title: Batch barcode scanning — the feature that keeps people hooked
product.plus: The ability to batch-scan books without interruption is repeatedly called the best part: people log 400 books in a couple of hours and catalogue whole shelves in one go.

product.title: Ads went from tolerable to a wall of video after every action
product.minus: Long-time users remember the app ad-free or with static banners, and now report 10–20-second video ads after every save plus fake close buttons hidden in the ad. The frequency is called "insane."

product.title: Books and whole shelves vanish out of nowhere, sometimes with the account
product.minus: The scariest class of complaint: people with hundreds or thousands of logged books log in to find lists, notes and shelves gone, the book count dropping on its own, the account seemingly reset — after long use it feels like a disaster.

product.title: Responsive support often rescues lost data within an hour
product.plus: The counterpoint to the data-loss fear: the support team earns praise again and again for replying fast, restoring accounts and transferring data — sometimes in under an hour. For many that's what keeps them.

product.title: A simple, lightweight interface with no forced social layer is exactly what they wanted
product.plus: Many were explicitly hunting for a private, non-social tracker: a clean UI, clear shelves, reading goals, no community features shoved in your face. After trying five to seven apps, this is where they land.

product.title: Custom shelves and wishlists make the catalogue genuinely your own
product.plus: Organisational flexibility is a frequent reason for love: separate shelves for TBR, read, gifts, library books, series, plus a wishlist to scan books "for later" in the store. You can even mark books as lent and to whom.

product.title: People expect a reader and get only a tracker — there's no "read" button
