product.title: No recurring or multiple alarms — you have to set it from scratch every night
product.minus: You can't set a weekday repeat or a separate weekend alarm, there are no multiple alarms, and you must set the time by hand every single night. For a daily alarm that's an astonishing gap — people automate the start themselves or just can't use it consistently.

product.title: The smart wake-up window misses by half an hour in either direction
product.minus: People love the idea of waking in a light phase, but in practice the window fires half an hour early, much later, or always at the very last minute — making a wide window pointless. Users lose sleep guessing when it will decide to get them up.

product.title: A beautiful, calming interface — praised even by the unhappy
product.plus: The design is called pretty, self-explanatory and relaxing: a unique look, a calm way of showing data, a relaxation mandala. Even reviewers who hammer the paywall or accuracy single out the lovely UI — a strength almost everyone concedes.

product.title: Empty by morning: you start tracking at night and wake up to nothing recorded
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people press start before bed for several nights in a row, and by morning the app is back on the start screen showing nothing was recorded.

product.title: The ad screams "free," but inside it immediately asks for a card for a paid trial
product.minus: People come in expecting a free app and are met only with a 3-day trial that demands a card upfront — they read it as outright false advertising.

product.title: Almost everything behind the paywall: you can't even play your own recordings or sounds without paying
product.minus: You get one recording and a couple of sounds; your own sleep data, the color noises and the rest are locked — what stings most is paying just to access your own data.

product.title: A $7-11 weekly price for a sleep app feels absurd
product.minus: Many are shocked the charge is weekly, not monthly: $7-11 a week against plenty of free or far cheaper alternatives reads as a rip-off.

product.title: Charges keep coming after you cancel and uninstall — and cancelling is nearly impossible
product.minus: People cancel before the trial ends or uninstall, yet charges keep coming for weeks; the cancel button is impossible to find, support is silent, and one cancellation even killed someone's Google One subscription.

product.title: Charges for an app people never even used — it feels like fraud
product.minus: Some users only glanced at the app or never subscribed at all, yet found charges, sometimes off a spouse's card; double charges show up and people reissue cards and go to their bank.

product.title: Sound classification is wrong: snoring gets logged as "pet," "talking" or "fart"
product.minus: The app can't tell sound sources apart: snoring gets tagged as talking, sneezing or an animal, a dog's bark counts as the user snoring, and a background TV throws off the whole picture.

product.title: It measures noise, not sleep: numbers clash with watches and reality
product.minus: The app gauges loudness rather than sleep: it shows 2-3 hours after 8-12 hours of sleep, disagrees with Garmin and Samsung Health, and mistakes a fan for being awake.

product.title: Crashes, freezes and force-closes about 10 minutes after tracking starts
product.minus: The app crashes overnight, freezes asking to close the window, and shuts itself down about 10 minutes after start; stats won't load, and tracking fails on newer phones like the S25.

product.title: The sleep sounds help people drift off — the one thing even critics praise
product.plus: The white-noise and relaxing-sound library gets genuine praise as soothing: it calms people down and helps them fall asleep, and most 5-star reviews are about exactly this.

product.title: Sounds loop in a crude 10-20 second clip that actually keeps you awake
product.minus: Those very praised sounds are undermined by crude looping: short clips repeat every 10-20 seconds with no smooth transition, there's no sleep timer, and it keeps people awake.

product.title: The dream analysis genuinely lands — a rare standout feature people remember
product.plus: The dream interpretation turns out surprisingly accurate and emotionally on-point: even people who cancelled single it out for matching what they were going through.

product.title: The flashlight heart-rate sensor burns your finger and returns nonsense
product.minus: Measuring pulse via camera and flashlight literally burns the finger, the reading is unreliable, and it absurdly reports the very "stress" its own burn caused.

product.title: One free lesson, then everything is locked
product.minus: People praise the content but complain in unison: you get exactly one free lesson, and lesson two onward requires a subscription. They call it pointless — one lesson isn't enough to judge whether it's worth paying for.

product.title: "Free trial" auto-charges a full year with no warning
product.minus: The trial requires a card and silently rolls into a paid plan: people report being charged a full year with no notice, no month-to-month option, and a separate fight with support to get a refund. Many call it dishonest and predatory.

product.title: Speech recognition rejects correct pronunciation
product.minus: The most frequent technical gripe: speaking exercises reject a word even when native speakers say it perfectly. People repeat a single word 10-20 times, while a deliberately exaggerated accent somehow passes. With no hint about which part is wrong, the exercise is useless for learning.

product.title: Speaking is required — but disabled for most languages
product.minus: A distinct pain: for many languages the speaking feature simply doesn't work or is disabled on Android, with no warning. People pay for a year specifically for speaking practice, then find it missing, and support leaves it unfixed for years.

product.title: Decline AI voice-data consent and speaking is blocked
product.minus: A recent change that enraged long-time users: to do any speaking you must now consent to recording, storing and using your voice to train AI. Decline and you're left with flashcards only. Paying users of many years are uninstalling on principle.

product.title: Narrow, heavily European language selection
product.minus: A huge number of people install it and can't find their language: no Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, Greek, Arabic, Hindi, Thai. The list is almost entirely European, and its narrowness often isn't flagged before install. Many never even start.

product.title: Russian missing while Ukrainian is offered upsets Russian speakers
product.minus: A notable group of Russian speakers is upset that the interface supports Ukrainian but completely ignores Russian — one of the most widely spoken languages in Eurasia. For them it means the app is simply unusable.

product.title: Dark onboarding: long questionnaire, then "pay up"
product.minus: Before you start, the app runs you through a long "personalized" questionnaire and asks for your email, only revealing at the very end that there's no free option. People call it manipulative — harvesting your contact and time before disclosing it's all paid.

product.title: Pacing spikes: hard phrases dumped without buildup
product.minus: A common gripe about the method itself: it jumps abruptly from simple sentences to long phrases full of words never taught first. Basics like the alphabet, numbers and colours are skipped and repetition is thin — beginners lose the thread and their interest.

product.title: No free review: the app forces you forward
product.minus: Even paying users complain they can't reinforce material at their own pace: the app blocks review and pushes you into new lessons you're not ready for. And a couple of mistakes often means redoing the whole lesson, not just the misses.

product.title: Crashes, black screens, locked out of a paid account
product.minus: A noticeable share complains about stability: the app hangs on loading, opens to a black or white screen, and forces landscape on tablets and folds. It stings most for people who've already paid but, on login, see only the payment screen.

product.title: Teaches grammar and the "why", not just rote drills
product.plus: The top reason people switch here from Duolingo: lessons actually explain grammar, conjugation and the logic of the language instead of just drilling cards. Topic structure and "did you know" notes make it feel like learning a language, not farming streaks.

product.title: Real-life dialogue and usable phrases, not textbook lines
product.plus: People like that the phrases sound natural and actually come in handy in real life — especially before a trip. The dialogues feel like genuine conversation, and the podcasts add real-world context; this is exactly what many are happy to pay for.

product.title: Short lessons and a choice of mode: read, write, listen, speak
product.plus: A format strength: short two-minute lessons that slot into a busy day, plus the freedom to choose how you review — flashcards, listening, writing or speaking. People with ADHD and busy schedules love it, and the calm, gamification-free interface gets praise.

product.title: Speech recognition rejects correct answers
product.minus: The app's core mechanic — speaking out loud — keeps marking correct answers wrong: people repeat a phrase five times, shout it, slow it down, and it still 'can't hear' them, trapping them on a single word for hours.

product.title: The mic flat-out stops working
product.minus: Beyond recognition errors, for many the mic simply stops responding for months: permissions granted, cache cleared, app reinstalled — yet the voice isn't recorded and the lesson can't be passed, leaving people stuck on the very first chapter.

product.title: Google sign-in freezes at the door
product.minus: New users can't even create an account: the 'Continue with Google' button does nothing or freezes the screen, email sign-up throws an error — and someone who downloaded the app to learn never gets past the login screen.

product.title: Teaches you to speak, not tap options
product.plus: The method of real video dialogues and speaking aloud feels like talking to a live person: people say they reach basic phrases and full sentences within days, and it sticks better than tapping an answer on screen.

product.title: Storytelling makes the alphabet easy
product.plus: Delivery through stories and charming tutors removes the fear of an unfamiliar script: people say Hangul felt hard until it was woven into a story, and the alphabet sinks in unnoticed and fun.

product.title: Beats the green owl for speaking
product.plus: Those tired of grinding the same things daily in Duolingo openly call Teuida faster and more practical for real speech — especially for Korean and Japanese, where the speaking focus delivers tangible progress.

product.title: Paywall and 'keys' choke the learning
product.minus: Enthusiasm hits monetization: a daily lesson cap and 'keys' for unlimited access force you to stop mid-stride, and teens and those who can't pay complain that an educational app locks the core behind premium.

product.title: Ads and forced Google Play kick-outs
product.minus: Ads for other games appear between lessons, and worse — you can't just close them: at the end the app forces open Google Play instead of letting you return to studying, which for some makes the product unusable.

product.title: Too few languages to choose from
product.minus: The app mainly covers Korean, Japanese, Spanish and French, and people regularly leave disappointed at the absence of Chinese, Norwegian, Thai, German or Arabic — demand for new languages clearly outpaces supply.

product.title: Crashes, freezes and a phantom streak
product.minus: On top of everything — instability: the app freezes the phone mid-lesson, crashes, stops opening, won't load videos, and a revived streak shows 'successful' yet still dies — striking at the main reason to keep coming back.

product.title: Drills two phrases at once, no reinforcement
product.minus: The lesson structure is questionable: the app introduces two new phrases at once without locking in the first, and grammar is buried inside long lessons with no separate review — for people with weaker memory it's hard to retain.

product.title: Speech recognition rejects correct answers
product.minus: The core pain: people say the phrase correctly — sometimes even as native speakers — yet the app keeps marking it wrong and won't let them continue. A simple word for 'tea' (thee/te) hard-stops lesson one with no way to skip.

product.title: Passes you on words you never said
product.minus: The flip side of the same broken engine: it doesn't just reject correct speech, it waves through partial or unspoken answers — marking words right when you never finished them. That defeats the whole point of pronunciation practice.

product.title: Speaking from day one — and it actually works
product.plus: The standout strength even critics admit: the 'repeat out loud' method gets you speaking from the start instead of guessing words in games. Many note that after Duolingo, where you never speak, here they finally feel real progress in speech.

product.title: Subscription ads after every lesson, longer than the lesson
product.minus: Paywalls and premium ads pop up after literally every lesson, and the lessons are shorter than the pitches. Before the first lesson people click past 10+ subscription offers — it reads as 'they only want your money'.

product.title: AI-generated sentences are nonsense and teach errors
product.minus: Deeper into the course the 'AI slop' shows: grammatically broken, absurd phrases like 'I have a bicycle in my breakfast' or 'It's a book with coffee?'. No native ever reviews the lessons — Swedish, Greek and Dutch are full of mistakes.

product.title: An update wiped progress and killed what people loved
product.minus: A recent update reformatted the app: situational conversations gone, progress wiped, no choosing a lesson or level. The old Falou was quietly moved to a separate app called Chats, while a 'second Duolingo' shipped under the Falou name.

product.title: Paid for premium — and it unlocked nothing
product.minus: People who paid (often ~$90 yearly) complain access never opens up: no skipping or reviewing levels, progress not tied to an account, and support emails go unanswered. The word 'scam' comes up, along with refund requests.

product.title: No way to revisit lessons or skip what you know
product.minus: The course structure is rigid: you can't revisit earlier chapters to recap, and you can't skip what you already know. Without a proper placement test, a beginner gets stuck in dull easy lessons while a B2 learner is fed A1 words.

product.title: Quickly teaches real phrases for conversation
product.plus: When the method clicks, the effect is real: people memorize practical, everyday phrases faster than elsewhere and feel they can already speak after a few lessons. Many love the focus on conversation over starting from raw grammar.

product.title: Price too high, with no monthly plan or trial
product.minus: The free tier lasts a couple of lessons, then it's a yearly subscription only — no monthly option and often no trial. For students and users in India and elsewhere the price feels out of reach.

product.title: Cuts you off mid-sentence and hangs during lessons
product.minus: The app often cuts the speaker off before they even start or right mid-phrase, and lessons hang to the point where not a single word registers. It breaks exactly when you're trying to speak.

product.title: The course serves lessons in the wrong language
product.minus: A recurring bug: past a certain chapter the app serves a different language instead of the target one — Spanish for French, Portuguese for Japanese, English with Spanish as the native — and gets stuck on that lesson with no way out.

product.title: Teaches without gamification — the logic of the language, not points and streaks
product.plus: The number-one reason people stay: no owls, no energy meters, no guilt-trip streak reminders. Mango explains why the language works the way it does instead of forcing rote memorization, and trusts you to decide when to move on.

product.title: Free through a library card — but only if you're lucky with your library
product.plus: A huge loyalty driver: many libraries unlock full Mango access for free with membership, and people thank the app specifically for this. Progress syncs between the app and the website.

product.title: Record and compare your pronunciation against a native speaker
product.plus: A beloved feature: you can record yourself and play it back against the native speaker to match your accent. For many it's the genuine game-changer.

product.title: No feedback on your speech: you record, but never learn if it was right
product.minus: The flip side of voice recording: the app asks you to repeat, waits, then gives no assessment or correction. There's no submit button, no penalty for hitting Next — you can just skip ahead without knowing if you're right.

product.title: Explains grammar and culture — not just words
product.plus: Mango gives grammar notes, the why-behind-the-rule, and cultural tidbits between lessons. Colour-coded words show how a phrase's translation maps together. It's exactly what people felt Duolingo lacked.

product.title: Teaches phrases in context — and you start speaking fast
product.plus: The 'build phrases in context, not random words' approach gives a feeling of real progress: people say they were speaking within a week and assembling full sentences rather than disconnected phrases.

product.title: Spaced repetition and flashcards that lock in what you've learned
product.plus: The SRS system and end-of-chapter review flashcards bring back what you missed, again and again, until it sticks. People note the material stays with them better than in other apps.

product.title: Early paywall: 3 free lessons, then subscribe
product.minus: Without library access the wall comes up fast: after a few lessons everything locks behind a subscription. Some are angry enough to call it a scam; others quit midway because they simply can't afford it.

product.title: Simple, clean interface and autoplay — learn while driving or on the go
product.plus: An interface with only what you need, bite-sized lessons, no ads. The autoplay/hands-free mode lets you listen while driving or doing chores. The one recurring design gripe is the missing dark mode.

product.title: Weak pronunciation support for non-Latin languages: no pinyin, romaji, kanji
product.minus: For Japanese, Mandarin and other languages far from English, the pronunciation aid is just an anglicised, often inconsistent spelling. No pinyin or romaji, advanced Japanese runs without kanji, and important sound distinctions simply aren't addressed.

product.title: Rare and endangered languages free — from Levantine Arabic to Gaelic
product.plus: A catalogue strength: a wide range of dialects and rare languages, including deep Levantine Arabic, Irish and Scottish Gaelic courses, with endangered languages often free. It wins over people Duolingo didn't serve.

product.title: Catalogue gaps: missing interface languages and the target languages people want
product.minus: For all the exotic breadth, people get turned away at the door: the interface doesn't support their native language (e.g. Indonesian), there are no Southern African languages, and sometimes you find 'Pirate' and Shakespearean English but not living languages spoken by millions.

product.title: Launch failures: app won't open after an update
product.minus: A slice of users can't get in at all: the app crashes on launch or stops opening right after an update, wasting their data. Separate complaints mention a crash when trying to view study stats.

product.title: The dictionary with examples and conjugations is the core value
product.plus: People come back for the rich entries: multiple usage examples, context, related terms and full conjugation tables for any verb. That is exactly what the app is loved for.

product.title: The free version is genuinely usable, not crippled into uselessness
product.plus: A rare kind of praise: the free tier gives real definitions, examples, conjugations and lessons. Users specifically thank the team for making it fully usable without paying.

product.title: A direct Duolingo rival — and it often wins
product.plus: After Duolingo "did some very stupid things," people switch here and stay: same formats but without the childishness, with real grammar and drills. Many flat-out call it better than the green owl.

product.title: Word tiles vanish on tap — making lessons impossible to pass
product.minus: The most painful bug: in the build-a-phrase exercises the tapped word disappears and never comes back, so every answer is marked wrong. Several users call the app outright unusable because of it.

product.title: Pronunciation by real humans, not a robot
product.plus: Words voiced by real native speakers (both Latin American and Spain variants) is a standout: you can trust the pronunciation, and the word is even read out slowly.

product.title: No dark theme — blinding, after years of requests
product.minus: The oldest unmet request: the interface is too bright for outdoors and evening study, and a dark mode still doesn't exist. Some refuse to buy a subscription purely over this.

product.title: Freezes, lags and crashes — especially on newer phones
product.minus: Stability is shaky: it lags while typing, freezes, crashes during vocab practice, and dies after thirty seconds on newer Pixels. For some it dropped the rating from five stars.

product.title: Ads are tolerable, but the subscription pitch hits the moment you open it
product.minus: Most call the ads unobtrusive and short, but the irritant is elsewhere: you're pushed to buy a subscription before you've even seen the app, and forced to sign in via Google/Facebook. For some that's a red flag.

product.title: It doesn't train speaking — only typing and picking words
product.minus: Anyone wanting speaking practice is let down: the app never asks you to say words aloud, only to type or choose them. For some that wasn't enough, and the male AI voice is hard to understand.

product.title: Grammar is genuinely taught — with videos and the logic of the language
product.plus: A real strength for serious learners: lessons explain why the grammar works as it does, with short teacher videos, conjugations and drills. It teaches how the language works rather than rote vocab.

product.title: It used to be a clean dictionary — now it's bloated and lost its definitions
product.minus: Some long-time users complain the good dictionary turned into an overloaded learning app: the actual definitions are gone (only example sentences remain), there's too much going on, and one even cites "thousands of ads."

product.title: It flags a word's region — Spain, Latam — but offers no dialect switch
product.plus: A detail serious learners value: the app marks where a word or phrase comes from (Spain, Latam) and teaches regional differences. But there's no dialect toggle, and Castilian Spanish specifically is missing.

product.title: Word of the Day quietly pulls users back in every day
product.plus: A simple but beloved hook: a daily notification with a new word and sensible example sentences. For many it's the main reason they open the app and the habit that keeps learning going.

product.title: Swapping hearts for energy is felt as ruining a once-loved app
product.minus: The switch from hearts to energy is the single most frequent and painful complaint: energy drains on every question, runs out after a couple of lessons, and forces you to wait or pay. Many users came back specifically to change their review and drop their rating over it.

product.title: Gamification turns studying into an addictive daily habit
product.plus: The app's core strength: learning feels like a game, lessons are engaging, and points and streaks motivate daily return. Many admit they got hooked and have kept their streak for years.

product.title: Great to start from scratch, but doesn't teach real fluency
product.plus: Users value how the app gently eases a beginner in from the very basics and simple phrases — an excellent starting point for a new language.

product.title: Teaches entertainment, not real speaking: no grammar, no depth
product.minus: Experienced users note the app consumes time via 'allegedly fun exercises' but gives no systematic grammar explanations and no real language progress. Removing the discussion centre with native speakers made it worse.

product.title: Aggressive ads feel like pressure to subscribe
product.minus: Ad volume has grown to 'egregious' levels: refilling energy means watching ever more videos, and users feel like 'hostages' to ads in an app that's supposed to teach a language.

product.title: Turned from a good cause into a money-extraction machine
product.minus: Long-time users mourn that the app went from a free public good to a 'for-profit' product manipulating micro-transactions: on top of regular Super there's now an even pricier Max.

product.title: Expansion beyond languages: chess, music, math
product.plus: Users love the new courses — chess, music and math; the chess character Oscar is a particular favorite. Being able to learn it all in one app is seen as a big plus.

product.title: Bugs: correct answers marked wrong, progress lost
product.minus: Serious technical failures: the app marks correct answers as wrong, breaks long streaks of right answers, energy drops from 20 to 10 by itself with no mistake, and levels sometimes have to be redone.

product.title: Speech recognition rejects correct pronunciation
product.minus: Voice exercises and the paid Max conversation mode often fail to register correctly spoken words: recognition ignores context and produces nonsense matches, undermining an expensive feature.

product.title: A patient 'strict teacher' that keeps you motivated
product.plus: Many see Duo as a kind but persistent mentor: the character reminds you to study daily, encourages you, and makes the process feel warmly human.

product.title: The app freezes and crashes, sometimes losing access entirely
product.minus: Instability breaks study sessions: the app crashes mid-lesson, won't open for days, won't log in via Google account — even for paying users who lose paid time and hard-won progress.

product.title: No support: AI bot can't help, no human to reach
product.minus: When something breaks with a subscription or account, users hit a useless AI assistant and silent support — ten days with no reply, a child's lost progress, and no way to get a refund.

product.title: You can't cancel from inside the app — there's no button
product.minus: There's no subscription management in the app itself: you're pushed to the website or to the third-party Paddle billing you also can't reach. People spend weeks emailing, get only bots back, and end up blocking their card.

product.title: They keep charging after you cancel and delete the account
product.minus: A textbook dark pattern: you delete the account inside the app while billing quietly continues. People cancelled months ago and are still being charged, sometimes two or three times in a month.

product.title: Support runs you in circles and refuses refunds
product.minus: Refund requests get template replies, stalling, or silence the moment you send screenshots. Almost no one gets money back — most have to dispute the charge through their bank.

product.title: "Premium" is still limited — you pay, then they ask for more
product.minus: After paying for a subscription you find out it's the basic tier, and the AI tutor and "unlimited" cost extra. The app bombards you with upgrade screens before you even open the first lesson.

product.title: Content stops at A2 — the promised B/C levels aren't there
product.minus: The listing promises "Rookie to Advanced", but the actual courses (Spanish, Italian, German, French) end around A1–A2. No new lessons appear for months, and the answer is just "read the books".

product.title: The test rates your level, but the app starts you from zero anyway
product.minus: A long placement test rates you intermediate or advanced, yet inside the app you're dropped into the most basic "me gusta" lessons you can't skip. Spending an hour testing out of levels doesn't help.

product.title: An endless "take the test" loop blocks all progress
product.minus: You press Continue, pass the test, get congratulated — and land back on the same screen. Ten times over; neither reinstalling nor support fixes it, and the app you paid for simply won't let you move on.

product.title: Setup and sign-up die on a false "network error"
product.minus: Plenty of users can't get past onboarding: "network error" / "server error" with working internet, across different networks and devices. Some delete the app without ever opening a single lesson.

product.title: Create an account after paying — and lose the subscription you just bought
product.minus: The flow is broken: you pay, then tap "create account" — your email switches to a different one, premium vanishes, and the "14-day money-back guarantee" no longer applies.

product.title: Broken translations and AI audio read other languages as English
product.minus: Spanish words are pronounced by English rules, translations give the wrong meaning out of context, and the AI voice sounds like a twenty-year-old machine translator. You can't trust the learning material.

product.title: The movie-clip-and-books method genuinely hooks people
product.plus: For those who get to actually learn, the mix of real-show video clips, narrated simplified books and games clicks — the language comes in context, it's not boring, and many report faster progress than with other apps.

product.title: Energy limits push you to buy instead of letting you learn
product.minus: Free and even on the basic plan you get about twenty minutes a day: energy runs out, a timer ticks, and when it ends you get a subscription screen instead of a lesson. Tests burn your energy for nothing.

product.title: An onboarding wall of dozens of questions scares people off
product.minus: Before you start there's a long sensory-overload questionnaire, and the price only shows up at the very end. People quit before the first lesson and suspect it's there to harvest personal data.

product.title: Video and audio buffer, stutter and cut out
product.minus: Books stop loading after chapter eight or ten, story audio breaks after five minutes, and clip sound is either muffled or too quiet even at the phone's max volume.

product.title: The paywall is hidden until the end of a long onboarding
product.minus: You spend 10-15 minutes on the questionnaire, level check and lesson plan, then discover the first lesson won't even start without a subscription. It feels like a bait-and-switch — they stay silent about the cost until your time is already spent.

product.title: Botched pronunciation undermines trust in the lessons
product.minus: The AI tutor mangles words — Italian sounds like an American faking it, Japanese kanji are read wrong. If the tutor itself speaks incorrectly, you can't trust what it's teaching you.

product.title: Praises you for answers you never gave
product.minus: The tutor announces "great, you're at A1" when the user never spoke the target language at all or the mic didn't work. Hollow praise instead of real assessment makes the feedback worthless.

product.title: Essentially an expensive ChatGPT wrapper
product.minus: Users see a plain text LLM behind the avatar: you can get the same thing from a free chatbot with a couple of prompts. The ad showing live pronunciation feedback turns out to be fake — it's just text with a talking head.

product.title: Cancelling and getting a refund turns into a quest
product.minus: They charge people after cancellation despite a confirmation email, don't send the cancel link, ignore emails. It gets so bad that users cancel their card just to stop the payments.

product.title: They demand a card before the first free-trial lesson
product.minus: The "free" trial won't let you start even the first lesson without entering card details — banking on you forgetting to cancel. Many refuse: they won't hand over a card before trying the product.

product.title: A thin language selection cuts off the audience
product.minus: No Polish, Russian, Arabic, Welsh, Gaelic, Greek, Breton — there's simply nothing for many users to learn. The ads promise "a lot of languages" while the actual selection is very narrow.

product.title: Quizzes ask about things never taught
product.minus: The post-lesson quiz throws in words that were never covered or gives options in the target language with no context — so you're guaranteed to fail. The tutor gets confused, repeats the same question twice, and doesn't notice its own mistakes.

product.title: Push-to-talk and lag break the live conversation
product.minus: You have to press a button every time you want to speak — no hands-free, useless while driving. The mic often doesn't pick you up, the tutor takes too long to start speaking, responses hang — the illusion of a live conversation falls apart.

product.title: Removes the fear of speaking and gives real spoken practice
product.plus: The core strength: you can speak out loud with no social pressure, at your own pace, and get instant feedback. People who can read and write but freeze up speaking finally practice the one thing they need.

product.title: The avatar tutor feels alive and welcoming
product.plus: Many find the tutor warm and human — you can ask a question mid-conversation, request an explanation in your native language, pick a character. After "cold" apps it's a relief that Skye/Tama react like a person.

product.title: Remembers context and adapts to the individual
product.plus: The AI remembers past answers and topics — even things said two weeks ago — and builds immersive, personalized learning on top of that. It feels like real progress that template-based apps can't match.

product.title: Hard subscription-only model with no monthly plan
product.minus: Only a yearly plan at ~$99-106 or three months — no month-to-month option and not a single free feature. Committing a full year to an unproven product feels like too big a risk, especially outside the US.

product.title: Only a couple of free chapters, then a hard paywall
product.minus: Users get through 2-3 chapters (often in about five minutes) and hit a wall: you can only keep learning by subscribing. Many feel misled after the «like Duolingo» pitch and uninstall right at that screen.

product.title: Short video lessons that are clear and addictive
product.plus: The core strength: bite-size lessons with real video (not 2D diagrams) that are easy to follow at your own pace. People say they learned more than in years of school classes, and that it's genuinely fun.

product.title: Auslan is promised in the title but isn't in the app
product.minus: Australians download it as an «Auslan resource» per the description, then at language selection see only ASL, BSL and Austrian ÖGS — no Australian sign at all. They feel duped by false advertising and uninstall immediately.

product.title: The subscription is steep — especially for those who need signing to communicate
product.minus: Prices around $17/mo or roughly $100-125/yr strike many as outrageous «in this economy». It hits hardest for deaf users, broke teens and people on fixed incomes, who feel learning to communicate shouldn't cost this much.

product.title: Self-paced learning is what people love most
product.plus: Going slow, calm and pressure-free is a key reason people get attached. They value that the app doesn't rush, recycles material and lets you feel daily progress.

product.title: No trial without a card, and cancelling is a nightmare
product.minus: Getting the «7 free days» requires entering card details before seeing a single lesson. Cancelling runs through 4 screens plus a mandatory Google Play step — users report being charged anyway and read it as a bet on people forgetting.

product.title: Multiple signers in the videos teach you to recognise variations
product.plus: A real strength of the method: signs are shown by several different people, so you learn to recognise one sign performed in different ways and see regional variations — closer to real-world conversation.

product.title: AI use is alarming: «it can't do hands»
product.minus: Users discover the app uses AI only after agreeing to the trial and start doubting the signs: the language is 99% hands, and AI is notorious for getting hands wrong. It breeds a fear of learning misinformation.

product.title: Too little content — the course runs out fast
product.minus: Even paying users complain there aren't many lessons: the course is done in a couple of months, leaving only review of what you've covered. People want more dialogues and ongoing content to keep progressing.

product.title: Manipulative notifications push people away
product.minus: Guilt-tripping pushes («you're hurting our feelings for not putting in 10 minutes») and nagging midnight reminders irritate users — some stop opening the app entirely after one.

product.title: It actually helps people communicate with loved ones and at work
product.plus: A strong emotional payoff: people learn to talk with a deaf child, brother, granddaughter or customers at work — and it works. For many, the app makes real communication attainable.

product.title: No way to slow down videos or set your own level
product.minus: Signs play at full speed with no slow-motion — if you miss it, you just rewatch over and over. There's also no placement test: people who already know the basics are forced to relearn «hello» and «thank you».

product.title: The "free trial" charges you immediately
product.minus: Over and over people describe the same thing: you accept a 14- or 3-day trial and the full amount (AU$94.99, £64.99, €80) is taken within minutes, sometimes even after cancelling and uninstalling.

product.title: Charges without consent and near-impossible refunds
product.minus: Dozens report money (3,800 pesos, $49.99, $140) leaving their GCash, e-wallet or card without their knowledge, while support answers with copy-paste AI replies or demands you "complete 10 lessons" before a refund is considered.

product.title: You paid, yet almost everything is still locked
product.minus: Paying doesn't unlock the app: users say ~90% of lessons still ask for extra payment, every lesson shows a lock, and "premium" turns out to be just a gateway to more purchases.

product.title: Speech recognition and the AI tutor just don't work
product.minus: The headline feature — a talking AI — fails for many: it doesn't respond to your voice, turns correctly spoken words into "rubbish", and role-plays freeze with no way to skip.

product.title: Built for English, fails learners of other languages
product.minus: Buying Spanish, French or Ukrainian, people find the AI and content are built for English: a Spanish speaker with an English accent, explanations only in English, and a Ukrainian course that never goes past beginner.

product.title: Misjudges your level: advanced learners get baby flashcards
product.minus: There's a placement test but it's ignored: pick advanced and you get basic flashcards and beginner-level lessons, with no real progression or level accuracy.

product.title: Freezes at plan setup — you never reach the lessons
product.minus: A recurring scenario: the app freezes on the "Your course is ready" screen, crashes during sign-up, or gets stuck on the splash logo — even a fellow mobile developer documented the onboarding bug.

product.title: The ads promise one thing, the app delivers another
product.minus: Slick ads lure you with a "native speaker" and a full AI conversation partner, but inside there are only boring flashcards, repetitive vocab drills and an AI that just repeats the sentence; the price at checkout suddenly differs.

product.title: Bite-sized 10–15-minute lessons actually keep you consistent
product.plus: Those who click with it praise the format: compact daily 10–15-minute lessons fit easily into a day and are what keep people coming back — even users who already have Duolingo and Rosetta Stone.

product.title: Shadowing, error feedback and culture notes — a strong method
product.plus: Those who get into it call out genuine strengths: scene-based shadowing for pronunciation, detailed feedback after role-play with more natural response options, clear explanations, and engaging culture notes.

product.title: Free premium for Ukrainians is a standout perk
product.plus: Ukrainian users specifically thank the app for free premium (learned via the state employment center) and the fun "Usyk mode" that keeps motivation up — a rare source of genuine delight in the review feed.

product.title: Without review, what you learn slips away fast
product.minus: Even happy users flag one gap in the method: lessons only push forward, old vocabulary barely returns, there are no tests or flashcard consolidation — and words are quickly forgotten.

product.title: A Plus subscription layered on top of already-paid Pro feels like a betrayal
product.minus: People who paid once for lifetime Pro found features hidden behind a new monthly Plus tier — they were promised a one-time fee for all features, and now feel demoted back to being free users.

product.title: After updates the app turned unstable: crashes, freezes, won't open
product.minus: Long-time users see the app crash right on launch, freeze at the login screen, or die mid-session — reinstalling and clearing the cache don't help.

product.title: Nagging 'no internet' popups break offline use
product.minus: Basic features used to work fine offline, but now every screen throws a 'Poor internet connection. Enter limited mode' popup — absurd for an app whose whole point is to pull you away from connectivity.

product.title: Basic functions — app blocking, charts, tags — are locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Blocking more than one app, creating a tag, or seeing your stats now requires a subscription — for cash-strapped students the app collapses into a plain timer.

product.title: Ads and Plus popups on every open are infuriating
product.minus: Even paying Pro users get ads and a 'buy Plus' popup on every launch; the 'take a break' button leads to a non-skippable ad — at odds with the very idea of a focus app.

product.title: Gamification and events turned from motivation into distracting noise
product.minus: Challenges, levels, events and endless popups, users say, keep you on the app instead of focused on your task — exactly contrary to its original purpose.

product.title: The new 'pause' button kills the blocking people installed it for
product.minus: The added pause lets you interrupt the blocking endlessly with no penalty, so a 25-minute session drags on for hours — the core feature people bought it for stopped working.

product.title: Login and sync wipe out years of accumulated progress
product.minus: Sudden account-creation prompts, 'invalid username or password', and sync failures cause trees and purchased sounds to vanish or get locked after logging in on a new phone.

product.title: The focus sound keeps playing after the timer ends
product.minus: White noise and nature sounds don't stop when the session ends (sometimes even after closing the app), so you can't tell by ear that time's up and have to keep watching the screen.

product.title: The 'focus → tree' loop genuinely makes concentration feel rewarding
product.plus: A forest that grows as you focus gives a tangible reward for each session: people are drawn to unlock new trees and decorate their forest, and that's exactly what gets them to sit down and study or work.

product.title: Cuts screen time and genuinely keeps you off the phone
product.plus: Blocking distracting apps during a session helps people with ADHD and students stay out of social media — many report their screen time dropped by nearly half.

product.title: Planting real trees and studying with friends wins people over
product.plus: Turning focus time into real tree planting and shared sessions with friends adds meaning and social motivation — people value it as something more than just a timer.

product.title: Responsive support that fixes bugs wins ratings back to five stars
product.plus: When the team responds fast and resolves issues — restoring accounts, fixing sound, shipping fixes — users restore five stars and note the developers actually listen to suggestions.

product.title: An ad after every tap turns a focus timer into a source of distraction
product.minus: Ads pop up on practically every single tap: open the app — ad, press a button — ad, stop the timer — ad. In an app built for concentration, this directly destroys the very focus people installed it for.

product.title: Ads even during the study session itself
product.minus: Leave the app to do other work and come back to check the timer, and an ad greets you. Users plainly ask for one thing: anything but ads while the study timer is running.

product.title: Long unskippable clips, sometimes two in a row
product.minus: The complaint isn't just frequency but format: unskippable 15-30 second clips, often two back to back after a single action. The "good" ads are described as the ones where you only wait 5 seconds.

product.title: The bunny-and-coins gamification genuinely motivates studying
product.plus: The most heartfelt praise: earning coins for study time, decorating the room and a cute bunny turn drudgery into a game. People with short attention spans admit they studied for hours for the first time just to keep the bunny happy.

product.title: Time tracking and colour-coded subjects give a clear picture of study
product.plus: Beyond the game, users value the tracker itself: you can see how many hours you studied and on which subjects, colour-code those subjects and review weekly and monthly progress. For many it's the main reason to stay.

product.title: The timer resets or glitches when the phone is locked or the app is closed
product.minus: A paradox: people put the phone away to avoid distraction, and because of that the timer stops, freezes on an old value, or simply won't count in the background. Sometimes it does the opposite — starting on its own and crediting hours that were never studied.

product.title: Data and progress can't move to a new device without paying
product.minus: Moving data between devices is paywalled, and cloud restore loses your check-in streak and purchased cosmetics. For multi-year users with years of accumulated history, that's a painful blow.

product.title: The app stopped working offline — no internet means no studying
product.minus: It used to work in airplane mode, cutting off distractions; now without a connection the app is essentially unusable. For people without a data plan, that's the loss of a core use case.

product.title: Flashcards and built-in study guides make it more than just a timer
product.plus: Beyond the timer, users praise the flashcards and the in-app guides on efficient study methods. For some, the flashcards were the thing that finally let them sit down and actually learn the material.

product.title: Too few coins for a long session undercuts the reward loop
product.minus: People like the reward system but find the economy stingy: a 60-minute session yields just 6 coins, so decorations take hours to save up for. Some feel the effort simply isn't paid back.

product.title: Premium sign-up and study-with-friends often just don't work
product.minus: Premium registration fails with a "registration failed" error, and the social "study with friends" feature either won't let you sign up or feels dead and empty. The promised collaborative functions don't deliver.

product.title: Harsh break penalties and the stress of keeping the bunny happy
product.minus: The same gamification turns into pressure for some: a break over seven minutes already counts as a violation, and constantly having to keep the bunny happy makes studying more anxious, not easier.

product.title: No phone-lock or background notifications — it doesn't actually keep you off your phone
product.minus: Users expect Forest-style mechanics from a focus app: blocking you from leaving and a sound notification when the session ends even with the screen off. As is, the app doesn't fence you off from your phone.

product.title: The pause before opening genuinely kills autopilot scrolling
product.plus: What people love most: the brief wait screen makes you think "do I actually want this?" for a second, and users close the app without even entering it. Hours of social media collapse into minutes.

product.title: The free version lets you block only one app
product.minus: The most common gripe even among fans: one free slot is a loophole, since people are hooked on several apps. Block Instagram, drift to YouTube Shorts or Snapchat. Many beg for at least 2-3 free slots.

product.title: Ads promise "pushups to unlock", but Android doesn't have it
product.minus: People install specifically for the pushup/squat unlocks pushed all over TikTok and Instagram, pay for a year, then find only breathing. The feature is iOS-only with zero mention of it in the Android app. Many call it false advertising and a scam.

product.title: Yearly subscription only, no monthly — a week's trial can't tell you if it works
product.minus: No monthly plan: a 7-day trial, then pay for a whole year up front (~$45-75). Habits take ~20 days to form, so a week can't tell you if it'll help. Some call the model predatory, a money grab.

product.title: The quotes at open hit right at the moment of impulse
product.plus: The inspirational lines on the wait screen are a separately loved touch: they nudge you toward something useful instead of scrolling and catch the moment of mindless opening.

product.title: Forced Google-only sign-in scares people off at the door
product.minus: The very first screen is "continue with Google" — no email, no guest, no username/password. For many that's overkill and they uninstall before trying it; some go straight to rivals like ScreenZen.

product.title: The pushup counter counts thin air and is easy to cheat
product.minus: Where exercises do exist, the detector is raw: it counts pushups when the camera sees nothing, sometimes hands you a free "automatic" rep — turning the lock into a formality you scroll right past.

product.title: The Android version clearly lags iOS and looks unfinished
product.minus: Android users feel second-class: the UI looks cheap, like a 2010 Android app, and half the iOS features are missing — at the same subscription price.

product.title: Works where blockers, timers and deleting apps all failed
product.plus: People who tried deleting apps, built-in limits and hard blocks say the gentle breathing pause is the only thing that actually gave them control — and they don't want to delete it precisely because it isn't strict.

product.title: People want a one-time/lifetime purchase instead of a subscription
product.minus: Even willing-to-pay users balk at subscribing for such simple mechanics: they propose a one-time fee, buying slots one at a time, "add 3 more apps" bundles, or a lifetime license — even at a higher price.

product.title: Small bugs break trust: the wrong app opens, streaks reset
product.minus: Annoying glitches erode the experience: after confirming, a different controlled app opens; streaks reset for no reason; the pause loads so slowly you're already sucked in before it appears. Some cancel their subscription over it.

product.title: Users ask for more challenge types: squats, reading, writing
product.minus: Those who like the "earn screen time" idea want variety: one kind of pushup gets stale. They ask for squats, reading pages, minutes of writing — to cover different interests and not only people who can do pushups.

product.title: Ad-free, no-paywall minimalism is the core reason people love it
product.plus: A clean interface, zero ads and no nagging to buy anything — users repeatedly call it the best pomodoro app precisely because of its austerity.

product.title: On-the-fly duration tweaking is the killer feature
product.plus: Being able to change work/break length mid-session and jump back to a previous cycle is the thing people will forgive everything else for.

product.title: The timer reliably runs in the background and with the screen off
product.plus: Many are surprised the timer genuinely keeps time in the background and works in sleep mode — by their account, a rarity among pomodoro apps.

product.title: The end-of-session notification stays on screen — and reads it without unlocking
product.plus: A noticeable notification with vibration and a loud-enough sound, plus checking the timer via the power button without unlocking, gets singled out as a real convenience.

product.title: The green palette and design aesthetic give a sense of calm
product.plus: The aesthetic and green colour are specifically called pleasant and calming — for a chunk of users this is a real part of the app's appeal.

product.title: The flip side of minimalism: no proper stats or reports
product.minus: Users constantly ask for detailed statistics, graphs and yearly reports; what exists feels raw — for instance, time is shown in minutes rather than hours.

product.title: No customizable notification sound
product.minus: The alert sound can't be changed — some say it sounds like their doorbell, others want it louder or a ticking option, and several ask for a sound-vs-vibration choice.

product.title: No tags, labels or categories for sessions
product.minus: Users want to label sessions (study, work, custom tags) and see per-label stats — without it they can't tell where their time went.

product.title: No landscape mode — useless on a tablet
product.minus: The missing landscape orientation is cited outright as a deal-breaker on tablets and docks; users also ask for widgets to run the timer.

product.title: No cloud sync or backup of progress
product.minus: Progress lives only on the device: switching phones loses it, and users call cloud export/backup the missing piece that would make it perfect.

product.title: Long-break autoplay and notification-time updates are buggy
product.minus: Several concrete bugs: the long break doesn't start automatically, and the notification time fails to update after a pause — painful for tracking.

product.title: Requests for a ticking sound and background noises to focus
product.minus: The lack of a ticking timer and background noises (rain, white noise) is a frequent ask; for one user the silent notification instead of ticking "defeats the whole purpose."

product.title: Hard blocking with no overrides actually works
product.plus: When a no-phone session is scheduled, there's no way around it — and that very rigidity is what keeps people off the screen.

product.title: Everything locked behind a $99/year subscription
product.minus: You can't use the app without subscribing, and for many the paywall itself is a barrier — especially when money is tight.

product.title: The Android version is noticeably weaker and rough
product.minus: Compared to the Apple version the Android app is unresponsive, won't let you pick specific apps to block, and struggles across timezones when travelling.

product.title: Support refunded the switch from Apple to Android
product.plus: A user who moved from iPhone to Android got a full refund on the Apple subscription so they could resubscribe on Android — the support turned a user into a fan.

product.title: Onboarding stalls on login and permissions
product.minus: Some users can't get past setup — one is stuck on the Google sign-in button, another can't proceed after granting the draw-over-apps permission.

product.title: Complaints of overcharging and refused refunds
product.minus: One review alleges being billed three times the listed amount with no refund — a red flag against the otherwise positive refund experience others report.

product.title: The garden grows from focus — and it genuinely keeps you at your desk
product.plus: The core loop works: focused time pays out coins and new plants, and the urge to watch the garden bloom turns studying into a game that beats procrastination on its own.

product.title: You can't friend someone on the other OS — the whole social hook is broken
product.minus: Android and iOS users simply can't add each other as friends, so the study-together and competition features many installed the app for just don't work, forcing people to coordinate through outside group chats.

product.title: Fully free with no ads — where rivals put up a paywall
product.plus: People specifically thank the app for keeping the core features — deep focus and the garden included — free and ad-free, while rivals like Forest lock the same things behind a subscription.

product.title: Step out of the app for a second and you lose all progress and coins
product.minus: Reading a message or googling a term means leaving the app — and the session resets along with the coins you earned, which enrages people, especially when the phone itself holds their study material.

product.title: No app whitelist — it blocks everything you actually need
product.minus: Deep focus is all-or-nothing: you can't whitelist even a couple of apps (calculator, notes, study messengers), so for online studying the timer becomes more of an obstacle than a help.

product.title: Constantly logs you out and complains about the internet
product.minus: The app logs people out multiple times a day and forces re-login, often blaming a missing connection while the network is fine — an irritating bug that breaks the basic flow for some users.

product.title: AI images instead of relaxing landscapes feel cheap and betray the concept
product.minus: Some users, artists especially, recoil at the swap to AI-generated landscapes: it looks cheap and contradicts the app's eco message, while the canned AI quotes at the start of a focus feel like a missed chance at real motivation.

product.title: It locks you off your phone — a lifeline for procrastinators and ADHD
product.plus: The very threat of losing a tree if you leave the app effectively kills the urge to grab the phone: people with ADHD, chronic doomscrolling and procrastination say Flora is the one thing that actually got them to focus.

product.title: The Android build is a stripped-down poor cousin of iOS
product.minus: The Android client is visibly poorer and looks different: features go missing (tasks, app-blocking, parts of the grand tour), the UI feels dated, and users openly demand it be brought up to the iOS level.

product.title: It mis-counts focus — false fails during real study, or counting when you do nothing
product.minus: The time-counting logic glitches both ways: sometimes it accuses you of using the phone during hours of honest study and burns your points, other times it silently keeps the timer running up to three hours after a session ends, skewing your stats.

product.title: You can't tag or revisit what a focus session was for
product.minus: Basic tagging and history are missing: the description you type vanishes when the session ends, you can't tap an individual tree to recall what you worked on, and there's no per-session breakdown — only a daily total.

product.title: Doesn't work offline — a letdown for studying on the go
product.minus: The timer needs a connection: with no internet you can't start a session, which hurts people who study on the move or watch their mobile data, and feels like a needless data drain.

product.title: A schedule won't block anything until you manually open the app
product.minus: The most common and damning Android bug: you set a schedule for 7am, but your blocked apps open freely until you open Brick yourself. Then it 'wakes up' and says you've been bricked for hours, even though you were scrolling the whole time. It defeats the entire point — relying on willpower is exactly what you were trying to avoid.

product.title: Schedules have no end time, so you can't leave the brick at home
product.minus: On Android you can only set a start time, not an end time — and the only way to unbrick is to physically tap the fob. So if you set a morning schedule you're forced to carry the brick everywhere, or you're locked out of apps you need all day. iPhone has end times, which infuriates people who bought it on a friend's recommendation.

product.title: The physical barrier genuinely breaks the doomscroll habit
product.plus: The core reason people love it: to reach social media you have to get up and physically tap your phone to a fob hidden in the garage, on the fridge, or in the car. That bodily hurdle does what built-in timers and Digital Wellbeing never could — it forces a beat of awareness about whether the scroll is worth the walk.

product.title: NFC reading is finicky — it takes ten taps to register
product.minus: On Android the fob registers maybe half the time: the phone vibrates as it reads the NFC, but the app does nothing. People take off their case, rub the phone around the brick, tap 10-15 times, sometimes burning 5-10 minutes just to unbrick. And their Tap-to-Pay and other NFC work fine — so it's the app.

product.title: Gave people their life, sleep, and focus back — not a metaphor
product.plus: The strongest reviews aren't about features but consequences: brain fog lifted, sleep returned, people finish whole novels, run 10Ks, notice their depression almost vanish. Screen time drops from 4 hours a day to one. For many it's the 'best purchase in years' and a gift they buy for friends and grads.

product.title: No website blocking on Android — the headline selling point is missing
product.minus: People buy specifically for website blocking — the ads and site promised it — and only learn after delivery that Android can block apps only. Block Instagram, then just open it in the mobile browser. Nobody wants to block their entire browser at work. Many say they're returning it over this. (Some later noted an update added the feature.)

product.title: Too easy to bypass: kill accessibility, recents pop-up, just uninstall
product.minus: For a device that promises 'impossible to get around,' the loopholes pile up. On Xiaomi you just toggle accessibility off and on. You can open a blocked app via a long-press from the recents view. The app 'goes to sleep' if you don't open it for a couple hours and the block falls off. And in non-strict mode it uninstalls in seconds the normal way.

product.title: Updates wipe schedules, modes, and activity history
product.minus: Several times the app started up after an overnight update as if freshly installed — every schedule, mode, and activity log gone. For others it silently reset permissions, so the schedule quietly failed for a couple of days. For a $60-100 device, losing your setup breaks the trust — you can no longer rely on it.

product.title: $60 for what is essentially a couple-dollar NFC sticker
product.minus: The price stings: the fob is an NFC tag you can buy in 10-packs for $5, sold for $60. The app is locked to their tags so third-party ones won't work. Many call it overpriced marketing and point to cheaper or free alternatives that do the same thing.

product.title: You can only brick by physical tap — but the friction is on the wrong action
product.minus: The friction is backwards: to brick your phone you have to get up and tap the fob (the 'hold the icon 3 sec' trick doesn't work on Android), when the hurdle should be on unbricking. People want to turn the block on from anywhere in one tap, and take it off only with effort. As is, the barrier fights you exactly when you're trying to do the right thing.

product.title: The team ships fixes and listens — reviewers upgrade to 5 stars
product.plus: A visible arc: people come back and raise their rating because promised features actually landed — Android website blocking, working 'hold to brick', steadier schedules, faster NFC. Support replies quickly, owns known bugs, and pulls people into the beta. For many it turns 'half-baked' into 'works now'.

product.title: Heavy permissions and phantom NFC triggers spook users
product.minus: Two trust worries. First, the scope of permissions: the app wants to read calls and messages and track everything in the background, and people don't see why — some return it over this. Second, the fob sometimes bricks on its own: on a phone restart, when charging after a dead battery, or randomly mid-day when the brick isn't nearby — leaving you locked out.

product.title: The 4.0 update broke the core function: blocking
product.minus: After the May-June update the app stopped blocking selected apps for a huge share of users: schedules don't fire, and a second tap often lets you straight into a 'blocked' app. Long-time fans are uninstalling because it no longer does the one thing they installed it for.

product.title: Screen-time stats are absurdly wrong
product.minus: Tracking shows physically impossible numbers: 16 hours in an app by 10am, a banking app at 19 hours, counts that don't reset after midnight and contradict the phone's own screen-time. For an app whose whole point is showing your time accurately, this destroys trust entirely.

product.title: Devours tens of gigabytes of mobile data
product.minus: Background data use is anomalous: users report 14-95 GB a month and real overage bills. For an app that barely needs the network at all, it reads like data harvesting and drives uninstalls even among people the blocking was helping.

product.title: Ads inside an 'anti-distraction' app
product.minus: To take a break you're forced to watch full-screen ads with audio, sometimes playable, with no close button, escapable only via the Play Store or a phone restart. The irony bites: a focus app feeding back the exact distraction it sells against, and the ads persist even for paying subscribers.

product.title: Paywall: 3 rules free, everything else by subscription
product.minus: The update retroactively locked what used to be free behind a subscription: a cap of 3 rules (people had 5-7 set up), strict mode, effective blocking. ~$9/month or ~£80/year just to 'block apps on your own phone' reads as a greedy cash grab alienating the user base.

product.title: When it works, it genuinely cuts screen time several times over
product.plus: The strongest theme: users repeatedly report dropping from 6-11 hours to 2-3 a day within a week or a month. Opal catches the unconscious tap, makes you wait before unlocking, and genuinely pulls people out of doomscrolling — for many it's the 'best productivity find' they keep coming back to.

product.title: The Android version is a stripped-down twin of iOS
product.minus: Switchers from iPhone say it in unison: on Android the gems/collectible stones, custom block screens, app passwords and friends are gone, replaced by ads that iOS never had. Opal only reached Android in 2026, and users feel like second-class citizens on a cut-down build.

product.title: On Android it lags hard — black screens and crashes
product.minus: The UI stutters on every action, scrolling is choppy, the clock hands won't follow your drag, and after the splash many users hit a black screen they can't get past. On powerful phones that run heavy games fine, Opal barely moves — clearly a build problem.

product.title: Drains the battery
product.minus: Alongside the data drain, the app noticeably eats battery — up to 20% of the charge — and it got worse after the latest update. Support promises to 'look into it' but it doesn't get fixed, and some users uninstall purely over the drain.

product.title: Bible verses on block screens, unasked
product.minus: Instead of the old calming scenes and countdown, the update started pushing Bible verses and 'trust God' on the pause screens. Non-religious users find it preachy enough to remove the rule entirely — and there's no setting to turn the preaching off.

product.title: Breaks got too easy: the escalating delay collapsed to 5 seconds
product.minus: The unlock delay used to grow with each break (10 → 30 → 90 sec), which is what broke the doomscroll spiral. After the update it's a flat 5 seconds or a paid 'hard mode' — the barrier is gone, and the app no longer holds people back from the apps they wanted blocked.

product.title: Alarming permissions and questionable privacy promises
product.minus: The app demands accessibility access that 'can see everything you do and even control your device,' which some users find excessive. A separate complaint: claims that 'your data never leaves your device' contradict its own Google Play disclosures about collecting and sharing data.

product.title: Login bug: kicked out and re-logging in on every open
product.minus: A frequent Android break: every launch logs you out, asks for your number and an OTP, sometimes creates a fresh username again — and occasionally the codes stop arriving so you can't get in at all. Paid subscriptions also fail to attach to the account.

product.title: Strict but kind — nudges you back gently
product.plus: For users whose app works, the tone wins: not aggressive but with breathing pauses, playful messages and encouragement. Streaks and gamification keep people engaged, and strict blocking with short breaks genuinely helps freelancers and students not relapse.

product.title: Often blocks essential apps with no way to whitelist
product.minus: Opal auto-files essentials as 'distracting' — a music tuner, alarm, Spotify, WhatsApp for calls, study apps, even a banking GCash app — and won't let you unblock or exclude them. There's no split between 'harmful' and 'work' apps, so the blocking gets in the way of studying and daily tasks.

product.title: The ticking sound can't be turned off and drives people mad
product.minus: Many users can't switch off the constant clock ticking and uninstall over it: it cuts through their music, distracts in a quiet room and ruins the whole point of focusing. A hidden mute button (swipe the bottom bar) exists, but almost nobody finds it.

product.title: The Android version is a stripped-down iOS app missing the promised features
product.minus: Switchers from iPhone are stunned: the Android build has no tasks, calendar, dark theme, customization or half the settings present on iOS and shown in the Play Store listing. Users feel deceived by the "fake" screenshots.

product.title: Daily goal and rounds never reset — the counter just keeps climbing
product.minus: The midnight auto-reset works for no one: sessions don't zero out the next day and there's no manual reset. Instead of "10 of 10 sessions" people end up seeing "118 of 10" and lose any way to track progress.

product.title: Just opening the app is a struggle — it crashes on launch
product.minus: On Pixel and Samsung the app crashes instantly on launch or gets stuck on the intro screen. Reinstalls, cache clearing and force-stops don't help — users delete it without ever seeing the timer.

product.title: Ads on the focus screen itself — a mockery of the whole concept
product.minus: A moving carousel of ads now sits on the very screen meant to help you concentrate. There's no way to remove it, and even Pro buyers still see footer ads. For many it was the reason to uninstall.

product.title: No settings menu — you can't set your own focus duration
product.minus: Many can't find any settings at all: it's locked to 25 and 5 minutes, with no way to change durations, pick sounds or add your own music — even though the description promises it. Without customization the app is "close to useless" for them.

product.title: The timer stops the moment you leave the app
product.minus: Minimize the app, rotate the phone or take a call and the countdown freezes or the round ends early. For a timer people rely on while studying this is critical: the time isn't counted and the alarm doesn't ring.

product.title: The end-of-session alarm either blares or fails to fire
product.minus: The end-of-timer sound is unbearably loud and piercing for some with no way to change it, and for others simply doesn't go off — so they never know the time is up. There's no volume control or alarm choice.

product.title: Minimalism that genuinely helps you focus
product.plus: What users love most is the simplicity: open it, start the timer, get to work. No complicated menus. Many studied with it for years, saw their focus and grades improve, and stick with it precisely for that clean, clutter-free interface.

product.title: Flexible long and short intervals instead of rigid 25/5
product.plus: Users for whom the settings work value being able to pick their own focus and break lengths rather than the default 25/5. It lets them tune the rhythm to themselves — especially helpful for people with ADHD who need frequent short breaks.

product.title: Session and stats tracking that motivates you to keep going
product.plus: When tracking works, users enjoy seeing how many sessions they did in a day, setting daily goals and watching progress over time. It turns studying into a visible game against yourself and nudges them to keep at it.

product.title: No dark mode or orientation lock — small things that grate
product.minus: Basic small things are missing: a dark theme (screen burn-in risk and a pain for night studying) and portrait-orientation lock — you can't lay the phone flat without a rotation breaking the timer. iOS has dark mode, Android doesn't.

product.title: Genuinely pulls people off the feed and outside
product.plus: The core praise: people say they finally stopped doomscrolling YouTube and TikTok in the mornings, finished schoolwork and projects, and literally went outside. The "earn your screen time" idea clicks for them.

product.title: The coin economy is poorly tuned — everything pays the same
product.minus: The most common gripe: activity rewards aren't thought through. Journaling pays the same as napping, almost everything is a flat 10 coins regardless of effort. Users explicitly ask for varying amounts per activity.

product.title: Rewards accrue by the hour, not per completed action
product.minus: A distinct pain inside the coin system: tasks are counted "per hour," so there are no quick wins — an hour of breathing for 10 coins feels absurd, and walking "doesn't pay" until a full hour adds up.

product.title: An update cut blocking to 3 apps behind a paywall
product.minus: A sharp breach of trust: a user who blocked 31 apps found the limit dropped to 3 after an update, the rest gated behind a 3-day trial. For a "get off your phone" tool, three slots simply don't cut it.

product.title: The block sometimes fails to actually stop the app
product.minus: A core technical failure: the chosen app still opens, and Unrot only later, on return, flashes "you're blocked, return to Unrot" — without actually cutting off access to the other app.

product.title: Free and unlike the rest — that's the hook
product.plus: Beyond results, people are won over by the concept itself: "free and different for once," "unique." It sets Unrot apart from the usual screen-time timers and blockers.

product.title: Saving the image fails en masse: «Failed to save image» instead of a result
product.minus: After updates, export collapses for a crowd of users with a Bitmap.compress null-reference error: people lose finished work at the very last step and leave for other apps.

product.title: Installing any font you want is the main reason people love it
product.plus: Loading your own TTF instead of being stuck with someone else's set is what keeps users coming back for years; it solves the «my font isn't here» pain other editors leave open.

product.title: A simple, intuitive app people have used for 5–15 years
product.plus: It does exactly one thing — text on photos — and does it easily; dozens describe it as their «go-to» that they reinstall on every new phone.

product.title: The Android version is cut down vs iOS: no zoom and missing exclusive features
product.minus: Users coming from iPhone complain you can't zoom for precise text placement on Android and some paid features are simply absent — the same app feels second-class.

product.title: Free with no aggressive paywall — valued in its own right
product.plus: Most of what you need is free and fonts aren't locked behind a subscription; users openly beg the dev «don't get greedy» and keep it that way.

product.title: No undo button — an accidental mistake means redoing from scratch
product.minus: Long-time users have begged for undo/redo for years: without it any accidental move or layout slip forces a fresh start, and it's the single most requested fix.

product.title: An uploaded image can't be cropped, resized or zoomed
product.minus: Basic operations on the picture itself are missing — you can't crop an inserted image or resize it, so people have to finish the job in another editor.

product.title: Loading photos and picking an image now misbehaves: empty folders and a partial gallery
product.minus: After recent updates the app loads images slowly, shows an empty folder or only part of the library — users can't find their photos and switch to another editor.

product.title: Paid «ad-free» doesn't stick: ads return and the purchase is lost
product.minus: Buyers of the ad-free upgrade report video ads returning after every edit, and some users lose their paid upgrade after switching devices or updating.

product.title: Saved projects and installed fonts vanish after an update or reinstall
product.minus: No account or cloud: an update wipes projects and a reinstall erases every manually added font — people lose months of work and ask for sync.

product.title: Indispensable for content: memes, covers, posters, watermarks, social media
product.plus: Content creators keep it as a core tool: quick adverts, k-pop theme banners, watermarks on icon edits, business posters — it covers real daily work.

product.title: Text controls fall short: sizing by guesswork, no centering, no per-word color
product.minus: Users miss a centering indicator, sizing by touch, and coloring a single word; the font panel covers the photo and you have to scroll back to a font you just used.

product.title: AI editing is advertised as free but is actually paywalled
product.minus: The app is titled "AI Photo Editor" and the first tutorial teaches the AI function, yet it carries no premium symbol — you try it and hit a demand to pay. Users call it dishonest bait.

product.title: The free features just duplicate the phone's built-in editor
product.minus: What you get for free — remove background, resize, change file type — your built-in editor already does. Without paying, people treat it as a 100% paid-only app.

product.title: The "unlimited" promised in the description is actually capped per month
product.minus: After paying premium for promised unlimited use, people hit a monthly cap on AI generations and a lockout until next month — a direct contradiction of the store description.

product.title: The Android version is a stripped-down port of iOS
product.minus: Android lacks curved text, video, image stretching, precise snapping, stop motion — at the same price. Long-time iPhone fans are let down after switching to Samsung/Pixel.

product.title: Premium is paid for, yet premium features don't work
