product.plus: Studying doesn't feel like a chore: memes between questions, customizable avatars and campfire, a game-like feel — both kids and adults have fun, and it genuinely motivates them and improves grades.

product.title: Paper mode doesn't work on the phone
product.minus: Paper mode is unavailable or won't start on mobile and its QR code doesn't work — teachers ask to bring it back the way old Quizizz had it, to connect the phone to a laptop.

product.title: Free access to the features — the key plus for students
product.plus: Users specifically value that the core features (including quiz creation and exam prep) are free — for students and those without a laptop, it's a decisive advantage.

product.title: Poorly optimized for phones and tablets
product.minus: The UI displays incorrectly on phones, you can't scroll through the questions, it gets stuck on tablets — the mobile version is at times simply unusable.

product.title: Helps prep for exams and reinforce topics
product.plus: As a tool for revision and exam prep it delivers: it helps spot weak points, analyze mistakes and raise grades, and is handy for last-minute studying.

product.title: Question generation from text and AI saves teachers real time
product.plus: Instead of typing questions by hand you can paste text or upload a worksheet and the app builds the quiz; teachers note the AI generation from materials works decently and cuts prep time a lot.

product.title: Anti-cheat and seasonal updates get in the way of studying
product.minus: The anti-cheat update flashes your name for no reason, and seasonal effects like snowballs or a festive background cover the answer options or simply won't turn on — these forced extras get in the way of answering.

product.title: False VPN detection blocks sign-in
product.minus: The system wrongly "detects" a VPN that isn't there and refuses to let you log in — especially when switching between mobile data and Wi-Fi; the only workaround is manual email-and-password login.

product.title: Spaced repetition genuinely drills knowledge into memory
product.plus: The core thing users love: daily spaced reviews really do lock vocabulary, facts and concepts into long-term memory. People credit it with passing exams, learning languages and memorizing hundreds of characters.

product.title: Steep learning curve and unfriendly UI scare off beginners
product.minus: The biggest pain: getting started requires watching tutorials and reading the manual. Many say they have no idea how to use it, find it unintuitive and far too complicated for someone who just wants to flip through some cards.

product.title: Free with no ads feels like a gift
product.plus: Users are stunned that such a powerful tool is completely free and ad-free. It comes up again and again: 'can't believe this is free', 'this is a gift'.

product.title: Customization, add-ons and custom decks give near-limitless flexibility
product.plus: Power users value being able to build their own decks, style cards with CSS, install add-ons and tailor everything. The flexibility is called a top advantage — it adapts to any way of studying.

product.title: Huge community library of ready-made decks on any topic
product.plus: A real strength is the community shared decks covering nearly any topic: science, languages, religion. You don't have to build everything from scratch — grab a ready-made set.

product.title: Cross-device sync is prized but painful to set up
product.minus: Sync across devices is praised as very useful, yet setup is hard and a bad sync can overwrite your data. Users get confused between 'web or app', can't link phone and tablet, and the backup-restore menu hides until decks break.

product.title: New/review card limits can't be clearly turned off and frustrate users
product.minus: People who just want to flip through cards anytime hit the review limits: 'congratulations, you're over your study limit'. There's no clear way to disable it in settings, and users don't understand why the restriction exists at all.

product.title: Random order and card selection from nested decks are broken
product.minus: A specific mechanical breakage: random repeat only loops the last two cards, 'all cards in random order' returns 'no cards match', and nested decks aren't picked up — you have to go through every deck manually.

product.title: Recent split-screen update wrecked the familiar interface
product.minus: The latest update introduced a split-screen view and side bar: the answer no longer shows full-screen, and the bar wastes space and is useless. Many ask to revert the interface and the grey background change.

product.title: New card opens carrying over the previous card's back text
product.minus: A recurring input bug: after saving a card a new one opens automatically, but its back side is already filled with the previous card's text. It appeared with an update and ruins deck creation.

product.title: Stylus support and drawing on cards are raw and buggy
product.minus: On the new study screen stylus (S-Pen) support is poor, strokes vanish and flicker when writing on the whiteboard, the drawing tool is called inconvenient, and image insertion/saving and crop break.

product.title: Strict text matching in typing mode marks correct answers wrong
product.minus: In typing mode correct answers are often flagged wrong over trivia — capital letters, punctuation, formatting. For language learning it's frustrating: instead of studying you fight strict text matching.

product.title: Just works: reliable, lightweight, cross-platform
product.plus: Those who've settled in value that it just works — reliably for years, on old phones and tablets, synced across platforms. The minimalist lightweight design with no heavy animations is seen as a plus for daily use.

product.title: Importing ready-made decks often fails
product.minus: Despite the rich library, importing purchased or website-downloaded decks often fails: cards won't load and the help walks you in circles. It especially frustrates people whose teachers recommended the app.

product.title: Core study modes are locked behind a subscription
product.minus: The defining complaint: the Learn and Test modes people actually relied on now hit a limit after two or three rounds and demand Quizlet Plus. The students the app was built for can't afford it.

product.title: Even your own cards are now locked
product.minus: What stings most is being unable to study or download the cards you made yourself for free. Paying for others' content is one thing — paying to use your own reads as pure greed.

product.title: Forced AI has crowded out making cards by hand
product.minus: Many can no longer build a set without AI — everything must be fed to a generator that mangles wording and won't let you fix it by hand. AI even got stuffed into the title for no apparent reason.

product.title: Endless "prove you're not a bot" checks
product.minus: The captcha pops up every few minutes, even after a short idle, and often just doesn't work — you have to hold a button while the page freezes. The Blast game won't launch for the same reason.

product.title: Billing: surprise charges, blocked refunds, premium that won't activate
product.minus: Free trials quietly roll into annual subscriptions, cancellation is impossible to find, refunds are denied, and paid premium sometimes never activates at all. One user threatens an FTC complaint.

product.title: Ads so frequent they interrupt studying
product.minus: Ads pop up nearly every 30 seconds and between game rounds, and a one-minute clip for half a minute of use is too much. Many would happily tolerate ads if it kept the app free.

product.title: Glitches: crashes, lost card inputs, lag
product.minus: The app lags on the simplest actions, throws you out, and freshly typed cards vanish if you switch away and come back for a second. Building a set glitches regularly.

product.title: Wrong answers and broken grading in Learn
product.minus: Community content can be wrong, grading marks right answers wrong and wrong ones right, and Learn is too lax on wording — leaving a false sense that you've mastered the material.

product.title: Android is crippled versus iOS and web
product.minus: On Android you can't study whole folders, the font is tiny and unadjustable, offline access is hit-or-miss, and features available on the web are missing from the app.

product.title: Fast last-minute cramming genuinely works
product.plus: When you don't hit the paywall, it's still a killer prep tool: people pass exams, certifications and tests by drilling definitions and terms in just a couple of days.

product.title: Gamification and varied modes make study less of a chore
product.plus: Game modes, multiple ways to review, and the freedom to pick a learning style keep motivation up: even procrastinators and people with ADHD say they retain material that never stuck before.

product.title: Huge library of ready-made sets and language support
product.plus: A core strength is the vast library of community sets for almost any subject or exam, plus audio playback and support for rarer languages like Traditional Chinese that rivals lack.

product.title: An ad after every action — the answer drowns in video spots
product.minus: Full-screen and video ads pop up on launch, before a question and after every answer; when you're in a hurry you burn minutes watching ads instead of studying.

product.title: Answers are frequently just wrong
product.minus: Users report it hands back wrong solutions — especially on math and multiple-choice tests; some got bad grades after trusting it.

product.title: Snap a question — get an answer with a clear, step-by-step breakdown
product.plus: The core value: you photograph a problem and the AI doesn't just give the answer, it breaks the solution into steps and explains it, so you actually understand the material.

product.title: Lifts grades and rescues homework
product.plus: Many say the app pulled their grades up from D's to A's and made homework and exams far quicker to get through.

product.title: Pricey subscription, and the free tier caps your questions hard
product.minus: Accurate answers and the unlock hide behind a costly subscription ($7/week, $8/month, $59/year), and the free tier gives just 20 questions a day — steep for students.

product.title: The camera and photo recognition let you down
product.minus: Recognition fails even on clear shots, the camera won't open or is oriented wrong, and on long problems the photo gets misread.

product.title: The floating ball is handy — when it doesn't vanish
product.plus: The floating overlay button is a favorite as a quick way to scan questions, but many complain it disappears or was removed entirely.

product.title: Long-winded explanations you can't skip
product.minus: The AI dumps a long explanation you can't skip, just repeats itself when asked to re-explain, and the actual answer gets lost inside paragraphs of text.

product.title: You pay — and the features never arrive
product.minus: People pay for premium but get no access: money taken, no benefits, the subscription dies on a new phone, and it can't be cancelled.

product.title: Slow, freezes, and loses your history
product.minus: The app can be painfully slow, unresponsive, won't let you log in, drains the battery, and loses your whole past conversation when closed.

product.title: A lifeline for anyone stuck on math
product.plus: Those who struggle with math and the sciences say the app solves problems fast and lays them out clearly enough to follow.

product.title: The go-to Gauth alternative — for those who jumped ship
product.plus: A chunk of users arrived after Gauth stopped working and rate Question.AI as the more accurate replacement, even if it lacks unlimited free questions.

product.title: Point the phone, get the object's name
product.plus: The core use case delivers: lift the phone to the sky and instantly read what star, planet or constellation you're looking at — no telescope required.

product.title: The base set is free and ad-free
product.plus: People are won over that a serious tool is usable for free with no ad interruptions — for many that's the deciding factor.

product.title: Indispensable for astrophotography and session planning
product.plus: Telescope hobbyists and astrophotographers treat it as standard kit: aiming gear at a target, planning a Milky Way shoot, working around a tree or obstacle.

product.title: Beautiful 3D sky and realistic textures
product.plus: The visuals draw their own praise: a smooth 3D sky, detailed planets, a night mode — it's simply pleasant to look at.

product.title: An educational tool that teaches and pulls you in
product.plus: Many come to learn: showing kids and grandkids the sky, learning constellations on a physics teacher's tip — and the app genuinely broadens their knowledge.

product.title: Live tracking of satellites, the ISS and Starlink
product.plus: A distinct fan-favorite is tracking moving objects: the ISS, rocket bodies, Starlink trains that add a real-world feel to the sky.

product.title: Pointing often lies and the compass stops working
product.minus: For some users the object "shines" nowhere near where the phone is pointed, and the compass ignores rotation — the app points the wrong way and loses trust.

product.title: Location resolves wrong — hundreds of miles off
product.minus: Geolocation drops in someone else's city (Westminster, Aldershot) hundreds of miles away, and small towns are missing from the list entirely, breaking the sky-to-place match.

product.title: The best features and ad screenshots are behind a paywall
product.minus: Some are annoyed by the constant push to buy Plus and that what's shown in the store screenshots is locked behind a subscription — and one user paid and "got nothing."

product.title: Bugs and lost purchases after updates
product.minus: After updates the app has to be restarted several times, and restoring a purchase or moving a lifetime subscription to a new device breaks.

product.title: A time machine for the sky — past and future of the stars
product.plus: Being able to scrub time to see the sky in the past or future, plus viewing daytime stars, is a delightful bonus people single out.

product.title: Catalog gaps and requests for new data
product.minus: Enthusiasts hit the catalog's edges: black holes like TON 618 turn up nothing, planets show generic moons instead of real ones, and James Webb imagery and Indian sky-culture languages are missing.

product.title: Card required before the first screen — "free" means "pay to even open it"
product.minus: The app sits among the free ones, yet you can't open it without a subscription and a linked card: users hit the paywall before seeing a single feature, unable to evaluate the very product they're supposedly buying.

product.title: Diagnosis yes, cure no — real help is hidden behind a separate expert fee
product.minus: The ads promise: photograph a sick plant, get the solution. In reality the app says "your plant is sick," offers a generic list of causes, and demands an extra $19.99 to talk to a specialist for the actual cure — on top of the subscription already paid.

product.title: Plant ID gets the most ordinary species wrong
product.minus: It calls a rose a mountain ash, morning glories sweet potatoes, green onions unhealthy garlic, a tomato a weed: even with a clear photo the AI confuses common garden and house plants, sometimes giving opposite verdicts on the same bush from different angles.

product.title: "Image too small" — the core feature simply won't run
product.minus: For many, the in-app camera flat-out fails: every photo triggers "image too small, retake" or "camera blocked" despite all permissions granted. People paid for a year and couldn't identify a single plant.

product.title: The subscription can't be cancelled — the button is hidden until after the first charge
product.minus: Cancelling within the 3-day trial is physically impossible to find: no button in the app or on the site, support stays silent, the phone line drops the call. Some users could only stop the charges by getting a new bank card issued.

product.title: Billing on their own terms: extra, duplicate and surprise weekly charges
product.minus: Users get charged three times, billed the yearly amount monthly, kept charged after cancelling, and find their "$19.99 a year" turned into $6.99 a week. Some never used the app yet saw money vanish — hence the constant cries of "scam."

product.title: Plant journals and entries vanish out of nowhere — and never come back
product.minus: The most devoted users — keeping journals on 15 to 50 plants with photos and notes — lose everything at once, two or three times over. Support stays silent, the data never returns, and it destroys the one thing that kept people loyal.

product.title: Ads show a miracle — coffee, milk, instant healing — that the app doesn't deliver
product.minus: The clips pour coffee or milk on a plant and it instantly revives; users come for that and get a boilerplate "over/under-watered or sun-scorched" verdict identical for every plant. The gap between promise and product is the chief source of fury.

product.title: When it works — a strong identifier and care tracker that actually saves plants
product.plus: For happy users it's exactly the tool they wanted: fast recognition, watering and fertilizing reminders, light placement tips — people genuinely revive roses, violets and 20-year-old plants by following its care advice.

product.title: Beyond plants: identifies rocks, insects and mushrooms too
product.plus: An unexpected upside — the app identifies not just plants but rocks, bugs and mushrooms; for nature lovers this turns it into an all-purpose pocket guide to everything they find in the garden and the woods.

product.title: Watering advice is absurd and dangerous to plants
product.minus: Water-amount recommendations are wildly off: a gallon every two weeks for a snake plant, a flood for bell peppers. Users who trusted it genuinely set healthy plants back after following the advice just once.

product.title: The info is shallow — free on Google, cheaper in a book
product.minus: Skeptics see no unique value: the same data is easily found online, ChatGPT and Google Lens give sharper diagnoses, and a $5 plant-care book replaces the paid subscription. No info on varieties — just generic species.

product.title: Sound ID is the app's core magic
product.plus: Users are thrilled that the app hears and names unseen birds in real time and highlights whichever one is singing right now.

product.title: Turns an ordinary backyard into a discovery
product.plus: The most common emotion in the reviews is amazement: people discover how many different birds live right by their home that they never knew were there.

product.title: Teaches you to recognise birds by their voice
product.plus: The app doesn't just name the bird, it helps you learn its song — users say they finally learned to tell birdsong apart on their own.

product.title: Free and ad-free — a rarity users cherish
product.plus: Users specifically note that such a powerful tool is fully free with no ads — and some even beg the developers to charge them.

product.title: Accuracy wins over even the skeptics
product.plus: Even people who don't consider themselves bird lovers note the identification is fast and accurate — the app "never failed" them.

product.title: The Clarkson's Farm effect — discovered via TV
product.plus: A noticeable wave of new users arrived after seeing the app on Clarkson's Farm and stayed happy — a powerful organic acquisition channel.

product.title: Constant logouts kill spontaneity
product.minus: The app repeatedly asks you to sign in again, and the slow login means you can't just whip out your phone and record a bird you hear — the top frustration of otherwise happy users.

product.title: No signal means getting kicked out
product.minus: On a bad or absent connection the app logs you out automatically — exactly the wild places where the birds are richest.

product.title: A Google Assistant clash breaks the microphone
product.minus: On some phones sound ID won't work at all due to a microphone clash with Google Assistant, forcing people to choose one or the other.

product.title: Saving sightings and the Life List are buggy
product.minus: Identified birds don't save to the Life List, and saving keeps demanding a manually named location even with geolocation on — losing the whole observation history.

product.title: A glutton for data and storage
product.minus: A single field session can eat hundreds of megabytes of data, offline databases weigh over a gigabyte, and they sometimes crash the app into unusable lag.

product.title: Sometimes misses quiet or distant birds
product.minus: With background noise or a too-quiet, too-distant bird the ID misses it — users ask for better filtering of stray sounds.

product.title: Camera freezes on capture — the observation never saves
product.minus: Live ID still works, but pressing the shutter hangs the app on a spinning wheel; you have to force-kill and restart it, and the observation is never recorded — for months.

product.title: After the model update, everything is a "dicot"
product.minus: It used to be accurate, but the recent "improved" model update tanked it: now nearly every plant stalls at "dicots" and the identifier won't reach species even on clear photos.

product.title: Wild misfires: a cat called a dog, a log pile called a human
product.minus: The identifier returns absurd answers on the obvious: a house cat logged as a dog or opossum, a rabbit as a cat, and a pile of boxes or logs taken for a human.

product.title: I used to love this app — now I'm uninstalling
product.minus: A recurring arc: users loyal for years drop their rating from five stars to one because over the past months the app stopped doing the one thing it exists for.

product.title: A real-life Pokédex: gamification that pulls you outside
product.plus: Collecting species with badges and challenges turns a walk into a thrilling "catch them all": people roam the neighborhood, explore nature with their kids, and learn for the sake of new badges.

product.title: Free, ad-free, no subscriptions — and it works offline
product.plus: The headline win: it's free, ad-free, no "7-day free trial", and identification works even offline out in the woods — against paywalled rivals that wins people over.

product.title: New phone = all observations gone
product.minus: Progress lives in the app, not the account: a reinstall or a new phone wipes out years of observations and badges without a trace, even when you're logged into iNaturalist.

product.title: No way to reject or fix a wrong identification
product.minus: Once the model is wrong, the mistaken species is logged straight into your found list, with no button to reject, delete or replace it with the correct one — a false observation stays forever.

product.title: You must get right up close — moving creatures get away
product.minus: To reach species you must hold the camera unnaturally close and long, and the zoom/focus is weak — the insect flies off or the animal leaves before the identifier even starts thinking.

product.title: A nagging pop-up before the camera steals the moment
product.minus: Every time you open the camera a disclaimer pop-up appears with no "don't show again", and the extra steps before shooting make you miss fleeting birds and insects.

product.title: It teaches and reconnects you to nature — especially with kids
product.plus: For families, teachers and nature lovers the app works as an educational tool: kids love it, walks become more informative, and adults rediscover the world around them.

product.title: Dangerous for foragers: false "accuracy" on toxic species
product.minus: The app claims accurate IDs with no warning against foraging, yet confuses deadly toxic plants and fungi — users see this as a direct danger to health.

product.title: Language resets to English after the very first photo
product.minus: For multilingual users the app shows names only in English: the chosen native language resets within a minute or after the first photo, and the bug has gone unfixed for over a year.

product.title: Often stalls at genus/family without reaching species
product.minus: Even on clear shots the identifier often stops at family or genus and asks for "a different angle", never naming the specific species — losing half its purpose.

product.title: The "free trial" charges a full year up front
product.minus: Dozens report the exact same thing: you sign up for a 7-day free trial and the full annual fee is deducted the very same day, with no warning and often no way to get it back.

product.title: It never warns the app is paid at all
product.minus: People only discover the subscription when they hit a paywall on first launch: nothing in the description or before download says it costs money or needs a card, so many uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Sound ID is where it fails most
product.minus: Audio recognition is the weakest spot: it stubbornly returns an owl or a crow for almost any recording, confuses a common cardinal with a finch, and gives three different answers to the same bird across three tries.

product.title: It doesn't know local birds outside the US
product.minus: The app is tuned for the US and Europe: users in the UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand get names of birds that don't live there at all, with no way to change region.

product.title: Accurate ID even from bad photos
product.plus: What fans love most: it confidently recognizes a bird from blurry, distant, low-quality shots — you take whatever picture you can and it still nails the species.

product.title: Rich species cards: songs, maps, habits
product.plus: After an ID, users dive into detailed cards: photos of male and female, audio of song and call, range maps, favorite food and feeder type — the app teaches rather than just names.

product.title: It opens up birdwatching for beginners
product.plus: Many say this app is what made them fall in love with birdwatching: now they recognize feeder visitors, keep a tally of species, and even credit it for their mental wellbeing.

product.title: Constantly compared to free Merlin — and loses
product.minus: A recurring refrain is the comparison to Merlin: free, more accurate, catches a whole chorus of singing birds, and lets you upload existing photos — next to it, paid Picture Bird looks pricey and clunky.

product.title: Cancelling the subscription is nearly impossible
product.minus: Even after cancelling the trial, people keep getting charged: the subscription shows up neither in Google Play history nor in the app, support stays silent, and the only escape is to block the card.

product.title: Complaints of aggressive ads and suspected harm
product.minus: Some users blame the app for a sudden flood of intrusive popup ads and even hijacked phone themes and icons that they couldn't get rid of short of uninstalling.

product.title: Crude recognition: it reads tree bark as a bird
product.minus: Beyond geography errors there are crude misfires: it identifies a bird from a photo of tree bark, calls everything a House Sparrow, and mixes up chicken breeds.

product.title: Dual input (photo and sound) praised for accessibility
product.plus: A genuine strength for the people it fits: two ID methods — photo and audio — are especially helpful for those who can't identify a bird by look or sound alone.

product.title: The «free trial» charges immediately, not after 7 days
product.minus: Dozens of users report the same thing: you sign up for a 7-day trial and the money (29.99, 30, 49.99, etc.) leaves your account that same day, sometimes a full year up front, with no warning at all.

product.title: Cancelled the subscription — charged anyway
product.minus: Users cancel during the trial or right after installing, get a confirmation, and the money is still taken anyway — with refunds denied.

product.title: The subscription is nearly impossible to cancel, and deleting the app doesn't stop it
product.minus: There's no cancel button in the app or in Google Play; the promised link can't be found; uninstalling doesn't stop the charges — people end up googling instructions or blocking their card.

product.title: You can't even try it without entering a card
product.minus: On first launch it immediately demands payment details under the guise of a «free» trial; many uninstall without ever using it.

product.title: Safety-critical info about whether a bug is dangerous is locked behind a paywall
product.minus: The thing you most need — whether a spider is venomous, whether a bite is dangerous to humans and pets — is subscription-only; it used to be free, and many find paywalling safety info cynical.

product.title: Misidentifies species, dangerously: calls the harmless venomous and vice versa
product.minus: It confuses species and even whole orders: it calls a ladybug a cockroach, labels a significantly venomous spider «harmless», treats all millipedes as one species. With errors like these the stakes are your health.

product.title: The camera won't focus and ruins the shot itself
product.minus: The built-in camera blurs sharp shots, endlessly demands you «focus», won't let you focus manually, and swaps the image — by the time you're done the bug has crawled away.

product.title: The species database is narrow and US-centric: your bug often just isn't there
product.minus: The catalog misses many genera and regions: it suggests species that don't exist in Europe, gives no native range, and the absence of the right species in the «correction» list cements a wrong result.

product.title: When the camera catches a clear shot — IDs are accurate and fast
product.plus: Many praise the high accuracy: it correctly identifies insects and spiders, often on the first shot, and beats rivals like Seek, iNaturalist and Google Lens.

product.title: The free tier is surprisingly generous — and many say it earns their money later
product.plus: Against the angry subscription reviews, a chunk of users stress that the free mode gives accurate IDs and plenty of info with no limits, the subscription popup closes with an X, and that's exactly why they'd eventually pay for premium.

product.title: The AI assistant answers any question about the bug — and users love it for it
product.plus: The built-in chatbot understands questions phrased any way, keeps context about the identified species, and serves up behavior, habitat and danger — for many it's the best part of the app.

product.title: Helps users overcome fear of bugs and raise curious kids
product.plus: Emotional payoff: the app reduces fear of spiders and bugs, gives parents peace of mind (is this bite dangerous to my kid or pet), and turns walks with children into eager ID hunts.

product.title: Pushy subscription popups and a Clippy-style assistant get in the way
product.minus: The subscription window and ads pop up at every step — on every open, navigation and scroll; a pushy Clippy-style AI helper was added too, and it all spoils a genuinely good ID feature.

product.title: Switching phones wipes your account and your whole find history
product.minus: Moving to a new phone breaks login, password reset doesn't recognize the email, and saved bug photos vanish; the out-of-date help is no use.

product.title: Google sign-in hangs — you can't even get into the app
product.minus: The only way in is the «Continue with Google» button, but after tapping it the app shows «Signing you in» and then nothing happens. People delete and reinstall, yet never get to see the app at all.

product.title: Charges keep coming after you cancel, and there's no way to unsubscribe
product.minus: The subscription is nearly impossible to cancel: there's no link in settings, emails go unanswered, and charges continue even after the app is deleted. People spend months chasing refunds and end up escalating to their bank.

product.title: Misidentifies plants — even the obvious ones
product.minus: The recognition misses even familiar plants: one user tested 10 plants from their own garden and it got just one right — it failed to recognize a peach tree with a peach hanging on it.

product.title: «Free» in the ads turns into paywall after the first photo
product.minus: Ads promise a free app, but in reality you get one free (and often wrong) identification, after which everything is locked behind a subscription. Many call it false advertising.

product.title: The price shocks: over $10 a week for a plant app
product.minus: The cost strikes people as wildly out of proportion: over $10 a week, which adds up to $40+ a month. Even those who praise the app's content find that price impossible to justify.

product.title: Descriptions are generic — little real care guidance
product.minus: Even when identification works, people complain they get generic descriptions they could just Google, with no concrete «how to care» guidance. The problem-diagnosis feature doesn't help either.

product.title: The mandatory Google account turns people off before they start
product.minus: There's no email login — only Google. Those who don't want to tie in their Google profile hit a wall and leave without ever trying the app.

product.title: When it works — it identifies accurately and genuinely helps
product.plus: The few who got past the sign-in praise the app: it does its job really well and pinpoints the exact plant. For them it's a genuinely useful tool.

product.title: Charges with no visible subscription read as a flat-out scam
product.minus: Money leaves the account weekly, yet no subscription shows up in Google Play, and people feel the app holds onto their card details. Hence the blunt accusations of fraud and calls to shut it down.

product.title: The "free trial" charges your card immediately and without warning
product.minus: Users describe the same pattern over and over: you sign up for a free trial and money leaves your card the same day, often before the promised period ends. The advertised 7 days turn out to be 3, and the price charged doesn't match the plan they picked.

product.title: Cancelling is nearly impossible, and charges continue even after you cancel
product.minus: The cancel button is hidden, support claims it can't stop the subscription "on their end," and charges keep coming for months or years even after the app is deleted. People resort to changing their bank cards just to make the billing stop.

product.title: It calls even an obviously dying plant healthy
product.minus: The most common complaint about the core product: photograph a wilting, blackened, yellowing plant and the app cheerfully replies "healthy, keep growing." Trusting that verdict, people lost plants they'd kept for 30 years.

product.title: Plant identification misses even the most obvious species
product.minus: Recognition confuses corn with garlic, calls a porcelain mushroom a coconut, and once identified the user's hand instead of a plant. People often have to type the name in by hand, and Google Lens or Gemini do the job better and for free.

product.title: The headline feature — disease diagnosis — is locked behind a paywall
product.minus: People install the app specifically for the diagnosis shown in the ads, yet that feature and any treatment advice require an extra payment. For free you only get generic symptoms you could have Googled anyway.

product.title: The ad promises one thing, the app does another
product.minus: Marketed as free, with specific home remedies (pepper, eggshells) and lawn or disease recognition. In reality it's a subscription, vague advice like "nitrogen/potassium," and broken features. Some of the ads are built from content stolen from creators.

product.title: One "signup" produces several stacked charges
product.minus: You pick a $9.99 plan and the same day a second charge of $49 lands that was never disclosed at checkout. People find two to four parallel charges for a single subscription.

product.title: It forces account creation and checkout before revealing it's a subscription
product.minus: First you register and go through the whole onboarding, and only then does it surface that the app costs money. A "Try for free" button with "Continue" makes it feel free to start, while features stay locked until you buy the trial.

product.title: Watering advice ignores the specific plant and conditions
product.minus: The watering schedule ignores soil, season, and plant type: it tells you to water something already growing in water, and doesn't register five days of rain for outdoor plants. The recommendations feel generic, like old wives' tales.

product.title: For committed users, the watering reminders genuinely save plants
product.plus: Those who stay praise the care discipline above all: reminders to water, mist, and fertilize keep dozens of plants alive. Several users say their home would be full of dead pots without it.

product.title: For beginners it builds confidence and teaches plant care
product.plus: The users it clicks with value the friendly, educational tone: tips help them avoid killing plants, make sense of unfamiliar species in the yard, and build knowledge over time — and it's pleasant to do with their kids.

product.title: Auto bird ID was pulled behind a paywall after purchase
product.minus: The core feature people bought a smart feeder for — automatic species identification — was switched to premium in a sudden update (Q1 2026). Buyers who had used it free for years, going back to the Kickstarter, saw it as a textbook bait-and-switch.

product.title: Without auto-ID, every bird must be identified by hand
product.minus: After the update, instead of an instant "species X visited" notification, the app sends generic alerts and makes you open each postcard, tap "identify" and wait for the AI. On a busy feeder this turns a pleasure into a chore and breaks the "ignore this species" feature.

product.title: Premium pop-up ads on every single action
product.minus: Every time a user identifies a bird, saves a photo, or just opens the app, a subscription ad pops up — often covering the photo itself. People call it dark patterns and nagging that rubs the lost feature in their face at the moment of use.

product.title: You can't escape the subscribe screen — only kill the app
product.minus: Tap the subscription icon by accident and you land on an upsell screen with no way back. To return to the app you have to force-close it from memory, sometimes clear the cache or even restart the phone.

product.title: The AI misidentifies even the most common birds
product.minus: Species ID frequently misses: the same sparrow gets tagged as a rare warbler all week, a common finch becomes a "mystery visitor", and a hummingbird is called a nutcracker. People spend more time fixing errors than enjoying the birds.

product.title: The feeder misses half the visits and records late
product.minus: The camera often ignores birds perched for 20–45 seconds, starts recording after they arrive, and sends notifications minutes or even hours late. Users complain they miss up to 75% of visits.

product.title: Painful Wi-Fi/Bluetooth pairing with near-absent support
product.minus: Initial setup is a recurring pain: the camera won't join Wi-Fi, Bluetooth pairing hangs and falsely reports success, and support is email-only with replies that take weeks. There is no live phone line.

product.title: Notifications are all-or-nothing, with no fine control
product.minus: You can't separate charging alerts from bird alerts, turn off the daily recap, or limit the flood of notifications from friends' feeders — it's all on or all off. Some users mute notifications at the OS level instead.

product.title: Sharing the feeder with your household requires a subscription
product.minus: After spending a couple hundred dollars, families find that without a subscription only one account can see the feeder: adding a spouse or second user knocks the first one out or costs ~$100/year. Transferring premium to another account is offered but doesn't work.

product.title: The bird-watching itself brings huge joy
product.plus: Despite all the monetization gripes, people genuinely fall in love with the product: getting postcards of visiting birds, discovering new species in their own yard and watching from indoors is, for many, the best gift they've received and a daily source of joy.

product.title: Crisp close-up photos and video
product.plus: Camera quality is the most-praised strength: crystal-clear photos and video where you can see every feather, and the chance to view hummingbirds or small songbirds up close. Even users frustrated with the app single out the camera.

product.title: Helps you learn and discover new bird species
product.plus: For many the app opens up the world of birds: people are amazed how many species visit their yard, read facts about each one, and learn alongside their kids and parents. Homeschooling families and older birders especially value it as an easy on-ramp into birding.

product.title: You can watch feeders from around the world
product.plus: Beyond their own yard, users love peeking into other people's feeders around the world and seeing birds from entirely different habitats — it turns the app into a small window onto nature across the planet.

product.title: The subscription can't be cancelled — money keeps coming out even after you cancel
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people cancel or close their account and the charges keep coming, week after week. There's no cancel option in Google Play or on the site, support doesn't reply, and users end up changing card numbers just to make it stop.

product.title: "Free" is bait: a 3-day trial, then $10 a week
product.minus: The ad promises a free identifier, but you only learn about the three-day trial and mandatory subscription after installing. It's a classic bait-and-switch — the price is hidden up front and it stings.

product.title: They charge without authorization — sometimes before the trial even ends
product.minus: Users report charges they never authorized: money taken straight from the bank account bypassing PayPal, sometimes twice a week or before the "free" period is even over. Many threaten BBB complaints and PayPal disputes.

product.title: Misidentifies plants — even basic ones
product.minus: The core feature misfires often: a lemon tree becomes a bell pepper, a hydrangea becomes a Bushy Lippia, and aloe, hibiscus and basil it can't identify at all. Users call the rival Picture This more accurate.

product.title: Permanently "under maintenance" — you simply can't use it
product.minus: Whole trial periods pass with the site "down for maintenance." People pay for a year and can't reach the features they paid for; some burn all three daily free tries on the maintenance message.

product.title: The app crashes on launch and while taking a photo
product.minus: After a recent update the app closes the moment you open it, or right when you take a picture. Only a reinstall helps — and only once, until the next close; meanwhile the paid annual access won't open.

product.title: The promised disease diagnosis is missing — you only get the plant's name
product.minus: The ad promises to tell you what's wrong with your plant and how to fix it, but that's paywalled — and the answer is often nonsense: everything gets diagnosed as "water deficiency," even lucky bamboo sitting in water.

product.title: The price shocks: up to $40 a month for what free AI tools do
product.minus: $9–17 a week reads as absurd — about $40 a month and over $550 a year. People compare directly: rival identifiers cost $10 a month, and Google and free AI do the same thing for nothing.

product.title: Demands location and reviews where neither is needed
product.minus: The app won't work unless you turn on location — which it doesn't need to name a plant — and nags for a subscription and a five-star review on every other screen, sometimes withholding results until you rate it.

product.title: When it works — fast identification with detailed care info
product.plus: Happy users praise instant recognition from a single photo, with plant history, care instructions and reminders. The toxicity notes for both humans and pets are a particular favorite.

product.title: For beginner gardeners — a simple, educational helper
product.plus: Plant novices value how easy and approachable it is: it helps tell a weed from a planted seed, organizes your collection into folders, and rescues wilting houseplants. One user even checked wild weeds for edibility before eating them.

product.title: Care advice is one-size-fits-all — it ignores the species
product.minus: Care advice is generic: a cactus gets weekly watering, misting and twice-yearly pruning, and tips boil down to water and light the user already knew. It hollows out the point of the app.

product.title: Basic features that were free for years got locked behind a subscription
product.minus: The single biggest grievance: people who used the app for years suddenly hit a paywall on what used to be free — export, multi-page scans, sending PDFs. It doesn't read as "now paid," it reads as "they took away what was mine."

product.title: A subscription for what is essentially "a camera with a filter"
product.minus: Users reject the model itself: scanning is a rare, occasional need, and paying $3–15/month or $10/week to photograph a sheet of paper feels absurd next to free alternatives. Many would happily pay once, but not subscribe.

product.title: Multi-page scanning is now pay-only
product.minus: A specific, recurring loss: combining several pages into one PDF was removed from the free tier. Now it's strictly one page at a time with no merging — which for many kills the entire point of the app.

product.title: A sharing cap of three documents, then it stops
product.minus: A brutal detail: emailing/sharing was throttled to an absurd number (three documents, and the counter ticks even if you cancel), and the most common use — "email myself a PDF a few times a year" — got blocked. People discover it at the worst possible moment.

product.title: Bought "forever" — now being asked to pay again
product.minus: A distinct tier of fury: people who bought Pro or lifetime years ago find, on reinstall or a new phone, that the purchase won't restore and access is behind a subscription again. It reads as outright deception and broken trust.

product.title: Documents vanish, accounts won't restore
product.minus: The most severe reviews: people lose hundreds or thousands of scans — after an update, on a phone switch, or just "in a glimpse." Sign-in fails, support goes silent. For small-business owners and students mid-exams this is a catastrophe, not an inconvenience.

product.title: Surprise charges and a subscription you can't escape
product.minus: Serious dark-pattern accusations: charges without warning, sometimes for an app never even used; cancellation is hidden or redirects to a blank Google Play page. Some users end up disputing the charge with their bank.

product.title: Intrusive ads and "AI features" that made scans worse
product.minus: On top of the subscription, the free tier got buried in ads — including a video with a screaming voice just to share once. The added "AI features" are widely seen as a downgrade: auto-crop chops off edges and scan quality dropped.

product.title: Updates complicated what used to be dead simple
product.minus: Separate from money: the UI redesign added extra steps, buried crop and rotate in menus, slowed things down, and broke auto-crop and the home screen. The refrain is "it was simpler before; update = made it worse."

product.title: For those who stayed: the best quick scanner in your pocket
product.plus: The standout strength for the happy cohort: for years (often 5–10, across several phones) it does exactly one thing — turns a photo of a document into a clean PDF — simply, fast, and reliably. Many call it indispensable and the best they've tried.

product.title: A workhorse for business, school, and travel
product.plus: A clear value scenario: teachers, small businesses, and travelers use it for invoices, receipts, tax forms, and digitizing documents on the go. With no printer or scanner around, it's a lifesaver that replaces a trip to Staples or the library.

product.title: Responsive support — when you reach it
product.plus: A bright spot against the "support is silent" complaints: some users praise fast, human email responses — recovered lost files, restored access, removed offensive ads. The contrast with those who got no reply at all is stark.

product.title: Scan quality and OCR — when it works, it works great
product.plus: Happy users praise auto edge detection, tidy PDFs, and OCR that actually works — quality compared to a desktop scanner. Yet a faction reports the opposite: blurry, fuzzy scans after updates, especially on books and curled pages.

product.title: Auto-crop nails the page border, even on a white desk
product.plus: The single most-loved feature: it finds the document edges by itself with almost no input from the user, even when a white page sits on a light surface.

product.title: It just works: download, scan, send — no fuss
product.plus: Over and over, people say it does exactly what it promises with no learning curve — that rare 'I downloaded it and it just did the task' experience.

product.title: Scan clarity is the reason to drop phone photos and old printers
product.plus: Users switch from plain photos and home scanners precisely for the quality: text is legible, images are clean, and the result beats their first attempt elsewhere.

product.title: Light and un-bloated — unlike CamScanner
product.plus: The small footprint and lack of clutter are a selling point of their own: light size, no ads, sane PDF sizes — explicitly contrasted with the heavy CamScanner.

product.title: Years of reliability: the one scanner that survives phone upgrades
product.plus: A huge base of long-time loyalists — the app survives phone changes, never lets them down, and stays 'the one' scanner for years.

product.title: A lifesaver at the hospital, at school, and at work
product.plus: The app becomes indispensable in high-stakes moments: sending paperwork from a hospital bed, turning in homework on time, replacing a broken office scanner.

product.title: The paywall grew: a yearly subscription instead of a one-time buy
product.minus: The most painful theme: what was a simple free scanner for years now demands a subscription, sometimes priced around $64, and people explicitly ask for a one-time purchase instead.

product.title: The basic tier hits an upsell wall when you send or share
product.minus: Core actions — sending a doc, sharing to other platforms, printing — are locked on the basic tier, and trying them throws an upgrade pop-up in your face.

product.title: Surprise charges and broken purchase restore
product.minus: A worrying money cluster: charges without consent, paid fax credits that never arrived, and a non-working restore-purchase button in the latest version with unresponsive support.

product.title: The scan series won't stop — it keeps shooting in a loop
product.minus: A recurring UX snag: after the first scan the app keeps scanning over and over, and people can't figure out how to end the series — short of force-closing the app.

product.title: Being asked to rate before the first scan is grating
product.minus: People are annoyed that the app begs for a rating before they've scanned anything — and some hand it a one-star in retaliation.

product.title: Weak flash and no always-on light — poor scans in the dark
product.minus: In low light quality drops: there's no always-on flash, and the manual one is so weak it's practically useless — sometimes the scan comes out blurry or unreadable.

product.title: The trial charges you instantly, with no consent or warning
product.minus: Users tap the «free trial» and money is taken the same second — most often 359 via GCash — with no explicit consent and no notice. They insist they never subscribed to anything.

product.title: Cancelling is impossible — the button is dead and the sub isn't even listed
product.minus: Even after cancelling, people keep paying: the unsubscribe button is dead and the subscription isn't in their Google list. Charges continue after cancellation and even after uninstalling.

product.title: You scan the whole document, then learn the result is paywalled
product.minus: It lets you scan the whole document, then demands payment to actually hand over the file. It hits hardest when you have a tight deadline and no time to find another app.

product.title: The free tier is just 3 documents, then a forced subscription
product.minus: After three scans (for some, just one) the app hits a wall and demands an upgrade. The «free» framing is misleading — you effectively can't save a file without paying.

product.title: An ad after every tap — unusable in practice
product.minus: Ads pop up after literally every action, every 30 seconds. In the free version the wall of ads makes it impossible to reach the scanner itself.

product.title: An extra promo page is baked into the finished PDF
product.minus: Every document gets a final page advertising the app — with no warning. You need another app to remove it or you waste a sheet when printing, which ruins sending official documents.

product.title: You can't find the saved file — no gallery export, no clear folder
product.minus: Even when a file is supposedly saved, users can't locate it: no save-to-gallery option and no clear storage folder. Some lost important scans after switching phones.

product.title: Scan quality stumbles: dirty edges, poor straightening
product.minus: Edge straightening works poorly, and a black border lingers along the document edge even on a contrasting background. Some users find the plain phone camera with cropping does a better job.

product.title: Once you pay, the scans are genuinely crisp and save the day
product.plus: Those who get past the paywall praise the clarity: scans are crisp enough to help with schoolwork and even rescue visa applications that were rejected due to blurry scans from other apps.

product.title: Snap-and-send: a fast, convenient «photo to PDF» flow
product.plus: For happy users the flow is simple and convenient: snap the paper, send a PDF. It's especially valued for distance learning and working from home — saving time, travel and copy costs.

product.title: Pricey for a feature rivals give away free
product.minus: The price feels steep for a basic feature: people directly compare it to free CamScanner, Adobe and clear scanner. The «subscribe for one scan» model itself drives them off.

product.title: Support does refund — if you manage to reach it
product.plus: Not all is lost: some users got their money back and found support responsive. The developer replies to reviews and points people to the free version.

product.title: The shortest path from photo to a finished PDF
product.plus: Users are won over by how PDF creation is boiled down to the fewest steps — they call it the simplest way to put a document together.

product.title: Genuinely useful with no learning curve
product.plus: People see the app as genuinely useful yet clear from the first launch, with nothing to figure out.

product.title: Free to scan, but you pay to do anything with the result
product.minus: Scanning is free, but saving, exporting to PDF and sharing are locked — and you only find out after you've already assembled the document. A textbook bait-and-switch.

product.title: The $9.99-a-week price only appears at the moment you try to send
product.minus: A 49-cent trial flips to $9.99 a week — about $40 a month, more than Netflix. The real price stays hidden until you hit the wall trying to send a finished scan.

product.title: There is no way to cancel — the app simply has no such button
product.minus: There's no cancel option inside the app, support says "go to your phone settings" or goes silent, and the charges keep coming. People end up disputing with their bank and filing complaints.

product.title: Charges keep landing even after you try to cancel
product.minus: Users report repeated and surprise charges — sometimes "without consent," sometimes after they'd already tried to cancel. Support doesn't answer emails, and it ends in a bank dispute.

product.title: It begs for a review before you've even used it
product.minus: The "rate us" prompt pops up after every action, sometimes four times a minute, interrupts the PDF render and forces you to start over. Some people give one star purely for this.

product.title: Multi-page scans fall apart — only the first page survives
product.minus: With several pages the app either duplicates the first one, drops everything after page one, or crashes on large documents. For anything beyond a single sheet it's effectively unusable.

product.title: Scanned files vanish — nobody can tell where they're stored
product.minus: Scans either go missing or save to some unknown place: the app never shows where, so you can't send a file via WhatsApp or email because you simply can't find it.

product.title: Scan quality lets you down: shadows, no auto-crop, no fixes
product.minus: The camera fails to find the page edges and grabs the whole frame, shadows stay on the final document, and there are no brightness or contrast tools. Many say their phone camera does it better.

product.title: Even the paid trial stamps a watermark on your document
product.minus: Saving without a watermark requires a subscription, and the 7-day trial still stamps one anyway — so you never actually get to try it properly.

product.title: Saving just fails outright — "something went wrong"
product.minus: Even after paying, some users can't send their document: email, OneDrive and Teams attempts all fail, and saving throws a "something went wrong" error.

product.title: When you do get to scan, it's genuinely simple and saves the day
product.plus: Those who actually reach the scanning step praise how easy and handy it is: a lifesaver when the home scanner dies, great for quickly digitizing work documents and pushing them to the cloud.

product.title: The real gripe isn't the price itself but a weekly sub instead of a one-time buy
product.minus: People are willing to pay — but for a one-time purchase or per-scan, not a recurring weekly subscription. Many like the product and leave purely because of the payment model.

product.title: The "free trial" charges a full year on the spot
product.minus: People tap "7 days free" and the same day see a full year charged — with no separate purchase confirmation. This is the single most repeated complaint about the whole app.

product.title: Money taken with no consent and no confirmation
product.minus: Money is pulled automatically with no transaction approval — it stings hardest for GCash and card users who see the amount vanish out of nowhere.

product.title: Cancelling doesn't stop the charges
product.minus: The most alarming pattern: people cancel the same day or months ahead, yet charges keep coming — sometimes again for the next year.

product.title: You can't save or export your document without paying
product.minus: You can scan, adjust, build the PDF — and then hit a paywall right at save/export, holding all the work you just did hostage.

product.title: Ads say "free", the price shows up afterwards
product.minus: It comes up first for "free scanner", but the subscription terms and the card request only appear after install — people feel misled before their first scan.

product.title: Refunds are promised but not delivered
product.minus: Refund requests go nowhere: support is silent or slow, instructions are confusing, and it escalates to card disputes and BBB complaints.

product.title: Scans lose color and detail, quality drops
product.minus: Color documents save as black-and-white, text comes out unreadable in places, the image is blurred — for people who actually scan, this defeats the subscription.

product.title: Files vanish somewhere deep in the phone
product.minus: The PDF opens inside the app, but outside — in the Documents folder or on a drive — it's nowhere to be found; attaching it to an email turns into a quest.

product.title: When it works — fast, simple scanning on the go
product.plus: The genuine strength fans praise: it grabs and crops the document instantly and the PDF is ready in seconds — a lifesaver when no scanner is nearby.

product.title: Simple and clear even for non-techies
product.plus: Happy users single out the friendly interface: even a non-technical person figures it out, and documents come out looking "professional".

product.title: Replaces a physical scanner for everyday work
product.plus: Teachers, students and travelers keep it on hand daily: scan a handwritten assignment, receipt or document and send it by email/WhatsApp right away — no printer, no paper piles.

product.title: A once-in-a-while user doesn't need a yearly plan
product.minus: Even users who like the app are trapped by the plan: they need one scan for the weekend but get pushed into a year; there's no sane one-off or monthly option, and switching plans is impossible.

product.title: The paywall appears at the end, once the work is already done
product.minus: Users describe a bait-and-switch: a tool looks free, you let it chew through hours of work and hundreds of pages, and payment is demanded only at the very end — when you try to save the already-finished result. It reads as "pay me or lose everything."

product.title: Basic editing is locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Many can't do even the basics without paying: you can view, but not edit, not add a single word, not build a PDF from your own images. For a free "PDF editor" that defeats the whole point of installing it.

product.title: Charges and a "free trial" that still took money
product.minus: Hard money stories: tapped the "free trial" and got charged anyway; instead of ₹85 they pulled ₹2529 for a "7-day subscription"; an unauthorized charge was refused a refund with the blame put on the user. Refunds via Google Play don't come through either.

product.title: The best all-in-one PDF toolbox
product.plus: The core love is one tool for everything: convert, merge, split, compress, password removal, OCR to text. People call it the best PDF toolbox and an Adobe alternative they return to for years, for both personal and work tasks.

product.title: Simple, clean interface anyone can use
product.plus: The interface gets praised for being clean and simple: good for beginners and pros alike, saves time, and makes document work fast and hassle-free. The design pleasantly surprises people who expected "just another web wrapper."

product.title: A lifesaver for students and work
product.plus: For study and work the app becomes indispensable: laptop-less students convert docs and write assignments, professionals rely on it for years for business and precise conversion. It helps "get the job done in a second."

product.title: Documents are quietly sent to the cloud
product.minus: It's unsettling that processing isn't on-device: the app uploads documents to the cloud with no notice at all. For people handling bank statements and personal files, this is a "sneaky practice" that makes them warn others to avoid it.

product.title: Demands access to ALL files on disk
product.minus: Instead of the standard secure pick-specific-files flow, the app demands blanket access to all storage — or it "won't work." That irritates users and raises questions about the developers, especially given the 80MB app size.

product.title: The free limit is just a couple of actions a day
product.minus: Free use is capped at 3 actions a day (or 5 conversions in a row), and you hit the wall too fast. Users point out rivals offer more generous limits and ask to raise the cap to at least 10–15.

product.title: Crashes, bugs and "Oops, something went wrong"
product.minus: Stability lets people down: a recurring "Oops something went wrong. restart", a 200-page scan lost after scanning, formatting issues and missing font characters. Some are openly puzzled by the high rating given how many bugs they hit.

product.title: Ads get in the way of even just viewing
product.minus: There are too many ads — to the point that they make it "impossible to even view" a document. Even users who like the app overall single out the intrusive banners as the main downside.

product.title: Small tool gaps: ordering, cropping, splitting
product.minus: Pinpoint feature gaps: images in a PDF don't keep the order you placed them; no page crop; won't produce more than two split outputs even with multiple page ranges set; weak annotation tools; and "extreme" compression squeezes 56MB down to just 55.

product.title: A familiar bridge to the loved web service
product.plus: Many come from the long-used iLovePDF website and are glad to have a native app: it's "just as easy," runs fast on desktop and Android, and people keep using it for years as a natural extension of the web.

product.title: Ads became a wall, not a backdrop
product.minus: The ad load grew to the point of making the app unusable: a clip to open a file, another one after returning from a neighbouring app, ads every 10 seconds. Long-time users say outright that their go-to app turned into an ad-watching simulator.

product.title: Basic functions moved behind the paywall
product.minus: What used to be free — signing a document, saving or sharing a PDF, downloading a scan — now hits a subscription. Without paying the app "won't work anymore," and people who recommended it for years now point others to alternatives.

product.title: The trial turns into an annual charge without consent
product.minus: The "free trial" turns into an instant or early charge for a full year — dozens of euros, pesos or dollars, often silently through GCash or the bank. No renewal notice arrives, and refunds are routinely rejected.

product.title: Refunds and support don't help
product.minus: Even refund requests filed within an hour of a mistaken charge get rejected, support replies with boilerplate that ignores the actual complaint, and unsubscribing turns out to be deliberately hard.

product.title: The subscription is too pricey for occasional use
product.minus: There's no monthly plan — only a yearly one, up to 60 € for a tool used a couple of times a year. For people who need a scan once a year, paying for the whole year feels unfair.

product.title: Scan quality and auto-correction are the core strength
product.plus: The app straightens photos shot off-angle, removes glare, shadows and reflections, boosts contrast and turns a dirty shot into a clean document. Many praise the high quality and the "magic pro" filter.

product.title: Simplicity and reliability proven over years
product.plus: Many have used it daily for 5-10 years: it's simple, always works and is well maintained. For students and office tasks they call it an indispensable helper and the "GOAT."

product.title: More than a scanner: PDF, Word, sharing and integrations
product.plus: Beyond scanning, the app converts documents to PDF and Word, recognizes text, edits and shares files, and integrates with OneDrive. That turns the phone into a full replacement for a scanner and printer.

product.title: A reliable document archive for years
product.plus: Users value that the app stores and gives access to documents accumulated over decades, sparing them the hunt for paper originals and preserving files well.

product.title: Forced watermark on free scans
product.minus: Without a subscription a watermark is stamped at the bottom of each page, spoiling the result. It can only be removed by paying, which particularly irritates many users.

product.title: Degradation and bugs after updates
product.minus: Some users complain the app started glitching and freezing, distorts images, deliberately worsens quality, loses files and downscales high-resolution shots. For one user it stopped working entirely after paying for the yearly membership.

product.title: Legacy buyers weren't grandfathered into the new model
product.minus: The app was once a one-time purchase with a key; after the switch to subscriptions long-time paying users weren't preserved, and now they get bombarded with ads and blocked features. Changing devices also risks a double charge.

product.title: Exodus to free alternatives
product.minus: Disillusioned users openly recommend switching to Adobe Scan, Google Drive, iLovePDF, FairScan or the phone's built-in scanner — free, ad-free and watermark-free. The brand survives more on habit than on being better.

product.title: Paid subscription and pushy paywall instead of an honest "free"
product.minus: The ads promise "free", but almost nothing works without entering a card; export and basic functions are locked behind a subscription, and users feel deceived before their first scan.

product.title: A trial that charges you, and refunds you can't get
product.minus: The trial turns into an auto-charge with no reminder: 9.99 leaves the card, and cancelling or getting a refund becomes a fight — many are left with months of paid but already locked subscription.

product.title: Virus-like ads: the app pops up and forces itself on you
product.minus: Promo banners pop up over other apps and force a download, interrupt music playback and won't close — users describe it as a virus that's hard to get rid of.

product.title: Crashes mid-task wipe out the entire unsaved scan
product.minus: The app crashes while cropping and straightening, and all the work is lost — dozens of scanned pages have to be redone, which stings most when a deadline is looming.

product.title: The area-measurement feature simply doesn't work on many devices
product.minus: People buy the subscription specifically for area mode, then get "your device is not supported" with no explanation of which phones actually work.

product.title: An overloaded AI-heavy interface confuses newcomers from minute one
product.minus: An overload of "smart" AI features adds friction instead of help: first-timers can't figure out how to digitize a page, there are no tutorials, and the UI is called slow and cluttered.

product.title: Scans hide in an inaccessible folder, with no save-to-gallery option
product.minus: Files land in an obscure folder you can't reach without the app itself; you can't pick a default folder or auto-save to gallery, and sharing documents is a struggle.

product.title: Poor PDF quality: pages shift, images shrink
product.minus: The finished PDF comes out unreadable: on assembly images get resized and shift, only the first page is straightened — a dealbreaker for any real paperwork.

product.title: For its fans — a simple, fast scanner where "everything just works"
product.plus: Those who get it praise the speed and intuitiveness: a document is scanned and sent in a couple of taps, with no learning curve, and the app does exactly what it promises.

product.title: AI enhancement and straightening make the scan better than the original
product.plus: Processing is the standout strength: the app straightens lines, cleans and brightens faded paperwork, makes documents legible and even auto-names scans by their content.

product.title: An indispensable work tool: sign, send, replace the printer
product.plus: For office, school and travel it fully replaces a printer and scanner: sign and send documents, digitize mail, email a scan to your wife — many have used it for years and can't imagine life without it.

product.title: When support is reached, bugs get fixed fast and trust is restored
product.plus: A pro subscription that suddenly drops, or bugs, sting hard — but those who reach support note the issue is resolved within hours and the stars come back up.

product.title: Auto edge-detection and auto-scan are the core reason people love it
product.plus: The camera finds the page edges itself and captures in a split second, even when white paper lies on a light desk; multi-page documents assemble themselves, leaving the user just to flip pages.

product.title: "It just works" — install, scan, send, with no learning curve
product.plus: People install it for a specific task and get it done immediately, with no signup or instructions; that no-fuss feel is exactly what makes it a workhorse for years.

product.title: Scan quality rivals a real scanner
product.plus: Output comes out sharp on the first try, legible, and straight to PDF; users rate it above a phone photo and even above their home printer's scanner.

product.title: Lightweight and ad-free — wins against bloated CamScanner
product.plus: Under 100 MB versus rivals several times fatter, no ads and no bloated PDFs; many switch here precisely to escape CamScanner.

product.title: A subscription wall hits you right at launch
product.minus: The first thing a new user sees is a pitch to subscribe; for some that's infuriating to the point of uninstalling, and only a hidden "continue with basic" button rescues the rating.

product.title: Basic actions like sending and printing are blocked behind a paywall
product.minus: Trying to send or share a document runs into an upgrade popup, and printing directly isn't available on basic; people feel something that used to be free was taken from them.

product.title: Billing breaks: charges without consent and vanished paid features
product.minus: Some users see charges they never signed up for, lose previously purchased lifetime access after an update, or pay for credits/fax and get nothing — and support doesn't respond.

product.title: A sharp price hike drives away years-long users
product.minus: People who used the app for years suddenly hit a steep yearly price they find out of proportion to the value — and leave, even though they loved the product.

product.title: Ending a scan series is confusing — it keeps re-scanning with no clear stop
product.minus: After a capture the app tends to keep scanning over and over, and users can't figure out how to end the series short of closing the app entirely — a small but recurring snag even for fans.

product.title: Spammed for a rating before the first scan
product.minus: The request to rate arrives before the person has scanned anything, which feels pushy and immediately drags the score down.

product.title: OCR and text recognition are tucked behind a fee
product.minus: Text recognition is paid-only, whereas some competitors give at least basic on-device OCR for free — a dealbreaker for some, an optional extra for others.

product.title: Indispensable for school, work, and digitizing personal archives
product.plus: Students hand in neat homework, professionals send documents straight from their phone, and some digitize family letters from the early 1900s and sheet music — one tool covers wildly different scenarios.

product.title: Features that used to be free got walled off behind a subscription
product.minus: Things people used free for years — maps, search, best efforts — now demand a subscription, and users read this as a betrayal rather than fair monetization.

product.title: Subscription popups interrupt almost every tap
product.minus: Premium prompts pop up on practically every other tap — sometimes two in a row just to finish an activity — and they sometimes block the record button outright.

product.title: Tracking drops activities right in the middle of a workout
product.minus: The app's single most basic job — recording an activity — fails: it "recovers from a problem" only at the end, and nothing was saved, wiping out half-marathons and long rides.

product.title: GPS distance is systematically wrong
product.minus: Distance gets undercounted or jumps around: 6 miles become 4.76, a 21-mile ride becomes 0.11, and routes cut through buildings and private yards, making the stats meaningless.

product.title: Charges with no consent and refusals to refund
product.minus: Users (especially via GCash in the Philippines) see 1,500–3,000 pesos pulled for a yearly plan they never knowingly bought, and refunds either drag on for weeks or get rejected.

product.title: Login breaks: removed Facebook sign-in and endless code loops
product.minus: After Facebook login was removed, people lost access to paid accounts, and the emailed one-time codes loop the login — "get a new code" over and over, especially on Samsung and GrapheneOS.

product.title: The screenshot intercept gets in the way of saving your own data
product.minus: Trying to screenshot your own activity triggers a "use our share function" window that can't be turned off — you can't take a scrolling screenshot or share the exact view you actually want.

product.title: Syncing with watches and third-party apps is unreliable
product.minus: It fails to pull from Samsung Health, Galaxy Watch, Whoop, Shimano, Huawei — distances disagree, swims and hikes don't import at all, forcing people to run two apps at once.

product.title: Support goes silent for weeks
product.minus: Tickets sit unanswered for weeks, people get banned with no explanation, and support replies with canned links or "just use the feature" instead of actually helping.

product.title: Accurate tracking and progress breakdowns are what people love
product.plus: When it works, Strava is treated as the gold standard: accurate GPS, detailed stat breakdowns, and visible progress keep runners and cyclists coming back for years.

product.title: The athlete social network motivates and keeps people consistent
product.plus: The friends feed, segments, leaderboards, and Kudos turn workouts into friendly competition — users call it the rare social network that's actually good for you.

product.title: Forced AI and extra animations annoy long-time users
product.minus: Recent updates pile on AI insights, AI workouts, an undisableable "muscle map", and laggy post-activity animations — veteran subscribers call it useless noise instead of fixing old bugs.

product.title: Coach Bennett's guided runs are the single biggest reason people love it
product.plus: The audio coaching turns a run from a chore into a guided session: the voice cues pace and effort in real time, motivates beginners, and walks people all the way to their first marathon.

product.title: Completely free with no ads — and that earns it a lot of forgiveness
product.plus: Full training plans, guided runs and tracking with no subscriptions or paywalls; ex-Strava users switch over precisely because the rival charges for plans.

product.title: The app crashes mid-run or right at the finish
product.minus: A crash at the moment you stop a run forces a delete-and-reinstall just to make the app open again — and the tracked workout is lost for good in the process.

product.title: Endless logouts: it makes you sign in again before every run
product.minus: It signs you out almost daily and re-entry needs an 8-digit email code that often never arrives — and it strikes at the exact moment you're ready to run.

product.title: Finished runs vanish — years of data lost
product.minus: People lose not just a single workout but their whole history: thousands of kilometres disappear from Nike's servers, shattering trust in the app's data security.

product.title: The stop button spins forever and only offers to discard the run
product.minus: When you finish, holding stop won't save the run and only offers to discard it: the timer keeps counting and the only escape is restarting the phone.

product.title: Distance and pace are inaccurate or freeze mid-run
