product.minus: Tracking freezes on one kilometre while you keep running: the distance is lost, pace spikes to physically impossible numbers, and a 30-minute run logs as 0.1 miles.

product.title: Auto-pause catches slowdowns but resumes only the timer, not the distance
product.minus: When you slow down or stop to tie a shoe, the app pauses the run and on resume keeps counting time while the miles stay frozen at where you stopped.

product.title: Watch and Garmin sync breaks — runs never reach the phone
product.minus: Runs from a watch get lost or sync hours late, and since the last update NRC stopped talking to Garmin Connect altogether, despite reinstalls and re-linking.

product.title: An infinite login loop won't even let you create an account
product.minus: You tap sign-in, confirm it's you, and the app loops you back to the login screen; the verification code email often never arrives, making registration impossible.

product.title: Interval and speed workouts break more than ordinary runs
product.minus: On interval and speed guided runs the app gets stuck on the rest step, fails to record intervals and won't let you save — discard is the only option, and the hard effort is wasted.

product.title: The training plans genuinely take beginners to half-marathons and marathons
product.plus: The structured 18-week plans work if you follow them: people go from "couldn't run 1km" to a first marathon in 4:30 and fall back in love with running.

product.title: No Spotify on Android and weak treadmill tracking with no way to calibrate
product.minus: Spotify linking is iOS-only, and treadmill runs are badly off: it logs 0.2 km out of a 2.4 km run, with no way to calibrate indoor tracking.

product.title: The plans and training structure are the core reason people love it
product.plus: People get back into running, hit PRs and finish their first half-marathons specifically because of the ready-made structured plan — no need to think it through yourself, just follow. Many call it a personal trainer in your pocket.

product.title: The app is sluggish and laggy on Android — 2-8 seconds per tap
product.minus: Every action takes 2-8 seconds to load, navigation is painfully slow and buttons don't register. It infuriates even multi-year subscribers and makes a paid app borderline unusable.

product.title: White screen and crash at the end of a run — workout data is lost
product.minus: The app routinely crashes to a white screen mid-run or at the end, and the only fix is reinstalling — which wipes the run you just recorded. Against a paid subscription that stings even more.

product.title: No Galaxy / Wear OS app — Android runners are cut off from their watch
product.minus: Only Apple Watch is supported — Galaxy, Wear OS, Huawei and OnePlus don't work, even though it was promised two years ago. People are forced to log runs through other apps, which defeats the whole all-in-one coach idea, and they refuse to subscribe over it.

product.title: GPS and tracking lie — it draws routes through houses and loses kilometres
product.minus: Unless the app is open on-screen the whole run, tracking falls apart: kilometres vanish, pace jumps around, the route runs in straight lines through buildings, and distance is consistently overstated. For a paid coach that breaks everything — it doesn't know your real pace.

product.title: The paywall now hides the app's whole point — pay after week 1
product.minus: Since 2026 the core value — the training plan — has been locked behind a subscription: only week 1 is free, then you pay. Long-time users are furious at the change, newcomers feel tricked, and plain run-tracking is available in any other app.

product.title: Expensive and bait-y onboarding — collect all your data first, bill you after
product.minus: The price ($120-190/yr, ~$20/mo) feels insane for a single-sport app, and onboarding makes you spend 5-10 minutes entering personal data before revealing there's no free option. Unsubscribing is a hassle too.

product.title: The "AI coach" is a templated plan with no real adaptation
product.minus: The plan doesn't adapt to what you actually do: runs outside the app are ignored, progress isn't accounted for, and the AI text insights are empty and data-free. Many say a free ChatGPT/Claude builds them a more tailored, personal plan.

product.title: Plans are too aggressive for beginners — injuries and shin splints
product.minus: The "beginner" level turns out brutal: starting near-sprint pace, distance jumping from 3.8 to 10 miles in two weeks. People get shin splints, dizziness and nausea, and end up injured — the app lacks proper baseline questions about real fitness.

product.title: The rigid plan doesn't forgive missed runs or injuries — you must restart
product.minus: Miss a workout or get injured and there's no proper way to shift the plan — only restart, after which the app nags you about "missed" sessions. There's no repeat-week option, no custom workouts, and your chosen run-days get ignored.

product.title: Garmin and Strava integration delights those for whom it works
product.plus: When a Garmin watch connects, runners love it: workouts and voice prompts land right on the wrist and everything syncs seamlessly. This pairing is often what keeps people subscribed.

product.title: The voice coach and live pacing are praised, but the voice grates
product.plus: Real-time pace cues and the built-in warm-up/cool-down land well for many — like a little jogging angel on your shoulder keeping you on pace. But the AI voice itself is called unnatural, cheap and too fast, and people often just switch it off.

product.title: App hangs on the logo and won't open after an update
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after an update the app gets stuck on the UA logo splash screen (or a white/black screen) and never loads. Reinstalling, clearing cache, and rebooting don't help — people can't buy anything for weeks.

product.title: Constantly logs you out and makes you re-enter password and code
product.minus: Skip a week and the app logs you out, then on sign-in it demands your password and an emailed code over and over. There's no "keep me logged in" and no biometric option. People spend more time typing their password than actually shopping.

product.title: Easy, friendly interface — when it works
product.plus: For those whose app actually launches, it delights: easy to search, filter, and check out, with clear navigation and categories, good photos and descriptions. Many have shopped UA exclusively through it for years.

product.title: Military and first-responder discounts via id.me — the main reason people stay
product.plus: The most-loved upside: the app links to id.me and auto-applies a 20–40% discount for military, veterans, first responders, and teachers. For many it's the sole reason they buy from UA rather than a competitor.

product.title: The login button does nothing and accounts get locked — you simply can't get in
product.minus: Beyond the constant logouts there's a harder failure: you tap "Login" and nothing happens, or the site says your account is locked and won't let you in even after a password reset. The reset itself is broken too — the emailed code vanishes from the field before you can type it.

product.title: Loads forever and lags — you reopen the app ten times
product.minus: Even when it doesn't freeze outright, it's "slow as molasses": spins the logo endlessly, opens on the tenth try, and lags when you tap a product. Some have to reopen it 10 times before anything shows.

product.title: Discounts and sale prices don't apply at checkout — bait and switch
product.minus: A sharp money pain: items show a sale price but land in the cart at full price, and promo codes are itemized in the summary yet never subtracted from the total. Users call it "bait and switch" and report being overcharged by tens or hundreds of dollars.

product.title: Product quality, fit, and fast shipping — what people love the brand for
product.plus: Separate from the app, people praise the product itself: quality gear, comfortable fit, hot/cold gear, Curry shoes for kids' basketball, fast shipping and free returns. The brand keeps loyalty in spite of the app.

product.title: Size filter is broken — it shows items not in stock
product.minus: An aggravating miss: you set your size in the filter and the app still shows shoes and clothes that aren't available in it. You find a pair you like only to learn your size was never in stock. In-app filters work worse than the website's.

product.title: Order history vanishes and the cart gets lost
product.minus: Trust-eroding: entire order history suddenly disappears from the account, and the cart doesn't save or gets wiped — one user lost a cart of 25 items. For people who've spent thousands at UA, it feels like their data is gone.

product.title: The app is crippled vs the website: no local pickup, different free-shipping threshold
product.minus: Users question the app's point: free shipping kicks in at $99 in-app but $50 on the web; you can't choose local pickup though it's advertised; you can't see in-store stock; you can't chat with an agent. "So what's the point of the app?"

product.title: Weak support and order failures: cancellations without notice, slow refunds
product.minus: When something breaks, support makes it worse: orders get cancelled without notice, refunds drag on for weeks, and you can't reach a manager. Review complaints get only a canned "make sure the app is updated" reply, which infuriates people further.

product.title: A once-free program got moved entirely behind a subscription
product.minus: Dozens of long-time users came back to find the program that was free for years (with ads) now demands a paid subscription, and they read it as naked greed and a betrayal of their loyal base.

product.title: Only the first few days are free — a hard paywall after week 1 or 2
product.minus: Users name the exact wall over and over: you get roughly 4 days or week 1 plus day 1 of week 2 free, then progress is locked — and you only find out when you hit the wall.

product.title: One-time purchases were voided by the subscription switch
product.minus: People who once paid a one-time fee (often promised lifetime access) are now hit with a subscription demand — the app doesn't honor their past purchase, which feels like a bait-and-switch and disrespect of paying customers.

product.title: Run/walk voice cues free you from staring at the phone
product.plus: The standout thing beginners love: a clear voice (or beeps) tells you exactly when to run and when to walk, so you never watch the screen and can just focus on the run — gold for anyone listening to music or an audiobook.

product.title: Gentle progression actually gets a non-runner to 5K
product.plus: Repeat users come back to it year after year for the soft, doable ramp: it genuinely takes complete non-runners — often older or overweight — all the way to a 5K, and each day feels like a small win.

product.title: The watch version freezes and loses the workout
product.minus: On smartwatches (especially Galaxy and Pixel Watch) the app routinely hangs, freezes the whole watch, auto-pauses when you glance at it, and fails to log the workout — exactly when people paid the subscription to run without their phone.

product.title: Opening the app kills your music or audiobook
product.minus: A recurring annoyance: opening the app cuts off your own player (Spotify, Audible, Samsung Music), its built-in music won't load, and rivals like Just Run merely duck the audio instead of killing it.

product.title: No internet or no location, and the app simply won't start
product.minus: For a "glorified timer" the app is bizarrely demanding: it won't open or recognize your paid subscription offline, and it refuses to start without location access — which many call pointless data-harvesting.

product.title: Backgrounding or screen timeout wipes the workout
product.minus: Switch to your music, unlock the phone, or let the screen time out, and the app crashes or drops the active session without logging the run — a killer bug for an interval timer.

product.title: A trusted old friend people come back to for years
product.plus: Many have used it for 10–15 years: they quit running, come back, and it's still there — simple and working, the trusted fallback they return to every time they restart their fitness.

product.title: A rigid plan with no customization and a brutal week-5 spike
product.minus: The plan is locked: no choice of intensity, length, or more than three days a week, and at week 5 the load suddenly jumps from 5 minutes of running to 20 — many physically can't make the leap and stall on a plateau.

product.title: GPS and route mapping get the distance wrong
product.minus: Those who rely on tracking complain the GPS is flaky and the route map is off: distance sometimes won't register or is inaccurate, you can't correct mileage on a treadmill, and rivals do better on the same phone.

product.title: The app logs you out every couple of days
product.minus: The single most common pain: users open the app and find themselves logged out, re-entering username and password multiple times a day. Everyone reports the same thing — it never happens on iPhone, only on Android.

product.title: Basic workout functions are locked behind a subscription on top of a plan you already bought
product.minus: You pay for a training plan, but moving a workout to another day or unpairing a wrongly matched workout still demands premium. People see this as a bare-minimum feature held hostage.

product.title: Deep analytics and training-load metrics are the core value for those who get it
product.plus: Once you understand the numbers, it's the best tool for tracking fitness: form, fatigue and load metrics, full training history in one place. Data geeks love it, especially the cues telling them when to back off and recover.

product.title: The coach-athlete link works flawlessly — it's why people tolerate everything else
product.plus: The number-one reason people stay: a coach remotely loads the plan, sees completed workouts and adjusts in real time, while the athlete just does what they're told. Even while travelling the link holds. For many it's irreplaceable.

product.title: The comment field doesn't show the text you're typing
product.minus: A specific, persistent bug: when writing a comment or workout note the text box is invisible, so you type blind. And rotating the screen can wipe a whole just-written race report.

product.title: The mobile app is a pale shadow of the desktop: you can't even build a workout in it
product.minus: The web version is excellent, but in the app you can't build a structured workout, edit steps, or delete an activity — half the actions send you to the website. Mobile feels like an afterthought, especially next to Garmin Connect.

product.title: The app is slow, freezes and crashes — often right in the middle of a workout
product.minus: A blank screen for 5 seconds on every launch, constant re-syncing, freezes on the 'Complete' button, crashes on recent Samsung and Pixel devices. Workouts aren't cached, so on weak signal you get a spinner instead of your plan.

product.title: The calendar shows the wrong day of the week
product.minus: An aggravating bug: weekdays don't match the dates. It's Wednesday but the calendar says Saturday; Thursday 25 September in Australia shows as Friday. It comes back every month and throws off planning.

product.title: A confusing, cluttered interface from the nineties: you need a PhD to navigate it
product.minus: Menus, screens and settings are scattered randomly, navigation is unintuitive, and the simplest actions are a chore. There's a ton of data but it's poorly presented; many say the app needs a ground-up redesign with a real UX designer.

product.title: Expensive, with aggressive upsell pop-ups — even for paying subscribers
product.minus: The price stings, and the app spams premium ads — pop-ups that hit even people who already pay for premium. Many say it's cheaper and more sensible to hire a real coach than to pay for this.

product.title: Device sync is flaky: Garmin loads halfway, Samsung and WearOS unsupported
product.minus: When integration works it's a favourite feature. But Garmin loads partial workouts, there's no sync with Samsung Health, Strava or WearOS watches, and users flatly call the support claims of 'major device support' a lie.

product.title: Support and billing are a weak spot: an AI bot instead of humans, charges after cancellation
product.minus: Support offloads everything onto an AI bot 'Sophie', drags people through hours of email with no result, and refuses refunds. The subscription can't be cancelled from the app, people keep getting charged after cancelling, and the account sometimes can't be closed at all.

product.title: Flexible choice and one-tap loading of ready training plans for an event
product.plus: A genuine strength: enter your event date and metrics and the app builds a plan, or load a ready program (8020, a 70.3 Ironman) in a couple of clicks, and the workouts lay themselves out on the calendar and fly to your watch. Just show up and train.

product.title: TrainingPeaks Virtual in the subscription makes it worth it — a Zwift rival
product.plus: A recent feature that flips the value of the subscription: a virtual training platform bundled into premium, workouts auto-populate into it, and the data-and-metrics overlay is rated better than Zwift's. For many this is exactly what justifies the price.

product.title: No dark mode — and the one shipped is broken: black text on a dark background
product.minus: Some users simply can't use the app without dark mode. And when it shipped, it was untested: black text over a dark background, no way to turn it off, and empty release notes.

product.title: Voice cues mid-run are the main reason people love it
product.plus: The app calls out your completed mile, pace and time right into your headphones — no need to pull out the phone and stare at the screen while running.

product.title: Silent shutdowns mid-run, with no warning
product.minus: The app quietly shuts down after a mile or two, and the runner only notices once back home — the run isn't saved and the distance is lost.

product.title: Accurate GPS even in forests and on trails — why people stay for years
product.plus: Distance and route stay accurate even where the signal drops — in forests, on trails, off-road; for many that's the deciding edge over rivals.

product.title: Was accurate for years — now it lies about distance and pace
product.minus: For long-time users distance and pace suddenly go haywire — 17 km logged instead of 7, impossible pace; reinstalling and clearing data don't help.

product.title: A decade of "it just works" — the brand's biggest asset
product.plus: People say they've used it for 10–15 years and it has never let them down — a rare "old reliable" reputation for a tracker.

product.title: Forced sign-up and data-collection consent at the door
product.minus: You can't use the app at all without creating an account, and declining consent to collect "sensitive" data instantly deletes your account — some people leave on the spot.

product.title: Random pauses in tracking mid-run
product.minus: The app pauses tracking on its own several times per run, or fails to resume recording after a short break.

product.title: Simple, clear interface right out of the box
product.plus: Starts and works without digging through settings: a clean interface, everything you need in plain sight, good for beginners and for people who don't want extra features.

product.title: The free version is enough — and ad-light
product.plus: Many stay on the free tier for years: it covers everything they need, ads are rare or absent, which sets it apart from paid rivals.

product.title: Paid plan is pushed, and subscriptions get charged without asking
product.minus: People are blocked from the free version unless they start a Pro trial, buried under subscription trials, and some got signed up for a paid plan without any consent.

product.title: Route history shows progress and keeps a "diary"
product.plus: Saved runs with a route map let people track progress, revisit old workouts and plan how to ramp up — for many that's the motivation itself.

product.title: Old settings reset, and a redesign broke familiar screens
product.minus: After updates pace units flip to mph on their own, the voice switches to female, splits jump to kilometers, and the route-history page was made "ugly and unclear."

product.title: Constantly nags for a rating and misses key integrations
product.minus: The app endlessly asks for a rating, yet won't integrate with Health Connect, can't connect to a Fitbit, and won't show stats offline.

product.title: Charged for a subscription with no warning, even after cancelling
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people cancel or delete the app, then get charged the full amount months later with no renewal reminder. Many only find out from a bank notification.

product.title: Refunds refused — they haggle 25–50% or hide behind fine print
product.minus: Even when people reach out the same day, support refuses a full refund and bargains "as a goodwill gesture" — 25%, then 50% — citing a 24–48h cancellation or 14-day window. Some only recover money via PayPal, their bank, or a complaint threat.

product.title: The "run a marathon, get your money back" challenge that never pays out
product.minus: The headline hook: run 26 miles / 42 km within your subscription for a full refund. People complete the distance (sometimes well over), then get denied — "wrong link", "bought via Play Store", "only outdoor GPS runs count".

product.title: The app freezes at the end of a run and loses the workout
product.minus: A recurring crash pattern: the run goes fine, then the screen freezes right when you save, wiping the workout and your streak. The only "fix" is to delete and reinstall — over and over.

product.title: GPS tracking is wildly off — a 5K logs as 0.3km or nothing
product.minus: Distance is logged with huge errors — a jagged line, lost kilometres, or double-counting. This wrecks both the plan (built off your first run) and the refund challenge, where only GPS distance counts.

product.title: No watch sync — phone in hand, or Apple Watch only
product.minus: It doesn't sync with Garmin, Strava, Samsung/Pixel/Fitbit or Android watches — effectively Apple Watch only. Runners are forced to carry the phone in hand, which for many is the dealbreaker.

product.title: Only outdoor GPS runs count — treadmill and indoor don't
product.minus: Even though onboarding asks about a treadmill, the app can't log indoor runs and won't let you add a run after the fact. In winter and cold weather this makes the plan and the challenge impossible.

product.title: Basically a pricey timer — Strava and Nike do it for free
product.minus: For $60–100 many feel they get just a timer offering "run for 10/20/30 minutes" and no real coaching plan. The constant comparison: free Strava, Nike Run Club, MapMyRun, C25K and Garmin do the same or better.

product.title: A gentle beginner plan that genuinely gets people running
product.plus: The top praise: the plan eases in someone who hasn't run in years or is recovering from injury. It doesn't overload, reassesses your level regularly, and builds people up to a 5K, half-marathon and their first race.

product.title: Voice coach and reminders keep run-haters accountable
product.plus: The voice coach encourages you at just the right moment — right when you want to quit — and tells you how far you've gone. Reminders and streaks keep people consistent who used to burn out or give up on running.

product.title: All-in-one — runs, warm-up/cool-down, strength and recipes — but the meal plan is rigid
product.plus: Many like the compactness: a run plan with warm-up and cool-down, strength work and simple tasty recipes for a weight-loss goal, all in one app.

product.title: Support is a lottery — some are rescued, others get dropped mid-chat
product.plus: Some users praise responsive human reps who actually solve the problem and end up refunding — sometimes after a public review.

product.title: Photos in the video moved behind a paywall — gutting the whole point
product.minus: The signature feature — up to 10 photos along the route in the free video — was moved to a paid tier. Without it the clip is no different from a plain map app, and users who loved it for years are leaving in droves.

product.title: Route trimming removed — forget to stop, and your stats are ruined
product.minus: The option to trim/edit a track after recording was removed in an update. Forget to stop at the finish and the drive home gets baked into the route, with no way to fix it — only delete the activity.

product.title: Shady subscription traps: charges with no reminder and no refund
product.minus: After the trial the card is charged with no warning, auto-renew turns itself back on, cancelling earns no refund, and unsubscribing is deliberately hard. People lose tens of dollars and call it a scam.

product.title: The track draws a straight line instead of the real route
product.minus: On GPS loss or in the background the app doesn't follow the turns — it draws a straight line from point to point, through houses, fields and lakes. The result is a fake route and distance.

product.title: "Oops, something went wrong" — the app just stops working
product.minus: For some users (especially on newer Samsung phones) every activity hits an "oops something went wrong" error, crashes when adding video, and lost ride data — all while the subscription is paid.

product.title: Distance and duration come out inaccurate
product.minus: Recorded mileage diverges noticeably from reality: 6 km becomes 4, 200 miles becomes 68, and the stats in the video don't match the activity figures. For a tracker, that breaks trust.

product.title: The free version is hollowed out — pointless without a subscription
product.minus: Users see steady degradation: things that used to be free (photos, custom covers, vertical video, max speed) get progressively hidden behind "Plus". Many call it enshittification and greed.

product.title: Every step nags you to subscribe, with "skip" hidden
product.minus: The app demands a subscription on every screen, hiding the "skip" button in corners and faint colors. Some people delete it within the first minute, never reaching the actual functionality.

product.title: When it works, the 3D route video genuinely delights and motivates
product.plus: This is what people love it for: a beautiful aerial clip of the path you covered with speed, distance and elevation. People relive old adventures, share with family, and feel proud of the activity.

product.title: Accurate track capture and smartwatch sync (Garmin)
product.plus: For a chunk of users it's the opposite — it pulls route and stats from Garmin accurately, impresses with elevation data, and turns out more precise than the default Android tracker. A reliable tool since 2017 for them.

product.title: Simple, easy interface and a "pay what you decide" model
product.plus: Newcomers praise the easy start: setting up and making the first video is simple, the result looks great, and the flexible — for some, generous — free version lowers the barrier to entry.

product.title: Music and video: a thin track catalog, length caps, and quality loss
product.minus: Even happy users tire of the same music set, want longer clips and Spotify integration, and find photos and videos go blurry once uploaded. A hard length cap exists even on premium.

product.title: Heavy battery and system-resource drain
product.minus: Recording an activity eats a noticeable chunk of charge and hammers the CPU — around half the battery on a single hike. For an app meant to run outdoors all day, that's a serious drawback.

product.title: The strap is visible to the phone, but the app refuses to pair
product.minus: The single most common complaint: third-party apps and the phone's own Bluetooth detect the H10/H7/OH1 fine, but Polar Beat itself can't connect or drops the link on the workout screen. The only fixes are rituals — pull the battery, reboot the phone, reinstall.

product.title: When it works — accurate live HR and clear zones
product.plus: The headline praise: paired with the H10/H9 chest strap the app gives the most accurate HR people have seen, with a live on-screen readout and a clear zone. Ideal for HIIT and zone-2 training.

product.title: No-nonsense simplicity is the main draw for many
product.plus: Many love Beat precisely for its minimalism: no social networking or bloat, a clean interface, big readable numbers, light on battery. It works without a Polar watch and (unlike Flow) even without a mandatory login, opening straight on the start screen.

product.title: Abandoned development: simple features missing for years
product.minus: Zones can't be customized, there's no audio alert when you exceed max HR, no CSV export, no "favorites" for exercises, no elevation on GPS routes. The same requests have sat for 5+ years unanswered — the app feels frozen.

product.title: The app demands a re-login and wipes out years of history
product.minus: Users get logged out without warning and can't get back in: the password is rejected even after resets, recovery emails never arrive, and a new account can't be made (the email is already in the database). This often comes with the loss of 10–15 years of training history.

product.title: Account and personal-data harvesting are mandatory, or your device is a brick
product.minus: Just to read HR from a strap you paid 100 € for, the app demands an account and consent to harvest a pile of personal data (even shipping it overseas). Decline and features are blocked citing "scientific need"; some users had their account closed mid-run.

product.title: The May 2026 update broke the app: crashes and failed syncing
product.minus: Since the update the app crashes when you try to open a workout summary, workouts stop on their own, and syncing with the H10 and the cloud falls apart. Viewing past logs became impossible — it crashes every time.

product.title: GPS is demanded even for indoor workouts, and the track is wrong
product.minus: The app nags you to enable location even for strength and indoor workouts that don't use GPS, and otherwise won't show your HR. And when GPS is on the track is wrong: 9 km becomes 4.5 km, points are joined by a straight line, distance is inflated.

product.title: Free with any Bluetooth HR strap — best of the free apps
product.plus: The app is free and works not only with Polar straps but with cheap third-party Bluetooth sensors too. For many it's the best of the free HR-monitor apps — everything you need at no cost, and no need to carry your phone.

product.title: The app gets stuck saving a session and loses the workout
product.minus: The "Save HR with sensor" mode breaks hardest: after a workout the data won't download off the strap, the app hangs trying to "download exercise", and Stop doesn't end the session — the screen loops. The only escape is reinstalling, which loses all the data.

product.title: Two Polar apps that confuse users and sync poorly
product.minus: Beat and Flow run in parallel, confusing users and barely cooperating: the sync between them isn't automatic and drags painfully, and the only way to push a workout to Strava is through Flow. Some workouts just get lost in the process.

product.title: Dated UI, and entering your birth date is torture
product.minus: The interface feels like it's from the 2010s and is plain clumsy in places: setting your birth date takes hundreds of swipes, the Stop button sits where you hit it by accident, there's no landscape support, and the sensor number is buried deep in menus.

product.title: Swapping the clock face for a scroll wheel doubled the taps needed per entry
product.minus: Time used to take two taps on the clock face; now you scroll wheels for hours and minutes, and logging a whole day after the fact takes many times longer. The defining pain of the update: dozens of parents beg for the analog clock back, or at least a toggle.

product.title: Sync between parents' phones is the thing the app is worshipped for
product.plus: The single most-loved scenario: mom and dad keep the app on two phones and feed, sleep and diaper entries appear on both almost instantly. It removes the need to ask each other and lets parents 'hand over' when one leaves for work.

product.title: A lifeline for the foggy-brained first weeks of no sleep
product.plus: Parents flatly call it a lifesaver: half-asleep, you can't hold in your head when the last feed was, which side, when the diaper was changed. The app counts and remembers for you, taking the anxiety out of the baby's first days.

product.title: Free, with no subscription and no pushy upsells
product.plus: A huge plus next to rivals: the app is free, no subscription, no AI, no pushing of 'useful' paid features. Ads are just a small bottom banner, and those who want can remove them for a small fee to support the developer.

product.title: The vanished edit button leaves false data stuck forever
product.minus: After the update parents can't find any way to fix or delete a wrong entry — and half-asleep, mistakes are constant (an accidental 14-hour nap). The record just sticks with false data, and the whole day is 'blacked out'.

product.title: Ads open AliExpress on their own and self-click without a touch — like malware
product.minus: A grave complaint: ads spontaneously launch the browser or apps (AliExpress, Shein, Lazada) mid-feed, with no tap at all. Users have googled that this is the Kaleidoscope ad fraud, and for a postpartum tool it feels like an infection.

product.title: Entries and whole sleep periods quietly vanish from the log
product.minus: Trust is undermined by data going missing: people log a feed or sleep, and later the entry is gone. Some have even built a habit of closing and reopening the app to check it saved — and even that doesn't help.

product.title: Sync regularly breaks and demands a reinstall
product.minus: The very sync feature people love stops working for some: a second device's entries don't pull through for a day, especially between Android and iOS. The fix is brutal — leave the group, delete and reinstall the app, sometimes weekly.

product.title: Perfect minimalism: everything you need, one tap on the home screen
product.plus: A beloved trait: the app does exactly what a newborn needs — feeds, sleep, diapers, growth — with no extra frills. Unwanted categories can be removed, everything shows on the home screen, entry is one tap, and daily summaries are ready for the doctor.

product.title: The interface is murky in places — sharing and switching babies especially
product.minus: Some parents struggle with navigation: it's unclear how to set up sharing across two phones, how to switch between babies (in places 'back' closes the app), or how to view one event's details. Profiles differ only by photo — easy to mix up babies.

product.title: Silent data loss when changing phones: there's a backup, but no way to restore
product.minus: A harsh failure: after a reset or new Android phone the data isn't there, though the app promised a Google Drive backup, and signing back into the old account fails. Some weren't even told backup had to be turned on manually — and lost weeks of records.

product.title: Weak twin and multi-child support pushes returning parents away
product.minus: Loyal parents come back for a second baby and can't find how to add another child or twins — the feature is hidden and not self-evident, so people are ready to leave for another tracker. After the update, managing multiple kids got even harder.

product.title: Timers and tallies miscalculate: phantom minutes, rounding, ounce jumps
product.minus: Accuracy fails right where a parent leans on it: the app adds phantom minutes at midnight and scares you that you 'waited too long to pump', rounds feeding duration, and ounce totals jump on their own. For tracking a baby's health that's alarming.

product.title: A years-loved tracker carried across several kids and years
product.plus: Deep loyalty: people track 3-4 kids in it, use it for 5-7 years, recommend it to other moms, and even get it recommended by a health visitor. It embeds into the routine and stays useful when the child is sick, even years later.

product.title: Swapping the clock face for scroll wheels killed input speed
product.minus: The top complaint: an update replaced the quick analog clock with scrolling hour-and-minute wheels. Time used to take two taps; now you scroll endlessly — far slower for a tired parent, especially when logging retrospectively.

product.title: Ads auto-open AliExpress and Shein with no tap
product.minus: Ads don't just appear — they open the browser and third-party apps (AliExpress, Lazada, Shein) with zero input. One user identified it as ad fraud; others uninstalled instantly. For an intimate tool it feels like an infection.

product.title: Cross-device sync is both the killer feature and the main failure
product.minus: Sync between phones is the most-praised feature — yet it regularly breaks: a partner's entries don't arrive, Android-to-iOS stops working, and people leave the group and reinstall weekly. When parents rely on a 'handover', a sync failure is costly.

product.title: Edit and delete vanished after an update
product.minus: Editing used to work; now the edit button is gone — and a mistaken entry (like a 14-hour nap) is stuck forever as false data. It's especially painful when both parents log and duplicates can't be deleted.

product.title: Entries and data silently disappear on their own
product.minus: What you enter doesn't stick: entries vanish after a while, sleep records delete themselves, feeds get logged but never appear in the day's timeline. People reopen the app just to check it saved — which destroys the trust a tracker needs.

product.title: Confusing navigation — basic things are unfindable
product.minus: Navigation is called baffling: it's unclear how to see one event's details or past notes, and 'back' in one menu closes the whole app. For a postpartum tool used through sleep fog, that's especially unacceptable.

product.title: Multi-child and twin support is hidden or missing
product.minus: Parents of a second child or twins can't find how to add another baby and leave for other apps. Profiles are nearly indistinguishable (photo only, no color or icons), so entries land under the wrong child by mistake.

product.title: Timers and time math lie — they add minutes by themselves
product.minus: The app adds time on its own: the gap between pumps balloons at midnight, feed durations round off, ounces vanish. A mother relies on these numbers to space her pumps, and the false data makes her panic for nothing.

product.title: Free, no subscription, no pushy ads — the core draw
product.plus: Again and again people celebrate that it's free, with no subscription and no aggressive ads — just a bottom banner. Against competitors that paywall basics, this is a core reason they love and recommend it.

product.title: A lifeline for the sleep-deprived brain
product.plus: The core emotional payoff: it removes anxiety and offsets 'mommy brain' — no need to remember when you last fed or changed a diaper. Parents flatly call it a lifesaver in the newborn days.

product.title: Summaries and charts you can hand to the doctor
product.plus: Parents value the clear daily tallies, charts and PDF export — nurses and pediatricians appreciate the readable summaries, and growth comparison against WHO charts helps at visits. It turns routine logging into a useful medical report.

product.title: Backup and restore fail when you switch phones
product.minus: After a reset or new phone, data won't restore: people can't log back into the old account, the promised Google Drive backup isn't there, and weeks of records are lost. Backup also isn't on by default, which users discover too late.

product.title: The AI swaps your baby's face for a different child
product.minus: Instead of just changing the background, the app generates a "prettier" AI version and returns a completely different baby — which defeats the entire point of keeping it your own child.

product.title: Paywalled at the front door — no trying it without subscribing
product.minus: You can't even get in without paying: the subscription is forced at the doorstep, and those unwilling to pay leave without ever seeing a result.

product.title: Charges keep coming after the subscription is cancelled
product.minus: Money keeps leaving the card even a month after cancelling, with no way to reach support and fix it — to parents it reads as a flat-out scam.

product.title: Subscribed for a year instead of the chosen week
product.minus: You sign up for a weekly plan but get charged for a full year at once, and support never responds — the billing doesn't match what the checkout screen promised.

product.title: Photo upload crashes and freezes
product.minus: Trying to upload a photo, the app keeps stopping and getting stuck — even for users who already paid a year in advance.

product.title: The subscribe button doesn't work — stuck on the checkout screen
product.minus: A paradox: the app demands a subscription, yet the checkout screen has nothing to tap or the tap does nothing — the user can neither pay nor move on.

product.title: Only a couple of shots come out well, the rest look fake
product.minus: Only a few cute shots actually land while most look unnatural; you need a perfectly clean background, otherwise the result is no better than an ordinary photo editor.

product.title: The core idea — preserving baby's childhood memories — wins parents over
product.plus: Even disappointed users admit the concept is great: creating artistic shots and milestone images of your child as a record of their childhood — an idea parents connect with.

product.title: Clean, intuitive interface from the first launch
product.plus: Those who reach the app itself praise the clean, attractive interface: navigation is clear even for first-timers and functions run smoothly without major lag.

product.title: Pricing stings even users who like the app
product.minus: Some parents praise the app but immediately note it's a bit pricey; for those who can't afford it, the cost becomes a reason to simply delete it.

product.title: Glowing ratings from users who haven't tried it yet
product.minus: A noticeable share of high ratings is given upfront — people openly say they haven't used it yet and will leave an honest review later; there's no real experience behind those stars.

product.title: Tells you it's not active labour when it actually is
product.minus: The app's most dangerous flaw: it repeatedly says you're not in active labour while you're already 7-10 cm dilated. Users describe nearly giving birth at home or on the way, and missing the epidural window, because they trusted that message.

product.title: Told them to go, and they made it in time
product.plus: The dominant flip side of the same feature: for most people the 'go to the hospital' prompt was spot on, matched their midwife's advice, and got them there just in time — sometimes still in time for the epidural.

product.title: Open and go — no signup, no setup
product.plus: The core loved trait: you open it and immediately start timing. No signup screens, no login, no setup — a big start/stop button and large numbers that stay readable even in panic and pain.

product.title: Free, with non-intrusive ads
product.plus: The core feature is free and, unlike rivals, the ads don't take over the screen. Many specifically praise that key features aren't paywalled, and buy premium only after delivery — just to support the developers.

product.title: Wrong frequency numbers, even negatives
product.minus: The math itself sometimes lies: it shows an 8-minute interval instead of a minute and a half, a 1.26-minute duration instead of 40 seconds, and occasionally negative frequency values. For a tool people lean on in labour, that's critical.

product.title: Can't reliably edit or delete an entry
product.minus: Miss a tap or make a mistake and it's hard to fix: the edit-time button doesn't apply changes and keeps the old value, you can't delete the last entry, and manually adding a missed contraction throws off the frequency math.

product.title: Pop-ups and ads block timing mid-contraction
product.minus: For some users pop-ups and ads appear right in the middle of a contraction and block starting the timer. The prompts behind them are called useless, and you have to dig into settings to turn them off.

product.title: A job for the partner who'd otherwise feel useless
product.plus: A distinct value for fathers and partners: while she's in pain, he can take over the counting and feel he's actually helping rather than just standing around. It shows up surprisingly often in reviews.

product.title: Rating contraction intensity — a rare extra
product.plus: Beyond duration and frequency, it lets you rate the intensity of each contraction on a scale — a feature many rivals lack, and one you can switch off. The data is handy to show staff on arrival.

product.title: Screen locks in the middle of a contraction
product.minus: The app doesn't keep the screen awake: the phone locks mid-contraction and you have to unlock it to stop the timer. As the pain ramps up, that gets harder and harder.

product.title: Payments and purchase restore fail
product.minus: Even people who want to pay sometimes can't: it won't accept Google balance or Visa cards, fails to restore purchases, and the in-app support button doesn't work. The developers are effectively turning down willing customers' money.

product.title: Won't load — endless spinner
product.minus: For a few users the app simply won't open: instead of the timer they get an endless loading spinner. At the most critical moment, that means a completely dead tool.

product.title: "Not in active labour yet" advice during real labour
product.minus: The most dangerous complaint: the app keeps insisting there's no active labour while the woman is already 7-10 cm dilated. Several mothers nearly gave birth at home or on the way after trusting the prompt.

product.title: "Go to the hospital" prompt landed exactly on time
product.plus: For most users it's the opposite: the leave-now recommendation matched reality and their midwife's advice. People arrived 4-7 cm dilated, made it in time for an epidural — for many the decisive moment of the birth.

product.title: Opened and worked instantly, no sign-up
product.plus: No registration, no settings, no intro screens — open it and press the button. Several people downloaded it mid-contraction and it worked from the first second.

product.title: Stripped-down interface with one big button
product.plus: A big start/stop button and large numbers you can read even in the panic of active labour. No extra features — that very simplicity is what lets people use it when they have no capacity for anything else.

product.title: Wrong frequency math — down to negative numbers
product.minus: Beyond the questionable advice, the arithmetic itself fails: users report 8-minute frequencies instead of the real 1.5, durations over a minute instead of 40 seconds, even negative numbers between contractions.

product.title: Gives the partner a way to feel useful
product.plus: An unexpected role — for the father/partner standing nearby with nothing to do. Counting contractions on the mother's behalf gives him a concrete job and removes the feeling of being useless.

product.title: Ads and pop-ups appear mid-contraction
product.minus: For some users pop-ups and ads invade the screen at the exact moment of a contraction and block the timer. The intrusive rate-the-app prompt at the worst possible time belongs here too.

product.title: Ads are unobtrusive, core features are free
product.plus: Paradoxically, many praise the lack of aggressive ads: nothing covers the screen, the key features are free, and people specifically thank the developers and beg them "not to sell out".

product.title: Can't reliably edit or delete an entry
product.minus: A frequent ask: let users fix or delete an entry. The edit button doesn't work for some and keeps the old time, back-dating contractions breaks the frequency math, and full editing is locked behind the paid version.

product.title: Helped tell false Braxton-Hicks from real labour
product.plus: A distinct value for anxious first-time mothers unsure whether it's labour at all. The app helped distinguish practice Braxton-Hicks from true labour and took away the uncertainty.

product.title: Screen locks and blocks stopping the timer
product.minus: Small but painful rough edges: the phone locks mid-contraction and you have to unlock it to stop the timer; you can't minimise the app; and there's no way to reset the timers short of reinstalling.

product.title: Payments and purchases often fail
product.minus: Ironically, people want to pay to support the developers but the payment fails — it accepts neither Google balance, nor Visa cards, nor Google Pay. Restoring a purchase and reaching support don't work either.

product.title: The video stream endlessly buffers — you force-close and reopen the app several times to get a feed
product.minus: The single most common complaint: the feed won't connect on the first try, it loads forever or freezes on the spinner. Users describe reopening the app 2-5 times as routine, spending more time restarting than actually watching the baby.

product.title: You're forced to start a subscription and enter a card just to activate a camera you already bought
product.minus: Parents are furious that the pricey hardware can't even be activated without a free trial and card details, and then 75% of the features land behind a paywall. Many call it a racket and predatory, especially when basic functions are blocked for people who already paid.

product.title: The Android version is noticeably worse than iPhone — it works on the partner's iPhone but not your Android
product.minus: The same story recurs: one parent has an iPhone where everything is stable, while the same account on Android constantly disconnects, buffers and crashes. That rules out the "it's your wifi" excuse — same network, the problem is the Android app itself.

product.title: Breathing monitoring and sleep tracking deliver genuine peace of mind, especially when the baby is sick
product.plus: The core reason people love Nanit: parents sleep easier knowing breathing is tracked. Many say it reduced postpartum anxiety, carried them through their child's respiratory scares, and the loud alarm on breathing stops gave confidence they won't sleep through an emergency.

product.title: Subscription ads pop up right over the face of the sleeping baby
product.minus: What especially enrages parents is the "Want to know when I fell asleep? JOIN INSIGHTS" banner slapped over the baby's video — with no close button. Many whose kids have outgrown the feature feel cheated: they paid for the camera, and now an ad covers their child's face.

product.title: Automatic logging of naps, feeds and diaper changes saves exhausted parents real effort
product.plus: Parents value that the app auto-tracks the day: naps, feeds, diaper changes, height and weight in one place. The next-nap prediction is called surprisingly accurate and a lifesaver with a newborn, and the weekly insights helpful for first-time parents.

product.title: The mic for soothing the baby by voice constantly throws "connection failed"
product.minus: The talk-to-baby feature works for people maybe 1 time in 10. It stings most at 3am when you want to tell a crying child to lie back down and the mic fails — by the time you get through, the child is already worked up.

product.title: Grandparents thousands of miles away get to see their grandkids every day
product.plus: A surprisingly frequent and touching use case: distant grandparents use Nanit to peek in on grandkids, hear them, and feel closer. For many it's the best part of the product — being present while 800 miles away or even abroad.

product.title: Background audio keeps playing even after the app is closed — and sometimes turns itself on
product.minus: The app doesn't exit cleanly: after closing, audio from the baby's room can start playing through the phone on its own, sometimes triggered by a humidity notification. Parents call it creepy and insecure — the phone effectively broadcasts the room unprompted, and the only fix is shutting the phone off.

product.title: Crib detection and sleep timings are wrong — it logs an empty bed as sleep, or counts nighttime as a nap
product.minus: The flagship paid feature is unreliable: the app misses that the baby is in the crib, mistakes a pillow for the child, fails to register wakeups, and logs absurd timings like 2am-to-6am as a "nap." At this price and subscription, parents expect at least correct data.

product.title: A nagging tooltip about controlling light and sound keeps popping up over the video
product.minus: A recent Android bug: the "control Nanit sound and light from the camera app" tooltip appears every time you open the app and won't dismiss no matter how many times you swipe it away. In night mode it even lights up the room and blocks the baby's face — pushing parents to the point of wanting to rip the camera off the wall.

product.title: The subscription is billed per camera, not per family — twins cost double
product.minus: An unwelcome surprise: after buying a plan, parents find it covers only one camera. With two kids (e.g. twins) you pay two separate subscriptions, plus a separate fee per additional user. Many say they'd have picked a different system had they known.

product.title: The picture and sound are crystal clear even in total darkness
product.plus: When the stream does work, parents praise the quality: a sharp image day and night, the baby visible in detail in pitch black, clear audio. Many note the crisp night view and good sound are exactly what keeps them with Nanit despite the app's quirks.

product.title: After an update, picture-in-picture shows a frozen frame instead of the live feed
product.minus: The beloved picture-in-picture broke after an update: the mini-window holds a frozen frame and the audio cuts out. Parents find out the hard way — thinking the baby is asleep on a static image when she's actually already awake and crying.

product.title: A "second brain" for parents with baby brain
product.plus: The core value is taking the load off an exhausted memory of when the last feed, nap and diaper change happened; parents repeatedly call it a sanity-saver in the postpartum chaos.

product.title: A recent update breaks saving and deletes logs
product.minus: After an update (especially on Android) the app stops saving feeds, bottles and sleep, and for some users wipes days of already-saved data — for a tracker that exists for exactly this, it destroys the whole point.

product.title: SweetSpot predicts the nap window almost telepathically
product.plus: The premium SweetSpot feature suggests the perfect time to put baby down and adjusts wake windows to logged sleep; parents describe it as uncannily accurate and a saviour from overtiredness and meltdowns.

product.title: Subscription costs more than Netflix and is pushed aggressively
product.minus: The premium price (£115/year, ~$15-30 a month) feels out of touch for mums on maternity pay, and constant upgrade pop-ups and emails — right in the middle of logging — feel pushy and tone-deaf.

product.title: Android is a stripped port without widgets or a watch app
product.minus: Android users pay the same money but don't get the widgets and smartwatch support iOS has; for one-handed night logging, the missing widget and quick entry is a constant pain.

product.title: Sharing with the second parent is a clumsy workaround
product.plus: When both parents are logged into one account, the shared log feed works great and helps them stay in sync on what happened with the baby while the other was asleep.
product.minus: But there's no real family access: you can't add a partner separately, you have to share a single login, and cross-device sync (especially iOS↔Android) either drops for days or doesn't work at all.

product.title: The Berry AI assistant frustrates more than it helps
product.minus: The newly added Berry AI asks questions instead of answering, runs in circles, contradicts itself and pretends to be a sleep expert — parents call it imposed "slop" in the bottom bar that only adds stress.

product.title: Scroll-wheel data entry is agony at 2am
product.minus: Entering times and values via oversensitive scroll wheels takes too many clicks and screens, is awkward one-handed and literally wakes the parent up; after saving, the app also dumps you on the reports page instead of home.

product.title: Lag, freezes and long load times on every open
product.minus: Nothing is stored locally, so every launch and screen change spends seconds loading from the cloud; the app freezes when entering bottles, hangs for up to a minute and is noticeably heavier on Android.

product.title: Weight and growth entry is broken after an update
product.minus: After a recent update the weight selector broke: it only lets you pick ounces or fractions of a kilogram, won't accept pounds/whole kg and blocks updating height and head circumference — some users note the bug was later fixed.

product.title: Won't open — stuck on the logo or login screen
product.minus: For some users the app won't launch at all after an update: it hangs on the Huckleberry logo, crashes before account creation, or loops back to the login screen, leaving a paid subscription unusable.

product.title: The free version paywalls the genuinely useful bits
product.minus: Basic tracking is free and enough for many, but the key features (SweetSpot, the "last fed" notification) are locked behind premium, and some feel important features were moved to paid like a pay-to-win game.

product.title: Charges and renewals without consent, cancellation trouble
product.minus: Users complain about accidental subscription taps that auto-renew a year later, charges for premium without ever starting a trial, and failed cancellations — money is taken even after cancelling or before it's due.

product.title: A lifesaver for multiple caregivers and a first baby
product.plus: First-time parents and families who take turns caring especially value it: the shared picture of the day, reminders and summaries (how many ml, how many wet diapers) give a sense of control and help when talking to the doctor.

product.title: A former one-time purchase became a subscription — and old buyers are furious
product.minus: The defining pain: people paid once years ago ($1.99–$6), used the app for previous kids, and on returning for a new baby find a subscription and no honoring of the old purchase. It reads as a betrayal and greed, not a model change.

product.title: Hard paywall: nothing visible without paying, no trial, no preview
product.minus: The app is listed as free, but everything is behind the paywall — no free tier, no trial, no ad-supported option. People refuse to pay blind for something they haven't seen and call it a dark pattern.

product.title: Fill out the profile and hand over data first — only then learn the price
product.minus: The price is hidden until the end of onboarding: users are made to create an account, enter personal info and due date, and only at the payment screen does the cost appear. It feels like a bait-and-switch and a waste of time.

product.title: Uncanny phase accuracy: open the app and it describes exactly what's happening
product.plus: The core strength for fans: when the baby is suddenly fussy for no clear reason, parents open the app and it shows the leap has just begun. It removes anxiety and feels almost magical.

product.title: Peace of mind for the exhausted parent: knowing the fussiness is a normal stage
product.plus: The strongest emotional upside: the app explains why the baby is fussy and removes the parental guilt of "what am I doing wrong." First-time moms in the "newborn trenches" value it most.

product.title: Only matches "on average": a real baby's leaps don't follow the calendar
product.minus: The flip side of "accuracy": for many, phases don't line up at all — calm days in the "fussy" phase and vice versa. Data is tied to the due date, not the actual baby, so for premature or simply individual babies the predictions miss.

product.title: The same info is free on Google, ChatGPT, or cheaper in the book
product.minus: The key value argument against the price: the content is just a digitization of a $10 book, and the same leap info is easily Googled or asked from AI for free. A $5/month subscription for known information reads as absurd.

product.title: Switched phones, lost access: restore-purchase and password reset are broken
product.minus: A widespread technical pain: after switching devices (especially iPhone→Android) the app doesn't recognize the old purchase, and password reset endlessly returns "something went wrong." Paid-for access simply vanishes.

product.title: White screen and crashes after updates — the paid app stops opening
product.minus: After recent updates the app simply won't launch for many: a blank white screen or a crash on open. Especially painful because access is paid up front for many months or years.

product.title: Responsive support actually restores old accounts — and flips the rating
product.plus: A counterpoint to the access complaints: when support replies, it quickly restores old purchases and migrates data between devices. Many edit 1-star reviews up to 5, with several praising an agent named Miranda by name.

product.title: Play ideas matched to the current skill — the favorite feature for development
product.plus: Beyond predictions, parents especially value the concrete play and activity suggestions for each phase: it gives them something to fill the wake windows and a sense of actively helping the baby develop, not just watching.

product.title: Confusing navigation: can't peek at other leaps, the UI lags and crashes
product.minus: Even for paying users the interface frustrates: you can't look ahead to the next leap, the back button closes the app, the diary loses entries, and scrolling lags. After updates many say it got worse.

product.title: Useless first month for preemies: everything is tied to the due date, no manual leap start
product.minus: If the baby is born early, the app still counts by gestational age: the first leap only comes a month after the due date, and you can't start a phase manually. You pay for months in which the app shows nothing.

product.title: Week-by-week baby-size comparison is the core hook and daily ritual
product.plus: Comparing the baby's size to fruit and objects is what people open the app for every day; it gives them something to look forward to in the dragging first trimester and makes the pregnancy feel tangible.

product.title: It doesn't abandon you after birth — it becomes a feeding and diaper tracker
product.plus: After birth the app automatically switches into a tracker for feedings, diapers, sleep, baby milestones and even the mother's own painkiller doses — users say the postpartum features turned out even better than the pregnancy ones.

product.title: Free and no subscription — a rarity users single out
product.plus: Against a sea of apps that paywall everything, WTE being free is itself a reason to love it; users explicitly praise the lack of a subscription and free access to all the content.

product.title: Due-date community and chats — support from moms on the same timeline
product.plus: The forums and due-month groups let users ask questions and connect with other expecting moms; for many it's the main reason they open the app almost daily.

product.title: Weekly videos and articles arrive right on time for the current stage
product.plus: Users eagerly await the videos and articles on the baby's development and their body changes — the content lands on the right week and helps them feel informed, especially first-time moms.

product.title: Works for dads, grandparents and partners — but lacks profiles built for them
product.plus: Dads and husbands specifically note the app keeps them in the loop on their wife's pregnancy and helps them prepare for the birth; for fathers who don't write reviews it's a rare exception.
product.minus: Yet there's no friendly separate profile for other family members — a grandfather or grandmother has nowhere to set up their own access to use the app meaningfully.

product.title: Sells your data — consent baked into sign-up with no opt-out
product.minus: The first thing you must agree to at sign-up is letting them sell your information and send promo emails, with no opt-out; users brace for endless spam and call it shameful.

product.title: Ads clutter the screen — users would pay just to remove them
product.minus: The app is so cluttered with ads that it stops being enjoyable and user-friendly; even satisfied users say they'd gladly pay for an ad-free version.

product.title: Heavy US bias — discounts and freebies are unavailable outside America
product.minus: Contests, registries and freebies are tuned for Americans only: Canadians, Australians and others can't qualify, and some users can't even sign up from outside the US.

product.title: Broken sign-in — passwords rejected, accounts not recognized
product.minus: Some users can't get in at all: passwords are flagged as incorrect, no reset email arrives, and no new password meets the requirements — locking them out of the content entirely.

product.title: Content goes stale — unsourced medical advice and repeating videos
product.minus: Some advice is plainly outdated and one-sided (supplements, sleep, attachment), with no studies cited, and the videos start repeating — the app flags 'new' clips the user already watched a trimester ago.

product.title: Small tracking gaps — lost photos, dropped data, divisive comment order
product.minus: Annoying losses pile up: photos aren't saved, kick counts get dropped from the monthly recap, and flipping the comment order from oldest-first to newest-first broke forum navigation with no way to switch back.

product.title: The 3D fetal model is the main emotional hook
product.plus: The animated week-by-week 3D baby model is what keeps people coming back: they show it to older kids, husbands and grandmas, and it sparks delight and a sense of bonding.

product.title: Week-by-week tracking calms first-time-mum anxiety
product.plus: The app clearly shows what week you're in and how much is left, and for first-time mums this becomes a lifeline: no need to track dates in your head, it's all clear and at hand.

product.title: Paywalling the 'important' info angers users
product.minus: The most useful pregnancy and baby info is locked behind Premium, and on top of already-expensive baby prep this feels like another bill for things you could google for free.

product.title: The fruit-size baby comparison is fun but inaccurate
product.minus: People love the fruit-size baby comparison for the visual, but users notice it doesn't match reality — and on Samsung the fetus even shows twice as big as on iPhone.

product.title: Crashes break onboarding and adding a pregnancy
product.minus: The app routinely freezes and crashes at critical steps: it won't continue after you enter your info, crashes when setting a due date, won't let you add a new pregnancy, and shows 'app not responding'.

product.title: Articles and weekly tips feel like a 'pocket doctor'
product.plus: Beyond baby growth, the app delivers articles, tips and facts on symptoms and pregnancy topics — it reassures, answers anxious questions, and feels like having a private doctor at hand.

product.title: Doesn't respond to miscarriage or status changes
product.minus: After a user switches their status to miscarriage, the app keeps sending baby-development updates — a painful failure at the most vulnerable moment; emailing the developers is futile, messages get ignored.

product.title: Engages partners, grandmas and the whole family
product.plus: It's not only for the pregnant: husbands get tips on helping their wife, grandmas follow their grandchild's weeks, coworkers track along — it brings the whole family around the pregnancy.

product.title: Bait pricing and nagging rating prompts
product.minus: The advertised '$2.50 a month' actually turns into a single $31.97 annual charge with no cheaper option, and even the paid version still begs for a rating every launch and runs ads.

product.title: No language switch and units stuck on UK/US
product.minus: You can't change the app's language without changing your whole phone's language, and baby size comes only in inches and feet — Europeans without centimetres simply can't follow the growth.

product.title: Accurate due dates, but factual content errors
product.minus: The due-date math is praised as accurate, even matching the real birth date, yet the content has factual errors: weeks 1-2 are described wrongly and the week-5 embryo looks like week 7-8.

product.title: Weight graph with no scale makes the tracker useless
product.minus: The weight tracker's x-axis has no scale and points sit equidistant whether measurements are a day or a week apart — it distorts the trend and makes a basic graph almost useless.

product.title: The price is hidden behind a long quiz — you find out only at the end
product.minus: You have to make an account, answer dozens of personal questions about your diagnosis and hand over your email, and only at the very last step does it reveal a $50/month or $200/year subscription. People feel tricked and uninstall before ever starting.

product.title: App pricing rivals a therapist — $50/month or $200/year
product.minus: Dozens call the price unaffordable and insulting: more than their phone and internet bills, out of reach for students, the disabled and people whose ADHD already hurts their income. Many say for that money they'd just see a real professional.

product.title: They charge after cancellation — and cancelling is deliberately convoluted
product.minus: People cancel and keep getting charged; the subscription isn't in Google Play, cancellation routes through a website with passwords and codes that never arrive. Charges of $200–400 hit months and even a year later, with refunds refused.

product.title: The promised pre-charge reminder never comes
product.minus: The app swears it'll remind you before the trial ends, but the reminder never arrives — instead you get a notice that payment already went through. Users call it a deliberate bet on ADHD forgetfulness.

product.title: "Predatory" targeting of ADHD users — the defining grievance
product.minus: Over and over, users say the app cynically exploits the very symptom it claims to treat: forgetfulness and trouble following through. Hard cancellation plus a costly subscription reads as a trap set for vulnerable people.

product.title: Freezes while typing — journaling becomes impossible
product.minus: After an update the app locks up on nearly every keystroke: journaling and posting in the community become painful, the screen freezes, and you have to restart repeatedly. Ironic for a tool built around written reflection.

product.title: Blank white screen and a phantom "update needed" — can't get in
product.minus: A large group reports the app opening to a blank white screen after login, demanding a non-existent update forever, or falsely claiming there's no internet. Verification codes never reach the inbox, locking people out entirely.

product.title: Too much reading and AI narration — not built for an ADHD brain
product.minus: Some users find the content a boring "textbook": long passages, a school-like layout and a synthetic AI voice that kills attention fast. For an app billed as made by people with ADHD, that lands as a failure.

product.title: Content is generic neurotypical advice, not actually ADHD-tailored
product.minus: Experienced ADHD adults complain the advice (time-blocking, eat-the-frog, pomodoro) is aimed at neurotypicals and often backfires, while the rest is common knowledge available free on YouTube. The promised personalization isn't there.

product.title: Quinn — an AI companion that genuinely helps in the moment
product.plus: The AI companion Quinn is the most-praised feature: users say it understands ADHD, is available 24/7, helps through anxiety and crisis, asks the right questions and feels like an understanding friend in your pocket. Even AI skeptics come around.

product.title: Bite-sized lessons that finally make you feel understood
product.plus: The core strength: short, gentle, practical lessons — "Duolingo for ADHD" — without overwhelm or lecturing. Especially for the newly diagnosed it brings relief, a feeling of being seen, and real tactics they actually manage to apply.

product.title: Community and live focus sessions keep people accountable
product.plus: Co-working "focus rooms", Sunday setups and the community forum are, for many, the best part: a supportive atmosphere where "everyone gets it" helps people finish tasks and not feel alone.

product.title: Coaching and live events were gutted — the thing they paid for vanished
product.minus: Long-time subscribers are angry the app removed free coaching and co-working (coaching is now a separate $30–90), stopped adding content, and pivoted to AI and clinical programs. To them it's a bait-and-switch.

product.title: Forced AI chat with no opt-out — a privacy and trust concern
product.minus: A subset actively doesn't want the AI: the chatbot wasn't disclosed up front, it's easy to open by accident, can't be disabled, and the AI is pushed for journaling even after you decline. Some see a privacy risk, others fear AI dependency.

product.title: UI doesn't fit the screen — text gets cut off
product.minus: On several phones (notably Samsung/Galaxy) content is over-zoomed: lesson text and buttons don't fit, quiz options can't be scrolled, and landscape mode is blocked. People pay but literally can't read the material.

product.title: For the newly diagnosed, a turning-point that restores hope
product.plus: The strongest reviews come from late-diagnosed adults: the app teaches self-compassion instead of self-blame, explains "why I'm like this" and hands over real tools. Many describe tears of relief and hope they hadn't felt in years.

product.title: Engaging chat that also helps clear up doubts
product.plus: People find it fun and engaging to talk to, and it genuinely helps them work through questions.

product.title: Message limit cuts off the one thing people came for
product.minus: Even users who love the app single out the cap on how many messages they can send.

product.title: Stuck on "..." replies and sign-in errors break the session
product.minus: The bot sometimes freezes and answers with just "...", and sign-in throws errors — people still rate it okay overall, but it stings.

product.title: No customization: no wallpaper, no avatar design
product.minus: Users want to change the wallpaper and design the avatar — the current background colour literally hurts their eyes.

product.title: Almost everything useful is locked behind a paywall
product.minus: Users repeatedly complain that only mood tracking is free, while exercises, courses, insights and statistics all require a subscription — and it feels like exploitation of exactly the people who need help most.

product.title: A quiet companion that checks in three times a day
product.plus: The thrice-daily questions become something users look forward to — small journaling moments that build a habit of noticing how you feel, gentle and without judgment.

product.title: Helps you come to your therapist without a blank mind
product.plus: Many use it as a bridge to therapy — the logs and bi-weekly reports give concrete topics to discuss with a doctor, make patterns visible, and users say it even makes the clinician's work easier.

product.title: After two weeks of questions, a report that tells you what you already knew
product.minus: The promised payoff — the 14-day report — disappoints many: it's either obvious or boils down to «your emotional health is poor, see a therapist», and then it too hits a paywall.

product.title: Updates took away what used to be free
product.minus: Long-time users (since the Moodpath/eMindLog days) bitterly note that features that were free for years — mood tags, meditations, «Take a Pause» — have crept behind the subscription, and it feels like a betrayal of trust.

product.title: Your own past entries got locked behind a subscription
product.minus: A special pain — being unable to see your own past months of mood history and journal entries without Plus: people lose years of data and major life events, and for a mood journal that feels absurd.

product.title: Insights are either obvious or too generic
product.minus: The promised «insights» often fall flat: too generic, repetitive, and context-blind — the app may label you «poor emotional health» even on a day you were genuinely happy.

product.title: A funnel to BetterHelp rather than help on its own
product.minus: Some users feel the app is essentially an ad for BetterHelp — it nudges you toward a paid therapist via a link, and people distrust that company given its reputation.

product.title: Sharp, thoughtful questions hit scarily on target
product.plus: Those who stay are struck by the accuracy: the questions make you really think, vary each time, and sometimes catch what other tools missed — users call the results «scary accurate».

product.title: Helped through the darkest times — like someone cares
product.plus: For some, the app became a lifeline in crisis: a safe, private place to vent, a distraction from dark thoughts, and a warm companion when no one else is there.

product.title: Hard technical failures: lost entries, broken payments, crashes
product.minus: The app fails technically: entries on stressful days don't save, the upgrade to Plus errors out, and some were charged without authorization — especially cruel for people who need reliability.

product.title: Doesn't account for those outside the «well and working» template
product.minus: The questions assume the user is physically well, employed and goal-driven — erasing disabled and seriously ill people; the emotion set is also too narrow to describe how you really feel.

product.title: The free version cuts you off behind a paywall after just minutes of talking
product.minus: The app advertises 'free unlimited chat', but after a handful of messages or a couple of hours communication is fully blocked by a subscription screen — mid-conversation, even while the AI keeps texting you itself.

product.title: The AI forgets everything you told it, even on the top-tier plan
product.minus: The headline promise — 'remembers everything' — fails: the companion loses memory within hours or days, doesn't recognize the user, and mixes old conversations with new ones. Even Max/Platinum/Ultra subscribers complain.

product.title: Only an $80–100 annual plan, no monthly tier — scares people off at the door
product.minus: The only option is a $70–100 annual plan paid up front; there's no cheap monthly or weekly tier to try it out. Many would happily pay monthly but walk away rather than hand over the full sum blind.
