product.minus: The attempt to "motivate" with snarky reminders about skipping a workout backfires on people who are injured or taking a planned rest day, and reads as an insult.

product.title: Questionable accuracy: spot-reduction claims and injury risk
product.minus: Careful users flag the lack of scientific correctness — you can't burn fat in one specific region as the app implies; and with no age check, children are doing the workouts and some have already gotten hurt.

product.title: Constantly logs you out — and people miss classes because of it
product.minus: The app drops you out of your account over and over, sometimes weekly, and won't remember your password. Until you log back in, notifications go silent — so people straight-up miss classes or get hit with a late-cancellation fee.

product.title: A March update broke schedule loading — the app became useless
product.minus: After an early-March 2026 update the app stopped loading the schedule and booked classes: endless spinner or "error loading." Booking and cancelling only work through the website, and the support email listed in the Play Store bounces.

product.title: The only fix is reinstalling — and even that doesn't always work
product.minus: The standard "fix" is to delete and reinstall the app, sometimes 3–6 times. Along the way you get "cannot connect to server," class history disappears, and after installing on a new phone the app doesn't recognize your account.

product.title: Notifications only fire if you open the app
product.minus: Push alerts about getting off the waitlist or about a class starting don't arrive until you open the app yourself. And once you finally log in, all the missed notifications dump at once — and the class reminder lands right at class start time.

product.title: No way to search or filter classes by level, type or instructor
product.minus: There's no filter by level (1, 1.5, 2), class name or instructor — you scroll the schedule horizontally day by day by hand. For an app whose whole point is finding the right class, that's a basic feature that stubbornly isn't there.

product.title: Multiple studios don't merge into one view
product.minus: Passport members have their classes and class count split per studio: to see everything you must keep switching studios. People have long asked for one shared calendar and a single class tally across all studios.

product.title: The class and credit counter is unreliable
product.minus: The app fails to count completed classes — sometimes for an entire studio at once for two weeks — and eats credits: it shows "out of credits" when you have them, or quietly removes the ones left. On a goal-and-progress app, this hits its very purpose.

product.title: The app says "booked" while the studio still has you waitlisted
product.minus: The most painful failure: the app says you're booked, you show up — and the front desk still has you on the waitlist. Your credit gets used anyway. People conclude you must book through the studio by phone, not through the app.

product.title: Evening and beginner classes are nearly impossible to get into, and cancelling costs you
product.minus: Popular evening and level-1 classes get booked weeks out, all riding on long waitlists. Switching days is nearly impossible, and cancelling within 24 hours costs a credit or a $20 fee — even with an unlimited membership people can rarely book a class.

product.title: Pricing stings, and cancelling the membership is deliberately hard
product.minus: At ~$250 a month, people are angry about a price hike after three months and hollow "rewards." Cancellation is set up so the app won't let you — it sends you to call, the phone line refuses and pushes you to email, where an undisclosed deadline conveniently went unmentioned.

product.title: The studios, instructors and Pilates itself are what earns forgiveness for the rest
product.plus: Nearly every positive review is about the real-world experience: knowledgeable, attentive instructors, friendly staff, clean studios and variety across every level. People explicitly separate "the studio is amazing" from "the app is awful."

product.title: The low-impact training genuinely relieves pain and restores movement
product.plus: The strongest reason people stay is the bodily result: back, knee and hip pain fade while strength, balance and flexibility grow. People with chronic illness, disc and stenosis issues, before and after surgery, describe Pilates as what made movement possible again.

product.title: When the app does work, booking and calendar sync are genuinely handy
product.plus: For some users it just works: booking is simple, classes sync straight to Google Calendar, and you can set goals and track activity. These reviews matter as a contrast — the app has potential; it's reliability, not the concept, that fails it.

product.title: After the intro class, a barrage of calls and texts begins
product.minus: The free intro class wins people over, but then aggressive outreach kicks in: 3–5 calls and texts every day. It puts people off enough to block the number and delete the app — even though they genuinely wanted to stay.

product.title: The "show less" and block-source buttons do nothing
product.minus: People spend years tapping "show fewer like this" on sports or obituaries, and the feed stays packed with the exact same topics. The personalization buttons act like an illusion of control: feedback goes nowhere, and it's the top reason for uninstalling.

product.title: Paywalls turn half the feed into unreadable links
product.minus: Clicking a headline too often lands you on some outlet's subscription page. Users don't want to sign up for a dozen subscriptions and treat these articles as clickbait rather than news.

product.title: Ads cover up the article itself
product.minus: Banners pop up, shift around, and cover most of the screen, video ads sit between paragraphs, and cookie prompts pile on top. The ads physically get in the way of reading.

product.title: The feed goes stale: stories linger for days and ancient ones resurface
product.minus: The same stories from the same sources stick around for 24-36 hours, and then a piece that's two months — or even a decade — old suddenly shows up. There's no sort-by-date, and trust in the "news" erodes.

product.title: The Share button has been broken for weeks
product.minus: Inside an article the Share icon simply does nothing, and it's been that way for weeks across different Android phones. Clearing cache and reinstalling don't help — users read it as the app being neglected.

product.title: Forced AI summaries replace access to the actual article and source
product.minus: A notification now opens an AI summary or a made-up query instead of the article, and audio mode swaps the NPR or Reuters feed for an AI voice with no way to turn it off. Users feel they're being herded into Google's AI metrics.

product.title: Articles stop loading partway down the feed
product.minus: Partway through the feed stories just stop opening, the local tab sits empty for days, and the app freezes, overheats the phone, and constantly asks to "retry." Basic reliability fails.

product.title: Lag and stutter while scrolling after the update
product.minus: Since the last update the feed stutters on plain scrolling across several devices at once — force-closing and clearing cache don't fix it. It's the update itself, not the phone's settings.

product.title: A handy aggregator of local and global news in one place
product.plus: The core value users love: a quick overview of every major event — from town to country to the world — without manually checking a dozen sites. For busy people it's the perfect morning briefing.

product.title: When the algorithm gets it right, the feed feels personal
product.plus: A chunk of users praise exactly the personalization: the app guesses topics from their interests and searches, and the feed feels tailored to them. It's the side of the algorithm people love — the opposite of the ignored-preferences complaint.

product.title: Clean, simple interface and trust in the source mix
product.plus: Loyal users single out the tidy, easy-to-read design, smooth navigation, and a broad set of trusted sources — it's why they trust it as their daily entry point to the news.

product.title: The AI audio briefing is liked, but users want it less US-centric
product.plus: The AI-voiced audio briefing is a standout favorite: people praise the convenience of "listening to the news" and the clean voices. The main ask is to add content from around the world, not just the US.

product.title: The content feeds the mind and soul — that's what people love
product.plus: The main driver of five-star reviews isn't the app but what's inside it: deep, well-researched articles that readers say change how they see the world and give them knowledge they don't get from other apps' endless scroll.

product.title: A calm haven without toxicity and mindless scrolling
product.plus: Users value the vibe: peaceful, free of hate and the stupid trends of other platforms, a place for heart-to-heart talk with like-minded people — many literally call it «home» and contrast it with Twitter and Instagram.

product.title: The article editor loses text and shoves you to the website
product.minus: The number-one writer pain: drafts fail to save, a version-conflict pops up, another app steals focus — and the words vanish «into a black hole». Some are forced to write in MS Word first and then paste it in.

product.title: Accounts get suspended instantly, and the appeal link is dead
product.minus: The most painful scenario: newcomers get suspended within hours or days with no reason given, and the in-app appeal link doesn't work — leaving people stuck waiting on an automated backend to respond.

product.title: You can't edit posts or settings — only via the browser
product.minus: Core author actions are stripped out: you can't edit a published post, change settings and subscriptions, or take out a paid subscription — for all of it the app sends you to the website, which users call unacceptable.

product.title: Notifications can't be fully turned off
product.minus: Users beg for a way to fully disable all notifications and reminders, but alerts keep arriving even from muted accounts — for some that was reason enough to uninstall.

product.title: The app just won't open and crashes
product.minus: For a chunk of users the app simply won't launch: it opens and immediately bounces back to the phone's home screen, despite reinstalling and trying everything.

product.title: Dark patterns: articles get cut off until you download the app
product.minus: The web funnel grates: you're shown half an article, then asked for email, then pushed to download the app even on desktop, and the app then demands a phone number — users call these dark patterns and dock stars.

product.title: The feed and algorithm ignore the user's choices
product.minus: The feed misbehaves: posts don't come in chronological order, important stuff gets missed, and the «show fewer notes like this» command is ignored — the same authors reappear on every refresh.

product.title: Buggy video and audio playback
product.minus: Media playback has long been broken: the video player barely works and only gets worse over time, the listening queue builds backwards, and text posts somehow keep the screen from timing out.

product.title: The best platform for writers and readers alike
product.plus: For many it's a «home» for self-expression: easy to publish thoughts, poems and stories while also reading others — people call it the best platform both for authors and for those who love to read.

product.title: The platform skips the small navigation and reading details
product.minus: For all the love of the content, the basic UX is raw: no index in long articles, no «go to top» button, no remembering your search; you can't highlight text, note comments don't work, and the interface confuses newcomers.

product.title: Scrolling reads a touch as a swipe and throws you out of the article
product.minus: A hypersensitive gesture: trying to scroll an article makes the screen slide left or right, loses your place and dumps you back to the feed. It reproduces on Pixel, Samsung and Motorola, so the fault is the app's, not the device's.

product.title: Ads open from an accidental touch while scrolling
product.minus: Ads are staggered throughout the article and trigger not on a tap but on a light touch while scrolling — a new ad screen opens and reading is interrupted. There are even audio spots that start playing on their own.

product.title: Ads stay even after paying for the ad-free subscription
product.minus: People buy the ad-free tier and the ads simply don't go away — down to Amazon redirects when tapping an article. The paid access also randomly resets itself to limited even while signed in.

product.title: The endless «Do you like the app?» pop-up drags the rating down
product.minus: The app asks several times a day whether you like it and begs for a review — even after one was already left. Many users give it one star specifically for this nagging.

product.title: The app demands you enable notifications or it won't open
product.minus: Just to read articles you are forced into settings to allow notifications; without that the app blocks you. The notifications themselves then come constantly all day.

product.title: Billing: charges after cancellation and no refunds
product.minus: A $1 trial turns into a $9.99 charge, cancelling doesn't stop the billing, and support refuses refunds even days after the charge and never sends renewal reminders.

product.title: Signing into a paid account is impossible — the button does nothing
product.minus: A paid subscription is useless because the «Sign in» link won't open from the home page or settings; the only link that works is the one to buy a subscription. Support's fix is to just use the website instead.

product.title: Articles won't load, paragraphs duplicate, cut off at «developing story»
product.minus: After recent updates articles hang on loading, duplicate paragraphs (looks like AI editing) and cut off after the first line with a «developing story» notice, while feeds throw a connection error on a working network.

product.title: After reading a story the feed jumps back to the very top
product.minus: Exit an article and the feed resets to the top story, forcing you to scroll all the way down again to find your place. Swiping back also fails to return you to where you were in the stack.

product.title: Bloated footprint: gigabytes of storage just to «read the paper»
product.minus: Users discover the app silently eats several — sometimes tens — of gigabytes, while the 256 MB install itself is several times heavier than rivals (~70 MB).

product.title: Even-handed, unbiased reporting is the core reason for loyalty
product.plus: Long-time readers value the app precisely for neutral, fact-based coverage without a partisan slant: for many it's the one source they trust, and they openly contrast it with «biased» rivals.

product.title: Clean, easy interface with concise, to-the-point summaries
product.plus: Those who like it praise the tidy navigation, fast clean layout and condensed summaries of the top stories with good photos and galleries — the feed is easily customised to the topics you care about.

product.title: Five local papers and topic variety at a reasonable yearly price
product.plus: Subscribers highlight the strong breadth: national news plus up to five local papers, sports, weather, puzzles and human-interest pieces — all in one app at a manageable yearly price.

product.title: They love the content and hate the app — two separate ratings
product.minus: Over and over subscribers give the journalism 5 stars and the app 1 star in the same review. The content keeps them for years, but the tech tears down loyalty — people say outright the brand's reputation has been tarnished by the app itself.

product.title: The world's best balanced journalism, without sensationalism
product.plus: The core magnet is balanced, deep, unbiased analysis on global topics. People have read it for 30-40 years, trust it like no other source, and feel it makes them smarter rather than dumber.

product.title: The audio player and queue management are the main technical pain
product.minus: For those who listen to articles, the player is a disaster: it forgets your place, replays things you've already heard, you can't clear or edit the queue, and after a week's worth it auto-dumps the next issue in with no way to remove items. The old «build queue» was removed and people threaten to cancel.

product.title: A forced update breaks the app on old but working devices
product.minus: The new version demands an update, but the update is incompatible with Android 9, older Samsungs, Chromebooks, tablets. The subscriber pays but can't open the app: an endless «update» screen that leads nowhere (and sometimes to the Apple App Store instead of Google Play).

product.title: Ads inside a paid subscription — an insult you can't turn off
product.minus: People pay hundreds a year and still get animated, sometimes strobing video ads right inside article text. There's no option to turn them off, and it directly ruins the reading experience — a frequent reason for downgrades.

product.title: The app is slow, freezes and crashes on launch
product.minus: Opening an article takes minutes even over Wi-Fi, the interface lags, and on various Pixels and Galaxies the app simply crashes on startup. People's only workaround is to switch to airplane mode or move to the browser.

product.title: Offline download is promised but doesn't work without internet
product.minus: The main reason to install the app is to read and listen on a plane or off-grid. But the downloaded issue never truly downloads: an endless «Downloading» status, failed loads, or content that won't open offline exactly when you have no network.

product.title: Cancelling is deliberately hard — people call it a scam
product.minus: There's no «cancel subscription» button in the app or on the site; to leave you must battle a chatbot for half an hour or call. Add the refund finger-pointing between Economist and Google Play, and trust collapses into words like «scam» and «fraudulent».

product.title: Login breaks even for active subscribers
product.minus: You've paid, but the app treats you as a non-subscriber: endless password resets, one-time emails that never arrive, a blank login page after an update. Support sends you in circles and access to the expensive content simply won't open.

product.title: Zero integration with Android Auto and smart home
product.minus: Those who listen while driving are furious: no Android Auto, car and earbud buttons rewind to the start of an article instead of skipping ±15 seconds, audio plays over navigation instead of pausing, no casting to a speaker. Every podcast app solved this long ago.

product.title: «Insider» video and AI narration annoy rather than please
product.minus: Intrusive auto-playing Insider video with a stuck-controls bug, and an AI voice that butchers names and sounds mechanical. Subscribers want to read in peace and hear human narrators, not an Instagram-style reel and robots.

product.title: A glutton for battery, storage and data
product.minus: The app drains the battery in a day (up to 60% of usage even when idle), eats over a gigabyte of storage, and aggressively leaks data to trackers — for some, DDG blocks over 1500 tracking attempts in the first hour.

product.title: When they fix it, people notice: after big updates the app genuinely revived
product.plus: It's not all bleak: after the 2025 updates many raised their rating — the app got faster, articles auto-bookmark, navigation is easier, a sleep timer appeared. People say outright that their feedback was heard and the wait was worth it.

product.title: The price stings, and AI-analysis rivals are closing in
product.minus: The subscription is expensive, prices keep rising, and given the app quality people start comparing it to the FT and even AI tools like SuperGrok that, for the same money, assemble analysis from many sources on demand. That's a real churn risk.

product.title: Readers love the journalism, hate the app
product.plus: The content is the near-unanimous praise: thoughtful, deep, beautifully written essays and reporting that readers trust as a source.

product.title: Ads bombard paying subscribers
product.minus: Despite an expensive subscription, articles are stuffed with ads — between paragraphs, full-page McDonald's banners, autoplay videos — with no way to turn them off.

product.title: Notifications open the wrong article
product.minus: Tapping a push notification either does nothing or opens a previously read article or the home screen — and the intended one then can't be found, even by search.

product.title: Profile button hides behind the Android status bar
product.minus: After an update the UI stretches under Android's system bars: the account icon sits behind the status bar and is unclickable, locking Pixel and Galaxy users out of their profile and saved articles.

product.title: Subscribed, but no access
product.minus: The app refuses to recognize a paid subscription: opening an article prompts you to subscribe or re-enter your password again, even though the same account works on the website and iOS.

product.title: Audio is its own disaster
product.minus: The audio player lags and freezes, won't play with the screen off, restarts after a pause, and runs a two-minute podcast ad before the AI narration.

product.title: Freezing, crashing and constant logouts
product.minus: The app is fundamentally glitchy: it freezes, crashes on launch after updates, flickers on touch, and keeps logging you out and refusing to recognize you on re-login.

product.title: Search can't find even an exact title
product.minus: Search barely works: an exact title returns nothing, an author query pulls up other authors, and recent articles from the website simply aren't available in the app.

product.title: Nagging for notification permissions
product.minus: After an update the app throws a popup begging to enable notifications the user deliberately turned off — every single launch — and often won't load until you dismiss it.

product.title: It remembers where you left off — and readers love it
product.plus: When it works, the app scrolls back to exactly where the reader stopped, even days later — a rarity among apps that gets singled out for praise.

product.title: Sharing an article is nearly impossible
product.minus: There's no plain share button: gifting an article means opening a browser and logging in again, even though easy sharing is exactly what would bring in new subscribers.

product.title: Support doesn't respond
product.minus: The Atlantic's support goes unanswered for weeks by email, phone or chat — leaving subscribers with double charges and no access to content.

product.title: A creeping paywall: what was free for years is now "subscribers only"
product.minus: The number-one complaint and the reason for mass uninstalls: more and more articles are locked behind a paid subscription while the app is billed as free. People tap an article, hit a pay demand, then just Google the same story or leave for ABC, NPR, AP.

product.title: Video auto-plays and follows you as you scroll — you can't just read
product.minus: After an update, opening and scrolling triggers auto-play video (often with sound) that takes "12 clicks" to close or won't close at all, blocking the story. For people who came specifically to READ the news, it's infuriating and drives them out.

product.title: Ads disguised as news, and clickbait widgets at the end of articles
product.minus: Ads have grown bigger than the stories, shift content as they load, flicker and reset the scroll; each article ends with cheap clickbait blocks "on par with online games" and dubious AI ads, some of which readers consider scams.

product.title: No dark mode — a basic accessibility feature still missing in 2025
product.minus: The app stubbornly refuses to add a dark mode or respect the device's system theme. For people with light sensitivity, cataracts and vision problems the white background is painful, and that alone becomes a reason not to use it.

product.title: Notifications can't be tuned — you get everything, including subscription ads
product.minus: There's no granular control: it's all notifications or none. Pushes arrive for sports you don't care about and — most maddening — for "subscribers only" content you can't open anyway without paying, which reads as ads dressed up as news.

product.title: The redesign stripped out local news and the familiar sections
product.minus: The new format took away what people valued: local news from their NBC affiliate and sections like science, sports, LGBTQ. The feed is no longer customizable, articles repeat, and the familiar quick evening rundown is gone.

product.title: Freezes, crashes, white screens — it's become heavy and slow
product.minus: Post-update the app barely loads the home page, freezes when opening a story, regularly shows a white screen and a "blue circle," hangs on splash screens and drains battery and phone resources. It used to open instantly — now it's nearly unusable.

product.title: The share button is gone — you can't send a story to friends anymore
product.minus: Longtime users noticed sharing is gone: the share button was removed or swapped for a "subscribe" button, especially on political stories. For people used to forwarding news to family, this became a reason to switch back to the browser.

product.title: The "live" stream cuts out and is forced on you, with no clear schedule
product.minus: Live video is forced on users, yet the "live" turns out to be the previous night's playback, cuts out to "we will be right back," runs commercial breaks and has no clear schedule. The beloved Nightly News got hard to find, and hosts' audio feeds were removed.

product.title: When it behaves, it's clean, fast reading of factual news
product.plus: The loyal core praises exactly what they came for: a clean, tidy format, readable real articles (not all video), timely accurate news and easy navigation. Many have trusted NBC as a source for decades.

product.title: Free, paywall-free access — the headline argument over CNN
product.plus: For a slice of the audience the decisive virtue is that the app is free and doesn't force a subscription to finish an article (unlike CNN). These users aren't nagged for money, and they give five stars precisely for that.

product.title: A window into the US for overseas readers — follow the world from anywhere
product.plus: A distinct grateful audience is readers outside the US: the app gives a clear picture of what's happening in America and the world from anywhere, an understandable presentation and breaking alerts. For them it's a handy, authoritative way to stay informed.

product.title: Content moved behind a paywall, and that killed the app for longtime users
product.minus: The dominant, near-universal complaint: what people read free for years now demands a subscription. Once the free-article limit hits, access shuts off, and users delete in droves for AP, BBC, Reuters and other free sources. What stings most is that the same content is freely available on the website and in a browser.

product.title: "I already pay CNN through cable" — double-billing for the same content
product.minus: A distinct grievance from people already paying for CNN via cable, YouTube TV, DirecTV or Xfinity: the app still asks them to buy a separate subscription. Signing in through a TV provider often doesn't unlock content, and some material demands yet another subscription on top.

product.title: You pay and still get hit with ads — and there are too many
product.minus: Ads enrage even paying subscribers: spots run during live broadcasts, and a ratio like "5 minutes of news then 15 minutes of ads" reads as a con. The same commercial repeats three or four times in a row. People cancel specifically over ads on a paid plan.

product.title: The app won't open: an endless CNN splash screen on launch
product.minus: A steady technical failure: after an update the app hangs on the red splash screen with the logo and never loads. Reinstalling, clearing cache and rebooting don't help. It fails especially often on newer Samsung S25/Galaxy devices and after One UI / Android updates.

product.title: Slow startup: 20+ seconds on the splash screen until you give up
product.minus: Even when it does eventually open, startup is painfully slow — the CNN logo sits there for 20 seconds or more. Content loads with a visible lag while ads appear instantly. People close the app before the news ever arrives.

product.title: You bought the subscription — the app "forgets" it and demands payment again
product.minus: A systemic billing breakdown: a paid subscription isn't recognized, and the app asks users to log in or subscribe again several times a day. They have to clear data and restart to get the account acknowledged. Some can't log in or re-subscribe at all — money is charged, access isn't granted.

product.title: Video is broken: black screen, audio-only, or out of sync
product.minus: Video is a weak spot: clips either won't play at all, show a black screen with audio only, or run with audio badly out of sync with the picture. For some, audio keeps playing even after they close it. For an app selling live streams, that's critical.

product.title: Aggressive Amazon/AliExpress banners jump to another app on any touch
product.minus: Huge Amazon and AliExpress ad banners fire not on a click but on any touch — even an attempt to scroll. The user gets thrown into another app and has to hit back several times to return. People flatly call it bad programming or deliberate manipulation of the touch event.

product.title: Disguised ads-as-news erode trust in the source
product.minus: For a news brand this hurts especially: the feed mixes ads, comments and editorial so heavily you can't tell a story from an advertisement. Blatant scam "hacks" (like a miracle Vicks trick) show up presented as CNN content. People uninstall precisely over this blurring of lines.

product.title: Fast, accurate breaking-news alerts — the reason people keep it
product.plus: When it works, the core value is lightning-fast, accurate alerts on major events. Many praise the speed of delivery and the global reach of on-the-ground correspondents, keeping CNN as their go-to source during natural disasters and world conflicts.

product.title: Clean, easy interface paired with strong reporting
product.plus: Satisfied users single out a clean, intuitive interface: headlines across politics, tech and world news are easy to scan at a glance, navigation is simple, and articles load fast. Combined with a reputation as a reliable, fact-checked source, it makes CNN a handy daily app.

product.title: No casting and no Google/Samsung TV app — a pain for paying users
product.minus: Paying subscribers miss the basics — a native cast-to-TV icon; instead they have to mirror the whole phone screen. There's no Google TV app, and on Samsung TV things either don't work or quietly require a TV provider, which you discover only after paying. The advertised "All Access" turns out to be not what they expected.

product.title: Login and TV-provider sign-in are broken, and cancelling is a chore
product.minus: Authentication fails at every step: the app stops keeping you logged in (so alerts stop), lies about a "connection issue" at sign-in, and your TV provider isn't in the list (COGECO and others). The subscription-help section returns "Access Denied," and people call cancelling extremely hard — even reporting years of unauthorized charges.

product.title: Alerts arrive ungrouped and off-topic (sports instead of breaking news)
product.minus: Notifications irritate on two fronts: they arrive as separate items instead of one grouped "CNN" stack, and they're off-topic — sports alerts to people who never signed up for them, instead of the major events they asked for. On top of that, subscriber-only content alerts go to non-subscribers.

product.title: Ads catch accidental taps while scrolling and fling you to third-party sites
product.minus: Full-screen banners register a scroll as a tap: people open Amazon, Walmart and other apps dozens of times just by swiping past them. Many call it borderline ad fraud and uninstall.

product.title: Mandatory cross-app tracking consent with no opt-out drives away longtime readers
product.minus: A recent update demands you allow tracking of your activity across other apps and sites: the only way in is to tap Accept, with no way to decline. For a reputable news agency this feels like a betrayal, and users of a decade uninstall in droves.

product.title: Endless 'update required' loop for an update that isn't in the Play Store
product.minus: The app locks behind an 'Update Required' popup, yet Google Play offers no update — only 'Open'. Reinstalling, clearing cache and rebooting don't help, and readers lose access to the news entirely.

product.title: Going back from an article dumps you at the very top of the feed
product.minus: After reading an article and pressing Back, you land not where you left off but at the top of the list, forced to scroll all the way down again each time. Many suspect it's done to force extra ad views.

product.title: Freezes and crashes mid-article, especially once a banner ad loads
product.minus: Articles stop scrolling, the screen goes black, the app crashes — often right as an ad banner loads. The same article opens instantly in a browser on the same phone.

product.title: Broken screenshots: a pushy 'Share' modal hijacks the capture
product.minus: Trying to take a screenshot, the whole screen is covered by a modal nagging you to share a link, making it impossible to save a paragraph or snippet. It pushes some users back to reading AP in a browser.

product.title: No real search or topic filter — unwanted sports notifications keep coming
product.minus: Search is essentially useless, and sports notifications keep arriving even after those sections are removed from preferences. There's little real control over what's pushed or shown.

product.title: Tapping a push notification opens the wrong article
product.minus: Tapping a headline notification opens the index of all stories or an unrelated piece, and the actual headline then has to be hunted down by hand. It's especially reliable at breaking when the app is already open.

product.title: Oversized, uncontrollable font makes articles unreadable
product.minus: Text sometimes balloons so that three or four lines fill the whole screen, and the font-size setting either doesn't help or resets on restart. Other times it flips to a tiny, computer-screen size.

product.title: Feed buried under sections and videos — fresh news hidden at the bottom
product.minus: Getting to the latest news means scrolling past photos, playlists, 'today in history' and most-watched videos. Many just want to read rather than watch, and the feed barely refreshes.

product.title: A reputation for unbiased, fact-based reporting is the main reason to stay
product.plus: Readers praise AP again and again as one of the few honest, well-sourced outlets left, with no left or right slant — a certified fact-checker they can trust every day. The journalism is what keeps even the frustrated around.

product.title: Developers fix breakages fast and respond to feedback
product.plus: When the update loop broke en masse, many users had a working app again within hours or a day and raised their rating back to five stars. The support responsiveness is explicitly cited as a reason to stay.

product.title: Free, no subscriptions, no paywall
product.plus: Against paywalls at rivals like the Guardian and Washington Post, readers value that AP delivers quality news for free with no subscriptions, opening access to people at any income level.

product.title: Reliable breaking-news push notifications keep you informed
product.plus: Some users grant AP the notification privilege they rarely give any app, because the breaking-news alerts are timely, relevant and high-quality — a grounding force through the day.

product.title: Watchlists keep emptying out — the core feature broke after updates
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after updates the watchlists vanish or show "empty" while desktop works fine. Only repeated "sync now", reinstalls, or waiting helps — there's been no lasting fix for months.

product.title: Crashes, freezes, and needs a daily reinstall
product.minus: The app crashes, hangs on the logo and spinning circle, and regularly needs a delete-and-reinstall just to work. The content and data are good, but it's so unstable it becomes unusable.

product.title: Live-stream is a gamble: loads, freezes, and drops
product.minus: People subscribe for CNBC's live feed, but it barely works: endless loading, drops every few minutes, freezing after commercials. It got noticeably worse after the rebrand and spinoff.

product.title: Best source for financial news — that's why people stay
product.plus: Despite everything, the content is the reason people love it: deep, timely, and (to many) unbiased coverage of global markets that's hard to find elsewhere.

product.title: Too much content got locked behind the Pro paywall
product.minus: CNBC was praised precisely for free access, but now articles, news, and the "five things" sit behind a subscription. Even signed-in users hit a CNBC Pro wall and a link to the paywall site.

product.title: Index tiles overlap into unreadable numbers
product.minus: After the redesign, the market-index boxes on the home screen overlay text from the line above, making real-time values unreadable. Some tiles disappear entirely until you restart.

product.title: Endless re-login demands even when already signed in
product.minus: The app logs you out daily, hides content, and asks you to sign in again — and when you try, it asks if you want to log out. Each forced login wipes the watchlists.

product.title: No dark mode — and it hurts the eyes of daily readers
product.minus: One of the most repeated requests: add a dark mode. Other finance apps and even CNBC's own iOS version have had it for ages, while here over 75% of the screen is a white background.

product.title: The redesign and new logo broke what worked
product.minus: Loyal users mourn the old version: tiny fonts, washed-out colors, a design that blends into the background, and the loss of the recognizable peacock. Many openly ask to revert the update.

product.title: Removed historical highs, lows, and multi-year price charts
product.minus: Updates cut investor-critical data: 52-week highs/lows, individual stock histories, and 5- and 10-year price views. Users explicitly ask for them back.

product.title: Slow to load and crawl to navigate — slower than the website
product.minus: Startup takes forever on the logo screen, navigation lags even on fast Wi-Fi, and quotes don't load. An app is supposed to be faster than the browser, yet this one is slower.

product.title: Articles refresh themselves mid-read — you lose your place
product.minus: The app refreshes on every open and resets the article you're reading: step away for work, come back, and it starts over. Rivals like Bloomberg and Google News cache it properly.

product.title: Complaints of bias and clickbait in the reporting
product.minus: Some readers feel the reporting drifts from facts toward opinion and narrative, headlines exaggerate ("DOW slides" on a 0.03% move), and the NBC source adds slant. They just want the facts.

product.title: A sudden paywall on nearly every article is the top reason people uninstall
product.minus: By far the most common complaint: after years of free reading, almost all content went behind a subscription overnight. People who read BBC for 10–16 years describe it as a stab in the back and uninstall on the spot.

product.title: "Publicly funded, yet now charging me": a sense of betrayed public-service mission
product.minus: Readers stress that the BBC is funded by UK fees and taxes, so charging for news feels not merely expensive but a betrayal of the public-broadcaster mission itself — especially painful for Brits living abroad.

product.title: The Android back button exits the app instead of returning to the previous page
product.minus: A persistent navigation bug: the system back button closes the whole app instead of returning to the feed, forcing users to scroll back up to a tiny arrow. Sometimes it logs you out too.

product.title: Ads open by themselves while you scroll — no tap required
product.minus: After a recent update the ad hit-boxes became hyper-sensitive: trying to scroll past a banner registers as a tap and throws you out to Amazon/Expedia. Users call it a potential gateway to malware.

product.title: You paid for a subscription — yet the ads and pre-roll video clips remain
product.minus: Paying users are furious that the subscription doesn't remove ads: articles still carry banners, and a short clip is preceded by a 30-second pre-roll — sometimes an ad for BBC's own podcast already available in the app.

product.title: The app won't open: a white or grey screen and constant crashes
product.minus: A frequent failure to launch: instead of news, a frozen BBC logo or a white/grey screen. Reinstalling and clearing cache don't help; the app crashes on incoming notifications, even on new phones running Android 16.

product.title: A poor replacement for BBC Sounds: glitchy audio, impossible programme search
product.minus: Former BBC Sounds listeners were force-migrated here, and for audio the app feels gutted: streams cut off when you leave the car or lose headphones, programmes are out of date, and finding a specific podcast is nearly impossible.

product.title: The new UI killed customization: gone are "My News", the widget and the sections
product.minus: A redesign chasing a "hip, modern" look stripped out the "My News" section of chosen regions and topics, the home-screen widget and many categories. The feed got simplified, articles feel fewer, and finding what you want is a slog.

product.title: The $50–90/year price stings, especially for seniors and those on a fixed income
product.minus: What repels many isn't the subscription itself but the amount: $9/mo or $49–90/yr costs more than streaming. People on limited incomes, seniors and the disabled ask for a tiered "news-only, no shows" plan — but there isn't one.

product.title: The paywall targets the US/North America — read as "targeting wealthy users"
product.minus: Users noticed the paywall is switched on specifically for heavy readers in the US and North America. Americans who valued BBC as a neutral outside view feel singled out right when a neutral source matters most.

product.title: Videos autoplay with sound and are pushed instead of text
product.minus: Readers complain that opening an article autoplays video with sound and there's no way to stop it; content is reshaped around video, and in the US the clips often fail to play at all.

product.title: Despite everything, still the best source of neutral, fact-based world news
product.plus: Those who stay value BBC as the closest thing to neutral English-language news in a polarized landscape: trustworthy reporting from conflict zones, broad coverage of culture, history and sport. For many it's the first app they open each morning.

product.title: Ads and pop-ups shove themselves over kids' photos every time you open the app
product.minus: The number-one pain: instead of the photo feed, users are met with a string of full-screen ad windows they have to dismiss one after another. Many report closing 3-5 pop-ups just to see a picture, and banner ads now sitting right on top of their children's photos.

product.title: The ideal way to share kids' photos with relatives while skipping social media
product.plus: What people love most: one album where parents post photos and the whole family — grandparents, relatives abroad — sees them instantly, without messaging each person and without posting publicly. For many it's the only way to avoid putting their kids online.

product.title: An app sold on privacy now hands children's data to advertisers and AI
product.minus: The core selling point — privacy — is seen as betrayed: complaints about data sold to advertisers, a rewritten policy full of loopholes, and an AI-company integration. It stings harder because it's children's photos, the very thing people came here to keep off social media.

product.title: Endless crashes and a 'this app has a bug' message force reinstall after reinstall
product.minus: For a chunk of users the app simply won't open: it crashes on launch with a message about a bug the developers supposedly need to fix. Only uninstall-and-reinstall helps — and only briefly, before the bug returns. It's especially bad once multiple users join an album.

product.title: Automatic date-sorting that keeps years of photos in order with zero effort
product.plus: A strength that keeps even the frustrated around: photos auto-sort by date, duplicates are hidden, and you can scroll back to see how little the kids once were. People keep 6-8 years of pictures organized in one place this way.

product.title: Once-free features migrate behind a paywall — the video limit got cut from 3 to 2 minutes
product.minus: Loyal users feel cheated: things that were free for years slowly become premium. The cut to video length and child-filtering locked behind a subscription rankle most. It reads as service decay, not honest evolution.

product.title: Free monthly prints and photo books that people genuinely love
product.plus: A perk often named as a favorite: 11 free prints a month for the price of postage, plus quality photo books, calendars and albums. For many it turns the app into a way to build physical keepsakes of their kids.

product.title: Spam notifications won't turn off even after you change the settings
product.minus: A separate nuisance is the push spam: marketing notifications and requests to enable notifications come back even after you turn them off. People report having to walk relatives through disabling the spam when inviting them.

product.title: Admins can kick each other out of an album — and support won't restore access to your own photos
product.minus: A frightening flaw in access control: another admin can remove you from your own album, and support says it can't do anything. People risk permanently losing years of their kids' photos, including when an account owner switches phones.

product.title: Rigid onboarding rejects anyone without a baby — no pets, no general photos
product.minus: Getting started is tied to baby photos: the app won't let you begin without a baby and won't get past the first page for people who wanted to store pet or general family photos. Some users bounce before they ever begin.

product.title: Support is nearly absent: no contact to be found, and replies can take a month
product.minus: When something breaks, help is hard to get: users can't find a way to contact support in the app, support emails bounce, and a reply by email reportedly can take up to a month. It turns any problem into a dead end.

product.title: No separate albums per child frustrates bigger families
product.minus: A structural limit: the app lets you make only one album, while parents want separate folders per child or for different sides of the family. The automatic child-tagging is also imperfect and offers no manual edits.

product.title: Photos vanish without a trace — the users' core fear
product.minus: The most frequent and most painful complaint: people open the gallery and find their shots gone — sometimes years of accumulated memories. For an app trusted to safeguard memory, this undercuts its entire reason to exist.

product.title: Backup turns itself back on like a zombie — even after you explicitly disable it
product.minus: People turn cloud sync off again and again, yet it's active again next time they open the app. Photos go to the cloud without consent, spread across other accounts, and become unreachable.

product.title: AI on your photos without asking — a privacy breach
product.minus: The new wave of AI features feels forced and unsafe: users are convinced their shots (including their kids') feed generative AI without explicit permission, and the edits can't be undone.

product.title: Storage fills up, then they demand money
product.minus: Seen as a money-grab machine: storage-full notifications, greyed-out inaccessible photos even on a paid plan, and no way to pull shots back to the phone without buying more space.

product.title: Updates break what used to work
product.minus: Constant "improvements" break familiar flows: simple cropping, search, the editor. Many feel that version after version the app gets worse and less intuitive.

product.title: The editor is broken: magic eraser lags, edits won't upload
product.minus: Once-instant tools now require a cloud upload and work intermittently: the eraser hangs for minutes, AI enhance ruins the frame, and edited photos can't even be posted to other apps.

product.title: The "Moved to bin" banner lingers forever and blocks deleting
product.minus: A specific micro-pain many name: the toast after deleting stays for tens of seconds, covers buttons, and stops you deleting shots in a row — and you can't swipe it away.

product.title: Crashes, hangs and lags — even on the latest Pixels
product.minus: Basic stability is shaky: the app closes by itself, hangs on the newest Pixels with hundreds of gigs free, and photos open as grey tiles.

product.title: Backup rescues memories when you switch phones
product.plus: Those it hasn't failed value it for exactly what it promises: lose or replace a phone and all photos, videos and contacts come back on their own once you sign in. That's the app's core promise delivered.

product.title: Word-based photo search and "Memories" — what people love
product.plus: Fans praise the smart search (finding a shot by typing a word that might be in it) and the memories feature that joyfully resurfaces old frames. For many that's the very magic of Google Photos.

product.title: A simple, friendly all-in-one interface
product.plus: Happy users note the app is easy to navigate, fast and responsive, gives everything you need for photos and video in one place — and shows no ads.

product.title: Creative edits are a joy — especially the new "Create"
product.plus: A chunk of the audience gets pure delight from the powerful creative tools: erase an object in the background, turn yourself into a cartoon, build a collage — and show it off to loved ones.

product.title: Backup re-enables itself even after you turn it off
product.minus: Users turn off cloud auto-upload again and again, but the setting silently flips back on the next time they open the app. Photos go to the cloud without consent, sometimes into several linked accounts at once, and the owner loses control over what gets copied where.

product.title: Storage fills up, then it's pay-or-nothing
product.minus: Storage fills up almost instantly, and the only escape the app offers is to buy more space. Deleting old photos to free up memory doesn't always work, and users feel pushed into a paid plan.

product.title: Photos simply vanish
product.minus: The scariest scenario for a gallery: pictures and videos disappear on their own, sometimes over time, sometimes right after an update. People lose years of memories despite being promised safe storage.

product.title: AI is forced on you and quietly grabs your photos
product.minus: The new wave of AI features feels like an intrusion: users are convinced their pictures feed generative models without explicit permission. It stings most when the photos are private — children's photos included.

product.title: Every update breaks what used to work
product.minus: Constant updates shuffle elements around, change menus and the editor UI, and routine actions like cropping turn into a chore. People are worn out from re-finding features and relearning a UI that's been redrawn yet again.

product.title: The editor glitches and the magic tools lag
product.minus: The once-premium editor has gone unstable: cut and erase sometimes don't work, AI enhance crops awkwardly, and Magic Eraser now needs a cloud upload and takes minutes instead of being instant.

product.title: The 'Moved to bin' banner blocks your next action
product.minus: After a delete, a banner offering to undo sticks at the bottom — and you can't swipe it away. It covers the UI for tens of seconds, blocking you from deleting or editing photos in a row. A small thing that infuriates during any bulk cleanup.

product.title: Photo search stopped finding things
product.minus: The signature feature — searching photos by words — broke for some users: queries that used to work now return "nothing found". For people who keep everything in one pile, that strips the app of its main point.

product.title: Too tied to the cloud: useless without internet
product.minus: The app constantly pulls from the cloud: you need internet just to view your own photos, and backed-up shots aren't always visible in the app — you have to go to the browser. There's no real offline mode and no album sort order.

product.title: Crashes, freezes and greyed-out photos you can't open
product.minus: The app closes itself, hangs and crashes even on the latest Pixels with plenty of free space. Some shots show up as grey tiles and just won't open — even for people paying for storage.

product.title: Memories hit home — old photos resurface on their own
product.plus: For the satisfied crowd, the standout is the Memories feature: the app surfaces old shots and screenshots on its own, and it lands emotionally. For many that's the single reason to stay with Google Photos.

product.title: Peace of mind for your photos plus an easy, simple interface
product.plus: Loyal users value that after losing or switching phones, all their photos, contacts and videos come back thanks to backup, and the interface itself is simple and friendly. Searching by a word in the photo feels like real magic that saves space and time.

product.title: Swipe-sorting turns gallery cleanup into a fast, almost enjoyable process
product.plus: The thing users love most is the «swipe up to trash, tap to file» mechanic. People sort thousands of photos in an hour, call it fast, simple and even addictive, and clear out galleries of 18,000–32,000 files.

product.title: Turning a free app into a weekly subscription is the number-one reason users feel betrayed
product.minus: The app was free for years, then locked basic functions behind a weekly subscription (~$52/year). Long-time users feel betrayed: they want a one-time purchase, not a perpetual fee for what used to be free.

product.title: Deleting in the app doesn't remove photos from the gallery — hours wasted
product.minus: The most damaging bug: people spend one to three hours marking hundreds or thousands of photos for deletion, hit the trash — and nothing is actually gone from the gallery. Often only noticed after checking, with all the effort wasted.

product.title: Filing photos into albums, not just deleting them, is a distinct draw
product.plus: Unlike simple «culling» apps, Slidebox lets you file photos into folders and create new albums with a single tap. It's a lifeline for people with ADHD, photographers and shop owners — anyone who needs structure, not just cleanup.

product.title: A forced subscription before the first screen scares people off at the door
product.minus: The app demands money or a post-trial payment agreement before it shows anything at all. The enrollment screen won't dismiss, photos stay locked, and users feel the promised «free» turned out to be a lie.

product.title: No safeguard against an accidental «Back» — one tap erases all the work
product.minus: No confirmation and no autosave: accidentally hit the system «Back» button mid-album and all the work vanishes without warning. People beg for a simple «Are you sure?» prompt.

product.title: A crash on a large deletion batch wipes out hours of work
product.minus: When you mark thousands of photos for deletion, the app freezes or crashes the moment you apply — and the whole selection is lost. Past ~2,000 photos crashes become routine; an autosave history is needed as a safety net.

product.title: Video audio keeps playing after the player is closed
product.minus: A persistent bug: play a video, swipe or exit, and the sound keeps running in the background and overlaps onto the next clips. The only way to stop it is force-closing the app.

product.title: After the update only the camera sorts — old folders and Downloads become inaccessible
product.minus: The old killer feature was sorting every photo from every folder at once. Updates broke it: now only camera and screenshots show, folders like Downloads are gone, and older photos are locked behind a date-based paywall.

product.title: No Google Photos or cloud integration — works only with local storage
product.minus: A big gap for cloud users: the app doesn't see Google Photos and won't sync with it. Deletions and albums stay local-only, and the main backlog living in the cloud stays out of reach.

product.title: The narrow album bar at the bottom is painful when there are dozens of folders
product.minus: The destination folders sit in a narrow scrolling bar at the bottom. With 50+ albums you have to scroll forever to the one you need; people ask for an alphabet index, colors, favorite folders or more slots on screen.

product.title: Charges continue after cancellation, and the cancel button is nowhere to be found
product.minus: Billing feels like a trap: charges continue a month after cancelling, money is taken even without a subscription, and «manage subscription» has no cancel option inside. Support via a broken email address doesn't respond.

product.title: Nagging review prompts after every action grate on users
product.minus: The app begs for a rating after nearly every album created or action taken — even from people who already left one. There's no way to turn it off, and it sours an otherwise pleasant flow.

product.title: Folders under «More» can only be deleted — the move buttons are missing
product.minus: The biggest folders end up under «More», where only delete and share are available and the «move to album» buttons are gone. Sorting — the app's headline feature — simply doesn't work there, which defeats the whole point.

product.title: Charged ₱1,990 for a yearly plan after the trial — with no warning
product.minus: The dominant complaint: people take the 7-day free trial, and after it ₱1,990 (or 140 SAR, $33.99) silently leaves their GCash or card. No separate notice, no confirmation, and many claim it was pulled even from an account they never linked.

product.title: Refunds take weeks of begging, support replies with one canned message
product.minus: After a charge people email every address the developer has — and get either silence or the same automated reply. Google Play denies the refund and points to the developer, who points back. The money was often meant for bills, medicine, or tuition.

product.title: Minute-long ads with no close button that sometimes freeze the app
product.minus: Ads pop up on every action, run for minutes, and for some users have no close button while covering the whole screen. Several say the ads now freeze or brick the app entirely.

product.title: Years-free features moved behind a paywall — veterans feel betrayed
product.minus: People kept the app for 6-15 years across many phones just for a simple grid. Now the basic grid, filters and touch-ups sit behind a subscription, and the old crowd leaves feeling robbed of what was free for years.

product.title: Free output means a watermark you can remove only once
product.minus: The free version stamps its logo onto your photos, and you can remove the watermark only once before paying. Users call it taking credit for someone else's work and uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Core features just break: blank screen, cropping, AI enhance
product.minus: Beyond billing, the product itself breaks for some: video collage shows a grey screen, crop doesn't crop, AI enhance returns the same image, the bottom of the grid gets cut off, and paid AI features throw "no internet" on a working connection.

product.title: Crashes, logs you out and re-asks for a subscription you already paid
product.minus: Paying subscribers report being logged out and asked to subscribe again, crashes when sharing from the gallery, an "out of memory" force-restart, and the AI eraser hanging at 99%.

product.title: Some do get their refund — and then praise support
product.plus: Against the wall of denials there are opposite stories: some users got their money back, by their account handled professionally and fairly, and then bumped the rating to 5 stars.

product.title: For a simple collage or resize — fast, clear, no learning curve
product.plus: People love the core: building a 9-photo grid, resizing for Instagram, stitching a collage — fast, intuitive and exactly as imagined. Many stay for years precisely for that simplicity.

product.title: A rare trick: mixes video with photos in one collage
product.plus: What stands out from other collage apps gets its own praise: you can mix video and photos in one grid, with plenty of layouts and easy editing. For content and thumbnail makers, that's the reason to stay.

product.title: Image quality and toolset — almost "too many" options
product.plus: Those who stay praise the high output quality and rich feature set — sometimes even joking there are too many options. For invitations, quotes and content design they call it professional.

product.title: Killed the monthly plan and lifetime license — leaving only the annual
product.minus: Even willing payers are angered by the pricing structure: the monthly option was removed in favor of annual-only, and some lost a lifetime license they'd already bought. Payers feel the choice was forcibly narrowed.

product.title: After the update the app stopped working properly with Google Photos
product.minus: Books used to come together in minutes straight from Google Photos, but the update broke the sync: an external browser opens, you can't tell which photos are already added, and on some Android devices Google Photos is no longer supported at all. Long-time loyal subscribers are leaving over exactly this.

product.title: Photos won't upload and you have to reinstall the app over and over
product.minus: Photos hang while loading, throw a "couldn't add" error, or simply vanish; to get the 60 photos in for a monthly book, people delete and reinstall the app several times. Uploads have to be babysat by hand — they won't resume on their own if you leave the screen.

product.title: The glitchy app forces you to redo the book three times over
product.minus: The app crashes, doesn't save progress, refreshes the album and loses all your work halfway through. People flatly say they build a single book 3-6 times before it saves correctly and goes to print.

product.title: Books never arrive and tracking doesn't work
product.minus: The site shows "shipped" and even "delivered," but books don't arrive for weeks and months; tracking isn't linked to any carrier and only shows a rough estimate. It hits hardest when someone orders 12 books as a Christmas gift and only three show up.

product.title: Credits expire and the subscription charges sooner than promised
product.minus: Promos like "12 books for $12, no expiry until December 2026" turn into a charge within a month, and accumulated monthly-book credits expire 30 days after you cancel. People experience it as theft: you paid, several months were left, and it all vanished.

product.title: Cancelling the subscription is nearly impossible
product.minus: There's no cancel button to be found in the app, and support loops you through a bot; some had to cancel the charges through their bank instead. Sometimes a one-time purchase is advertised but an auto-subscription gets set up that you can't cancel without phoning the company.

product.title: You can't crop, only zoom — and photos cut off heads
product.minus: The editor only lets you zoom within a fixed frame, with no way to crop off the excess; the result is photos that aren't centered and cut off heads. You can't change text size, font, or color, and cropping became painfully slow after the last update.

product.title: The finished product is adored: small, durable, kids won't put them down
product.plus: Despite the app pain, people love the books themselves: perfect size, durable pages that survive toddlers, great print quality. Kids and grandkids carry them everywhere and look through them again and again — and put up with the glitches for it.

product.title: Support saves the day where the app falls short
product.plus: Time and again people praise the warm, responsive support: it's like chatting with an old friend, and they fix problems fast and willingly. It's the quality of service that keeps many around despite the bugs and rework.

product.title: Priceless for busy moms: get memories out of the phone in a couple of minutes
product.plus: The core value is simplicity: you can assemble a monthly album while rocking the baby or feeding at night, without editing every photo to perfection. People preserve years of memories without the cloud or scrapbooking, and the family awaits each new book like an event.

product.title: The app forces a date on the cover and date-based ordering
product.minus: The book rigidly arranges photos by capture date and prints a month and year on the cover that often can't be edited; to make an event book you have to hunt for an empty "month." Dragging pages and reordering by hand became clumsy after the update.

product.title: It used to pull photos from social media itself — now it's just a printer
product.minus: The original hook — automatically pulling finished, captioned shots from Instagram and Facebook — disappeared without notice. Now the app only reaches the camera roll, and people who came to print Instagram albums have to manually move photos back into the camera roll.

product.title: Dark-pattern ads kick you out of the app mid-browse
product.minus: Full-screen video ads with countdowns and hidden close buttons open the store even when you try to dismiss them, and a slow swipe registers as a click. Many say they have to fully close and reopen the app to continue, with ads firing every 3-4 photos.

product.title: A perfect Android-to-iPhone bridge for family and friends
product.plus: The number-one reason people love it: lets people on different phones see the same photos in one place without social media. Families — especially grandparents off social media — stick around precisely for the cross-platform sharing.

product.title: Built for group events: tours, weddings, reunions
product.plus: Its strongest use case is pooling everyone's photos from a single event into one place. Travel agents, teachers, wedding and reunion organizers love that no one person drowns in collecting every shot and everyone can contribute their own.

product.title: Compresses photos and videos, killing the original quality
product.minus: Some users find HD shots crushed (4MB down to 4KB) and offloaded copies turning lo-res. For anyone who wants to print or work with originals this makes it useless — even though others, notably, praise it for preserving quality.

product.title: No computer or browser access without paying
product.minus: Web access is locked behind a paywall and there's no web uploader at all: photos from a 'proper' camera are a pain to upload, and desktop downloads become a multi-step zip-then-pdf ordeal. Several drop to one star simply because the service requires an app at all.

product.title: Hard caps on photo uploads and video length
product.minus: Videos are cut off at one minute and batch uploads are capped at 40 photos instead of the old hundred — and the limits were tightened even on the paid plan. For people recording loved ones' lives in full, the one-minute ceiling stings most.

product.title: Simple enough even for grandparents
product.plus: A minimalist, intuitive interface is a recurring compliment: uploads are instant, albums are easy to browse, and even relatives in their 80s and 90s manage with no trouble.

product.title: Mass bans with no explanation after a content-policy change
product.minus: After a policy change the app began deleting accounts and all their content, with whole groups of people permanently banned — even those who never posted or left the groups long ago. People lose years of family photos with no explanation given.

product.title: Keeps photos off social media — a private family album
product.plus: Privacy is a big draw: people can share photos of their kids and grandkids without putting them on Facebook or Instagram. It's a closed circle for family and friends, free of influencers and an algorithmic feed.

product.title: Broken sign-in, sign-up and stuck updates lock users out
product.minus: For some, the sign-in and sign-up buttons simply don't respond, and the app demands an update that endlessly 'updates' but never installs. The result is loyal users locked out of their own photos for weeks.

product.title: Preserves quality and metadata while freeing phone storage
product.plus: Despite the compression complaints, a notable share praises the opposite: photos and videos stay crisp, metadata is kept, and phone storage is freed up for new shoots. For many it's a dependable vault for memories.

product.title: Messy sorting and ordering, missing key tools
product.minus: Photos upload and export in a random order rather than by date taken, breaking the timeline; there's no 'select all' for downloads, no album search, and no way to group circles. With hundreds of circles and albums, people get lost and re-sort by hand every time.

product.title: Free and copyright-free is the main reason people stay
product.plus: YouTube and social creators value that the content is genuinely free, with no watermarks and no copyright strikes — the core argument over paid stocks like Getty.

product.title: Downloads regularly fail with an error
product.minus: A frequent complaint: trying to download a photo or video throws an error, files won't download at all or come down corrupted — and it's getting "worse day by day".

product.title: High-quality photos and videos impress
product.plus: Users single out the resolution and aesthetics: "on top of this world", real photos by real people, great material for wallpapers and video editing.

product.title: Slow, laggy and crash-prone
product.minus: Some users complain about constant crashes, stutter when searching and scrolling, and general glitchiness — especially noticeable on certain devices like Galaxy.

product.title: An essential tool for content creators
product.plus: For editors, faceless channels and social media it has become a go-to working tool: easy to find backgrounds, b-roll and clips for specific scenes.

product.title: Simple and easy-to-navigate interface
product.plus: Many note it's easy to navigate and quick to find what you need — a low barrier to entry that beginners in video editing especially appreciate.

product.title: Videos download as images or won't open
product.minus: A painful failure: after spending time downloading, the user ends up with an image instead of a video, or a corrupted file the gallery can't open.

product.title: Video downloads are too slow
product.minus: Video downloads drag on so long that some users lose patience and uninstall, even though they like the content itself.

product.title: Eats mobile data while downloading
product.minus: Even a happy user notices abnormal data usage: 2-3+ GB of traffic spent on videos that weigh under 300 MB altogether.

product.title: Missing basics: dark mode, grid view, password recovery
product.minus: Users ask for obvious things — dark mode, a grid view for browsing — while a broken password reset cost one person access to all of their work.

product.title: Search doesn't always find what you want
product.minus: Sometimes the library falls short on coverage: people can't find the specific topics or figures they installed the app for, and walk away disappointed.

product.title: No ads and no clutter
product.plus: People specifically value the absence of ads and "junk" — a favorable contrast with rivals like Zedge that keeps the experience clean.

product.title: Full-screen ad the moment you open the app
product.minus: Ads hit users before they do anything: people describe a full-screen video right on launch and endless impressions they have to push through just to reach the editing.

product.title: Watermark and paywalled basic actions
product.minus: Edited photos keep a watermark, and removing it or adding a photo right away forces you to watch an ad — people say they'd gladly pay a small ad-free fee, but no real option exists.

product.title: Sky replacement has become less realistic
product.minus: Longtime users complain the new sky now lays a faded layer over the old one instead of replacing it fully, covers objects, and doesn't match the picture — the very feature they installed it for has degraded.

product.title: Sky replacement is the magic people come for
product.plus: When the sky lands well, the effect transforms the whole shot: users love how a single sky swap changes the mood of a photo, especially fans of cloud pictures.

product.title: Soft, warm filter colors
product.plus: The filters deliver soft, beautiful tones: people say the app makes gloomy shots feel as warm as they actually felt, and praise the color palette itself.

product.title: Simple and easy for everyone
product.plus: The interface is praised for being friendly and minimal: people note its smoothness, sensible simple controls, and that anyone can figure it out.

product.title: Consistent result over many years
product.plus: Review veterans come back after 4-5 years and say the app works as well as it did before, in places even better — rare loyalty for a photo editor.

product.title: Missing a video mode
product.minus: Fans repeatedly ask for video editing: they love the filters, but the lack of a video mode feels like the main missing piece.

product.title: Objects get outlined, looking unnatural
product.minus: Even happy users notice that object edges come out with artificial outlines and the result sometimes looks not quite realistic enough — you can tell it's AI.

product.title: Photos don't save, and no zoom/autofocus
product.minus: Beyond filters, functional gaps surface: complaints that the app doesn't save photos, has no zoom, and that without holding perfectly still shots come out blurry due to weak autofocus.

product.title: Already-hidden photos get suddenly locked behind a paid subscription
product.minus: People keep their photos in the vault for years, then one day the app declares "premium expired" and demands payment just to open their OWN files. This isn't "selling a feature" — it's holding already-trusted data hostage.

product.title: The "switch to basic" button doesn't work — there's no way out
product.minus: They nominally offer a "basic mode", but the button is either dead or simply absent. So you can't decline the paid plan and take your photos — the only path to your own data runs through the payment screen.

product.title: Photos and videos vanish on their own — especially after an update
product.minus: Again and again people open the vault and find it empty: thousands of photos, gym-progress videos, wedding pictures — all gone on their own, with no warning and no way to recover. Several outright warn: don't update the app, it deletes everything.

product.title: Forget the password and you're locked out: there's no recovery
product.minus: The most common trouble after the paywall is a forgotten PIN/password with no working reset. No email is linked, no recovery option, just a running timer. People plead in the reviews because there's nowhere else to turn.

product.title: The calculator disguise locks the owner out of their own vault
product.minus: The fake-calculator trick backfires: set it up and you can't get back in, and on one device enabling it wiped all the photos outright. Protection from strangers turns into protection from yourself.

product.title: Money is charged without consent and never refunded
product.minus: Billing behaves aggressively: charged for a trial, charged for a yearly plan twice, money pulled twice over — and refund requests get met with endless screenshot demands or plain silence.

product.title: Support goes silent once the data is already lost
product.minus: At the exact moment photos are gone or money is taken, people need a real reply — and there isn't one. Emails go unanswered, follow-ups are ignored, and a store review becomes the only channel left.

product.title: Free at first — the charge only appears after you've loaded your photos
product.minus: The scheme feels like a trap by design: download free, hide your photos, and after 30 days or right after you set a password the demand to pay arrives. People call it outright fraud and blackmail, because the timing is chosen so you can no longer walk away.

product.title: Videos won't play, and files can't be moved to an SD card
product.minus: Even setting money aside, there are basic technical failures: videos throw an error on play, photo loading fails on full signal, and the whole vault is stuck in internal storage with no SD-card move — and has been for years.

product.title: When it works, it's a beloved, simple vault for private stuff
product.plus: Those who haven't been burned genuinely love it: simple, convenient, the password prompt comes up right at launch, personal photos and videos behind a solid lock. Many keep it for 3-4 years as their main private album.

product.title: The encryption turned out less private than promised
product.minus: For an app whose entire value is privacy, the heaviest accusation: a user claims the developer can access "encrypted" photos and decrypted them. True or not, the mere existence of that doubt undermines the whole point of a vault.

product.title: Ads have flooded an app that used to be clean
product.minus: On top of the paywall, long-time users note the app has become ad-ridden. They liked the old version, while the current one feels like a different, greedier product.

product.title: You can't peek inside without a card and a subscription
product.minus: Right after install the app collects your email and full name, then slams you into a payment screen — no demo, no look at the interface, not a single session without a card on file. People delete it within minutes.

product.title: Silent annual auto-renewal with zero warning
product.minus: After the trial the app defaults to a full annual charge ($180-225) with no reminder email and no receipt. Many only discover it from a bank statement months later.

product.title: Cancellations ignored, refunds refused
product.minus: People cancel the same day and still get charged; support hides behind a "no refunds" policy even at zero usage. Some report charges after cancelling and end up disputing with their bank.

product.title: Since the Pliability rebrand the app constantly crashes
