product.minus: Full-screen autoplay videos and pop-ups fire on every tap, pause the radar and force a 1–2 minute wait before you can even see the forecast — for many it "makes it impossible to use".

product.title: The forecast and rain chances are often flatly wrong
product.minus: People stand in a downpour while the app shows 0% rain or "partly cloudy", and the temperature is off by several degrees — the inaccuracy breaks trust and ruins plans.

product.title: Pre-installed bloatware that can't be uninstalled
product.minus: The app ships baked into the firmware (Motorola, Google, etc.), can only be "disabled" not removed, and some say it reinstalls itself and keeps sending notifications even when disabled.

product.title: The radar only shows the past, never the future
product.minus: After a redesign the radar loops the past ~4 hours with no future motion, the resolution dropped and the timeline is off — pushing users to check the web or TV instead.

product.title: A forced news feed shoved in front of the weather
product.minus: On open the app greets you with a news feed and AI articles you must dig through to reach the forecast; people plainly ask for "just the weather, no news" and threaten to leave.

product.title: Paid for ad-free — the ads came back anyway
product.minus: Buyers of lifetime premium say the developer switched to a subscription, brought ads back and ignores support emails — felt as a bait-and-switch and a "scam company".

product.title: Nagging notifications and irrelevant alerts
product.minus: The app fires several notifications a day (including nags to re-enable it), and wildfire or hurricane alerts arrive from thousands of kilometers away — with no way to dismiss or mute them.

product.title: Widgets and the status bar glitch after updates
product.minus: The persistent status-bar temperature shows only a cloud icon with no number, the widget fails to pick up location and shows random hours, and it either won't place on the home screen or won't refresh.

product.title: The location keeps resetting to the wrong city
product.minus: The banner sticks to a previously visited city and reverts there on its own within hours, lasting 1–2 weeks; sometimes two tabs of the same location show different forecasts.

product.title: Longtime fans loved the widgets, design and alerts
product.plus: Before the forced AI and ads, this was many people's favorite weather app: a beautiful transparent interactive widget, clean navigation, precise hourly forecasts and instant alerts for storms, tornadoes and floods.

product.title: The app lags, freezes and crashes
product.minus: Slow loads, freezes and crashes after tapping the radar or right after opening; after some updates it won't launch at all and vanishes from the phone.

product.title: Privacy alarm: data harvesting and fake "virus" ads
product.minus: Users notice the app pulls and sells personal data for ads, see pop-ups warning of "viruses" and fake malware-laden updates, and find that even when disabled it still pings ads with their location.

product.title: The whole trip in one place — and it genuinely delivers
product.plus: Those who push past onboarding fall in love: flights, hotels, reservations, places, and notes assemble into one day-by-day plan. It replaces the whole Google Docs + Excel + maps + email-folder stack.

product.title: The map-with-pins turns chaos into a day's route
product.plus: A favorite for many — seeing the day's places on a map in relation to each other, optimizing the route, and getting travel time between stops. Especially valued in an unfamiliar country.

product.title: Shared planning lifts the load off the lone «planner»
product.plus: Planning together with family and friends in real time is a frequent reason for the love. Responsibility is shared, updates show instantly, companions add their own places and notes.

product.title: Budget tracking and splitting costs between companions
product.plus: The budget tracker and the «who owes whom» split are a separately praised plus for group trips. Everyone logs expenses and the app computes the balance.

product.title: An exhausting onboarding: dozens of questions before the first screen
product.minus: Before you can even type a city, you're forced through dozens of questions, splash screens, and data collection. Many delete the app before ever reaching the planner — it feels like your data is being farmed.

product.title: «Free» turns out to be a 7-day trial that demands a card
product.minus: Advertised as free, but after install it demands card details for a 7-day auto-billing trial. People call it bait-and-switch; some were charged without consent and then had to fight to delete the account.

product.title: Lag and freezes make the app unusable as the trip grows
product.minus: Once you add a reasonable number of places, the app slows, freezes, and stops responding — to the point that Android offers to kill the process. The web version works; mobile doesn't.

product.title: Constant Pro popups annoy even satisfied users
product.minus: Banners, popups, and pushy tutorials about upgrading appear at every step, even when the user is happy with the free version. An app that should simplify keeps getting in the way.

product.title: Email reservation import — a promise that often misfires
product.minus: The signature feature (auto-parsing emails) fails for many: Airbnb bookings aren't recognized, tour and theater tickets are ignored, some entries get duplicated. You end up entering it all by hand — defeating the point.

product.title: AI features break the itinerary instead of helping
product.minus: Trying the AI leads to losses: it wipes a whole month's plan, dumps every item onto one day, and crashes. The «smart» optimizer can't account for places' opening hours.

product.title: Dark mode and basic essentials locked behind the paywall
product.minus: What grates isn't paying as such, but that basic things like dark mode require a subscription. And it's annual-only — wrong for people who travel a couple times a year; they ask for a one-time purchase.

product.title: Front-door breakages: stuck language picker and account bugs
product.minus: After updates the app gets stuck on a language-selection popup where «Continue» does nothing — mid-trip. Plus login failures, being logged out on every launch, and a keyboard that closes itself.

product.title: Login dies on an "unexpected error" — reinstalling and resetting the password don't help
product.minus: The single most common complaint: tapping sign-in throws "An unexpected error occurred" and goes no further, even though the same account opens fine on the website. People reinstall and reset passwords to no avail, losing access to years of saved trips.

product.title: Fails exactly mid-trip: internal server error on travel day, access returns once you're home
product.minus: The vault for all your tickets and bookings quits at the worst possible moment — at immigration or on departure day: "internal server error," app won't open. Several users spotted the pattern: it breaks precisely on travel days and recovers afterward.

product.title: Random sign-outs every few days kill the core value prop — "everything at hand"
product.minus: The app logs you out on its own — sometimes every few days, sometimes mid-action — forcing a fresh login. Users rightly wonder why data isn't cached locally: if you can't depend on it, the whole convenience value evaporates.

product.title: The auto-parsing of emails — the whole reason to use TripIt — increasingly fails
product.minus: The headline feature — forward an email, get a ready itinerary item — has decayed: it misses bookings even from major vendors (AirBNB, Cathay Pacific, Accor), reads only the first flight leg, ignores PDFs. You end up entering everything by hand, defeating the point.

product.title: Pro subscribers get no delay or gate-change alerts — the very thing they pay for
product.minus: Paid Pro promises live flight updates, yet people sit delayed on the tarmac, have five emails from the airline, and TripIt still shows "on-time." Gate and delay alerts arrive late or never — so what is the $99/year for.

product.title: Sign-up trips over the password: "too weak" or "doesn't match our records" on a brand-new account
product.minus: People can't even create an account: the page rejects passwords as not complex enough (even 20-character ones), and on sign-up throws the absurd "email/password doesn't match our records" — for a new account that doesn't exist yet. Many quit right here.

product.title: Demands for full name, DOB and inbox access read as surveillance and intrusion
product.minus: To keep using it, the app suddenly demands date of birth, full name and address, and above all — standing access to your entire inbox. Users read this as a privacy invasion ("reads every email"), threaten regulator complaints, and uninstall.

product.title: Geo-blocking locks out travelers: "unavailable in your region" mid-trip, with no VPN on
product.minus: A paradox for a travel app: login is blocked by country/region — users in the US, Asia, Canada are told the service isn't available there, sometimes even with the VPN off. It cuts people off from their own itineraries exactly when they're actually traveling.

product.title: Editing an itinerary is painful: can't delete a part, duplicate conflicts won't resolve, sharing breaks
product.minus: When auto-import fails, manual management becomes a slog: you can't delete a single item without nuking the whole trip, updates pile up as duplicates with unresolvable "conflicts," and an invited traveler can't link the shared trip to their account.

product.title: When it works it's the best trip organizer: everything in one place, auto-from-email, indispensable for years
product.plus: What people love: forward your emails and get a tidy timeline of all flights, hotels and bookings in one place, available offline and shared with family. Dozens of 10-15-year users call it indispensable — "practically more important than my passport."

product.title: Pro pays for itself in real money: refunds on price drops and compensation for delays
product.plus: For some users Pro tangibly justifies its price: it monitors fare drops and helps claim a travel credit for the difference, secures compensation for excessive delays, and at the airport surfaces gates and baggage carousel faster than the boards themselves.

product.title: Pro pricing repels: ~$50-99/year for what used to be free, many call it a rip-off
product.minus: Many balk that useful features (gates, airport maps, updates) moved behind a $49-99/year Pro that used to be free. The free tier now feels like an empty duplicate of an itinerary, and the price is called astronomical.

product.title: Past trips and the memories in them — the reason people stay for years
product.plus: A strength for long-time users: TripIt keeps a full history of trips with notes, addresses and phone numbers — years later you can revisit it "like a second vacation." It turns a utilitarian organizer into a personal travel archive.

product.title: Support ping-pongs you to the airline or hotel — no one owns the booking
product.minus: When something goes wrong, Hopper support just repeats "not possible", tells you to call the airline or hotel, and they bounce you back to Hopper — you spend hours going in circles with no resolution.

product.title: "All taxes and fees included" — then you pay extra at check-in
product.minus: The app explicitly promises all fees are included in the final price, yet at the front desk you get hit with resort fees, deposits and surcharges of tens to hundreds of dollars that were nowhere to be seen at checkout.

product.title: Paid cancellation/insurance doesn't deliver: the credit dies or can't be used
product.minus: People pay extra for "cancel for any reason" and insurance, then lose the money on cancellation: the credit is locked to the same flight or route where seats are "never available", or the refund drags on for weeks and months.

product.title: Hotels turn out filthy and nothing like the photos
product.minus: Arriving on their booking, people land in roach-infested, smelly, run-down rooms that don't match the app's pictures — and Hopper does the bare minimum and refuses refunds for the filth.

product.title: Bookings collapse: hotel closed, renamed, or never heard of Hopper
product.minus: The worst-case scenario is arriving to find there's no booking: the hotel doesn't honor Hopper reservations, has been closed for renovation for two years, or simply changed names — and you're left with nowhere to sleep.

product.title: The "deals" cost more than the hotel's own site or other apps
product.minus: Users compare against Google Flights, Expedia and the hotels' own sites and routinely find the same rooms and flights 20–30% cheaper — Hopper's margin is baked in.

product.title: The date or number of nights gets scrambled at booking
product.minus: Somewhere at the payment step the booking gets swapped: a mid-July date becomes "tonight", two paid nights turn into one, and changing or cancelling it is nearly impossible.

product.title: Pay-walled: the price tracker is now locked behind Pro
product.minus: The signature feature — price watching and predictions — moved behind a paid Pro subscription; the entry flow forces you to pick three destinations you don't want, and the UI is buried in upsells and microtransactions.

product.title: Double charges, payment bugs and absurd card authorizations
product.minus: At checkout the app throws connectivity errors but charges you anyway — sometimes twice; one user got hit with 100 authorizations and an attempt to charge $43,676 for a $436 booking.

product.title: From India there's no way to reach support — just a bot
product.minus: For users in India the only channel is a call to an international US number (costly and impractical), with no email and no live chat — just a useless AI assistant.

product.title: The price tracker and "when to buy" alerts — what people love it for
product.plus: Fans track flights for years via Flight Watch: the app tells you whether a price will drop or rise and nails the moment to buy — and it genuinely saves money.

product.title: Disruption insurance actually pays out — sometimes even without buying it
product.plus: When a flight is delayed or cancelled, Hopper monitors it and refunds you — sometimes in full and even for people who never bought the insurance; for many that's the genuine WOW moment.

product.title: Spammy notifications and pushy suggestions annoy users
product.minus: The notification stream can't be sorted: genuine price-drop alerts drown in spam about "cool places you said you liked", and the pushes just open the app without showing the date or the price.

product.title: Easy interface and all-in-one breadth
product.plus: Many praise the intuitive, clear flow: flights, hotels, cars and homes in one place, with handy search and filters — especially loved by first-time travelers and people booking on the go.

product.title: Price Freeze and paid seat/leg-room add-ons don't deliver
product.minus: The paid "Price Freeze" doesn't guarantee the price and is non-refundable, and paying extra for a seat or leg room simply doesn't work — Hopper says it doesn't handle seating.

product.title: One feed instead of spamming photos across every messenger
product.plus: The core reason people love it: post once and all your family and friends see the route, photos and comments — without flooding WhatsApp, Instagram or Facebook with separate updates.

product.title: The route map turns a trip into a visual story
product.plus: The line on the world map with «steps» pinned along it is the standout feature: you can see how you move from place to place, and the people back home know exactly where you are right now.

product.title: A diary that reminds you where you've been
product.plus: People keep it as a personal trip journal: photos plus day-by-day notes help them not mix up place names afterwards and relive the route years later.

product.title: The printed photo book at the end is what keeps people loyal
product.plus: The auto-assembled book with route, weather and photos is a recurring reason for praise on its own: people look forward to it and buy it as a physical keepsake of the trip.

product.title: A clean private circle — no ads, no peanut gallery
product.plus: Being private and ad-free is valued in its own right: only a chosen audience can follow, only your own people comment, and there's barely any visible monetisation.

product.title: GPS tracking draws straight lines instead of the real route
product.minus: The most painful technical issue: even on «high accuracy» with every setting dialled in, the route collapses into straight segments, and switching to a less accurate mode wipes earlier waypoints entirely — a bug that's lived for years without a fix.

product.title: You can't pick a step's cover photo or caption each shot
product.minus: The single most common request, even from 5★ fans: the step cover is always the first photo, and to change it you have to drag a shot to the front and break the order of the rest; you also can't caption an individual photo.

product.title: Comments attach to the step, not the individual photo
product.minus: Followers can't like or comment on individual photos — only the whole step; you also can't see who liked a particular post, which clips the social side of the app.

product.title: Editing after the fact breaks the route tracking
product.minus: Going back to fix text or photo order in a published/draft step throws off the tracking and loses the edits; after one update you also couldn't change the arrival date anymore.

product.title: Adding a trip retroactively is a struggle
product.minus: The app doesn't use the location data baked into photos to place steps, so reconstructing a route after you get home is hard; if you forgot to «start» the trip on time, there's no obvious way to backfill past places.

product.title: Sign-in, device verification and invite links fall over
product.minus: For some users the app dies at the very entrance: sign-in works through neither Google nor email, there's an «error verifying your device», and an invite link to someone's trip doesn't actually open the trip after install.

product.title: Notifications about new posts arrive unreliably
product.minus: Even happy users get flaky pushes: notifications about friends' new steps don't always arrive, or are simply wrong, so people have to open the app and check manually.

product.title: Used to be free, now paywalled — the subscription killed what people loved
product.minus: Dozens of long-time users open the app to find that without a subscription ($35–65/yr) you can barely do anything — not even plan your own route. The grievance isn't «too pricey», it's «they took away what used to be free».

product.title: «There was a problem creating your trip» — the trip simply won't generate
product.minus: A very common scenario: trying to create a trip throws the same error over and over. People toggle Wi-Fi, try exact addresses, reinstall — nothing helps, and even in the paid trial no itinerary loads.

product.title: Auto-renewal with no notice and near-impossible cancellation
product.minus: The subscription renews with no reminder email, and cancelling is hard: on Android you have to email support and «ask permission». Many got charged for years of non-use, and refunds are refused.

product.title: Makes you pay before showing a single example
product.minus: The app makes you enter a pile of info, walks you through questionnaires, then dead-ends at an upgrade prompt — never showing what it does. People are willing to pay but want to see a sample trip first.

product.title: No Android Auto — nothing to use behind the wheel
product.minus: The app doesn't support Android Auto (CarPlay only), so after planning you still have to re-enter waypoints into Google Maps by hand. For a navigation app, users see this as a fundamental failure.

product.title: Lag, freezes and crashes — you have to restart after every edit
product.minus: The app constantly freezes, scrolls slowly and crashes; making a single change to the route often means closing and reopening it — and this hits paying premium users too.

product.title: Doesn't work outside the US — Canada, Europe and the UK fall flat
product.minus: Outside the US the app is essentially useless: Canadian and European addresses aren't recognized, and searching Paris only returns Paris, TX. The limitation isn't stated up front, so people pay before finding out.

product.title: No offline mode — without signal on the road the app goes dead
product.minus: The core pain hits during the trip itself: without internet the app won't load data or routes, and the promised premium offline maps can't be found. It dies exactly where it's needed most.

product.title: Forced AI autopilot instead of manual planning — and it doesn't work
product.minus: Many users want to pick their own route and stops, but the app pushes an AI «autopilot» that frequently freezes or errors out. Experienced travelers say flatly: «I do not want you to plan my trip».

product.title: The absorbed Campendium got worse — RVers lost their favorite data
product.minus: Roadtrippers absorbed Campendium and, in users' eyes, ruined it: free overnight spots (Walmart, rest areas, churches) vanished, the Campendium Android app was dropped, and campground data thinned out. A distinct pain for the RV community.

product.title: Reordering stops and setting dates is agonizing
product.minus: Dragging stops barely works — they don't move or jump too far; new points land at the top of the list instead of the bottom; and one long stay auto-rewrites the dates of every stop after it. A simple route edit becomes a fight.

product.title: Worse than free Google Maps at its core job — finding interesting stops
product.minus: The paid app's paradox: it suggests only chains like Chick-fil-A and Starbucks, shows attractions at the destination instead of along the way, and serves stale data. Again and again the conclusion is the same — Google Maps does it better, for free.

product.title: For loyal fans — the best trip planner they've used for years
product.plus: A core of users adores the app and won't travel without it: up to 150 waypoints per route, day-by-day breakdown, reservations, budget, notes, and a shareable link for family. People plan 4+ week, 6,500-mile trips with it for years and consider the annual fee well worth it.

product.title: Strong concept: it surfaces cool stops you never knew existed
product.plus: When it works, it nails its core job — finding interesting, quirky and free spots along the route, revealing things you'd otherwise drive right past. It's this discovery value that keeps people coming back despite the flaws.

product.title: One screen, every way to get there — including routes you'd never think of
product.plus: The core value: it lays out train, bus, ferry, taxi and flight between any two points on earth and surfaces non-obvious combinations you'd never have considered on your own.

product.title: Indispensable for car-free, self-guided travel
product.plus: For solo travellers and non-drivers it's a pocket travel agent: it gives them the confidence to use public transport in unfamiliar countries and plan a trip from their own doorstep to anywhere in the world.

product.title: Prices, timetables and ticket-buying links right in the results
product.plus: Beyond routes it shows approximate cost and journey time and links out to buy tickets — users note prices are often spot on, occasionally the best they've ever found.

product.title: Beats Google Maps where Google Maps gives up
product.plus: Users directly compare it to Google Maps and pick Rome2Rio for ferries, intercity buses and places Google doesn't cover; its public transport integration is called superior.

product.title: The data lets you down: phantom routes, wrong timetables and non-optimal paths
product.minus: The most dangerous complaint: the app confidently shows buses and routes that don't exist, timetables that don't match reality, and far-from-optimal paths — risky to rely on when planning.

product.title: The app is a stripped-down website with key features missing
product.minus: Many love the website but stall on the app: missing route prices, missing ferries, no experiences or trips search, clunkier navigation — on the phone you lose almost everything the website is loved for.

product.title: Input is broken: can't change endpoints, reverse them, or enter coordinates
product.minus: After the first search the app gets stuck: you can't change origin/destination, there's no reverse button, you can't paste GPS coordinates, and the only cure is a reinstall.

product.title: Constant crashes, freezes and "check your connection" with the internet working
product.minus: The app freezes and crashes, goes unresponsive on some Android devices, and throws a routing error even with a working connection — long-loyal users are leaving precisely because the bugs go unfixed.

product.title: Abandoned by the devs: last update ages ago, bugs are known
product.minus: Users point out there have been no updates since November, the devs know about the bugs but don't fix them — an app that was number one for years now looks outdated and abandoned.

product.title: Can't book, can't save: no login, no sync, no multi-stop
product.minus: You see the route but there's no buy button — it kicks you to a browser; you can't log in, save a route or sync with the computer, and you can't add multiple stops — which defeats the point of a planner.

product.title: Opens Google Maps instead of itself — so why use a Google Maps alternative?
product.minus: For directions the app hands you off to Google Maps with no option to pick another navigation app; users fairly ask what the point of a "Google Maps alternative" is if it just launches Google Maps.

product.title: Core navigation features are locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Voice, sound, zoom control, lane guidance, Android Auto — the things rivals give away for free are paywalled here. Without paying you drive blind, with no voice prompts, and miss your exit right on the highway.

product.title: The "lifetime" license was taken away and you're forced to pay again
product.minus: People bought navigation "forever" years ago, and now voice and other paid-for features have been stripped out and moved into a subscription. Longtime users see it as outright betrayal and leave for Google Maps and Waze.

product.title: Full-screen ads for camper and motorbike modes even for paying subscribers
product.minus: Even after buying Premium, users keep getting intrusive banners and full-screen pop-ups pushing caravan or motorbike add-ons — sometimes right while driving at night. It's annoying enough that people refuse to renew.

product.title: Routes send you on detours, into oncoming traffic and down roads that don't exist
product.minus: The app plots pointless detours, demands U-turns on motorways, sends you the wrong way down one-way streets and onto roads that aren't even finished. For a GPS this is the core job — and here it fails worse than free Google Maps and Waze.

product.title: Crashes and freezes, especially a few minutes into Android Auto
product.minus: The app reliably crashes or freezes to a black screen 5–20 minutes into a drive, and restarting it while driving is nearly impossible — you have to shut off the car. Many keep Google Maps on standby precisely because of this.

product.title: Maps and POIs are years out of date, new streets are missing
product.minus: Housing estates and streets 5–6 years old are still missing from the map, points of interest are stale, and there's no way to report errors. For a paid service where map data is the whole point, falling this far behind free rivals is fatal.

product.title: Speed limits are shown wrong and update too late
product.minus: The app shows the wrong speed limits — 70 where the sign says 40, mislabels school zones, and only updates a few kilometres after the limit changes. This triggers false warnings and leaves you unable to trust the number on screen.

product.title: Search can't find addresses or places by name
product.minus: To find anything you need the exact address: search by a shop's name returns nothing, or suggests a location thousands of miles away. People end up looking the address up in Google Maps and typing it in here — using two apps at once.

product.title: Offline maps won't download and still demand an internet connection
product.minus: Map downloads stall at 80–90% or never start, and even already-downloaded offline maps refuse to work without a connection — the app says "no internet". This strikes at the very reason people buy Sygic in the first place.

product.title: Beautiful, readable maps and interface — even when the rest fails
product.plus: Looks are what nearly everyone praises, even the unhappy ones. Clean graphics, pleasant map colours, and clear turn and junction cues that many find easier to read than Google Maps. It's often the reason people add a star.

product.title: Indispensable on travels without signal: offline maps, cameras, curve warnings
product.plus: Loyal users have relied on Sygic for years on trips across Europe, national parks and mountains where there's no signal: maps live on the device, use no data and just keep working. Speed-camera alerts, sharp-curve warnings and live speed are what brings them back.

product.title: An over-chatty voice confuses turns with "curves" and floods you with needless prompts
product.minus: The voice assistant endlessly repeats "keep going straight", calls ordinary turns "curve" (or even "curb"), mangles its grammar and distracts the driver with a stream of pointless instructions. Some just mute it or switch to terser rivals.

product.title: Double charges, refused refunds and billing confusion
product.minus: People get charged twice — both by Sygic and by Google Play — a yearly plan is billed as monthly, a purchase won't transfer to a second phone, and refunds are denied. Support replies with canned templates and drags on for months, deepening the sense of being scammed.

product.title: Proximity-based auto-routing is the headline reason people love it
product.plus: Enter your dates and where you're staying and it lays out attractions across days, sorts them by proximity and calculates travel time between stops. For short city breaks it saves hours of planning.

product.title: Turned into a storefront for paid tours instead of a build-your-own planner
product.minus: Many come to assemble their own route of sights and instead get a feed of paid tours, excursions and partner offers. Adding your own places often isn't possible — precisely because the app makes no money on them.

product.title: Can't add your own: hotels by name and non-commercial places simply won't go in
product.minus: A signature pain is the 'add your hotel' feature: searching by name or address returns 'no matches found', and you can't drop in your own address or a sight that isn't on their list. The plan stops being yours.

product.title: Pushy location prompt that won't go away after you decline
product.minus: To browse a distant city the app demands GPS, and if you refuse the prompt keeps popping up over and over — sometimes the app just hangs. The logic infuriates anyone planning a trip from home.

product.title: Stale and wrong data: hours, addresses and shut-down attractions
product.minus: It lists attractions as open when they've long since closed or burned down, gets opening hours and addresses wrong. On the ground this wrecks plans, and there's no way to report the error.

product.title: Ready-made plans for short visits take the stress out of planning
product.plus: For the time-pressed, the built-in 1-2-3-day plans hand you a ready list of top sights in the right order. It's easy to pick your pace and just follow the route.

product.title: The itinerary editor is clumsy: everything dumps into day one, times won't budge
product.minus: Try to customise and it falls apart: additions default to day one even with day three selected; times and order change themselves and can't be reverted; you can't drag stops around or slot in a lunch break.

product.title: Crashes, won't open and fails offline — especially after updates
product.minus: It crashes, hangs on a white screen or won't launch at all without a connection — and that hits right in the middle of a trip, with plans already built. Offline maps fail to finish downloading and network errors pile up.

product.title: Thin city coverage: too few destinations, nothing offbeat or smaller
product.minus: Many open their target city only to see 'coming soon' or nothing at all; it mostly covers big tourist capitals, while smaller or offbeat places are missing or shown only as a list of tours.

product.title: Travel times and transport mode are wrong, no public-transit choice
product.minus: The app decides for you whether to walk or drive, won't let you pick public transit, and travel times are often absurd — up to '19622 min' where it's a couple-minute walk. That blows the day's schedule apart.

product.title: Paywall and billing: 'free' but everything's locked, plus charges after cancelling
product.minus: It's advertised as 'free' but everything's locked without a subscription; some paid and still can't use it, others cancelled their account and were charged anyway — while support ignores the emails.

product.title: A city guide in your pocket: returning users carry it around the world for years
product.plus: The most loyal use it for years across dozens of cities as a personal guide: descriptions, prices, time-to-sights, offline mode and the confidence to explore further. For them it's an indispensable travel companion.

product.title: Login breaks exactly when you need the app most — mid-trip
product.minus: The single most common complaint: after an update, login stops working — "An unexpected error occurred", endless auto sign-outs, a dead Sign in button. Reinstalling doesn't help, the website sometimes works while the app doesn't. Users lose access to years of trip history right when traveling, standing at immigration.

product.title: The app silently signs you out in the middle of a trip
product.minus: A distinct bug from the broken login: the app signs you out by itself every few days or right in the middle of a trip, sometimes crashing too. What infuriates many is that data isn't cached locally — with no connection and no login the itinerary is simply gone, even though that's its one job.

product.title: The headline feature — auto-building trips from email — stopped working
product.minus: Email parsing of confirmations — the whole reason people install it — now regularly fails even for major vendors (AirBNB, Cathay Pacific, Accor, Expedia). Travel-agent PDFs aren't read, many emails land in Unfiled, and everything has to be entered by hand. At that point the app loses its purpose: a spreadsheet is easier.

product.title: Doesn't update flight statuses — which is the whole point of paying
product.minus: Pro subscribers pay mainly for delay, gate-change and reschedule alerts — and that's exactly what fails. The app shows a flight "on-time" while you sit delayed on the tarmac, misses reschedules, and won't show gates. For a paid travel service this is fatal.

product.title: Sign-up dies on the password — users never reach the app
product.minus: A barrier at the very door: creating an account demands a draconian password (15+ chars) and rejects even strong generated ones, or absurdly says "email/password doesn't match our records" — on the new-account screen. People burn minutes and leave for competitors without ever trying the product.

product.title: Demands personal data and reads your whole inbox — privacy backlash
product.minus: The app suddenly demands date of birth, full name and address to continue, and for parsing wants access to your entire inbox, even firing notifications on non-travel emails. Many call it "intrusive" and "malware", threaten a regulator complaint and delete their account — clearly excessive for a map organizer.

product.title: Region-locks you out — even at home in your own country
product.minus: A bizarre geo-blocking mechanism: users in the US, Canada, Asia are denied "from a region where the service isn't available" — with no VPN, sitting at home. For an app whose whole point is traveling the world, refusing to work abroad nullifies its value.

product.title: Duplicates and conflicts: an updated import spawns copies you can't delete
product.minus: When importing an updated itinerary the app can't tell it's an update and just adds a duplicate; conflicts can't be merged, can't pick the latest, can't even be deleted — you have to wipe the whole trip. Plan management is crippled overall: you can add items but can't delete or reorder individual ones.

product.title: When it works — it's the best way to keep a whole trip in one place
product.plus: People genuinely love the core for years — 10 to 15 of them: forward confirmations to an address and the app builds a clean timeline of flights, hotels, cars and activities by itself. Everything in one place, available offline, no ads — many call it indispensable and "more important than my passport".

product.title: Pro pays for itself in real money — but the ~$50-99/yr price scares people off
product.plus: The best Pro reviews are concrete: it tracks price drops and refunds the difference, wins compensation for delays, updates info at the airport faster than the boards and airline apps, and shows the baggage carousel. For frequent flyers it pays for itself many times over.

product.title: Trip sharing is broken exactly where it matters most — couples and families
product.minus: Shared travel is a core use case but it fails: an invitee can't add themselves as a traveler, sharing is email-only (still no link in 2026), invites don't get sent, and a spouse can't see the shared trip in the app — only in a browser. So everything ends up entered by hand again.

product.title: Android is a cut-down iOS: no search, broken Notes field, calendar bugs
product.minus: Android is clearly poorer than iOS: no search, the Notes field is one unreadable line, Google Calendar sync either fails or sets the wrong time zone, the widget drops out, and times show with no AM/PM. For the same price users get a visibly second-class product.

product.title: The core value is honest reviews from real people
product.plus: Again and again people come back for one thing: to read the reviews of those who have actually been there and to vet a place before booking. For many it is the first step of every trip and a habit built over years.

product.title: An update replaced lists with a map — and it infuriates people
product.minus: After the latest update users get only a map with rating numbers and no descriptions instead of a list of restaurants or hotels. People are openly begging for the list back and calling the app useless.

product.title: The suspicion that reviews are filtered and bought
product.minus: Users notice their low ratings get rejected without explanation and conclude that the visible reviews may be skewed toward whoever pays. It strikes at the app's very foundation.

product.title: Direct booking of tours and hotels inside the app
product.plus: Many value that they can go beyond reading reviews and book a tour, safari or hotel right away — and the experience with the guides and excursions turns out consistently good.

product.title: The go-to starting point for planning a trip
product.plus: For regulars it is the first place they open when planning: it helps gather ideas, surface hidden gems and makes them feel like their own travel agent.

product.title: Navigation is confusing, you keep going back and forth
product.minus: Even loyal users complain: the interface is overloaded and too prescriptive, you cannot search your own way, and a simple task like getting a list of restaurants becomes a struggle.

product.title: Intrusive 'Ask AI', ads and upsells
product.minus: Before letting you leave a review or just look something up, the app buries you in quizzes, ads and offers. The 'Ask AI' that is on by default cannot be turned off.

product.title: Prices jump, hidden mark-ups at booking
product.minus: The advertised price shoots up when you check availability, discounts turn out not to apply, and you only learn about military and other deals after a non-refundable booking.

product.title: Bugs: trips won't load, random password resets, sluggish
product.minus: For some users saved trips stop loading, the app keeps sending password-reset emails and logging them out on its own, and pages load slowly after the update.

product.title: Forced location access and a US-phone lock-in
product.minus: Opening the map demands precise location, while rewards and activation hinge on a US phone number — for users elsewhere this is both annoying and a blocker.

product.title: A favorite tool for people who write reviews themselves
product.plus: Many not only read but also leave their own reviews straight from the phone — on the plane, on the way to the next place — to help fellow travelers. Rewarding good service matters to them.

product.title: Stale data: old ratings, closed places
product.minus: A hotel's rating can stay high on reviews that are years old while reality has long since changed; searches surface out-of-date and already-closed listings.

product.title: Time-tested: trusted for years around the world
product.plus: Long-timers have used it for 20+ years and trust it more than the main rival 'beginning with a G': it feels like an old friend that rarely steers them wrong.

product.title: Loses your place and keeps resetting chapters to the start
product.minus: The most frequent pain: the app won't hold your listening position. It either restarts the chapter or jumps back to where the previous session began, while the timer freezes and stops moving. Many users reinstall the app weekly just to get sync working again.

product.title: Car autoplay that no setting will turn off
product.minus: The moment the phone connects to the car's Bluetooth, Audible starts playing a book on its own — even with autoplay switched off in settings. No toggle helps, and several users uninstalled or cancelled outright just to make it stop.

product.title: The credit-and-subscription model feels like a money trap
product.minus: One credit a month, credits don't roll over, and the new "standard" tier turned into a rental — cancel and you lose access to what you paid for. Users call it a silent money-eater and figure it's cheaper to buy a book elsewhere than to pay for the membership.

product.title: Post-update redesign makes the library hard to find and browse
product.minus: Recent updates buried the library, made the menus a maze, and the app always loads onto a pointless "home page" instead of what people actually want. Long-time users uniformly call it a major downgrade.

product.title: Freezes, crashes, and a grey screen that locks the controls
product.minus: For a purely audio app there's a startling amount of breakage: the screen greys out for hours and accepts no taps, the player freezes, and any network hiccup crashes it. The devs' stock answer — "log out and back in" or reinstall — drives users up the wall.

product.title: Login, verification, and Amazon-routed support are a nightmare
product.minus: Switching phones or using a passkey gets you locked out for "suspicious activity," buried under endless phone-number verifications and bounced between Audible and Amazon. Recovering a hacked account with years of purchased books is near-impossible, and support replies in canned scripts.

product.title: Promos, discounts, and charges that never break the customer's way
product.minus: A discount is offered but full price is charged; "3 months free" turns into one; a cancelled subscription keeps billing for months. Promo credits you earned have to be clawed back by manually "activating" them, and some users simply feel cheated.

product.title: AI narration and AI features feel forced and unwanted
product.minus: More and more titles ship with robotic AI narration that users call laughable. A new AI on the book page spoils the plot, and instead of real support you get a forced, pre-scripted AI chat where you can't even type your own message.

product.title: A huge library and great narrators are the core reason people love it
product.plus: A massive catalogue covering almost any subject, professional narrators, and clean sound — this is what keeps people on Audible for years. Many find 98% of what they wanted, love human narration with distinct character voices, and value adjustable narration speed.

product.title: Turns chores and commutes into time well spent — listen while your hands are busy
product.plus: The core love is hands-free listening: in the car, at work, while cleaning, cooking, or falling asleep. Long drives and dull tasks stop being a drag and become a story instead of ad-filled radio. For many it's a daily "me time" ritual.

product.title: A lifeline for people with dyslexia, ADHD, and failing eyesight
product.plus: A distinct and deeply grateful audience are those who struggle to read with their eyes. For people with dyslexia and ADHD, Audible opens up books that were otherwise out of reach; for those with eye strain or failing sight, it's a way to keep "reading" without the strain.

product.title: Pushy recommendations, ad notifications, and streak gamification
product.minus: Recommendations routinely miss — pushing the wrong genre, refusing to forget a removed book, with no "block this topic" button. Meanwhile the ad push notifications and "30-week streak!" counters work flawlessly, which annoys people more than the bugs themselves.

product.title: Free with a library card — the core, undisputed value
product.plus: The single thing people love most is simple: books and audiobooks are free with a local library card. For anyone who can't afford an Audible-style subscription, it's a direct replacement and a way to support their library.

product.title: Hold queues for digital copies — weeks and months of waiting for popular titles
product.minus: The most frequent complaint: a popular title has one or two licenses and a long line. People wait weeks, sometimes 45 days, and if you don't finish you go back to the end of a 19-20 week queue.

product.title: Random crashes and dropouts in the middle of an audiobook
product.minus: Audio stops every couple of minutes and kicks people out, especially while driving. For some it takes twice as long to finish a book because of the constant glitching.

product.title: A huge selection of books, audiobooks, magazines and comics
product.plus: Many are struck by the sheer volume: novels, comics, manga, magazines, audiobooks — all in one place. You can link multiple libraries to widen the collection even further.

product.title: Silent auto-return — no overdue items, no late fees
product.plus: Books return themselves, so late fees simply don't exist. A nice touch many call out is the bouquet of flowers you get for returning a book early.

product.title: Cross-device sync simply doesn't work
product.minus: Shelf, tags and reading position don't carry over between phones. It shows the right percentage but opens to the wrong page, and tags vanish and never come back.

product.title: A lifeline for the vision-impaired and those who can't get to a library
product.plus: For people with vision challenges and those who can no longer drive or physically reach a library, Libby's audiobooks bring back the ability to "read." It's mentioned with real gratitude.

product.title: Confusing navigation: 'back' closes the app, tags are baffling
product.minus: The interface is called counterintuitive even after years of use. 'Back' closes the app, the tags/favorites system feels impossible to grasp, and changes like the suspend/unsuspend holds flow made it harder.

product.title: Audiobooks for the commute, work and chores
product.plus: The signature use people love is listening while driving, working out, knitting or doing chores. Adjustable speed and offline listening on long drives make it indispensable.

product.title: Won't open, crashes after updates, downloaded books disappear
product.minus: The app stops opening after an update, crashes even on titles downloaded for offline use, and sometimes has to be fully deleted and reinstalled just to get audio back.

product.title: Offline mode fails: downloaded books won't open without a connection
product.minus: Downloaded books behave as if they were never downloaded: they won't open on the way to work and won't load over data or WiFi. You can get stuck on a plane without the book you thought you'd saved.

product.title: Location and card-linking break during onboarding
product.minus: The app fails to find the nearest library even with location on — offering a city six hours away or claiming the town doesn't exist. Linking the library card itself also fails.

product.title: Added AI features triggered rating downgrades from some readers
product.minus: Some loyal users dropped their rating specifically over the rollout of generative AI: the features are called unwanted and unwelcome, and a few tie them to a perceived drop in quality.

product.title: Opening a book lands on a black or white screen, only a restart helps
product.minus: The single most common complaint: opening a book or switching back from another app leaves a black or white unresponsive screen. The only fix is force-quitting, rebooting the phone or reinstalling — and it happens every day.

product.title: Constantly loses your place and resets you to the start
product.minus: You're halfway through, and the next time you open it the book starts over. Bookmarks don't save you, sync with the e-reader and other devices breaks, and every session means hunting for your place again.

product.title: Freezes, crashes and closes mid-read
product.minus: The book freezes mid-page, the app closes itself, sometimes it locks the whole phone. Clearing cache and reinstalling don't help — you have to open and close it several times just to read at all.

product.title: Demands internet to open books you already downloaded
product.minus: The whole point of a reading app is offline reading, yet it won't launch without a connection. On a plane, the tube or a trip, your downloaded and paid-for books are out of reach.

product.title: The 'My Books' page loads for minutes or not at all
product.minus: With a large library the 'My Books' tab spins for minutes and often won't open on the first try. The Kobo e-reader itself doesn't have this issue — it's clearly an app bug.

product.title: Lose the subscription, lose the books: no real ownership
product.minus: Books read under the plan vanish when you cancel, and some purchased titles disappear forever when rights or cover art change. People have lost hundreds of dollars of paid-for content.

product.title: Audiobook player has no bookmarks and broken seeking
product.minus: Audiobooks have no bookmark feature — standard on any player — so if you doze off you lose your spot. Playback also resets to the chapter start and stutters every 15-20 seconds.

product.title: Google Pay broken by WebView, payment forced onto the website
product.minus: You used to pay via Google Pay (e.g. with Opinion Rewards balance), but the app now uses WebView and throws an error. You're pushed to buy on the website, and gift-card balances don't show.

product.title: Won't let you into your own account, though the website works
product.minus: You create an account, buy a book — and the Android and iOS app rejects your login with a generic error, sometimes never serving the captcha. The web version logs you in fine with the same details.

product.title: Huge catalogue at good prices, and not Amazon
product.plus: The top reason people stay: a wide selection of books and audiobooks, fair prices, Kobo Plus and VIP points. For many it's a principled Amazon alternative that treats authors and small business fairly.

product.title: Spot-on weekly book recommendations delight readers
product.plus: The weekly emails suggesting new titles to a reader's taste are called uncannily accurate — through Kobo Plus people discover new authors and series they'd never have found otherwise.

product.title: Your whole library always with you in your phone
product.plus: When it works, people love that forgetting the e-reader at home is no problem — the same book opens on the phone, hundreds of volumes in your pocket, perfect for travel and waiting rooms.

product.title: Flexible font and brightness settings make phone reading pleasant
product.plus: For those who actually read in the app, the customization options — font, size, brightness, orientation lock — are a highlight. Many find the reading interface nicer than Kindle's.

product.title: Walled garden: can't open outside EPUBs, can't take yours out
product.minus: The app is useless for EPUB files you already own, won't share books to other readers and never shows up in 'open with'. Kobo purchases are locked to its ecosystem and often need the branded e-reader.

product.title: Audiobook credits don't apply to all titles
product.minus: The promised monthly credit only works on part of the catalogue — authors that were available suddenly sell at full price only, and the 'free' credit covers a narrow selection, which feels like a bait-and-switch.

product.title: Pay-to-own instead of subscription is the main reason people love Chirp
product.plus: Books are bought once and kept forever, with no monthly fee or limits — users explicitly call this the best alternative to Audible.

product.title: Low prices and constant sales
product.plus: Cheap books, weekly discounts and sales from 1 to 10 dollars — for many it's a way to listen a lot without going broke.

product.title: "Free" is a false hook to get the install
product.minus: The ads promise "hundreds of free audiobooks," but everything inside costs money — people feel deceived and uninstall.

product.title: Playback stops on its own and crashes
product.minus: The book keeps going silent, the app closes every few minutes and hands control to Spotify — especially dangerous while driving.

product.title: Downloading doesn't make a book offline — internet is still required
product.minus: The file isn't truly saved on the device: the book plays through a browser and fails without a connection — a dealbreaker for listening in the car.

product.title: Purchased books don't show up in the library
product.minus: People pay for books and then can't find them in their library — money charged, nothing to listen to.

product.title: Good narrators and audio quality lift the books
product.plus: Narrators voice characters distinctly, add drama and nuance — listeners praise the clarity and quality of the audio.

product.title: Aggressive spam after sign-up
product.minus: After signing up users get flooded with spam emails and now spam text ads they can't opt out of — even after cancelling.

product.title: Storage hog: books can't be deleted or moved
product.minus: Files are nearly impossible to delete and can't be moved to an SD card, so storage fills up until you can't even update the app.

product.title: Clumsy search and missing filters make it hard to find what you want
product.minus: You can't sort the library by author or title, there are no real filters, and the list scroll resets every time you go back.

product.title: Android Auto and car listening — on again, off again
product.plus: When Android Auto works, Chirp is praised as a great road companion; but the integration breaks for years at a time or ships missing key features.

product.title: Stops working after updates and on older devices
product.minus: After an update the app declares the device unsupported or simply stops launching — loyal multi-year users are left with no books.

product.title: Per-book prices bite anyone hunting for a specific title
product.minus: Sales are great for random discovery, but the specific book you want can easily cost 20-30 dollars — pricier than subscription rivals.

product.title: Ads promise «photo the cover, hear the whole book» — in reality you scan every page
product.minus: The single loudest complaint: the ads show that snapping the cover is enough to get the whole book read aloud. In reality it only reads the text on the cover, and to read a book you must photograph and crop every page one by one. People discover this only after paying.

product.title: The engine skips words, whole sentences and paragraphs, and reads out of order
product.minus: The core function breaks: it swallows words and letters, skips whole paragraphs, reads sentences out of order, and sometimes speaks the punctuation aloud. For a paid subscription people expect the full text read, not a selective version.

product.title: Price is hidden until the end of onboarding, and only an annual plan is offered
product.minus: The cost isn't shown up front: first you're pushed through a long series of questions and setup, and the $100+ yearly price only drops at the very end. There's no monthly plan — you must pay a year in advance, which deters students and one-off users.

product.title: The subscription is nearly impossible to cancel, and charges land after cancelling or without consent
product.minus: There's no cancel button in the app, the link sends you into login loops, and the subscription doesn't show up in Google Play to cancel. Many are charged for a year even after cancelling during the trial — or with no subscription at all.

product.title: You pay for the subscription — then get charged again for the library books
product.minus: After paying for premium, people find that access to the book library costs extra on top, and each book may demand another payment. They feel nickel-and-dimed, and the promised thousands of books turn out to be a thin set.

product.title: The voice suddenly switches to a robotic one mid-read
product.minus: The chosen human-like voice switches to a robotic one for no reason, or changes accent right in the middle of a document. It's most noticeable on long texts and when the app plays in the background — disorienting and irritating.

product.title: A long, invasive onboarding with a pile of questions before you can start
product.minus: Before letting you read a single line, the app runs you through questionnaires, tutorials and settings — sometimes for half an hour. The questions feel inappropriate and invasive, and money is asked at the end; some uninstall before ever using it.

product.title: The library won't load — only reinstalling the app helps
product.minus: After updates the library and uploaded documents stop opening: infinite loading or an empty screen offering to «upload your first document». The only working workaround is to uninstall and reinstall — over and over.

product.title: Won't play in the background — your phone is locked up while Speechify runs
product.minus: Minimize the app or lock the screen and the reading stops. You can't listen to a book while driving or doing anything else, and support gives contradictory answers about whether background mode even works.

product.title: For dyslexia and auditory learning — genuinely life-changing when it works
product.plus: People with dyslexia, ADHD and vision issues call the app a lifesaver: it lets them «read» textbooks, notes and fiction by ear, helps them study and pass exams. Many wish they'd had it in school.

product.title: Quizzes, AI podcasts and high-quality voices — strong study features
product.plus: On top of reading, there's quiz generation from your documents and AI podcasts from your notes — praised as genuinely useful for exam prep. The voices are called natural and high-quality, with adjustable speed and voice cloning.

product.title: «When it works, it's the best» — but the stability isn't there
product.minus: A recurring refrain: the idea and the quality delight in good moments, but the app only works part of the time. Hangs, crashes, endless loading and post-update regressions make an accessibility tool unreliable — since 2021.

product.title: Loud ads between chapters hit hardest the people listening to fall asleep
product.minus: Ads are several times louder than the books and burst in between chapters without warning. For an app with a sleep timer that's fatal: people say they wake up from a sudden ad blast, and pausing or closing the app won't stop it.

product.title: Ads keep playing even after the app is closed — and over other players
product.minus: The most alarming bug: ads keep sounding after the app is force-closed, and play over other audio apps entirely. Users pause, force-stop, clear notifications — nothing helps, and it feels like something shady is going on under the hood.

product.title: A vast collection of classics read by real human volunteers is the core love
product.plus: Thousands of public-domain books — Dracula, Conan, Frankenstein, Jane Austen — for free, voiced by real people rather than AI. People come back for years for finds that aren't on commercial services, and treasure the range of voices and inflection.

product.title: This is an unofficial app profiting off a free volunteer project
product.minus: Many are furious to learn the app isn't made by LibriVox itself: a third party runs ads and charges money off volunteers' work, while the real project is non-commercial, ad-free and free. It reads as grifting off a non-profit.

product.title: The app crashes and buffers, losing your place in the book
product.minus: Stability is shaky: it hangs on the splash screen, crashes on launch, lags when you hit play and buffers every couple of minutes. After a crash it takes ages to get back to where you left off, and bookmarks sometimes fail.

product.title: Chapters with huge tails of silence and duplicates break continuous listening
product.minus: A recurring technical glitch: after a chapter ends there's an hour or two of silence before the next starts, or chapters duplicate with gaps. For bedtime listeners it's especially painful — the app goes silent and they wake up.

product.title: A cheap lifetime ad-removal unlock is a real plus for those who pay
product.plus: Those who pay a small sum for the ad-free version (the one-time/lifetime license for pennies gets a lot of praise) are happy: clean listening to the classics, convenience, and gratitude to the project. The price feels like token support.

product.title: Downloading books for offline makes the app handier than the official site
product.plus: Being able to download a whole book (even to an SD card) and listen offline is prized by people on the road, at camp or without wi-fi. Many note it beats downloading and unzipping archives from the site, and the app remembers where you left off.

product.title: The app drains battery and runs in the background even after closing
product.minus: Users notice heavy battery drain and background activity: the app won't close without a force-stop, keeps running with battery-saver restrictions on, and eats 10-11% of charge while idle — abnormal for an audio player.

product.title: Forced sign-up with a card on file triggers fraud fears
product.minus: Some users are alarmed that the app forces a Google login and asks for a card 'with no charge' — then the bank flags a suspicious 34.96 charge. Others fear a Google sign-in 'backdoor' and data collection just to access public-domain books.

product.title: Search is clumsy and the catalog is stuck in old books
product.minus: The interface and search are called awkward: 'search' is buried, there's no advanced search by author/genre, no playlists. Plus the catalog is old classics only, with no contemporary titles, and some readers want more new material.

product.title: Narration quality is a lottery: volunteers range from brilliant to hard to follow
product.minus: Because amateur volunteers narrate, quality swings wildly: some voices are praised as better than paid Audible versions, others are called poor and hard to understand. Many cope by just picking a different reader or another recording of the same book.

product.title: Half the catalogue is region-locked — and you find out only after paying
product.minus: The single most common pain: titles that show up in search and ads throw "Audio format not available in your region" only after you've subscribed. There's no filter for what's actually available in your country, so people pay blind and feel cheated.

product.title: The subscription stopped being unlimited: many books now cost extra on top
product.minus: Everything used to be included in the monthly fee; now a large slice of the catalogue costs another €10-25 per title. Subscribers see it as a betrayal of the whole point of the service and leave for Audible.

product.title: The player loses your place and rewinds on its own
product.minus: The book suddenly jumps hours back or forward, minimizing the app returns you to an old bookmark, and an accidental tap on the progress bar throws you to the start with no way back. People waste time hunting for where they left off.

product.title: The broken sleep-timer dialog rewinds your audio
product.minus: When the sleep timer expires a dialog pops up with no "don't rewind" option; ignore it and it skips the audio back to where the timer ended. On top of that an "off" timer still fires, making the app unusable for people who listen while working.

product.title: Marketed as free, but without a subscription you can't listen to anything
product.minus: Many download it thinking it's free and hit a paywall right after login — you can't even sample a book or excerpt first. With no trial, people feel misled before they reach a single page.

product.title: You can't create an account: your country isn't in the list
product.minus: Sign-up forces you to pick a home country, but the list has no USA, Canada, Portugal or Nigeria — a dead end at the front door for many. Login itself also often fails with "something went wrong".

product.title: Books vanish from your library mid-listen
product.minus: Licenses expire without warning and a series or title disappears when you're halfway through. Often, instead of an honest "removed", the app shows a vague "check your language settings", which stings even more.

product.title: Seeking and buffering struggle even on downloaded books
product.minus: The -15s controls lag and freeze, streaming stalls on full 5G, and the app buffers even an already-downloaded book. Functionality that should be table-stakes for an audio player works worse than Spotify's.

product.title: AI is flooding the catalogue: voices, covers and descriptions
product.minus: Long-time subscribers revolt against AI narration that mangles names, AI cover art, wrong AI descriptions, and whole AI-generated "books". For many it's a direct reason to cancel — and there's no button to even report a synthetic narration.

product.title: Search can't find books, and chapters are jumbled with no table of contents
product.minus: Search misses even exact titles and authors, you can't separate English from other languages, and a 15-hour book is often one long file with no table of contents — misclick the timeline and you hunt for your spot by hand.

product.title: A huge multilingual catalogue at a fair price — what users love most
product.plus: For those it fits, the draw is the unlimited multilingual catalogue (Bulgarian, Arabic, Malayalam and more), a price that beats Audible, and quality human narration. For many it's their most-used app.

product.title: Switching read↔listen is loved, but you can't do both at once
product.plus: A prized feature: one subscription gives both the audiobook and the e-book, letting you switch between them and tune the narration speed.
product.minus: But you can't co-read — only one version is open at a time, even when a title has both. Learners who follow audio alongside text sorely miss this.

product.title: Playback speed was capped at 2x — and power users are furious
product.minus: Higher speeds used to exist; now the ceiling is 2x, which is too slow for many — co-readers and people used to 3x can't use the service as before. They want the high speeds back, plus finer steps (e.g. 0.95x).

product.title: Billing charges, access never activates, and you can't cancel
product.minus: Money is charged (sometimes twice), yet access never opens; you can't cancel in the app, and the website insists your account doesn't exist. Support is just a chatbot with no refunds; people experience it as a scam.

product.title: Intrusive promo pop-ups inside a paid subscription
product.minus: Despite paying, the app buries you in recommendations and promos for other books before and after each title, while the home screen loops the same pushed picks. Users just want to listen to their choice, not fend off promoted books.

product.title: In-car and on-watch use barely works: Android Auto and watch are buggy
product.minus: For commuters it's critical that Android Auto/Car keeps logging you out and syncs poorly with the phone, Sonos plays the wrong title, and books downloaded to the watch say "you are offline". Next to Spotify it feels half-baked.

product.title: Bluetooth headphones drop out specifically in this app
product.minus: For some users, launching Storytel makes their Bluetooth headset connect and disconnect on its own — and only with this app. Listening to audiobooks on headphones, the very reason they subscribed, becomes impossible.

product.title: Cancellation is deliberately buried: not in-app, only via website or a phone call
product.minus: The single most common complaint: you can't cancel inside the app. Support sends you to a billing page that some users say doesn't even exist, live reps are off on weekends, and the card gets charged before you can reach anyone.

product.title: A genuinely simple, easy-to-use interface — the top thing people praise
product.plus: Over and over: the app is light, clear and easy to navigate. You find a book in seconds and start listening immediately, with nothing getting in the way. For most happy users this is the whole reason they stay.

product.title: Charged money for the "free" trial
product.minus: People are offered a free trial and then charged immediately — $15–16 on the day they download. Some are told it's refunded after three days if you cancel in time, but those who forget get charged anyway. The recurring takeaway is feeling deceived.

product.title: Strong selection — people find titles missing elsewhere
product.plus: A big library with big names, and frequently it has the exact titles people couldn't find on other services. For many that's the deciding factor when switching from Audible.

product.title: You pay twice: ~$15/month subscription and then again for the books
product.minus: The "subscription plus credits" model confuses people: $14–15 a month buys one credit — one book — and the rest costs extra. Users openly ask why they pay twice, and resent finding a restrictive subscription when they wanted a service without one.

product.title: Great audio quality and offline listening without bloating storage
product.plus: The audio on downloaded books is praised as clean and high quality, and the ability to listen offline — commuting, driving, no internet — comes up constantly. For listeners on the move that's the core value.

product.title: Credits soft-expire after 3 months — questionable for a prepaid balance
product.minus: Purchased credits only live three months before a soft expiry; you can call to reinstate them, but users find it deceptive and infuriating. The model forces you to grab books in a hurry so credits don't lapse — by which point the interest is gone.

product.title: A solid Audible alternative — more flexible, no Amazon lock-in
product.plus: Many arrive deliberately to escape the Amazon ecosystem and stay satisfied: the price is comparable, the library is close, and it feels less locked-in. The bonus VIP books read as a nice extra on top of credits.

product.title: Loses your place — you have to hunt down the chapter again
product.minus: A recurring pain: after a restart or a notification the app forgets where you stopped and you have to find the chapter by hand. It also doesn't rewind a couple of seconds back after a notification interrupts playback.

product.title: Rich player: speed control, sleep timer, bookmarks, read-along
product.plus: Listeners like the player features: speed from 0.5x to 4x, sleep timers (including end-of-track), bookmarks, notes and faster playback. The ability to listen and read along at the same time is singled out as a favorite.

product.title: The VIP book section is sparse and dated, and disappoints
product.minus: The free VIP books that come with the subscription are often old, from obscure authors, or seemingly public domain. In favorite genres the choice is tiny, and the books people actually want still cost extra.

product.title: Pricey for one credit a month — the common caveat even from fans
product.minus: Even users who like the app routinely add the same caveat: it's a bit expensive. Especially for heavy readers, one credit a month isn't much and credits aren't cheap. Price is what knocks a star off an otherwise five.

product.title: The switch from unlimited to 1-3 monthly "unlocks" gutted the core value
product.minus: For years you paid a flat price for unlimited reading and listening, and people went through 10-30 books a month. The new model gives just 1-3 unlocks for the same or more money — and subscribers en masse call it greed and leave for Audible, Libby, Libro.fm, Kobo Plus.

product.title: Unlocked books are taken away the moment your subscription lapses
product.minus: Unlike Audible, where credit-bought books are yours forever, here cancelling or pausing your subscription kills access to everything you already "unlocked" and paid for. People lose 30+ audiobooks and call it a scam — renting dressed up as buying.

product.title: The audio player loses your place and jumps to the start or chapters back
product.minus: The most common technical complaint: the book stops after a couple of minutes, and on restart the app doesn't return to where you left off — it starts over or jumps several chapters back. Happens even with downloaded books.

product.title: Downloaded books won't play offline — they buffer and burn data
product.minus: Download technically exists, but offline or in airplane mode the book won't open, and even with a connection a "downloaded" audiobook still streams and eats data. That defeats the whole point of downloading — listening on the road, on a plane, out of coverage.

product.title: Saved titles suddenly turn "premium" or vanish from your library
product.minus: After the model change, books that sat in personal libraries for years all flipped to "premium" and became unavailable without an unlock — or simply disappeared. Some users see only dozens of their 400 saved titles still accessible.

product.title: The app glitches, freezes and crashes — sometimes won't open at all
product.minus: Frequent crashes, error popups asking to retry, an endless "please update" prompt that reappears after updating, and the screen freezing on scroll. For some users a recent update left the app refusing to launch entirely.

product.title: Search and catalog are weak: authors don't surface, series stay incomplete
product.minus: The magnifying-glass search often doesn't work or fails to surface a specific author, though that author can be found by accident in someone else's results. Series are clipped — book one or two exists, the rest missing for years; series order isn't shown either.

product.title: Cancelling and the free trial are made deliberately painful
product.minus: The cancel button loops you around or the screen goes blank after it; the trial can't be cancelled until it ends, and access is cut if you cancel early. Several people report still being charged after they no longer have an active subscription.

product.title: Credits don't roll over and expire, with no room to undo a wrong pick
product.minus: Unused unlocks don't carry to next month and expire, and if you accidentally open the wrong book in a series or the wrong format (text instead of audio), you can't undo it — the credit is spent. Against this, Audible wins on rolling credits over.

product.title: The "premium" UI is dishonest: unclear what's included, and release dates lie
product.minus: The app doesn't show which books are unlimited versus premium — you discover the limit only by hitting it. The "unlock" button sometimes does nothing, and promised availability dates ("available 4/4") linger for weeks past the date.

product.title: A huge catalog of rare and niche material — a treasure trove for diggers
product.plus: Those who stay love the breadth and depth of the catalog: esoterica, Chinese and Sufi poetry, crochet patterns, psychology, historical and rare documents found nowhere else. For researchers and the curious it's a genuinely unique find.

product.title: Cheaper than Audible and bundles ebooks AND audiobooks — best value
product.plus: The top reason happy subscribers love it: for half Audible's price you get more books a month plus both text and audio in one subscription. Many deliberately left Audible for the savings and the ability to switch between reading and listening.

product.title: Support is responsive and actually fixes things — once you reach it
product.plus: In contrast to complaints about "nonexistent" support, some users praise fast, human help: replies within minutes-to-hours, escalation, untangling double-account confusion, and even shipping feature requests (flexible playback speeds).

product.title: Sign-up locks you into the wrong country and Swedish
product.minus: On install the account silently lands in the Swedish store or a wrong region you can't change later: the UI, emails and confirmation all come in Swedish, with no way to fix it inside the app.

product.title: You can't filter out the locked language — search drowns in Swedish
product.minus: The default language (Swedish, Dutch, Finnish) can't be unselected — it's locked in the filters, so every search and category leads with those books and finding anything in English is nearly impossible.

product.title: Payment is gated by card country — you simply can't pay
product.minus: The account is pinned to one region and a card from another country (or PayPal) is refused — you only learn about the restriction on the payment page, after already creating the account.

product.title: Cancelling the free trial ends the trial itself
product.minus: To try the service in peace you'd cancel auto-renew up front — but that immediately kills the trial too, so the only way to use it is to forget to cancel and get charged.

product.title: Cancelling is a maze, and they keep charging after it
product.minus: Cancelling is buried in settings or pushed to the browser, you click 'cancel' five times, and they still keep charging and refuse refunds even for unused months.

product.title: Hours run out mid-book — the ending costs another month
product.minus: The hour cap burns out in a couple of days (worse at higher speed), cutting you off 15 minutes from the end, and you can't top up to finish now — you wait until next month.

product.title: Books 'expire' with no warning, and paid access vanishes on cancel
